sections.section: What does a successful fit buy us?
sections.text: The invoice service wants to predict active review minutes when a document arrives. A schedule based on these estimates could help allocate reviewer capacity. It could also repeatedly underestimate difficult work. Before choosing a model, specify the decision time, what is observable then, and what outcome will eventually be measured. Our input x is the page count available at intake. The target y is active review minutes measured under one declared review workflow. Waiting in a queue is excluded from y. Changing reviewer tools could change y even for the same document. These are design choices, not facts about a deployed service. A feature is an input available to the predictor. A label is the outcome used to judge a prediction. A parameter is a number fitted from training examples. A hyperparameter chooses aspects of that fitting procedure, such as penalty strength. A baseline is a credible simple alternative evaluated on the same cases. Learning here means choosing a predictor from data; generalization concerns its behavior on cases outside that fitting process. F04 showed that reducing training loss can worsen an unseen prediction. A01 develops the missing evaluation design. F02 supplies the loss/denominator distinction, and F03 supplies the requirement to compare the same population under a declared protocol. No prior diagnostic answer is assumed.

sections.section: Fit a small predictor before a large one
sections.text: Reuse F04’s zero-intercept model, predicted minutes = wx. Its strong assumption is that time grows proportionally with pages, without fixed setup time. Use two invented training cases: (1 page, 2 minutes) and (2 pages, 4 minutes). The squared loss for one case is (prediction − outcome)². The mean squared error (MSE) averages it over cases. Here: L(w)=(w−2)2+(2w−4)22=52(w−2)2. Thus w=2 minimizes training MSE, with value zero. A constant baseline predicts the training mean, 3 minutes, for every case; its training MSE is 1 minute². Squared errors penalize large deviations heavily. Also report mean absolute error (MAE), in minutes, so an operator can interpret the scale. Neither metric alone measures whether scheduling actually improves customer outcomes. Now lock both predictors and evaluate two invented validation cases, (1,1) and (2,2). The fitted predictor gives [2,4], so MSE is (1+4)/2=2.5. The constant baseline gives [3,3], so MSE is (4+1)/2=2.5 as well. A perfect training fit did not beat the baseline here. The validation set differs in its relation between pages and time; that was deliberately constructed, not discovered empirically. The training objective is an average over observed fitting cases. The desired deployment risk is an expectation of loss over the intended future population, with the predictor fixed. An average on held-out data estimates that target only to the extent that the sampling and information conditions match it. An unseen row is not necessarily a new independent document, supplier or time period.

sections.section: Penalize flexibility, then test the choice
sections.text: Consider a penalized objective J(w)=L(w)+λw², with λ≥0. Differentiate the quadratic: J′(w)=5(w−2)+2λw. Setting this to zero gives wλ=105+2λ. The positive curvature 5+2λ makes this the unique minimum. For λ=0, 2.5 and 7.5, the weights are 2, 1 and 0.5. In this example units and loss scaling are fixed; multiplying features or replacing mean loss by sum loss changes the numerical meaning of λ. The penalty is a preference for smaller weights, not evidence that smaller weights are always better. Candidate Weight / prediction rule Training MSE Validation MSE Constant baseline Always 3 1 2.5 λ=0 2x 0 2.5 λ=2.5 x 2.5 0 λ=7.5 0.5x 5.625 0.625 Select λ=2.5 using this validation set. It has worse training fit but better validation fit among these candidates. This is not a general recommendation for λ=2.5. If deployment followed y=2x instead, the unpenalized predictor would be preferable. Regularization can trade fit for stability, but it cannot repair a label that contains future information or a test set chosen for easy cases. Reserve a separate final test with cases (3,3), (4,4), which has not influenced the candidate grid or selection. The frozen selected model has MSE 0 there; the constant baseline has MSE 0.5. These tiny exact examples illustrate the bookkeeping, not an estimated production advantage. If the final cases instead followed y=2x, the selected model’s MSE would be 12.5. That counterexample exposes the missing transport assumption. For a real study, use training folds to fit parameters and development folds to choose features, penalties and other settings. Fit normalization, missing-value handling and feature selection inside each training fold. Reserve an outer test for evaluating the complete selection procedure. Once its results influence changes, it is development evidence for those changes. Calling it “test” does not restore independence. A final refit on all development data is a new fitted model; evaluate that actual frozen model rather than reusing earlier numbers as though its weights were unchanged.

sections.section: Zero error from the wrong split
sections.text: Here is a separate, deliberately adversarial dataset. Four underlying documents each have two near-identical revisions with the same assigned target. Each document has two pages. Metadata are: Document Organization Template family Revision IDs Assigned minutes D1 A X D1r1, D1r2 2 D2 A Y D2r1, D2r2 4 D3 B X D3r1, D3r2 6 D4 B Z D4r1, D4r2 8 A lookup predictor remembers training labels by document ID and falls back to the training mean for an unknown document. Put each r1 in training and each r2 in validation. All four validation predictions are exact. This is one possible row-split allocation, not the expected result of every random split. It tests recognition of previously labeled documents, not prediction for new documents at intake. The use of prior labels also needs to match what is available at decision time. Now train on both revisions of D1 and D2, and evaluate both revisions of D3 and D4. Every validation document is unseen. The fallback is 3, giving MSE ((6−3)²+(8−3)²)/2=17. The constant baseline has the same MSE. The zero-error advantage vanished. Duplicating each target does not produce twice as many independent documents. Organization separation is still not template separation: X appears in both A and B. This is not automatically an error. New customers may use familiar templates. But it cannot establish performance on unseen templates. Grouping by the pair (organization, template) also fails to separate either individual attribute. If both organization and template must be unseen, group connected components of the graph whose edges join shared organizations or shared template families. Here the X connection joins A and B; all four documents belong to one component. There is no nonempty disjoint train/test partition satisfying both constraints. Collect more disconnected groups or narrow the claim; do not manufacture independent evidence by splitting the component.

Intended claim Proposed holdout What it still cannot establish New documents from existing suppliers Later intake period; no document family crosses partitions; features reconstructed as of intake Performance for unknown suppliers or changed review procedures New suppliers, possibly familiar templates Entire organizations held out; retain all revisions of each document together Unseen-template performance if templates overlap New template families Entire template families held out New-organization behavior unless also separated Both unseen organizations and templates Disconnected organization/template components held out Future stability or representativeness of missing components For a temporal evaluation, choose training labels that were already available at the fitting cutoff. A document arriving before cutoff but resolved afterward cannot contribute its outcome to that historical fit. Route all revisions of a case together, or exclude boundary-crossing cases under a declared rule and report the exclusions. At prediction time reconstruct only the evidence then available. A correction published next week is not an intake feature today. Use development partitions that mimic the same deployment boundary as the final holdout. A grouped final test combined with row-leaking model selection can still choose a poor procedure. Keep an audit record of case IDs, group membership, timestamps, label availability, feature schema and transformations. Count overlaps directly. Inspect a sample for hidden duplicate documents, renamed suppliers and template variants that exact IDs miss.

sections.section: Distribution change can reverse the winner
sections.text: Even valid held-out evidence concerns a population. Suppose model P has subgroup MSE 1 on routine cases and 9 on exceptions, while Q has 4 and 4. At 90% routine, P’s weighted loss is 1.8 versus Q’s 4. At 50% routine, P’s loss becomes 5, and Q wins. The crossover solves 9−8r=4, giving routine share r=5/8. This is F03’s workload-mix reasoning applied to losses. It assumes each subgroup’s error rate remains unchanged; a changed review process can invalidate even that assumption. Report performance by relevant groups, the target mix, missing outcomes and severe underestimation. A change in inputs can be visible before labels arrive; it does not prove quality declined. Outcome monitoring needs matured labels and their availability lag. A frozen model that changes who gets reviewed also changes the feedback data, so evaluate the full workflow separately before claiming causal business benefit. Prefer the simple baseline until added complexity earns its cost on an evaluation matched to deployment. More data from the same repeated template need not answer a new-template question. More parameters need not provide useful information absent from intake features. For language models, prompts, demonstrations, retrieval corpora and thresholds are also choices in the evaluated procedure. The same information-boundary discipline applies, while unknown pretraining exposure limits claims that a benchmark is entirely unseen.

Derive the constant baseline and all training/validation MSEs in the candidate table. Derive wλ and explain why the units/scaling of λ matter. Select a candidate using validation, compute its final test MSE and MAE, and compare the baseline. Change the final targets to 6 and 8. What claim does that defeat? Reproduce the lookup predictor’s zero-error row allocation and its grouped MSE of 17. Identify the independent document count and what the two evaluations measure. Construct the organization/template connected components. Explain why grouping by their pair is insufficient, and propose a feasible response when all records form one component. Write a one-page split plan for future new documents from existing suppliers, then revise it for new suppliers with unseen templates. Specify label cutoff, revision handling, preprocessing, baseline, tuning and final evaluation. Derive the routine-share crossover for P and Q. Specify one monitoring observation that would invalidate reweighting, and distinguish model quality from a causal improvement in scheduling.

Specify decision time → define feature/label availability → name the future population → split at its independence boundary → fit all transformations inside training → select on development → freeze → evaluate once → monitor matured outcomes. Record the unit and denominator beside each score. Field Value ID / revision / date A01 answers · 1.0 · 2026-11-09 Prerequisites F02–F04 and A01 core Capability developed Defend what a score establishes and repair the information boundary of an evaluation Source-check status R13 and R02 inspected passages and URLs in the core evidence table Experiment status Exact standard-library Python checks executed below; no production prediction experiment These are reference solutions, not learner responses or evidence of mastery.

Expand each squared residual. Keep the penalty separate from reported unpenalized MSE. Use frozen parameters; do not fit to the final labels. Ask whether the lookup key was already observed with a label. Shared membership is transitive through graph paths, even without a direct shared attribute. Split before fitting transformations. Arrival time and label-availability time differ. Weight losses, not winners. Then ask whether conditional losses remain stable.

For a constant c, training MSE is ((c−2)²+(c−4)²)/2 = (c−3)²+1, minimized at c=3. Its training and validation MSEs are 1 and 2.5. For wx, training loss is 2.5(w−2)². Adding λw² and setting the derivative 5(w−2)+2λw to zero gives w=10/(5+2λ). Positive curvature establishes a minimum. For weights 2, 1, 0.5, the training MSEs are 0, 2.5, 5.625 and validation MSEs are 2.5, 0, 0.625. Report these prediction losses, not penalized objective values, when comparing on a common validation criterion. The baseline is fitted from training labels only. Changing minutes to seconds multiplies label scale and fitted weights. Rescaling pages changes the numerical weights and penalty effect. Replacing mean squared loss with a sum also changes relative penalty strength. A λ value without its objective and feature units is incomplete. Criterion: Correct residuals, unique minimum, explicit loss scaling; do not claim regularization must improve every dataset.

Validation selects λ=2.5 and w=1 among the declared candidates. On final inputs 3 and 4 with targets 3 and 4, predictions are exact: MSE=MAE=0. The baseline predicts 3 for both: MSE=0.5 and MAE=0.5 minutes. If final labels become 6 and 8 without changing the model, residuals are −3 and −4. MSE=12.5 and MAE=3.5. The baseline has residuals −3 and −5, giving MSE=17 and MAE=4. The unpenalized model would be exact on these changed labels. Thus validation selection is not a guarantee under a changed input–outcome relationship. Two constructed test cases cannot establish deployment accuracy or uncertainty. Criterion: Freeze weights, distinguish the selected candidate from a hindsight winner, and state the test’s limited population.

Training on r1 of all four documents stores D1→2, D2→4, D3→6, D4→8. Every r2 lookup returns its assigned target, yielding zero MSE. The example has eight rows but only four underlying documents. The row allocation has no entirely unseen validation documents. Training on D1/D2’s four revision rows gives mean (2+2+4+4)/4=3. Unknown D3/D4 receive 3. Squared errors are 9,9,25,25, averaging 17. The constant baseline does exactly the same. There are two held-out documents, not four independent validation cases, and even those may share supplier/template effects. Do not form a confidence interval treating all revision rows as independent draws. Criterion: Explain the task mismatch, not merely the numerical score change. Reusing known documents is not inherently forbidden if that is the actual application and labels truly existed at prediction time; it is wrong evidence for the stated new-document question.

A links D1 to D2; B links D3 to D4; template X links D1 to D3. The resulting path connects all documents. Holding out B separates organizations but leaves template X shared. Grouping by (A,X) and (B,X) as different pairs still shares X; grouping (A,X) and (A,Y) separately still shares A. There is one connected component, so a nonempty train/test split cannot keep both organizations and templates disjoint. Acquire disconnected groups, restrict the intended claim to new organizations with known templates, or report the desired estimate unavailable. Dropping bridging records can create a different, selected population; document any exclusion and do not claim it represents all intake. Criterion: Show the connecting path and acknowledge infeasibility rather than quietly weakening the holdout.

sections.section: 5. An evaluation plan that matches deployment
sections.text: For future documents from existing suppliers, choose a historical fitting cutoff and a later test-intake window. Fit only on documents whose labels were available by cutoff. Keep a whole document family in one partition; declare boundary-crossing families excluded from this evaluation and count them separately. Reconstruct page counts and other permitted features at original intake, without later corrections. Track unknown suppliers separately from the intended existing-supplier population. Within the pre-test period use earlier-to-later development splits with the same label-availability rule. Fit preprocessing and each candidate only on that fold’s training data. Compare the training-mean baseline with the page predictor and predeclared penalty grid. Choose using development MSE, report MAE and severe underestimation, then freeze all choices. If refitting on development data, evaluate the actual refit on the untouched final period. Record failed/missing predictions and delayed labels under declared rules rather than dropping them. For new suppliers with unseen templates, reserve entire disconnected organization/template components, keeping every document’s revisions together. The development procedure must use analogous component holdouts. Add a time cutoff if future deployment is also part of the claim. Confirm enough separate components exist; this toy dataset fails that feasibility check. Report both case-weighted and, if relevant, organization-weighted outcomes with explicit denominators. More rows from one organization do not supply more independent organizations. Criterion: Decision-time inputs, label maturity, group/time boundaries, training-only transformations, baseline and final lock. There is no compulsory 80/20 split: the number and representativeness of independent groups matter.

Let r be routine share. P’s loss is r+9(1−r)=9−8r; Q’s is 4. P wins for r>5/8, ties at 5/8 and loses below it. At r=0.9 its MSE is 1.8; at r=0.5 it is 5. Reweighting assumes unchanged subgroup losses. If reviewer tooling changes minutes per page within routine cases, the old conditional MSEs may no longer apply. Newly matured labels showing that within-group change would invalidate simple reweighting. Input drift without outcomes is an alert to investigate, not a measured error increase. Better minute predictions do not by themselves prove better schedules. Queue policies, reviewer behavior and opportunity costs intervene. A controlled workflow evaluation using F03’s unit, outcome and interference discipline is needed for a causal benefit claim. Criterion: Correct threshold, a concrete failed assumption and separation of predictive quality from customer impact.

The following uses Python’s standard library. It checks the constructed arithmetic, the memorization counterexample, component feasibility and a metamorphic independence check: changing final labels cannot change selection that consumes only training/validation data. It does not estimate sampling uncertainty or validate a production data pipeline. from fractions import Fraction as F from itertools import product train = [(1,2),(2,4)] valid = [(1,1),(2,2)] test = [(3,3),(4,4)] def mse(data, predict): return sum((predict(x)-y)**2 for x,y in data)/F(len(data)) def mae(data, predict): return sum(abs(predict(x)-y) for x,y in data)/F(len(data)) mean = sum(F(y) for x,y in train)/len(train) assert mean == 3 assert (mse(train,lambda x:mean),mse(valid,lambda x:mean)) == (1,F(5,2)) lambdas = [F(0), F(5,2), F(15,2)] weights = [F(10)/(5+2*l) for l in lambdas] assert weights == [2,1,F(1,2)] assert [mse(train,lambda x,w=w:w*x) for w in weights] == [0,F(5,2),F(45,8)] assert [mse(valid,lambda x,w=w:w*x) for w in weights] == [F(5,2),0,F(5,8)] for l,w in zip(lambdas,weights): assert 5*(w-2)+2*l*w == 0 for d in [F(-1),F(-1,10),F(1,10),F(1)]: objective=lambda z:mse(train,lambda x:z*x)+l*z*z assert objective(w+d)>objective(w) def select(validation): return min(weights,key=lambda w:mse(validation,lambda x:w*x)) w=select(valid) assert w==1 and mse(test,lambda x:w*x)==mae(test,lambda x:w*x)==0 assert mse(test,lambda x:mean)==mae(test,lambda x:mean)==F(1,2) changed=[(3,6),(4,8)] assert mse(changed,lambda x:w*x)==F(25,2) assert mae(changed,lambda x:w*x)==F(7,2) # Final labels never enter selection, even under 25 alternate target pairs. for y1,y2 in product(range(5),repeat=2): alternate_test=[(3,y1),(4,y2)] assert select(valid)==w # doc, organization, template, revision, target; fixed two-page inputs. docs=[('D1','A','X',2),('D2','A','Y',4),('D3','B','X',6),('D4','B','Z',8)] rows=[(d,o,t,r,F(y)) for d,o,t,y in docs for r in [1,2]] def lookup_mse(tr,va): memory={r[0]:r[4] for r in tr} fallback=sum(r[4] for r in tr)/len(tr) return sum((memory.get(r[0],fallback)-r[4])**2 for r in va)/len(va) assert lookup_mse([r for r in rows if r[3]==1],[r for r in rows if r[3]==2])==0 tr=[r for r in rows if r[1]=='A'];va=[r for r in rows if r[1]=='B'] assert lookup_mse(tr,va)==17 assert not {r[0] for r in tr}&{r[0] for r in va} assert not {r[1] for r in tr}&{r[1] for r in va} assert {r[2] for r in tr}&{r[2] for r in va}=={'X'} # Enumerate all 14 nonempty document partitions: none separates both axes. feasible=[] for mask in range(1,15): left=[d for i,d in enumerate(docs) if mask>>i&1] right=[d for i,d in enumerate(docs) if not mask>>i&1] if all(not {d[k] for d in left}&{d[k] for d in right} for k in [1,2]): feasible.append(mask) assert feasible==[] for r,expected in [(F(9,10),F(9,5)),(F(1,2),F(5)),(F(5,8),F(4))]: assert r+9*(1-r)==expected print('PASS: fitting, penalties, validation/test arithmetic, 25 label changes,') print('revision leakage, grouped MSE, all 14 group partitions and mixture threshold.')

Field Value ID / revision / date A02 · 1.0 · 2026-11-09 Prerequisites F04 vectors, matrix products and fitted parameters; A01 information boundaries and evaluation Capability developed Calculate attention, identify allowed information flow and distinguish an operation check from a model-quality claim Source-check status R14, author-submitted arXiv v7: §§3.1–3.5 and §4 inspected; precise locators below Experiment status Constructed matrices and executed standard-library numerical checks; no training run or model benchmark Companion Hints, worked answers and checks

Suppose a document system represents each token occurrence with a vector. A token is an item in the model’s input sequence; it need not coincide with a word. The same text fragment in two positions can need different representations because its surrounding information differs. Our question is narrower than whether a generated answer is correct: how can one row of numbers incorporate information from other rows? We will implement a deliberately tiny operation. The numbers below are assigned, not learned from invoices. They have no calibrated meaning such as confidence or probability that a document is correct. That distinction follows F04’s warning about interpreting geometric scores and A01’s distinction between passing a constructed check and demonstrating generalization. Use rows for token vectors. A matrix with n rows and d columns represents n positions with d features each. Multiplying a row by a projection matrix changes its coordinates. The projection parameters are shared across positions, but the resulting vectors depend on the input row. No diagnostic answer or prior familiarity with neural networks is assumed.

For input X of shape n×d, define Q=XWQ, K=XWK and V=XWV. Queries Q and keys K have width dk; values V have width dv. We use the scaled dot-product rule from R14 §3.2.1, eq. 1, extended with an explicit allowed-position mask: S=QKT/dk,A=softmaxrows(S+M),O=AV. M is zero for allowed pairs and negative infinity for forbidden ones. In the executable version we omit forbidden entries from the denominator instead of representing infinity. Each query must have at least one permitted key. An all-forbidden row is rejected as invalid input in our contract. Quantity Shape Meaning WQ, WK d×dk Shared query/key projections WV d×dv Shared value projection Q, K n×dk One query/key per position V n×dv One value per position S, M, A n×n Row i refers to query i; column j to key/value j O n×dv One weighted result per query The transpose in QKᵀ aligns the feature coordinates. Entry Sij is the dot product of query i and key j, divided by √dk. These scores determine mixing weights; the corresponding value vectors supply what is mixed. Query, key and value are computational roles, not a claim that a token consciously asks a question. For allowed scores s1,…,sm, softmax returns exp(sj)/Σ exp(sk). Exponentials are positive and normalization makes the row sum one. Equal scores produce equal weights. Adding the same constant to every allowed score changes neither the ratios nor the output. Subtracting the row maximum before exponentiating therefore avoids unnecessarily large exponentials without changing the mathematical result. For this operation, each output is a convex combination of permitted values: each coordinate lies between their minimum and maximum. This property applies to AV before later projections, residual additions or other transformations. It is not a bound on the final model’s output.

Choose n=3, d=2, dk=1 and dv=2: X=[100211],WQ=WK=[10],WV=[1001]. Consequently Q=K=[1,0,1]ᵀ and V=X. Because dk=1, the scaling divisor is one. With all positions allowed, S=[101000101]. Let e=exp(1) and Z=2e+1. The first row’s weights are [e/Z,1/Z,e/Z], approximately [0.4223,0.1554,0.4223]. Its output is eZ(1,0)+1Z(0,2)+eZ(1,1)=(2eZ,2+eZ)≈(0.8446,0.7330). The second query is zero. All its scores are zero, so its weights are thirds and its output is the mean (2/3,1). The third query equals the first, so its output also equals the first. Different original rows can receive the same attention output; the operation does not guarantee that every position remains distinguishable. Now change only the last value from (1,1) to (1,7), leaving Q and K fixed. The first and third output’s second coordinate each increases by 6e/Z; the second output’s second coordinate increases by 2. We can realize this change by altering X’s last second coordinate: our chosen WQ and WK ignore that coordinate. This test isolates value flow from score changes. With other projections, the same input change could alter Q and K too.

sections.section: A mask changes what information may flow
sections.text: For a causal version allow key j only when j≤i. The first query can use only position 1. The second can use positions 1 and 2. The third can use all three. Query row Permitted keys Weights across all three columns Output 1 1 [1,0,0] (1,0) 2 1,2 [1/2,1/2,0] (1/2,1) 3 1,2,3 [e/Z,1/Z,e/Z] (2e/Z,(2+e)/Z) The mask is applied before normalization. If you normalize all three scores and merely zero forbidden weights afterward, a row may sum to less than one. For row 2 that faulty procedure produces (1/3,2/3), not (1/2,1). It has silently changed the operation. Under the causal mask, the last-value perturbation leaves outputs 1 and 2 unchanged, while output 3 changes. This follows because their allowed terms contain neither K3 nor V3, and their own queries are unchanged. It is a local guarantee of this layer with fixed projections. In a larger network, earlier input representations must themselves have been computed without future leakage. A causal final layer cannot repair representations that already incorporated future targets. For another test, remove the connection from query 3 to key 2. Its remaining equal scores yield [1/2,0,1/2] and output (1,1/2). Only row 3 changes in this one operation. In later layers, its changed representation may affect any positions permitted to use it. Padding and causality are different constraints. Padding marks absent sequence items; causal masking marks future positions relative to a prediction. A combined mask must preserve a valid key for every real query or specify another explicit policy. Do not silently interpret an undefined all-masked row as a useful representation.

sections.section: Position, multiple heads and the surrounding network
sections.text: R14’s architecture places attention within encoder/decoder stacks with residual connections, normalization and position-wise feed-forward layers. It projects multiple attention heads, concatenates them and applies an output projection. Its decoder combines causal self-attention with attention to encoder outputs. It adds positional information to embeddings and maps decoder representations to token probabilities. These are properties of the cited historical architecture, not a specification of every current model. Here is a shape-level extension of our own example. With two heads, each producing a 3×2 matrix, concatenate across features to obtain 3×4. A 4×2 output projection returns 3×2, which could be added to the original X. Concatenating across rows would produce 6×2 and would not preserve one output per input position. Different heads need not correspond to named human concepts, and more heads do not guarantee better task performance. Without positional inputs or an order-sensitive mask, our operation cannot distinguish a permutation of the sequence from the corresponding permutation of its outputs. If P permutes rows, then X becomes PX, the score matrix becomes PSPᵀ, and row softmax followed by the permuted values produces PO. This is an algebraic property, checked over all six permutations of our three rows. It explains what position information must change: the computation needs a way to represent order when order matters to the task. It does not imply that an orderless set-processing task always needs positional inputs. For cross-attention, query and memory lengths can differ. Three query rows attending to five key/value rows produce a 3×5 weight matrix and three output rows. The number of keys must equal the number of values; dk must match between queries and keys. The output width is dv, not the number of memory items. These shape checks catch interface errors before any semantic interpretation.

sections.section: Training and inference use different available inputs
sections.text: Consider a separate next-token task whose desired output is [A,B,C]. A shifted training input is [START,A,B], paired with targets [A,B,C]. A causal row can use its current shifted input and earlier rows without seeing its own target through that input path. All these known training-input rows can be evaluated together under the mask. Supplying [A,B,C] unshifted as input for predicting [A,B,C] would instead expose the answer at each diagonal connection. Parameter fitting adjusts projection and other model weights using a loss and an update rule, as F04 introduced. During the inference procedure considered here, weights are fixed: begin with START, obtain a token, append it, and use that actual prefix for the next prediction. The correct next token is not supplied by a teacher. Evaluating against known prefixes and generating from one’s own prefixes answer different questions; A01’s evaluation discipline still applies. No training or decoding implementation was executed in this pack. Attention weights normalize over available positions. Output token probabilities normalize over a vocabulary after another transformation. Neither normalization alone establishes factual correctness, permission to act or supporting evidence. Our numeric operation would mix values from fabricated text just as readily as from verified text. A03 will separately evaluate retrieval and answer support.

sections.section: Where sequence length enters the cost
sections.text: Count the explicit dense algorithm, one head and one sequence, ignoring batch size and datatype overhead. QKᵀ performs n² dot products of width dk, costing order n²dk multiply/add work. AV costs order n²dv. An explicitly stored score or weight matrix contains n² scalars. Doubling n at fixed widths quadruples those pair counts: n=3 has 9 positions, n=6 has 36. The causal mask has n(n+1)/2 allowed pairs, but computing a full matrix and masking it afterward still does dense work. The projections additionally depend on n and feature widths. These counts do not establish runtime, memory traffic, optimizer storage or the allocation strategy of an optimized implementation. They also do not describe the cost of one incremental generation step automatically. A04 will examine serving and retained state in more detail. Choose a full-context or causal operation according to what information the task may use, not just which scores look better. Restricting context can reduce candidate interactions but can remove needed dependencies. To justify a change, compare complete task outcomes under the same information contract and measure actual resources. A faster result obtained by leaking future labels is not an improvement for that contract.

Derive Q, K, V, S and every unmasked output from the supplied X and projections. Explain what the softmax axis means. Derive the causal outputs. Remove only row 3’s connection to key 2, then compare with the erroneous mask-after-softmax procedure for row 2. Change X3 from (1,1) to (1,7). Identify which unmasked and causal outputs change and by how much. State why the claim needs the chosen projections. Give shapes for three queries attending to five values with dk=4 and dv=2. Then describe the two-head concatenation/projection example and a residual shape error. Explain the [START,A,B] input/target arrangement, what goes wrong with unshifted targets, and why a later causal mask cannot undo earlier leakage. Distinguish fitting from fixed-weight generation. Derive dense and allowed-pair counts for n=3 and n=6. Explain the permutation test, then propose a task evaluation that could reject a cheaper context restriction despite passing all arithmetic checks.

sections.section: Reference card, evidence and open questions
sections.text: Write shapes → score query/key pairs → exclude forbidden pairs → normalize each query row → mix values → check the downstream shape. Specify whether inputs already contain future information. Separate weights over positions from probabilities over tokens and from verified truth. Basis Inspected locator Scope R14, Vaswani et al., 2017; inspected arXiv v7 dated 2023-08-02 Versioned text, §3.2.1 eq. 1; §§3.2.2–3.2.3 Scaled attention, learned projections and masking R14, same version §§3.1, 3.3–3.5; §3 opening and §4 Architecture context, shifted decoder inputs, position information and complexity discussion. No reported benchmark result adopted. Original derivations and constructed inputs This pack and companion executable checks Numeric trace, mask counterexamples, perturbations, permutation property, shape/count calculations and proposed tests Continuity F04 matrix/parameter bridge; A01 leakage/evaluation boundaries Previously saved prerequisites, not new measurements R14’s detailed mechanism is now passage-checked beyond the original catalog entry. The toy projections are not trained weights and the three vectors are not a tokenizer or language model. The checks cover a single deterministic attention operation without dropout, normalization, feed-forward layers or optimization. Real tokenization, positional scheme, masks, precision, architecture, resource use and task quality require application evidence. No learner mastery is inferred. Next is A03: retrieval, external knowledge and provenance.
1.0 — 2026-11-09. Three-position attention trace, mask and leakage counterexamples, architecture context and six exercises with separate checks.

title: Hints, worked answers and executable checks

sections.section: Hints, worked answers and executable checks
sections.text: Field Value ID / revision / date A02 answers · 1.0 · 2026-11-09 Prerequisites F04, A01 and A02 core Capability developed Verify attention arithmetic and test information-flow boundaries without overstating model evidence Source-check status R14 versioned passages and locators in the core evidence ledger Experiment status Standard-library Python checks executed; no neural model training, benchmark or generation experiment These are reference solutions for later self-assessment, not inferred learner answers.

Multiply rows by projection columns before forming query/key products. Recompute the denominator after changing permitted keys. Check whether the changed coordinate participates in WQ or WK. The output retains query count and value width. Write each input next to its target before discussing parallel computation. Count allocated pairs separately from permitted pairs and measured work.

WQ and WK select the first feature: Q=K=[1,0,1]ᵀ. WV preserves both features, so V=X. S has rows [1,0,1], [0,0,0], [1,0,1]. Because dk=1, scaling makes no numerical change in this case; it is still part of the general formula. With Z=2e+1, rows 1 and 3 of A are [e/Z,1/Z,e/Z]; row 2 is [1/3,1/3,1/3]. Outputs 1 and 3 are (2e/Z,(2+e)/Z), approximately (0.844638,0.733044); output 2 is (2/3,1). Row normalization distributes one query’s mass across keys. Column normalization would answer a different algebraic question and is not this contract. Criterion: Correct projection and multiplication order, normalization axis and value-weighted output. Attention weights are not vocabulary probabilities or truth estimates.

Causal rows are [1,0,0], [1/2,1/2,0] and [e/Z,1/Z,e/Z]. Their outputs are (1,0), (1/2,1) and the original third output. Disallowing key 2 for query 3 leaves two equal scores, producing [1/2,0,1/2] and (1,1/2). Rows 1 and 2 are unaffected by that single connection change. If row 2 is normalized over all three positions first and the final weight is then zeroed, the remaining weights are [1/3,1/3,0]. Their sum is 2/3 and the output is (1/3,2/3). Renormalizing the surviving positive weights would repair this particular finite example, but masking before the stable softmax directly implements the declared contract. All-masked rows have no valid distribution; the code rejects them. Criterion: Show the changed denominator and distinguish a forbidden connection from a small score.

Changing X3’s second coordinate from 1 to 7 leaves Q/K unchanged because their projections use only the first coordinate. V3 increases by (0,6). Unmasked output differences are (0,6e/Z), (0,2), (0,6e/Z). Causal differences are (0,0), (0,0), (0,6e/Z). With projections that use the second coordinate, K3 and Q3 may change too. Causality still excludes position 3 from outputs 1 and 2 if their inputs were causally constructed, but the third output’s difference would not generally equal a fixed weight times 6. If earlier representations already encoded future content, their queries or permitted values could change, violating the premise of this layer-local argument. Criterion: Separate changes to scores from changes to values and identify the upstream information assumption.

Q is 3×4, K is 5×4 and V is 5×2. Scores and weights are 3×5; AV is 3×2. The divisor is √4=2. Five keys paired with only four values is invalid, as is a query width unequal to the key width. For two heads each returning 3×2, feature concatenation produces 3×4 and a 4×2 output projection returns 3×2. That can be added elementwise to a 3×2 residual. Concatenating along positions produces 6×2 and cannot be added to the original X without redefining the operation. Even matching shapes do not guarantee matching feature meanings, as F04 showed. Criterion: Identify both multiplication compatibility and semantic correspondence. Self-attention and cross-attention need not have the same query/key lengths.

The training pairs by row are START→A, A→B and B→C. At row 2 the allowed input prefix is [START,A]; the target is B. With input [A,B,C] and the same targets, row 2 could inspect B directly through the diagonal connection. A causal index rule alone would not stop this labeling error. Fitting updates parameters based on loss. In the fixed-weight generation procedure, each new input prefix includes actual earlier generated tokens; target tokens are not available in advance. Parallel computation over known shifted training inputs does not imply parallel availability of unknown generated tokens. A prefix error can change subsequent inputs, so evaluation should match the intended generation procedure. If an earlier unmasked representation already mixed C into row 1, a later causal attention layer can read that contaminated row 1. The mask controls its own edges, not the entire history of its input tensors. Criterion: Explicit input/target alignment, fixed versus updated weights and an upstream leakage counterexample. No conclusion about current proprietary models is required.

Dense pair counts are 3²=9 and 6²=36; causal permitted counts are 3·4/2=6 and 6·7/2=21. Full matrix computation followed by masking does not by itself save the work on the forbidden positions. With fixed dk and dv, the two attention matrix products scale with n²; projections and the rest of a network contribute additional costs. Under a simultaneous row permutation of position-free X, Q/K/V permute consistently. The score matrix permutes in both axes, weights follow those changes and outputs permute by the same row order. The six-permutation check below tests this property. Holding positional vectors fixed while permuting token content is a different transformation, so it need not preserve the result. To evaluate a cheaper local-context restriction, freeze candidate settings on development data and compare both systems on the same held-out document tasks. Include cases where necessary evidence is farther away than the permitted window, and keep revision/organization boundaries from A01. Measure supported correct answers, missing evidence, latency and resource use. If local arithmetic passes but long-distance evidence cases fail beyond a declared tolerance, reject or revise the restriction. Test limits and costs must come from the application; no numerical deployment threshold is invented here. Criterion: Distinguish count models from benchmarks, state what is permuted, and propose a test that can falsify the cheaper design.

The implementation uses finite values and explicit Boolean allowed masks, with one permitted key required per query. Dropout and other Transformer components are absent. Tolerances reflect floating-point calculation, not statistical uncertainty. The expected expressions, metamorphic checks and deliberately wrong normalization provide checks beyond simply rerunning one function. from math import exp, sqrt, isclose from itertools import permutations def shape(a): assert a and a[0] and all(len(r)==len(a[0]) for r in a) return len(a),len(a[0]) def mm(a,b): na,da=shape(a);nb,db=shape(b) assert da==nb return [[sum(a[i][k]*b[k][j] for k in range(da)) for j in range(db)] for i in range(na)] def transpose(a): shape(a) return [list(c) for c in zip(*a)] def softmax(scores,allowed): if not any(allowed):raise ValueError('no permitted key') top=max(s for s,ok in zip(scores,allowed) if ok) terms=[exp(s-top) if ok else 0.0 for s,ok in zip(scores,allowed)] z=sum(terms) return [t/z for t in terms] def attention(q,k,v,allowed): nq,dq=shape(q);nk,dk=shape(k);nv,dv=shape(v) assert dq==dk and nk==nv and shape(allowed)==(nq,nk) scores=[[s/sqrt(dk) for s in row] for row in mm(q,transpose(k))] weights=[softmax(row,mask) for row,mask in zip(scores,allowed)] return weights,mm(weights,v) def close(a,b): assert shape(a)==shape(b) assert all(isclose(x,y,rel_tol=1e-10,abs_tol=1e-10) for ar,br in zip(a,b) for x,y in zip(ar,br)) def fails(fn,kind): try:fn() except kind:return raise AssertionError('expected rejection') X=[[1.,0.],[0.,2.],[1.,1.]] W=[[1.],[0.]];I=[[1.,0.],[0.,1.]] q=k=mm(X,W);v=mm(X,I) full=[[True]*3 for _ in range(3)] causal=[[j<=i for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)] e=exp(1);z=2*e+1 expected=[2*e/z,(2+e)/z] a,o=attention(q,k,v,full) close(a,[[e/z,1/z,e/z],[1/3]*3,[e/z,1/z,e/z]]) close(o,[expected,[2/3,1.],expected]) ac,oc=attention(q,k,v,causal) close(oc,[[1.,0.],[.5,1.],expected]) for mask,wts,out in [(full,a,o),(causal,ac,oc)]: for flags,row,value in zip(mask,wts,out): assert isclose(sum(row),1) assert all(w>=0 and (ok or w==0) for ok,w in zip(flags,row)) for col in range(2): permitted=[v[j][col] for j,ok in enumerate(flags) if ok] assert min(permitted)-1e-10<=value[col]<=max(permitted)+1e-10 newmask=[r[:] for r in causal];newmask[2][1]=False _,om=attention(q,k,v,newmask) close(om,[[1.,0.],[.5,1.],[1.,.5]]) wrong=mm([[1/3,1/3,0]],v) close(wrong,[[1/3,2/3]]) assert not isclose(sum([1/3,1/3,0]),1) # Changing a feature ignored by Q/K isolates the value path. x2=[r[:] for r in X];x2[2][1]=7 close(mm(x2,W),q) _,o2=attention(mm(x2,W),mm(x2,W),x2,full) _,oc2=attention(mm(x2,W),mm(x2,W),x2,causal) close(o2,[[expected[0],expected[1]+6*e/z],[2/3,3.], [expected[0],expected[1]+6*e/z]]) close(oc2,[oc[0],oc[1],o2[2]]) # Every ordering without positions/masks must permute outputs consistently. for p in permutations(range(3)): xp=[X[i] for i in p] _,op=attention(mm(xp,W),mm(xp,W),xp,full) close(op,[o[i] for i in p]) # Stable softmax is invariant to a common score offset. close([softmax([1001,1000,1001],[True]*3)],[a[0]]) fails(lambda:softmax([1,2],[False,False]),ValueError) fails(lambda:attention(q,k,v[:2],full),AssertionError) fails(lambda:attention([[1,2]],k,v,[[True]*3]),AssertionError) # Rectangular case checks dk scaling and query count, not just square shapes. qr=[[1.,0.,0.,0.]]*3 kr=[[2.,0.,0.,0.]]+[[0.,0.,0.,0.]]*4 vr=[[1.,0.]]+[[0.,1.]]*4 ar,orr=attention(qr,kr,vr,[[True]*5 for _ in range(3)]) close(ar,[[e/(e+4)]+[1/(e+4)]*4]*3) close(orr,[[e/(e+4),4/(e+4)]]*3) assert shape(orr)==(3,2) for n,dense,allowed in [(3,9,6),(6,36,21)]: assert n*n==dense assert sum(j<=i for i in range(n) for j in range(n))==allowed print('PASS: projections, analytic attention, masks, convex bounds, value perturbation,') print('all six permutations, stable softmax, invalid shapes/masks, rectangular scaling and counts.')

Field Value Title Retrieval, external knowledge, and provenance ID / revision / date A03 · 1.0 · 2026-11-10 Prerequisites S02 versioned evidence, A01 evaluation boundaries, A02 attention; S06 authority bridge below Capability developed Locate a failed evidence-to-answer stage and defend what a citation actually establishes Source-check status R15 arXiv v4 methods and experimental setup inspected; R11 mediation passage rechecked Experiment status Constructed corpus, fixed scores and executed finite checks; no live retriever, language model or semantic verifier evaluated Companion Hints, worked answers and checks

sections.section: The answer changed; which part should change?
sections.text: A reviewer asks, “What delivery reference is published for tenant A’s D17 now?” S02’s example has an older revision with delivery reference X and a newer revision with Y. A model can produce fluent text containing either. The decision is whether the answer is supported by the intended revision and whether this reviewer is allowed to see it. Keep frequently changing, tenant-specific and auditable facts in a versioned evidence system when those properties are required. Model parameters can supply learned language patterns, but a plausible remembered answer does not identify the document revision used. Retrieval makes particular source material available to the answering procedure; it does not by itself establish that the procedure uses it correctly. A corpus is the stored collection. An index is a representation used to find candidates. A passage is a bounded piece of source material. A ranking score orders candidates under a rule. A context is the evidence actually delivered to the answer-producing component. A citation identifies claimed support. These objects can disagree: a source may exist without being indexed, a retrieved passage may be dropped before generation, and a valid link may accompany an unsupported claim. Our lesson uses a deterministic document query before discussing open-ended answers. No learner readiness is assumed. S02 supplies immutable revision identity; S06 supplies the distinction between a caller’s request and their authority; A01 requires that evaluation reflect the intended decision time. A02’s normalized attention weights do not certify truth or access rights.

All metadata, scores and times in this case are invented. Time is measured in arbitrary units. Revision 2 was published at t=5, revision 3 at t=15. The query arrives at t=20. An authoritative head lookup selects revision 3; this is a system fact, not a conclusion inferred from similarity scores. Current read permission allows tenant A’s D17 only. Passage Tenant / document / revision Content fixture Score old A / D17 / 2 Delivery reference X 97 other B / D17 / 3 Delivery reference Z 95 note A / D17 / 3 Review notes; no delivery reference 93 new A / D17 / 3 Delivery reference Y 88 A score of 97 is simply larger than 88 under this assigned ranking. It is neither 97% confidence nor evidence of freshness. Identical document IDs in different tenant namespaces do not identify the same document. Our proposed sequence is: Establish the authenticated principal and exact question: current published state, a named revision, or historical state as of a time. Resolve the permitted document and selected revision using authoritative metadata. Search only eligible passages, or ensure equivalent enforcement before any unauthorized content reaches an untrusted component. Retrieve a candidate set, rank/select evidence under a context budget, and preserve stable locators. Produce an answer or an explicit insufficient-evidence outcome. Check each consequential claim against the selected evidence and enforce permission at disclosure under the declared freshness contract. Applying tenant/document/revision constraints leaves note and new. Top-1 by our score retrieves note and misses the fact. Top-2 contains both. But a one-passage context that keeps the first score-ranked passage still drops new. Increasing retrieval depth alone did not solve evidence selection. For this structured query, a simple field-aware selector preferring passages with the requested delivery field chooses new. For prose questions, that relevance judgment needs its own evaluation. An exact fact lookup on (tenant, doc, rev, field) is a strong baseline here. A general semantic search is useful when questions or source phrasing are varied, but it must earn its complexity against that baseline. Do not make a precise record lookup harder merely to use generation.

sections.section: Four failures, plus a handoff loss
sections.text: The desired answer is “The published delivery reference is Y,” linked to the exact location in revision 3. A diagnostic must compare intermediate artifacts, not only the final sentence. Controlled failure Observation to inspect Repair candidate and remaining limit Correct evidence missing Authoritative revision manifest expects the delivery fact, but the indexed corpus lacks new Repair ingestion/index publication; a larger k cannot recover absent content Present but not retrieved new exists and is eligible, but top-1 is note Examine query/ranker/index approximation; top-2 repairs this fixture only Retrieved but dropped Candidate IDs include new; delivered context contains only note Repair selection/truncation; log the actual context, not merely retrieval results Retrieved and supplied but ignored Context contains new; answer says X without valid current support Evaluate answer construction, contradictory memory and abstention; retriever recall is already adequate Cited without support Answer says “Payment is settled” and cites new Resolve the citation and compare the claim with its passage; a delivery reference says nothing about settlement The first, second, fourth and fifth rows instantiate the curriculum’s required four failure cases. The third separates a common handoff ambiguity in “retrieved.” They are controlled constructions, not observed incident frequencies. In a real failure several defects may coexist. Report the earliest failing stage for triage while retaining later failures rather than pretending each case has one universal cause. For debugging, supplying known sufficient evidence directly can isolate downstream behavior. If the answer remains wrong, changing only retrieval cannot fix that controlled run. Such an oracle-evidence test does not estimate deployed quality because it bypasses the retrieval difficulty. Conversely, improved recall does not prove improved supported-answer rate if context selection or generation remains defective.

Store a citation record with tenant/document identity, immutable revision, passage identifier, source-byte reference, extraction/rendering version and a locator such as page/region or offsets into that exact rendering. Preserve enough bytes to reproduce the source. A digest can detect mismatch; it cannot recreate a deleted document. Re-resolve permissions before disclosing retained evidence. This extends S02 and S06 rather than replacing them with a model prompt. Check three different properties: Resolution: the cited object and span exist and identify the source version claimed. Support: that span, possibly together with explicitly identified additional evidence, justifies the actual claim at its stated scope. Applicability: the source belongs to the requested object, time and authority context and is permitted for this principal. A citation can resolve perfectly and fail the other two. An old passage supports “revision 2 listed X,” but not “the current revision lists X” at t=20. A delivery reference supports an extracted field claim, not that goods physically arrived or a payment settled. Source support is also distinct from source truth: an authentic invoice can itself contain a false assertion. When an answer has several claims, check each. A single source at the paragraph’s end does not necessarily support every sentence. For a conclusion combining passages, retain the combination and explain the inference. Conflicting eligible sources should trigger the declared source-precedence rule or an unresolved result, not a silent choice of whichever scored highest. In the companion, support is a manually assigned exact fact relation. It validates the example’s bookkeeping. It is not an algorithm for determining arbitrary textual entailment. Real support assessment needs a rubric, human-labeled cases and an evaluation of the assessor’s errors.

sections.section: Freshness and authority are separate clocks
sections.text: For a historical question at t=10, the published revision is 2 and X is appropriate. For the same question at t=20, revision 3 and Y are appropriate. Neither answer should use a mutable “latest” link to reconstruct what was seen earlier. Record query time, source publication time, indexed snapshot and selected revision. If the head advances before the new index is ready, do not silently substitute old evidence while claiming current state. One policy is to return “current evidence unavailable” until the revision is searchable, or use an authorized direct lookup. Another is to offer a clearly labeled older result if the product contract permits it. Choose and test that contract explicitly. Updating source bytes without rebuilding affected passages/index entries is not a complete retrieval update. For access control, relevance is never permission. Do not send all tenants’ passages to an external model and ask it to ignore forbidden ones. It has already received them. Post-filtering can also hurt recall: selecting global top-1 and then removing ineligible results can yield an empty set even when eligible evidence exists. The fixture demonstrates this without measuring any search engine. A permission can change between retrieval and display. Our proposed immediate-disclosure policy requires a current authorization decision coordinated with disclosure; merely storing a policy version does not enforce that ordering. If permission cannot be established, withhold the protected answer. If a system deliberately allows bounded staleness, declare and evaluate that weaker policy. An answer cache must respect principal scope, source revision and permission changes; a query-string-only cache fails these requirements. R11’s complete-mediation passage explicitly includes remembered authorization decisions. Retrieved text is untrusted data and cannot grant new privileges by claiming to be an administrator. Authority must be enforced outside the generated response, as S06 established. These are design obligations, not security guarantees provided by R15.

sections.section: What the original RAG paper contributes
sections.text: R15 combines a DPR-based retriever, a dense Wikipedia index and a BART generator. Its RAG-Sequence formulation marginalizes one latent passage across an output sequence; RAG-Token marginalizes passages at each output-token step over the retrieved set. During fine-tuning it updates the query encoder and generator while keeping the document encoder/index fixed. These are specific mechanisms, not a definition of every later retrieval pipeline. Inspect §2.1–2.4, pp. 3–4; §3, p. 4 states the corpus setup. An original two-passage calculation makes the distinction concrete. Let retrieval weights be 0.6 and 0.4. For a fixed two-token target and its fixed prefix, let conditional token probabilities be (0.8,0.5) under passage 1 and (0.2,0.9) under passage 2. With these hypothetical normalized weights: Psequence=0.6(0.8)(0.5)+0.4(0.2)(0.9)=0.312, Ptoken=[0.6(0.8)+0.4(0.2)][0.6(0.5)+0.4(0.9)]=0.3696. The second expression includes cross-passage contributions between token positions. It does not require fetching a new corpus on each step. Neither number is a probability that the answer is true or a permission decision. The paper’s model is not implemented by our deterministic field selector, and our fixture does not reproduce its experiments.

sections.section: Evaluate the whole path without hiding failures
sections.text: Define success for our query as a correct, supported answer for the selected revision with no unauthorized disclosure. Track abstention, incorrect answer and missing evidence separately. A safe abstention can be preferable to fabrication while still failing an answer-completion objective. Questions outside the supported population need a declared separate denominator. Imagine 20 eligible test queries, each requiring one evidence item. Four lack it in the corpus; four more miss it during retrieval; two more lose it during selection; three more fail downstream; seven succeed. These stages are nested and exhaustive by construction. Corpus coverage is 16/20, conditional candidate hit rate 12/16, conditional selection retention 10/12, and supported completion given sufficient context 7/10. Their product is 7/20=35%. Reporting only 70% on the sufficient-context subset conceals upstream losses. This is an accounting identity for this suite, not an independence assumption or predicted production rate. For multi-evidence questions, replace a single hit with a sufficient-evidence-set criterion; one relevant passage may be inadequate. Freeze corpus snapshots, permissions, query interpretations and answer rubric before final evaluation. Use A01’s group/time boundaries, keep document revisions together and exclude information unavailable at decision time. Compare exact lookup, lexical matching and learned retrieval under the same task contract. Measure ranking, selected-context sufficiency, claim support, abstention and full-task outcomes as well as resource costs. Do not transfer a public QA score to private invoice correctness.

Trace eligible passages, top-1, top-2 and one-passage context for the t=20 query. Compare a field-aware selector with exact lookup and score-only selection. Construct the four required failure cases and the selection-loss case. For each, name the artifact to inspect and a controlled test that distinguishes it from adjacent stages. Compare “revision 2 listed X,” “current reference is X” and “payment is settled” with citations to old or new. Separate resolution, support, applicability and source truth. Change query time to t=10, then restore t=20 but remove new from the index. Add a permission revocation before display. Specify an honest response policy for each case. Recompute the two probability expressions and explain why passage weights, attention weights and claim correctness are different quantities. Derive all stage rates for the 20-query suite. Propose an evaluation that could reject a higher-recall retriever, including context budget, access controls, missing answers and deployment-aligned splits.

Identify the question’s object/time → enforce authority → verify corpus/index availability → inspect candidates → inspect actual context → assess each claim against exact evidence → retain the source version. A resolvable citation is a starting point for verification. Basis Inspected locator Use and boundary R15, Lewis et al., 2020; arXiv v4 dated 2021-04-12 Versioned paper, Figure 1 p. 2, §§2.1–2.4 pp. 3–4, §3 opening p. 4 Concrete retriever/generator model and experimental corpus scope; no performance result adopted R11, Saltzer and Schroeder, 1975 Basic Principles, §I.A.3 c, Complete mediation Access checks and updating cached decisions; our disclosure protocol is an application design Earlier packs S02 evidence identity; S06 authority; A01 evaluation; A02 attention limits Continuity, not fresh deployment validation Original synthesis Corpus, fixed scores, failure cases, two-passage calculation, stage accounting and companion checks Constructed values and explicit assumptions, not measured model behavior Open inputs include real corpus completeness, grouping, source accuracy, index publication latency, permission synchronization, ranker behavior, context budgets and support-assessor error. No essential source-access blocker remains. Learner answers/mastery remain unknown. Next A04 studies inference serving and memory economics.
1.0 — 2026-11-10. Versioned retrieval case, stage diagnostics, provenance/authority boundaries and six exercises.

Field Value Title Retrieval, external knowledge, and provenance — worked answers ID / revision / date A03 answers · 1.0 · 2026-11-10 Prerequisites S02, S06, A01, A02 and A03 core Capability developed Separate evidence availability, retrieval, context delivery and claim support Source-check status R15 methods and R11 mediation; exact URLs/locators in core Experiment status Executed finite fixtures and exact arithmetic; no live search, generation or semantic entailment experiment These are reference solutions, not learner responses or mastery assessments.

Apply eligibility before interpreting a ranking; inspect the context actually supplied. Change one stage at a time while keeping the query and required evidence fixed. Read the claim’s temporal and business scope, not only its nouns. A missing index entry and a revoked grant call for different explanations. Compare sum-of-products with product-of-sums using the same probabilities. State every denominator. A component metric can improve while task success falls.

At t=20, the authoritative head is revision 3. old is stale for the current query; other is a different tenant. Eligible candidates are note at 93 and new at 88. Top-1 is [note]; top-2 is [note,new]. Keeping only the first candidate loses the delivery evidence even with k=2. The declared field-aware selector chooses new because it contains the requested field. For this exact tenant/document/revision/field question, direct fact lookup is the natural baseline and returns Y with its frozen locator. More general search might help with paraphrases or unstructured documents, but that benefit is not demonstrated by this fixture. If multiple eligible passages claim conflicting delivery values, an explicit resolution rule is required; the field-aware selector alone does not resolve truth. Criterion: Separate eligibility, candidate recall and context sufficiency; no confidence interpretation of scores.

Missing evidence: remove new from the indexed corpus while retaining the authoritative manifest expectation. Compare expected versus indexed revision contents; k changes cannot fix it. Present but not retrieved: restore new, use k=1, and observe only note. Force new into the candidate set to distinguish a retrieval miss from downstream problems. Retrieved but dropped: use k=2, then retain only score-first note. Compare candidate IDs with actual context IDs. Supply new directly to the answering component as a diagnostic, without calling that oracle run deployed performance. Supplied but ignored: context includes new, yet the answer states delivery X. Inspect the exact model input and output and their claim-level comparison. A higher-recall retriever cannot fix this already-sufficient context on its own. Cited without support: retain context [new] and emit “Payment is settled” with that citation. The locator resolves, but the fixture contains no settlement fact. Validate the claim–passage relationship rather than counting citation syntax. Criterion: One controlled intervention per boundary, with observable artifacts. Real cases can contain several failures; a triage label is not proof of a unique root cause.

sections.section: 3. Provenance is necessary but narrower than truth
sections.text: old supports “revision 2 listed X” if the old bytes and locator resolve and the reader may access them. It does not support the current-state claim at t=20, because the head is revision 3. new supports “revision 3 lists Y,” and supports the current published-reference answer only with the authoritative head/time link. Neither passage supports settlement. A claim “X” cited to new fails the assigned fact comparison. A claim “payment settled” cited to new fails even though the citation is syntactically valid and current. An authentic passage can still be factually wrong about the world. Distinguish “the source states Y” from independently verified delivery. Keep exact tenant/document/revision/passage identity, bytes, rendering/extraction version and locator. Replacing old evidence with current bytes destroys historical reproducibility. A digest is an integrity check, not a substitute for retained content. Multiple claims need individual coverage; missing support is not repaired by adding more unrelated citations. Criterion: Correct scope, source identity and permission; no inference from link existence to semantic support or physical truth.

At t=10, revision 2 is the published head; X is the answer for that historical state, assuming current permission to view its retained evidence. The query-time snapshot and the disclosure-time access decision are different controls. At t=20 with revision 3 selected but new absent from the index, report current evidence unavailable, or perform an authorized direct lookup. An older answer is acceptable only as an explicitly labeled older result under a contract that allows it. Quietly returning X as current fails. If permission is revoked before display, withhold the protected content under the selected immediate-disclosure policy. A previously allowed retrieval or cached answer is insufficient. An unavailable policy check also does not establish permission. Coordinating the check with disclosure is a deployment requirement, not a feature proved by the fixture’s Boolean grant. Criterion: Distinguish source publication, index readiness, query time and authorization freshness. Do not present delayed ingestion as “no such fact exists.”

For the fixed target sequence, sequence-level mixing gives 0.6×0.8×0.5 + 0.4×0.2×0.9 = 0.24+0.072=0.312. Token-level mixing gives (0.48+0.08)×(0.30+0.36)=0.56×0.66=0.3696. Their difference is 0.0576. The product-of-sums includes cross-passage contributions; it does not mean an observed output is guaranteed to combine correct facts. The second-token probabilities are conditional on the same specified first-token prefix, not unconditional token frequencies. The two passages form the entire normalized toy distribution here. The paper uses a top-K approximation; these numbers are not its reported outputs. For a single-token target the two forms coincide, as summing over the same one-step terms yields the same result. Retrieval weights concern passages given a query; A02 attention weights mix representations over positions; a correctness assessment concerns an answer’s claims against evidence and reality. Matching a mathematical normalization pattern does not equate these targets. Criterion: Correct conditioning, arithmetic and interpretation; no fabricated measured model accuracy.

sections.section: 6. Stage accounting and a falsifiable evaluation
sections.text: Corpus coverage is 16/20=80%. Conditional candidate hit rate is 12/16=75%. Retention of sufficient evidence is 10/12≈83.33%. Supported completion after sufficient context is 7/10=70%. Multiplying yields 7/20=35%, because the nested counts cancel. No independence assumption is needed. Overall candidate hit rate is 12/20=60%, a different denominator from 75%. For a higher-recall candidate, freeze the same eligible query population, target revisions, permissions, corpus snapshot, context budget and downstream procedure. Include new documents/groups according to deployment, keeping revisions together. Measure sufficient-evidence retrieval and actual selected-context sufficiency, supported answer completion, unauthorized exposures, abstentions, latency and cost. Keep missing/unanswered cases in the declared outcome population. A retriever could increase candidate recall while adding distractions that crowd out the required evidence under the context budget. It could improve recall on authorized cases yet expose another tenant’s data. Either can invalidate deployment. Use direct lookup as the baseline for exact field questions, and a separate relevance/support rubric for open-ended questions. Independent adjudication of contested support cases is needed; our hand-assigned fact map is not that adjudication system. Criterion: Nested denominators, comparable policies and a concrete way the seemingly better component can fail the full contract.

This code implements only the declared fixture rules. The facts relation is an oracle supplied by the author, not inferred from prose. Authorization and head selection are sequential model inputs; concurrent policy changes, actual identity verification and index/storage failures are not simulated. Fixed rankings are not search-engine measurements. from fractions import Fraction as F from itertools import permutations # (tenant, document, revision, field, value) is the exact fact identity. def passage(pid,tenant,rev,score,facts): return dict(id=pid,tenant=tenant,doc='D17',rev=rev,score=score,facts=facts) corpus=[ passage('old','A',2,97,{'delivery':'X'}), passage('other','B',3,95,{'delivery':'Z'}), passage('note','A',3,93,{}), passage('new','A',3,88,{'delivery':'Y'}), ] def head(t): if t<5: return None return 2 if t<15 else 3 def eligible(p,t,grant=True): return grant and p['tenant']=='A' and p['doc']=='D17' and p['rev']==head(t) def candidates(rows,t,k,grant=True): return sorted((p for p in rows if eligible(p,t,grant)), key=lambda p:(-p['score'],p['id']))[:k] def select(rows,field='delivery'): return sorted(rows,key=lambda p:(field not in p['facts'],-p['score'],p['id']))[:1] def ids(rows):return [p['id'] for p in rows] def supports(claim,p): tenant,doc,rev,field,value=claim return (tenant,doc,rev)==(p['tenant'],p['doc'],p['rev']) and p['facts'].get(field)==value def disclose(claim,citation,context,t,grant=True): p=next((p for p in context if p['id']==citation),None) return bool(p and eligible(p,t,grant) and supports(claim,p)) claim=('A','D17',3,'delivery','Y') assert ids(candidates(corpus,20,1))==['note'] assert ids(candidates(corpus,20,2))==['note','new'] context=select(candidates(corpus,20,2)) assert ids(context)==['new'] and disclose(claim,'new',context,20) assert not disclose(claim,'new',context,20,False) # revoked before disclosure assert not candidates(corpus,20,2,False) assert ids(candidates(corpus,10,2))==['old'] assert head(4) is None and head(5)==2 and head(14)==2 and head(15)==3 assert not candidates(corpus,4,4) old=corpus[0] assert supports(('A','D17',2,'delivery','X'),old) assert not disclose(('A','D17',2,'delivery','X'),'old',[old],20) assert disclose(('A','D17',2,'delivery','X'),'old',[old],10) assert not disclose(('A','D17',3,'payment','settled'),'new',context,20) assert not disclose(('A','D17',3,'delivery','X'),'new',context,20) assert not disclose(claim,'invented',context,20) assert not disclose(claim,'new',[],20) # Filtering only after global top-1 loses eligible results. global_first=sorted(corpus,key=lambda p:-p['score'])[:1] assert not [p for p in global_first if eligible(p,20)] assert len(candidates(corpus,20,1))==1 # A second tenant's score cannot alter the result under this fixture's prefilter. for score in [-100,0,1000]: changed=[dict(p,score=score) if p['id']=='other' else p for p in corpus] assert ids(select(candidates(changed,20,2)))==['new'] # Storage order is irrelevant because ranking has an explicit tie rule. for rows in permutations(corpus): assert ids(select(candidates(rows,20,2)))==['new'] def diagnose(rows,cands,ctx,answer,citation): if not any(eligible(p,20) and supports(claim,p) for p in rows):return 'corpus' if not any(supports(claim,p) for p in cands):return 'retrieval' if not any(supports(claim,p) for p in ctx):return 'selection' if not disclose(answer,citation,ctx,20):return 'answer/support' return 'success' missing=[p for p in corpus if p['id']!='new'] one=candidates(corpus,20,1);two=candidates(corpus,20,2) assert diagnose(missing,candidates(missing,20,4),[],claim,'new')=='corpus' assert diagnose(corpus,one,one,claim,'new')=='retrieval' assert diagnose(corpus,two,two[:1],claim,'new')=='selection' assert diagnose(corpus,two,context,('A','D17',3,'delivery','X'),'new')=='answer/support' assert diagnose(corpus,two,context,('A','D17',3,'payment','settled'),'new')=='answer/support' assert diagnose(corpus,two,context,claim,'new')=='success' # Enough candidate depth cannot recover physically missing evidence. for k in range(1,6): assert not any(supports(claim,p) for p in candidates(missing,20,k)) seq=F(3,5)*F(4,5)*F(1,2)+F(2,5)*F(1,5)*F(9,10) tok=(F(3,5)*F(4,5)+F(2,5)*F(1,5))*(F(3,5)*F(1,2)+F(2,5)*F(9,10)) assert seq==F(312,1000) and tok==F(3696,10000) and tok-seq==F(576,10000) rates=[F(16,20),F(12,16),F(10,12),F(7,10)] product=F(1) for rate in rates:product*=rate assert product==F(7,20) and sum([4,4,2,3,7])==20 print('PASS: time boundaries, eligibility, ranking/selection, five failure fixtures,') print('revocation/citation checks, 24 orderings, score perturbations, marginalization and stage rates.')
