title: Hints, worked answers, and assessment criteria

sections.section: Hints, worked answers, and assessment criteria
sections.text: Field Value ID / revision B01 answers / 1.0 Date 2026-11-02 Prerequisites B01 core pack Capability developed Judge whether an evidence plan can change a concrete build decision Source-check status R19 locators in core §10; answers are original teaching examples Experiment status Arithmetic assertions executed; no customer or market experiment conducted All organizations, offers, inputs, and outcomes below are hypothetical. These are worked possibilities, not the learner’s answers or results from research participants.

A role is not necessarily a different person. Name who feels the problem and who can change the process. One hypothesis should concern the existing problem; the other should concern behavior toward an offer. Ask for a reconstruction, not a rating of your idea. Include an opportunity to say the existing process works. Convert minutes to hours before multiplying by an hourly value. Include review and onboarding. Identify whose behavior changed, what it cost them, and what terms they accepted. A gate authorizes the next bounded investment. It does not certify an entire market.

A useful example segment is purchasing teams receiving 100–200 supplier invoices weekly and manually matching them to delivery evidence. The trigger is invoice receipt. The operator is the matching clerk; the intended outcome is an evidence-complete case ready for a correct approval decision. The assumed buyer is the manager responsible for that budget, but this role must be verified. A separate data or systems approver may exist; it is unknown here. The current alternative combines documents, a spreadsheet, and employee judgment. It must be evaluated as a complete process, including exceptions. “Uses a spreadsheet” does not establish dissatisfaction or a business opportunity. An internal tool variant would replace a purchase hypothesis with a commitment of staff time and workflow ownership.

Problem hypothesis: In the defined segment, assembling matching evidence creates material active workload or consequential delays. Evidence against it includes several relevant recent cases showing quick matching, low recurrence, or a different dominant delay. A participant who has not encountered an exception recently is useful negative evidence, provided their workload belongs to the chosen segment. Adoption hypothesis: An authorized team will allocate permitted cases, a reviewer, and a dated trial if assistance preserves source traceability and approval. Adverse evidence includes refusal after the concrete terms are explained, inability to obtain necessary permissions, or higher-priority work repeatedly displacing the trial. Diagnose reasons before generalizing. Lack of authority in the interviewed person is a recruitment problem as well as a limit on their commitment. Neither hypothesis requires pretending that five conversations yield a population estimate. The bounded batch is a practical investigation design. A later decision to estimate prevalence needs a sampling plan, addressed in F03.

Reconstruct the last invoice requiring extra checking from receipt to resolution. Which steps needed active work and which involved waiting? What record could help check the distinction? What consequence followed, and what would have happened under the normal process? Over the last defined working week, which cases needed this work and which did not? What did the team change previously, and what remains useful about that approach? For the most recent workflow tool adopted, who approved spending and data access, and what did adoption require? These questions can reveal a mistaken premise. “How much would you pay for our AI that saves hours?” embeds both a benefit and a preferred solution. Rewrite it around actual work before discussing a real offer on explicit terms.

Quantity 8-minute baseline 4-minute baseline Current work, 120 invoices/week 16 h/week 8 h/week Proposed review: 120 × 3 / 60 6 h/week 6 h/week Proposed recurring overhead 2 h/week 2 h/week Recurring capacity released 8 h/week 0 h/week Onboarding: 12 h / 8 weeks 1.5 h/week 1.5 h/week Net released capacity during assessment 6.5 h/week −1.5 h/week Assigned value at ₹300/h, before fees ₹1,950/week −₹450/week The original baseline’s assigned labor value is 16×₹300=₹4,800/week. Before onboarding, the potential released capacity is valued at 8×₹300=₹2,400/week. These are conditional arithmetic results. If salaried hours cannot be reduced or usefully reassigned, released time may not reduce cash expenditure. If work quality falls or extra reviews appear, the model is incomplete. Even a correct capacity estimate does not reveal an authorized budget or accepted price. Compare the same outcome quality and count each work category once. The eight-week horizon is an assumed evaluation convention, not a prediction of a sales cycle.

Fictional signal What it supports What remains unknown Developer praises demo Appeal to that developer Target user’s pain, buyer’s authority, adoption Clerk estimates weekly burden Reported problem magnitude from one perspective Accuracy, recurrence, alternatives, budget Sponsor schedules trial with resources Specific intent to test on those terms Actual execution, outcome improvement, renewal Payment for custom integration Demand for that scoped transaction Repeatable product demand and delivery margin Repeated manager-mandated use Compliance or workflow dependence Voluntary preference, net benefit, willingness to renew A signal can be genuine and still answer the wrong question. Preserve the terms, roles, and context. Do not transform these fictional examples into measured customer evidence.

Proceed to trial design if two independent organizations supply relevant recent episodes and one authorized sponsor agrees to a bounded trial with cases, reviewer, date, and success criterion. This is the exercise’s proposed gate, not a proven universal threshold. Before execution, define how complete correct cases, active work, and exceptions will be checked against the current process. Revise if evidence identifies a different bottleneck or if the interested operator lacks the required approval route. Stop or defer this particular investment if repeated relevant evidence indicates little consequence, adequate existing alternatives, or no feasible adoption path within the chosen constraints. Record the investigation limit so a later change can justify revisiting it. With the new finding that missing delivery records create two-day delays, fast extraction does not itself provide the absent information. Investigate where records originate, who can obtain them, and why retrieval stalls. A follow-up plan could observe one missing-record episode and compare it with a routine case. Do not immediately commit to a reminder agent: the cause could instead be a supplier process, access restriction, or incomplete shipment. Reassess the problem before selecting a mechanism.

Dimension A useful answer demonstrates Specificity Segment, workflow, roles, alternative, and consequential outcome Falsifiability Adverse evidence for both problem and adoption claims Interview design Recent episodes, neutral framing, and an approval-path question Evidence discipline Separates account, measurement, inference, and hypothetical inputs Decision quality Bounded next step with explicit revise/stop conditions Transfer Changes the plan when the bottleneck or authority changes Different coherent plans can satisfy these criteria. No learner score or mastery state has been recorded.

from fractions import Fraction n, review_minutes, overhead, hourly = 120, 3, 2, 300 onboarding = Fraction(12, 8) new_hours = Fraction(n * review_minutes, 60) + overhead assert new_hours == 8 and onboarding == Fraction(3, 2) for old_minutes, hours, recurring, net, value in [ (8, 16, 8, Fraction(13, 2), 1950), (4, 8, 0, Fraction(-3, 2), -450), ]: baseline = Fraction(n * old_minutes, 60) assert baseline == hours assert baseline - new_hours == recurring assert baseline - new_hours - onboarding == net assert net * hourly == value assert 16 * hourly == 4800 assert 8 * hourly == 2400 print('PASS: two scenarios, units, onboarding allocation, and value arithmetic') The checks validate calculations from assigned inputs, not the inputs themselves. Editorial checks matched all six exercise prompts to worked answers, reviewed claim scope and timestamp locators, and verified that no interviews, outreach, trial outcomes, or demand measurements were claimed. Audit A remains pending.

title: Unit economics, pricing units, and sensitivity

sections.section: Unit economics, pricing units, and sensitivity
sections.text: Field Value ID / revision / date B02 · 1.0 · 2026-11-12 Title Unit economics, pricing units, and sensitivity Prerequisites F02 expected values; B01 problem and commitment evidence; A05 outcome contracts Capability developed Build a cost model with defensible units, expose its breakpoints and choose the next measurement Source-check status R20 unit metrics, R21 packaging and R12 elasticity passages inspected Experiment status Original hypothetical ledger; exact arithmetic and sensitivity checks executed; no customer or billing experiment Companion Hints, worked answers and executable checks

sections.section: Which unit pays for the work?
sections.text: The invoice service prepares supported evidence for a human reviewer. A cheaper model call sounds attractive, but the buyer needs a correct, timely result. A call can fail, require another call, create review work, or produce nothing billable. The decision is whether an offer can deliver its promised outcome at a sustainable cost, and which uncertain input is worth measuring before investing further. F02 introduced an expected value: multiply each possible quantity by its probability and add. B01 separated useful released capacity from actual cash savings. A05 separated a contract-correct refusal from a supported draft. B02 combines these boundaries into a deliberately simple service model. It is managerial reasoning, not a set of accounting, tax or investment recommendations. R20 distinguishes technical efficiency metrics from business unit metrics. R21 treats packaging as different feature/usage arrangements for customer groups. These practitioner sources motivate our choice of units; they do not supply the numbers or prove that a customer will pay them. R12 provides historical reasoning about provisioning risk, not current cloud prices.

sections.section: Define a case before counting money
sections.text: Use one monthly intake cohort. A case is one eligible submitted invoice requiring one supported evidence package. Revisions, retries and duplicate requests remain attached to that case. A run is an execution within it; a call is a resource-consuming operation. Billing a retry as a new case would change the offer, not improve delivery. For this lesson a successful case has a verified, supported package delivered within the agreed deadline, with no unauthorized disclosure or effect. An unresolved case may be a correct safe response but is not a billable success under this invented offer. This differs intentionally from A05’s broader contract-success metric. A human still approves any payment; producing evidence does not grant payment authority. Before measuring, specify eligibility, verification rubric, deadline, duplicate identity, dispute/refund rules and the observation window. Count offered, eligible, attempted, successful, unresolved and rejected cases separately. Here every eligible case is attempted once by a fixed procedure; any internal calls are included in that procedure’s cost. The optional retry extension below is a separate scenario. Let N be eligible attempted cases, p their success probability, P the price per verified success, c the expected variable cost per attempted case and F the fixed cost over the month. Price is a contractual revenue unit; cost is a resource unit. They need not use the same denominator.

sections.section: Build a ledger with mutually exclusive costs
sections.text: Every numerical input in this pack is invented, in a common currency unit called U. No number is a provider quote, customer observation or forecast. Assume success proportion p=0.8 and N=1,000. We use exact counts of 800 successes and 200 failures for the worked ledger; the probability model generalizes it for planning. Cost category Assigned rule Monthly amount Compute and storage directly attributable to processing 0.4 U per attempted case, including internal calls 400 U Routine verification 2 active minutes per attempted case × 0.5 U/minute 1,000 U Routine support 0.2 U per attempted case 200 U Additional failure handling 2 U per failed case, beyond routine review/support 400 U Fixed service overhead 1,500 U per month within the stated capacity range 1,500 U Assume the review labor can be purchased proportionally at this rate. If it is salaried staff already paid regardless of work, the cash-cost classification changes: record the committed salary and usable capacity separately rather than counting both salary and the same minutes as expenses. Similarly, failure support must exclude minutes already in routine verification. Every ledger category needs an owner and a non-overlap rule. Expected variable cost per attempt is c=0.4+2(0.5)+0.2+(1−p)2=3.6−2p. At p=0.8, c=2 U. Total variable cost is 2,000 U; variable cost per successful case is 2,000/800=2.5 U. Including the fixed overhead gives 3,500/800=4.375 U per success. Reporting only the 0.4 U compute charge omits most of the delivery cost. For actual observed counts use total attributable cost divided by actual successes. For planning, c/p is a ratio of expected totals under stable assumptions. It is not generally the expectation of the random ratio cost/successes; a small month can have zero successes. At zero successes report incurred cost and no finite unit-success ratio.

Suppose P=4 U per verified success, with all qualifying invoices collectible, no refunds and no payment fees in this toy model. Expected revenue is NpP=3,200 U. Contribution is revenue minus variable delivery cost: 1,200 U. It is the amount left to cover fixed costs, not company profit. Our modeled monthly operating remainder is Π=N(pP−c)−F. Here it is 1,200−1,500=−300 U. This remainder excludes taxes, financing, acquisition costs, unlisted development and other expenses; even a positive value would not establish total company profitability. Actual cash flow also depends on collection timing and upfront payments. A positive accrued margin cannot fund next week’s payroll if cash arrives later. Define contribution per attempt m=pP−c. If m>0 and F stays fixed, modeled break-even volume is F/m. At the baseline, m=1.2 and break-even is 1,250 attempted cases. At m=0 no positive fixed cost is recovered; when m<0, more identical work deepens the loss. A volume forecast is still required: algebra does not recruit customers. The contribution fraction of revenue is 1,200/3,200=37.5% in this definition. Do not label it gross margin without defining which costs that accounting measure includes. A per-case contribution and a percentage of revenue answer different questions.

Compare an alternative on the same population, outcome rubric, price and overhead. Assign compute cost 0.1 U, routine review 3 minutes at 0.5 U/minute, routine support 0.3 U, success p=0.7, and unchanged 2 U extra failure handling. Its variable cost is 0.1+1.5+0.3+0.3×2=2.5 U per attempt. Per success it is 2.5/0.7≈3.571 U, worse than the baseline’s 2.5. At 1,000 attempts, revenue is 2,800, contribution is 300 and modeled remainder is −1,200 U. The compute component fell 75%, but additional labor and failure handling erased that saving. This is a counterexample, not evidence against any named model. Re-evaluate p, review time and support together on matched cases. Holding success constant while claiming labor savings from a changed review process can conceal a weaker verification standard. Keep authority and quality gates independent of the economic objective; no attractive margin licenses an unsafe output.

With baseline costs and P=4, m=4p−(3.6−2p)=6p−3.6. Positive contribution requires p>0.6. At 1,000 attempts, covering F=1,500 requires p≥0.85. A success rate of 80% clears the first gate but fails the second. Change from baseline Contribution per attempt Monthly remainder at N=1,000 p=0.6 0 −1,500 p=0.8 1.2 −300 p=0.9 1.8 300 P=3, p=0.8 0.4 −1,100 P=5, p=0.8 2.0 500 Routine support becomes 0.7, p=0.8, P=4 0.7 −800 At baseline quality and volume the price needed to cover the modeled costs is (c+F/N)/p=4.375 U. This is a cost-covering threshold, not willingness to pay. A price increase may reduce demand, change customer mix or raise service expectations. A one-variable sensitivity table is a diagnostic; a scenario must change related variables together. For example, N=500,1,000,1,500 at baseline assumptions yields remainders −900,−300,300 U. Now suppose serving more than 1,500 cases requires an additional 600 U monthly capacity block. At N=1,501, remainder becomes −298.8 U, despite more demand. It returns to zero at N=1,750, assuming this second capacity tier is sufficient. Fixed costs are fixed only over a range and time horizon. Do not extrapolate the first break-even line indefinitely. R12 §6.1 discusses over- and under-provisioning risk. Our step cost is an original abstraction. Real queues, reserve commitments, hiring delays and latency can change both cost and p. A service may be memory-feasible and still miss deadlines, as A04/C02 established.

Consider one additional attempt only for baseline failures. Let r=0.25 be the chance of recovering a success among those failed cases, and d=1 U the incremental cost of the retry including its added review. Original handling cost is already sunk; do not charge it again. Assume recovery remains within the original deadline and uses the same verified-success rubric. Then p_new=p+(1−p)r=0.85, and incremental contribution per original case is (1−p)(Pr−d). With P=4, r=0.25 and d=1, this is zero: 200 retries cost 200 U and add 50 billable successes worth 200 U. More successes need not improve contribution. It might still matter for retention or a quality obligation, but those are additional premises. Do not reuse the unconditional 0.8 as the retry recovery rate. Failed cases can be systematically harder. Nor does 1−(1−p)^k apply without the appropriate independence and identical-success assumptions. Measure the conditional recovery and resource distribution of the actual retry policy.

sections.section: Choose a pricing unit without confusing it with value
sections.text: Offer hypothesis Revenue driver Main question to test Per attempted case Accepted submissions Will buyers pay for unresolved work; can duplicate billing be prevented? Per verified successful case Agreed outcome evidence Who verifies success, resolves disputes and pays failure costs? Subscription with included usage and overage Account, allowance, extra work Does the allowance cover variable workload without surprising either side? R21’s packaging discussion supports examining feature/usage boundaries for different customers. These three offers are original hypotheses, not recommended prices. Outcome billing can align a useful unit while introducing verification and dispute costs. A subscription can simplify budgeting while exposing the supplier to heavy usage. Keep the workload/cost model for each customer segment, not just an average across unlike accounts. An internal deployment may have no sales revenue. Replace revenue with a separately justified benefit measure and budget decision; do not invent external sales or call released staff time cash savings. B01’s buyer, approver and operator roles still matter. B03 next examines how an offer is found, adopted and retained.

Record case identity and cohort, versions, eligibility, success verification and time, calls/retries, attributable charges, non-overlapping review/support minutes, refunds, realized billing and shared-cost allocation. Reconcile totals with the accounting window; amortize onboarding only over an explicit horizon and also report its upfront cash requirement. Segment routine and difficult cases. Investigate missing cost tags rather than assigning their cost to zero. Estimate p and effort from representative held-out work, preserving supplier/document dependence. Compare plausible joint scenarios and severe-loss cases, not only averages. This model omits rare consequential harms; adding an expected loss term can aid a decision but does not replace safety constraints or tail analysis. No sample size or empirical confidence interval is claimed here. Reference card: define the case and success → separate cost and billing units → include failures and labor once → calculate contribution → subtract horizon-matched fixed costs → check capacity tiers → vary coupled assumptions → collect the evidence that could reverse the decision.

Rebuild the baseline monthly ledger and both variable/full cost-per-success ratios. Explain the cash-labor assumption. Calculate contribution, revenue fraction, operating remainder and break-even volume. Explain why none proves company profitability. Compare the cheaper-model alternative. State what matched measurements could overturn this constructed result. Derive success and price thresholds, the support sensitivity and the capacity-tier discontinuity at 1,501 cases. Derive the retry policy’s new success rate, incremental cost and contribution. Find the conditional recovery threshold for positive incremental contribution. Compare the three pricing units for the same job. Propose a bounded evidence collection plan that could reject a seemingly profitable offer.

Field Value ID / revision / date B02 answers · 1.0 · 2026-11-12 Title Unit economics, pricing units, and sensitivity — worked answers Prerequisites F02, B01, A05 and B02 core Capability developed Audit denominators, cost boundaries and conditional decisions Source-check status R20/R21/R12 passages and URLs in the core evidence table Experiment status Exact Python arithmetic executed; no observed prices, customers or revenue These are reference solutions, not learner responses or mastery assessments.

Failed cases consume routine resources too. Separate their additional handling. Subtract variable costs before fixed overhead. Check the sign before dividing. Replace all changed inputs, not just compute price. Solve an inequality under one capacity range, then check whether the solution belongs to that range. Use the recovery probability among failures. Original costs are already included. A billable event needs a definition, evidence and a dispute rule.

There are 800 successful and 200 failed cases. Compute costs 400, routine verification 1,000, routine support 200 and additional failure handling 400 U. Total variable cost is 2,000; adding 1,500 fixed cost yields 3,500 U. Variable cost per attempt is 2, per success 2.5, full cost per attempt 3.5 and full cost per success 4.375 U. Routine verification applies to all 1,000 cases. Dividing only successful-case expenditure by 800 would hide failed work. The 2 U failure charge must be incremental to routine review/support. If the review minutes are salaried capacity rather than proportional purchases, revise the cash ledger; do not charge the same labor twice. Report capacity usage even when cash cost is fixed. Criterion: All rows reconcile, units and denominators are explicit, and labor/cost categories do not overlap.

Revenue is 800×4=3,200 U. Contribution is 3,200−2,000=1,200 U, or 1.2 per attempted case. Its revenue fraction is 1,200/3,200=3/8=37.5%. Modeled operating remainder is −300 U. At unchanged costs and quality, 1,500/1.2=1,250 cases cover the modeled fixed cost exactly. For integer attempts and positive margin, round a noninteger break-even threshold upward. If margin is zero, positive fixed cost cannot be recovered; if negative, volume makes the result worse. This formula assumes sufficient demand and unchanged capacity cost. It excludes unlisted company expenses and collection delays. Contribution is neither total profit nor cash in the bank. Criterion: Preserve the time horizon, positive-margin condition, cost scope and demand limitation.

Alternative variable cost is 0.1+3×0.5+0.3+0.3×2=2.5 U per attempt. At 700 successes, revenue is 2,800, variable costs 2,500, contribution 300 and modeled remainder −1,200 U. Variable cost per success is 25/7≈3.571 U. Baseline cost per success is 2.5 U. Compute fell from 0.4 to 0.1, but the complete system lost 900 U in monthly contribution. Compare matched eligible cases with frozen verification standards, recording actual calls, active review/support, failures and deadline-qualified successes. A new model with lower review effort or higher success could reverse the result. The hypothetical ledger establishes only that compute price alone is insufficient. Criterion: Recalculate the whole service; do not infer measured superiority or weaken quality to lower apparent cost.

Baseline cost c=3.6−2p, hence contribution m=6p−3.6 at P=4. It is positive above p=0.6. With N=1,000 and F=1,500, the remainder is 6,000p−5,100, so modeled break-even requires p≥0.85. At p=0.8, the cost-covering price is (2+1.5)/0.8=4.375 U. Support rising from 0.2 to 0.7 adds 0.5 per case. Margin becomes 0.7 and the monthly remainder is −800. With overhead fixed at 1,500, baseline N=500,1,000,1,500 produces −900,−300,300. Above 1,500 the new overhead is 2,100; N=1,501 yields 1,801.2−2,100=−298.8. This tier breaks even at 2,100/1.2=1,750. Assume that volume fits the tier; do not extend it beyond a known capacity range. The table varies one input at a time. For a real scenario, higher price can change N and customer mix; higher load can increase review delays and reduce p. Cost thresholds do not establish an acceptable offer. Criterion: Correct inclusive versus strict thresholds, discontinuity and explicit coupling assumptions.

Of 200 failures, recovery rate 1/4 produces 50 extra successes. The new rate is 850/1,000=0.85. Incremental cost is 200×1=200 U, incremental revenue 50×4=200, and incremental contribution zero. Total variable costs become 2,200, revenue 3,400, contribution remains 1,200 and remainder stays −300. For 0≤p<1, positive incremental contribution requires Pr>d, or r>d/P for positive P. Here r>1/4. At p=1 there are no failures and therefore no retry increment regardless of r. At P=0 and positive d no paid recovery can improve contribution. The recovery rate is conditional on the failed-case population; independence is not assumed. A late or unverified recovery does not qualify under this contract. Criterion: Do not double-charge original handling or treat retries as independent new cases. Preserve deadline and verification rules.

Per-attempt billing exposes the buyer to unsuccessful work; it needs an agreed eligibility and duplicate policy. Per-success billing exposes the supplier to failure costs and requires agreed verification/disputes. Subscription plus allowance requires workload limits and overage rules; averages can hide a costly heavy-use segment. These are hypotheses for customer testing, not commitments already obtained. A bounded plan: select an authorized sample from the intended segment; freeze the success rubric; log all cases, costs and non-overlapping labor; reconcile invoices and observe a complete outcome window. Include failed and disputed work. Independently check a subset of success labels. Reconstruct who can authorize payment and what alternatives they use. Seek an explicit trial on stated terms rather than treating favorable interview comments as revenue. No outreach is performed by this file. Reject or revise if permitted data cannot be obtained, actual review/failure costs exceed the feasible range, the buyer rejects the billing unit, useful outcomes fail quality/authority gates, or demand cannot cover fixed commitments. Preserve reasons and uncertainty; a single refusal is not proof of no market. Separate the cash ledger from the customer’s released-capacity value. Criterion: Operationally observable units, matched evidence, explicit rejection conditions and no invented willingness to pay.

The script checks constructed counts, exact thresholds, ledger reconciliation, capacity tiers and conditional retries. The grid is sensitivity analysis, not sampling or an empirical confidence interval. from fractions import Fraction as Q from itertools import product def cost(p, compute=Q(2,5), minutes=2, support=Q(1,5)): assert 0 <= p <= 1 return compute + minutes*Q(1,2) + support + (1-p)*2 def ledger(n,p,price=4,fixed=1500): revenue=n*p*price variable=n*cost(p) return revenue,variable,revenue-variable,revenue-variable-fixed p=Q(4,5) assert cost(p)==2 assert ledger(1000,p)==(3200,2000,1200,-300) assert Q(2000,800)==Q(5,2) and Q(3500,800)==Q(35,8) assert Q(1200,3200)==Q(3,8) assert ledger(1250,p)[3]==0 and ledger(1249,p)[3]<0 assert cost(Q(7,10),Q(1,10),3,Q(3,10))==Q(5,2) assert 1000*Q(7,10)*4-2500-1500==-1200 assert Q(2500,700)==Q(25,7) assert ledger(1000,Q(3,5))[2]==0 assert ledger(1000,Q(17,20))[3]==0 assert ledger(1000,p,Q(35,8))[3]==0 assert [ledger(1000,x)[3] for x in [Q(3,5),p,Q(9,10)]]==[-1500,-300,300] assert [ledger(1000,p,x)[3] for x in [3,5]]==[-1100,500] assert 3200-1000*cost(p,support=Q(7,10))-1500==-800 assert [ledger(n,p)[3] for n in [500,1000,1500]]==[-900,-300,300] assert ledger(1501,p,fixed=2100)[3]==Q(-1494,5) assert ledger(1750,p,fixed=2100)[3]==0 # Exact observed partition agrees with the expected-cost formula. for successes in range(1001): p0=Q(successes,1000) observed=400+1000+200+(1000-successes)*2 assert observed==1000*cost(p0) assert (4*p0-cost(p0)>0)==(p0>Q(3,5)) assert (ledger(1000,p0)[3]>=0)==(p0>=Q(17,20)) # Retry extension: all original failures offered exactly one extra attempt. checks=0 for p0,r,price,d in product([Q(0),Q(4,5),Q(1)], [Q(0),Q(1,4),Q(1,2),Q(1)], [Q(0),Q(4),Q(5)],[Q(0),Q(1),Q(2)]): newp=p0+(1-p0)*r extra=(1-p0)*d delta=(1-p0)*(price*r-d) assert p0<=newp<=1 assert newp*price-(cost(p0)+extra)-(p0*price-cost(p0))==delta if p0<1 and price>0: assert (delta>0)==(r>d/price) checks+=1 assert checks==108 assert p+(1-p)*Q(1,4)==Q(17,20) assert (1-p)*(4*Q(1,4)-1)==0 # Cost per observed success is undefined at zero, not zero cost. def per_success(total,successes): return None if successes==0 else Q(total,successes) assert per_success(3600,0) is None assert per_success(2000,800)==Q(5,2) print('PASS: ledger, thresholds, 1001 success counts, capacity tiers, 108 retry cases and zero-success handling')

sections.section: A good component can still be a poor offer
sections.text: A document model can extract invoice fields accurately while the purchasing team continues using a spreadsheet. Perhaps nobody reaches the budget owner. Perhaps importing records takes longer than matching them. Perhaps the team cannot send data outside its environment. These are different bottlenecks; a better extraction benchmark does not resolve them all. The question is: why would a particular customer find, adopt, keep and pay for this offering when alternatives improve? Distribution is the path to a qualified customer and an authorized adoption decision. Product boundary says which work and responsibilities the supplier accepts. Defensibility is a hypothesis that a valuable advantage can persist despite substitution or imitation. None is established by a feature list. B01 asked whether the problem matters. B02 asked whether a useful unit can support its delivery costs. Here we hold the customer job constant while changing how the work reaches the customer and who performs it. The framework and cases are original teaching designs. Practitioner sources supply questions to investigate, not verified demand.

sections.section: Start narrow enough to observe the whole job
sections.text: Retain the fictional purchasing workflow: assemble invoice and delivery evidence for a human payment reviewer. Choose an initial segment of small purchasing teams that repeatedly match a limited set of document formats, have an identifiable operations buyer, and can authorize a bounded pilot. This is a proposed segment, not a claim about its prevalence. Teams barred from external processing require a different deployment path. The job ends when an authorized reviewer receives a supported, timely evidence package or a clearly unresolved case. Payment approval remains outside the product. An assistant that silently guesses missing evidence fails the contract even if the user likes its writing. The clerk uses the output, the operations manager funds it, and a data/security owner permits access. One person might fill several roles; do not assume that a willing user can authorize all of them. A first distribution route could be introductions through a bookkeeping practitioner who already works with this segment, followed by a workflow demonstration to its buyer. That is a channel hypothesis. It requires permission and a credible reason for the practitioner to introduce you; it is not an audience you already possess. A fallback is a narrowly relevant professional community with an approved demonstration. Count distinct organizations, record referral incentives, and separate warm contacts from independently reached customers. R22 recommends manual early recruitment and attentive service, including doing work manually before automating it. Its founder anecdotes motivate a small learning route, not a causal claim that handholding creates a scalable business. R19’s budget and authority discussion motivates checking who can actually approve the change.

sections.section: Model adoption as several observable transitions
sections.text: Define events before collecting counts. A qualified organization fits the segment and has a relevant recent problem. Activation means completing the first permitted real workflow to the agreed quality bar, not opening an account. Repeat use means another eligible workflow cycle with the same success definition. A paid contract and a useful outcome are separate events. For an invented completed outreach cohort, suppose 40 distinct organizations are reached, 12 qualify, 6 agree to a demonstration, 3 activate, and 2 complete a second eligible cycle. Every later set is a subset of the earlier one, and all organizations have enough follow-up time. Overall repeat-use fraction is 2/40=5%. Conditional fractions are 12/40, 6/12, 3/6 and 2/3; their product equals 2/40 by cancellation. No independence assumption is needed for these nested observed fractions. Multiplying rates from different cohorts would require additional transportability assumptions. The six demonstrations and only three activations suggest investigating onboarding, access or fit. They do not prove onboarding caused the loss. Track refusal reasons and elapsed time: an organization waiting for approval is not the same as a completed rejection. Recent cohorts without a second cycle yet are not mature retention cohorts. In small samples, a single organization changes the percentage substantially. If recruitment and demonstrations cost 600 U, acquisition cost per activated organization is 600/3=200 U. Cost per repeated-use organization is 300 U, a different descriptive ratio. Neither denominator implies payment. With zero activations, report 600 U spent and an undefined finite acquisition ratio rather than zero cost.

sections.section: Three boundaries around the same job
sections.text: All options preserve evidence traceability, access control and customer payment approval. Their completion promises and operational owners must be explicit. Dimension Self-serve hosted tool Managed evidence service Internal deployment Offer Software assembles a draft; customer operates checks and exceptions Supplier operates assembly and first review; customer authorizes final use Customer runs the workflow inside its controlled environment Buyer / route Operations buyer; focused demo, documented trial and self-onboarding Operations buyer; scoped proposal through trusted introduction Operations sponsor plus IT owner; internal budget and deployment review Onboarding Customer maps fields and imports permitted records Supplier helps map records within a bounded engagement Customer integration, access policy, release and rollback process Required trust Hosted data handling, traceable outputs, export and support terms Same plus named human access, confidentiality and escalation ownership Local operator competence, controlled dependencies, patching and incident ownership Variable labor Customer verification; supplier support still exists Supplier verification and exceptions; customer final review persists Customer verification and operations; external support only if separately purchased Maintenance burden Supplier service changes; customer mapping changes Supplier process/staff training plus software changes Customer runtime, connectors, evaluation and upgrades Switching friction Mapping/export and user retraining Replacement of process knowledge and service handoffs Migration of integrations, policies and operational knowledge Supplier exposure Hosted/API price, policy, availability and bundling Those dependencies plus labor availability External model/package dependencies can remain even with local hosting Internal deployment does not automatically mean offline operation. A locally installed interface calling an external model still exports data. Draw the actual boundary. Likewise, a managed service is not a transfer of every liability: the final approval owner and unresolved-case escalation remain named. R21 describes packaging through feature and usage differences for customer groups. Our three responsibility boundaries go beyond pricing columns. A plan becomes misleading if it sells a managed outcome while budgeting only for software delivery.

sections.section: A worked comparison with both sides of the ledger
sections.text: Every number below is invented, in a common unit U. These are new B03 scenarios, not edits to B02’s baseline. Compare one organization with 100 eligible cases per month over six months. Assume matched quality, deadlines and authorized access have already passed feasibility checks. That premise must be tested before any real choice. Customer labor is valued at 30 U/hour. Current handling takes 8 minutes per case: 400 U/month. It is capacity value, not automatically avoidable payroll. All recurring customer minutes include verification, residual handling and allocated operations time; all one-time customer hours include setup and switching. No category overlaps. Input per organization Self-serve Managed Internal Monthly supplier fee 120 U 180 U 0 U Customer recurring minutes per case 4 2 3 Customer one-time onboarding hours 4 2 12 Customer recurring infrastructure cost 0 U 0 U 40 U/month Supplier variable monthly delivery cost 40 U 120 U Not a supplier revenue offer here Supplier one-time onboarding cost 60 U 90 U Not applicable Let H be months, n cases/month, b baseline minutes/case, t new minutes/case, w labor value/hour, f monthly fee, i monthly infrastructure cost and o onboarding hours. Customer modeled net capacity value is V=H[n(b−t)w/60−f−i]−ow. This subtracts fees and setup from valued capacity. It excludes unmodeled risk, financing and benefits unrelated to handling time. It is not a willingness-to-pay estimate. At H=6, self-serve gives 6(200−120)−120=360 U; managed gives 6(300−180)−60=660 U; internal gives 6(250−40)−360=900 U. Internal has the highest modeled value, but its feasibility depends on the actual IT owner and maintenance allowance. If that owner cannot support it, the ranking is irrelevant. For a permitted outsourced pilot with no internal operator, managed is the tentative choice, conditional on its effort estimates. Now examine the supplier. Monthly contribution before shared overhead and acquisition is 80 U for self-serve and 60 U for managed. Assign the same hypothetical acquisition cost of 200 U to each newly activated paying organization for this comparison. Six fully paid months leave 6×80−60−200=220 U for self-serve and 6×60−90−200=70 U for managed, before shared overhead. Managed creates more modeled customer value yet leaves less supplier contribution. Both sides must work. Continuous-month recovery of acquisition plus supplier onboarding is 260/80=3.25 months and 290/60≈4.83 months. With contribution collected at month end, recovery first occurs after months 4 and 5. These are conditional payback calculations, not lifetime-value forecasts. If service ends after three paid months, remainders are −20 and −110 U. No constant churn assumption rescues a cohort that has not been observed.

Suppose managed customer effort is actually 5 minutes/case because exceptions require customer rechecking. Its six-month value becomes 6(150−180)−60=−240 U. The managed recommendation fails even though the supplier fee and demo accuracy are unchanged. The next measurement should capture total customer effort and correct completion, not only supplier review time. Alternatively, an internal variant with an additional 6 hours/month of customer maintenance adds 180 U/month. Its modeled value falls from 900 to −180 U. This is incremental maintenance beyond the original table’s allowance, not the same hours counted twice. “Runs internally” is a location, not a maintenance budget. Manual onboarding can reveal repeated problems worth automating. It can also mask a different bespoke workflow for every customer. Keep a work log split into reusable setup, customer-specific setup, recurring operations and exceptions. Move toward self-serve when repeat customers can complete the workflow with documented setup and measured support effort. Keep a service boundary when valuable recurring human judgment remains necessary and its costs can be funded. Stop or narrow the offer when neither boundary satisfies the joint quality, customer-value and supplier-cost conditions.

sections.section: The supplier bundles your main feature
sections.text: Treat this as a hypothetical stress test, not news about a named supplier. Assume a customer’s existing platform adds equivalent extraction at zero incremental fee. First ask whether it also solves evidence mapping, authorization, exceptions and review. A free component may still require costly workflow work. Assign the bundle 5 customer minutes/case and 3 onboarding hours, with no additional infrastructure charge. Its six-month value is 6×150−90=810 U. Under those premises it beats the managed offer’s 660 U by 150 U. The bundle is not automatically inferior because it lacks our interface, nor automatically equivalent because its extraction score matches. For managed to tie that bundle while retaining 2 customer minutes/case, solve 6(300−f)−60≥810: f≤155 U/month. At 155, supplier six-month remainder is 6(155−120)−90−200=−80 U. The supplier needs f≥120+290/6≈168.33 U to recover these modeled costs within six months. There is no feasible price interval under these assumptions. Negotiating the price alone cannot repair this scenario. Reduce delivery/acquisition costs, prove additional customer value, choose a different segment, or decline the offer. Bundling may also reduce the supplier’s own compute bill; that is a separate scenario requiring evidence.

sections.section: Turn a moat claim into a test
sections.text: Claimed advantage Mechanism to test Evidence against it Workflow knowledge Faster correct onboarding across new organizations Every setup remains bespoke; partner handles it equally well Evaluation corpus Permitted representative cases detect failures competitors miss No reusable rights, stale cases or no outcome improvement Distribution relationship Repeat access to qualified buyers at acceptable effort Referrals depend on one person; channel costs erase contribution Integration and trust Useful reliable handoffs plus credible data/control practices Bundle already provides the same end-to-end outcome More customer data Authorized feedback improves a defined outcome for later customers Data cannot be reused or more data adds no measurable benefit These are original testable hypotheses, not an empirical taxonomy of winning businesses. More records do not by themselves establish a network effect; demonstrate how another participant improves value for existing participants under permissible reuse. Switching friction can delay departure without proving satisfaction. Offer usable exports, preserve evidence identifiers and test migration; voluntary renewal despite a credible alternative is more informative than retention caused by trapped records. No source inspected here establishes an actual moat for this service.

Prepare a short comparison when studying later; no learner response is required for production. Specify segment, user, buyer, approver, acquisition route and activation event for the invoice job. Identify one rival explanation for low activation. Recalculate the nested cohort fractions and both acquisition ratios. Explain the zero-activation and incomplete-follow-up cases. Rebuild the three customer-value results. State the feasibility condition that makes the highest numerical value unusable, then evaluate both labor shocks. Rebuild supplier contribution, six-month remainders and both payback conventions. Evaluate departure after three paid months. Calculate the bundled alternative and the managed customer’s fee ceiling versus the supplier’s cost floor. Decide whether price alone can fix the offer. Propose a bounded pilot and a defensibility test. Name trust boundaries, a stop rule, a counterexample to a data-moat claim and evidence that changes the recommended product boundary. B01 contributes problem/authority evidence; B02 contributes explicit units and cost scope; S06 preserves authority independently of sales promises; A05 preserves whole-task evaluation. C04 will turn these into a fuller decision memo, and C06 will examine supplier replacement. B03 teaches the comparison mechanism rather than completing those later assignments. Reference card: name one job and segment → map buyer and approval roles → define acquisition/activation/repeat events → assign responsibility and labor → compare customer and supplier economics → test a stronger alternative → name the observation that changes the choice.
