These are application inputs, not blockers to this lesson. No learner mastery is inferred.
1.0 — 2026-11-13. Distribution transitions, three responsibility boundaries, two-sided economics, supplier-bundling counterexample and six exercises.

Field Value ID / revision / date B03 answers · 1.0 · 2026-11-13 Prerequisites B03 core pack, B01 and B02 Capability developed Audit distribution denominators, compare responsibility boundaries and reject an economically inconsistent offer Source-check status Uses the core’s verified R22/R21/R19 passages; proposals and numbers below are original Experiment status Embedded exact-arithmetic checks executed; no customer, acquisition or supplier experiment Assessment convention Criteria assess a future answer; no learner response or mastery is assumed

Hint: A customer is an organization with a workflow, not every person who likes the demonstration. Worked answer: Target small purchasing teams with repeated invoice/delivery matching, a restricted format set and authority for a bounded pilot. Clerk: operator. Operations manager: budget owner. Data/security owner: access approver. Payment reviewer: final business decision owner. A bookkeeping practitioner’s introduction to the buyer is a proposed route, contingent on permission and incentive; no introduction has happened. Activation is one permitted real workflow completed to the agreed supported-evidence/deadline contract. Logging in, uploading an unusable document and viewing a canned demonstration are not equivalent. A low activation fraction could reflect difficult setup, but could also reflect absent data approval, a weak problem, immature follow-up or the wrong audience. Record the reason and time in state before choosing a repair. Assessment: Names the distinct roles, an observable event and a rival explanation. Does not treat operator enthusiasm as purchase authority.

Hint: Write each transition as later-set count divided by earlier-set count. Worked answer: Qualification is 12/40=30%; demo agreement is 6/12=50%; activation is 3/6=50%; second-cycle completion is 2/3≈66.67%. Their product is 5%, equal to 2/40. Nested sets explain this identity without statistical independence. This is descriptive repeat use within this constructed cohort, not a paid-retention estimate or a forecast. The 600 U spend yields 200 U per activated organization and 300 U per repeated-use organization. Reporting the latter as “cost per acquired paying customer” would be unsupported. With zero activations the ratio has no finite value; keep the spend and zero count visible. Organizations that have not reached their next eligible cycle require pending/censored status and cohort-age tracking, not automatic classification as churned. A paid acquisition metric needs actual contracts/payments and consistently attributed sales costs. Assessment: Correctly changes denominators, preserves set nesting and refuses to turn missing time or payment evidence into observed behavior.

Hint: Count customer work and supplier work on different ledgers. Fees are a customer outflow and supplier inflow, not a new combined resource cost. Worked answer: The baseline is 100×8/60×30=400 U/month. Self-serve releases 200 U/month before its fee; net is 6×(200−120)−4×30=360 U. Managed releases 300 U/month; net is 6×(300−180)−2×30=660 U. Internal releases 250 U/month; net is 6×(250−40)−12×30=900 U. These are valued-capacity comparisons, not guaranteed cash savings or prices customers accept. Internal ranks first only if it meets quality/access requirements and the organization can operate it within the stated allowance. An unavailable IT owner invalidates that option regardless of its arithmetic. Managed at 5 customer minutes gives 6×(150−180)−60=−240 U. Internal with six additional maintenance hours/month gives 900−6×6×30=−180 U. Neither cost shock authorizes relaxing quality or access controls to restore a positive number. A counterexample to “managed always saves more customer time” is a service whose ambiguous exception notes force the customer to repeat the original matching. Measure total effort from intake to verified completion, including rework. If customer labor is fixed payroll, freed time needs a useful next use before its assigned value becomes an actual benefit. Assessment: Obtains all five results, states units and does not double-count baseline maintenance in the incremental shock.

Hint: Supplier onboarding is distinct from customer onboarding. Include both where appropriate, but never on the same party’s ledger unless that party actually bears both. Worked answer: Self-serve contribution is 120−40=80 U/month; managed is 180−120=60. After six paid months, self-serve leaves 480−60−200=220 U and managed leaves 360−90−200=70 U. This excludes shared overhead and all unlisted costs; the remainders do not prove company profitability. Acquisition plus onboarding is 260 versus 290 U. Continuous recovery times are 3.25 and 29/6≈4.83 months. With payments/contribution realized at month end, the earliest sufficient receipts are in months 4 and 5. Three paid months yield −20 and −110 U. The model assumes steady volume, full collection, unchanged variable costs and no extra cancellation costs. Billing in advance, late payments or refunds changes cash timing. Annualized revenue does not supply the missing cash automatically. The 200 U acquisition assumption is applied equally to isolate delivery differences; real channels could have very different costs. The earlier cohort contains activation counts but no payments, so this comparison explicitly assumes each modeled acquired organization pays. It does not claim that the cohort demonstrated that assumption. Assessment: Distinguishes contribution, recovery, profitability and collection; names at least one empirically unknown premise.

Hint: Derive the customer’s maximum fee and supplier’s minimum fee separately before looking for overlap. Worked answer: The hypothetical bundle releases 150 U/month and costs 90 U to onboard, yielding 810 U over six months. Managed’s value at fee f is 6(300−f)−60=1,740−6f. To match 810 requires f≤155. Its supplier remainder is 6(f−120)−290; nonnegative remainder requires f≥505/3≈168.33. Since 155<168.33, there is no fee satisfying both constraints. At f=155 the supplier loses 80 U on this limited ledger. At the supplier floor the customer gets 730 U, which is 80 U less than the bundle. Price alone cannot resolve the conflict. At f=155, supplier variable monthly delivery cost must fall to at most (930−290)/6=320/3≈106.67 U for six-month recovery. That is a conditional cost target, not permission to remove necessary review or a prediction of automation savings. Possible next evidence: the bundle may fail the required provenance/authorization contract; managed may create measurable value beyond handling time; reusable onboarding may reduce costs. Each possibility changes a premise and must be measured. If the bundle matches the whole job and the cost target cannot be met, decline or change the segment. The free component’s existence is a scenario assumption, not a current supplier announcement. Assessment: Shows both inequalities and rejects a purely rhetorical moat defense. Accepts a different choice only with explicit changed assumptions.

sections.section: 6. A bounded pilot and a moat test
sections.text: Hint: The pilot should resolve a decision, not collect favorable anecdotes indefinitely. Worked analysis: Propose one four-week learning pilot with two authorized organizations from the narrow segment, followed by an agreed second workflow cycle where timing permits. This small scope is a practical learning budget, not statistical sufficiency. No outreach is executed. Freeze eligibility, source revisions, case identities, output rubric, deadlines and approval roles. Compare managed and existing-process results on matched permitted cases. Record total active minutes by role, errors, unresolved cases, rework, fees, non-overlapping supplier labor and setup time. Preserve case-level discrepancies rather than presenting only the average. Start in a non-effecting evaluation mode: outputs do not approve or dispatch payment. Human supplier access must be expressly scoped; an internal interface must not hide external calls. Stop processing on an unauthorized disclosure/effect, unresolved authority issue or inability to preserve required evidence. Pause expansion if recurring labor exceeds the budget or quality falls below the agreed contract. A negative value result can justify changing the offer rather than expanding the pilot until a favorable average appears. For the workflow-knowledge advantage, ask whether setup on the second organization reuses a documented mapping procedure and lowers effort without weaker quality. A new organization with unrelated formats may falsify repeatability. For a data advantage, ask whether rights permit reuse and whether that permitted corpus improves held-out whole-task outcomes relative to a credible alternative. More records with no reusable rights are not a reusable data advantage. No measured effect means the improvement claim stays unknown. Choose self-serve if ordinary customers can operate the same workflow reliably with bounded support. Choose internal if access restrictions rule out external processing and a funded owner can maintain it. Keep managed if recurring operator expertise produces valuable outcomes at sustainable cost. If a bundle matches the whole task and both parties’ economics cannot be satisfied, stop or redefine the offer. A paid pilot alone does not establish repeated demand, scale or a moat. Assessment: Contains a bounded decision, authority limits, effort/quality measures, stop rule, rival explanation and observable conditions for changing boundaries. Does not invent trial results.

The following Python standard-library script was executed during production. It verifies the constructed ledger and decision boundaries, not real business behavior. Fractions avoid floating-point ambiguity at equality. Grid checks complement exact boundaries rather than proving behavior outside this model. from fractions import Fraction as Q from math import ceil H, n, b, w = 6, 100, 8, 30 def value(t, fee, infra, onboarding): return H * (Q(n * (b-t) * w, 60) - fee - infra) - onboarding*w def remainder(fee, variable, onboarding, months=6): return months*(fee-variable)-onboarding-200 counts = [40, 12, 6, 3, 2] product = Q(1) for before, after in zip(counts, counts[1:]): assert 0 <= after <= before product *= Q(after, before) assert product == Q(2, 40) == Q(1, 20) assert Q(600, 3) == 200 and Q(600, 2) == 300 def per_activation(spend, count): return Q(spend, count) if count else None assert per_activation(600, 0) is None assert [value(4,120,0,4), value(2,180,0,2), value(3,0,40,12)] == [360,660,900] assert value(5,180,0,2) == -240 assert value(3,0,40+6*w,12) == -180 assert remainder(120,40,60) == 220 assert remainder(180,120,90) == 70 assert remainder(120,40,60,3) == -20 assert remainder(180,120,90,3) == -110 assert Q(260,80) == Q(13,4) assert Q(290,60) == Q(29,6) assert [ceil(Q(260,80)), ceil(Q(290,60))] == [4,5] bundle = value(5,0,0,3) ceiling, floor = Q(155), Q(505,3) assert bundle == 810 assert value(2,ceiling,0,2) == bundle assert remainder(floor,120,90) == 0 assert ceiling < floor assert remainder(ceiling,120,90) == -80 assert value(2,floor,0,2) == 730 assert remainder(155,Q(320,3),90) == 0 # Exact equality and values immediately on both sides. for delta in [Q(-1,100), Q(0), Q(1,100)]: assert (value(2,ceiling+delta,0,2) >= bundle) == (delta <= 0) assert (remainder(floor+delta,120,90) >= 0) == (delta >= 0) # 2,401 fee points from 0 through 240 U at 0.1-U spacing. for k in range(2401): fee = Q(k,10) customer_ok = value(2,fee,0,2) >= bundle supplier_ok = remainder(fee,120,90) >= 0 assert customer_ok == (fee <= ceiling) assert supplier_ok == (fee >= floor) assert not (customer_ok and supplier_ok) # 25 maintenance increments, 0..12 h/month at half-hour spacing. for k in range(25): hours = Q(k,2) assert value(3,0,40+hours*w,12) == 900-180*hours print('PASS: cohort, ledgers, labor shocks, payback, exact thresholds, 2401 fee points, 25 maintenance points') Limitations: no statistical confidence interval, cash-flow simulation, empirical retention curve, supplier equivalence experiment or security verification was performed. Those require actual data and an implemented system. Source provenance remains in the core’s evidence ledger.
1.0 — 2026-11-13. Six mapped solutions, conditional pilot and executed arithmetic checks.

Field Value ID / revision / date C01 · 1.0 · 2026-11-07 Type Synthesis decision memo Prerequisites F01 remembered state and invariants; S02 durable evidence; S03 atomic decisions; S04 replicated decisions Capability developed Place duplicate prevention at the boundary that controls the promised effect, and revise a retry policy when that boundary changes Source-check status R10 author-copy pp. 2, 6–7 and R07 §8 p. 13 inspected; supporting passages and limits below Experiment status Executed finite state and crash-cut checks; no real payment, network, database or consensus deployment tested Companion Worked analysis and executable checks

For the fictional invoice workflow, put approval uniqueness, immutable evidence references and the successful request receipt in one durable application transition. If approval also initiates an external payment, commit a payment intent in that transition and require the payment authority to enforce a stable payment identity. A queue or reliable transport may reduce repeated work, but it cannot alone establish that one business operation had one effect. The baseline decision assumes a hypothetical provider with an explicit atomic identity contract. If that provider cannot prevent repeated effects or authoritatively resolve an uncertain attempt, change the policy: pause an ambiguous payment for reconciliation instead of automatically submitting it again. This sacrifices automatic progress to protect the at-most-once target. It does not turn uncertainty into proof of failure. This memo extends the earlier D17 case. It is a design exercise, not guidance for a named payment product. Approval and payment are distinct outcomes. We promise at most one accepted proposal per (document, approval epoch) and at most one provider payment per authorized payment intent. We do not promise at most one payment across every future correction of an invoice: that broader business rule would need a durable obligation identity and additional guards across epochs.

sections.section: Fix the assumptions and identity before choosing machinery
sections.text: An approval request contains tenant, operation key k, document D17, expected epoch 7, revision 2, actor, evidence reference and payment details. Treat the full canonical tuple as its payload; a hash alone is not the equality definition. Tenant namespaces prevent unrelated customers’ keys from colliding. Authentication and authorization are required before disclosing receipts or creating effects; S06 will develop that boundary. The caller preserves k across retries of the same intent. A new key is a new request identity, but does not bypass the occupied approval slot. Reusing k with a different payload is rejected. A different payment amount or destination requires a new authorized business decision, not silent reinterpretation of an old key. The application authority provides a serialized conditional transition, durable across the modeled process restart and failover. It retains receipts, epoch history and unsent intents. Every mutation path obeys the same guard. A successful decision includes both its immutable evidence reference and receipt. Storage media loss, malicious replicas and broken authorization are outside the finite model; they remain deployment obligations. The hypothetical provider atomically binds payment identity p to the exact payment payload, records the effect and its outcome, returns the same result on identical retries, and rejects conflicting reuse. This contract covers concurrent attempts and survives its modeled restart. Its identity records remain valid throughout the application’s retry horizon. These are strong premises to verify, not features assumed of every provider. A timeout means the caller lacks a result. It does not identify which side of a durable transition the system reached. Progress additionally needs eventual communication, a functioning authority and provider, and a dispatcher that continues trying. At-most-once effects alone can be achieved by doing nothing; that is not useful completion.

sections.section: The failure that chooses the responsibility boundary
sections.text: All events below are constructed. Suppose a worker records no durable payment identity and calls a provider that treats each request as a new payment. Step Application / client Provider What survives? 1 Worker sends payment for D17 Receives request No local completed receipt 2 Waits for reply Executes payment One external effect 3 Reply is lost; worker crashes Effect remains Application still lacks outcome 4 Replacement retries the payment Executes new request Two external effects 5 Replacement saves “paid” One local receipt describes two payments Moving the local marker before the call merely changes the failure: crash after marking but before sending leaves “paid” with zero payments. Holding a database lock during the call does not make the provider’s effect part of the database commit. Rolling back that transaction cannot undo an already executed payment. R10 explains why application retries can create distinct network messages for the same operation, and why a meaningful storage acknowledgement must come from the layer that can establish storage completion. R07 §8 explicitly adds client request identities and remembered responses to its consensus discussion. These support the placement argument; the payment protocol here is our own synthesis under the declared contract.

sections.section: Compare alternatives under the same objective
sections.text: The objective is to preserve both at-most-once invariants while allowing eventual completion when the stated dependencies recover. Assume multiple application workers and lost replies for every option. Option Useful contribution Missing guarantee or cost Disable repeated UI clicks Reduces accidental concurrent submissions Does not cover restart, retries or another client Worker-local set of seen keys Fast filtering within one process Another worker or a crash loses the shared history Transport or queue duplicate filtering Can reduce redundant delivery A new message can represent the same business operation; completion boundary may end before the provider effect Atomic application receipt plus guarded approval Prevents duplicate approval, preserves evidence and resolves its lost reply Does not atomically control an independent provider Durable intent plus provider-enforced payment identity Allows repeated delivery while preventing repeated provider effects under the contract Requires provider cooperation, retained identities, monitoring and reconciliation Stop after an uncertain attempt Avoids blindly creating a second attempt Can leave an operation incomplete indefinitely; delayed first attempts still need resolution Choose the fifth option for the baseline and retain the fourth as its local foundation. Lower-layer filtering remains an optimization worth measuring, not the authoritative source of business truth. Consensus protects an ordered state transition against its modeled failures; it does not make an incorrect transition correct or extend a transaction into an arbitrary external service.

The application transition first checks a previously accepted receipt for (tenant,k). If the canonical payload matches, it returns the historical receipt; if not, it rejects reuse. A historical receipt says what happened then, not that the approval is still current after reopening. For a new key, the transition checks authority, expected epoch, expected revision and an empty owner. On success it atomically writes the owner, evidence reference, receipt and one pending payment intent. Assign p from the accepted intent’s durable unique identity, not from a dispatcher attempt number. It records a status such as approved/payment_pending, never paid merely because the intent exists. Stale or occupied requests cannot create intents. A dispatcher reads pending intents and calls the provider with the same p and payload on every attempt. It persists the returned authoritative result before marking the intent complete. Crash before the call leaves pending work; crash after the effect but before recording its result causes a repeat call with p. Under the provider contract, that repeat returns the prior result without another effect. Multiple dispatchers need not create duplicate effects if they use the same p and the provider enforces the contract atomically; leases can still reduce wasted calls. The pending-intent record is often called an outbox. The name supplies no guarantee: its crucial property here is commitment with the accepted decision, followed by retryable dispatch. Sending first and creating the intent afterward restores the original crash gap. The local invariant proof reuses F01’s state reasoning. Initially each epoch is empty. The only accepting transition consumes that epoch’s empty slot and creates exactly one receipt and intent together. A replay creates neither; a competing fresh key sees an occupied slot. A reopen creates a fresh epoch without deleting history. Thus every epoch has at most one acceptance. S02 supplies durable recovery requirements; S03 supplies the atomic guard; S04 supplies the replicated-state boundary when deployed that way. The external proof is conditional: every dispatch of one intent uses one p, and the provider’s only effect-producing transition creates p’s first record atomically. Repeated p cannot produce another effect. This proves at most one effect per p, not eventual success, and not uniqueness across independently created intents for the same real-world obligation. Reopening does not cancel a dispatched payment. For this case an accepted intent remains authorized after reopening; a later correction creates a separately authorized adjustment. If the business requires reopening to revoke a pending payment, it needs an explicit dispatch/cancellation protocol with provider support. A new epoch alone cannot retract a message already in flight.

sections.section: Change one constraint: the provider has no identity contract
sections.text: Keep the same application authority and business objective, but replace the provider with one that has neither deduplicated payment identities nor an authoritative operation-status query. Now two histories look identical locally: H0: the send never reached the provider; no payment happened. H1: the provider paid, but its reply never reached the application. Both leave the same durable intent and missing outcome. Retrying can complete H0 but duplicate H1. Never retrying protects H1 from a second attempt but may leave H0 unpaid. A local timestamp, a new leader, a longer timeout or more copies of the intent cannot distinguish these histories. Revise the decision to record outcome_unknown, prevent automatic resubmission and reconcile using authoritative external evidence. Human review is a workflow for obtaining evidence, not proof by itself. Even a “not found” query would need semantics excluding a delayed original execution before a fresh attempt is safe. If the provider cannot supply such evidence or cancellation/fencing, retain the unresolved state, or change providers or the business guarantee. Do not label an unresolved payment failed and issue a fresh key.

Write a one-page decision memo before reading the companion. Use exactly the baseline assumptions above, then the changed provider constraint. Draw a lost-reply timeline and state separately what the client knows, what the application committed and what the provider did. State the two at-most-once invariants, payload-binding rule and evidence-retention requirement. Explain the different roles of k, p and epoch. Choose among the options and identify the atomic boundary. Give a concrete counterexample to one inadequate fix. Trace crashes before local commit, after commit/before dispatch, after provider execution/before its reply, and after reply/before local completion. Include two competing keys and a retry after reopening. Revise the decision under the changed constraint. State what evidence would permit resumption and which progress claim must be withdrawn. For application transfer, ask whether two independently approved documents can represent the same payable obligation. If yes, the invariant needs a domain-specific obligation identity beyond this exercise’s scope. Do not assume content equality alone decides that business question.

Basis Verified locator Role and boundary R10, Saltzer, Reed and Clark, 1984 Author copy, p. 2 principle; p. 6 Duplicate message suppression; p. 7 Transaction management Placement and acknowledgement argument; no historical performance figure adopted R07, Ongaro and Ousterhout, extended 2014 paper Primary PDF, §8 p. 13 Retried commands, remembered responses and authoritative reads; not an external payment guarantee F01, S02, S03, S04 Existing packs, especially F01 §7 exercise 6, S03 “Add the delayed request,” S04 retry contract Prior continuity, not newly measured deployment evidence This memo and companion Original histories, conditional proof and finite checks Hypothetical provider contract; no current product guarantee asserted Reference card: name the effect → define identity and payload → locate the authority → commit decision, evidence and receipt together → preserve identity across retry → resolve unknown outcomes at the effect boundary. Retention must cover delayed delivery and restoration, not just the ordinary client timeout. Expiring a provider’s identity while an old intent can still be sent invalidates the proof. Open questions are actual provider semantics, retention, safe cancellation, access control, evidence availability, failover durability and obligation identity. They are deployment inputs, not blockers to this synthesis. Next S06 develops authority, isolation and reliability objectives.
1.0 — 2026-11-07. Decision memo, changed-provider constraint, five assessment tasks and separate executed finite checks. No learner answers or mastery inferred.

Field Value ID / title C01 answers · Duplicate-effect responsibility Revision / date 1.0 · 2026-11-07 Prerequisites F01, S02–S04; C01 memo Capability developed Evaluate an invariant across a transaction boundary and revise an uncertain-outcome policy Source-check status R10 pp. 2, 6–7 and R07 §8 p. 13; exact links in the memo Experiment status Executed standard-library Python finite checks below; atomic transitions assumed, not deployment-tested This is a reference analysis for later self-assessment. It does not report your answers or mastery. A different design can be defensible if it preserves the stated invariants and openly changes any progress promise.

Missing knowledge and missing effects are different facts. Put each actor in its own column. Count accepted decisions and provider effects separately. Identify what equality means at each layer. Ask what happens between the effect and the durable record used to suppress its retry. On restart, retain only what the model says was committed. Replay the original identity, not a fresh attempt identity. Find two histories with identical local evidence and different provider outcomes. A local policy sees the same input in both.

A valid timeline is: application commits approval and pending intent p; dispatcher sends p; provider atomically executes and remembers p; reply disappears; dispatcher restarts with p pending. The application knows the approval committed but does not know whether the provider completed. The provider knows its own result. The client may know neither if its initial approval reply also disappeared. An approval retry with k resolves the application decision. A provider retry with p resolves the payment under the baseline contract. These are different queries. Returning a historical approved/payment_pending receipt must not be presented as a fresh assertion that payment is still pending or that the approval is still current. Use a separate authorized status read for current lifecycle information. The inadequate design sends without provider identity, then saves a local marker. A crash after the effect creates the possibility of two payments even though only one local receipt eventually exists. In the alternative marker-first design, a crash before send creates zero payments while the application believes it finished. Assessment: Name both durable states and the lost observation. “The timeout means payment failed” is incorrect under the model.

Write acceptances(doc,epoch) <= 1 and effects(p) <= 1. These count different events. The first is enforced by the application’s atomic empty-slot transition. The second is enforced by the provider’s atomic first-use transition. The application contributes by mapping every dispatch of one intent to the same p. k identifies the caller’s intended approval request, including a canonical payload. p identifies the external payment intent created by a successful approval. Epoch distinguishes successive business rounds even when the published revision remains unchanged. Neither leadership term nor retry attempt count is a replacement for epoch. Tenant scope and authenticated receipt access are necessary operational boundaries. Evidence references identify the revision and exact source used by the accepted decision. Keep the source bytes retrievable; retaining a digest without the bytes cannot reconstruct the document. S02’s immutable revisions and S03’s retained receipts supply this continuity. Replaying an accepted k after reopen returns historical information; a fresh key carrying the old epoch is rejected. Receipt/provider-identity retention must include delayed deliveries and recovery from older application state. An arbitrary cache TTL is not sufficient. If provider history expires while a dispatcher can replay p, the provider may treat p as new. Preserve a tombstone or establish that old attempts cannot recur before removing the distinguishing information. The exact mechanism depends on provider support. Assessment: State both invariants, payload binding and retention scope. A key alone does not prevent two different keys from representing the same real-world obligation.

The baseline chooses a guarded, durable application decision plus pending intent and provider-enforced p. The application must atomically preserve owner, receipt, evidence and intent. If intent creation were separate, a crash after approval could leave no dispatchable payment; creating the intent first could pay for a decision that never committed. Every external dispatch uses the saved payload and p. Provider result recording can occur later because replaying p is safe under the provider contract. That asymmetry is the reason the design can cross the boundary without pretending both databases share one transaction. A local set improves performance but lacks shared durable state. A global lock without atomic durable effect control still leaves the external crash gap. More application replicas preserve intent information but cannot infer an unobserved provider result. A queue may repeatedly deliver the same intent safely only when the effect authority supplies the corresponding identity guarantee. Assessment: Identify the exact atomic writes and the external assumption. Do not claim that an outbox, consensus or a unique database row alone gives exactly-once payment.

Cut Durable state after restart Safe baseline continuation Before local commit No accepted receipt or intent Retry k; it may create the decision once After local commit, before dispatch Approval, receipt and pending p Dispatch p After provider effect, before reply Pending p locally; provider remembers effect Repeat p; receive existing result After reply, before local completion Same durable uncertainty as preceding row Repeat p or use an authoritative status operation After local completion Recorded result and completed intent Return saved result; no new dispatch needed For competing keys A and B in epoch 7, whichever valid transition consumes the empty slot first wins. The other cannot create another intent. A repeated delivery of the winner returns its original receipt. This applies to all three distinct orders of A,A,B checked below. The model does not estimate how often any order occurs. After reopen to epoch 8, replaying the winner of epoch 7 is historical retrieval, not a new consumption of epoch 8. A new key with epoch 7 is stale. A properly authorized new request for epoch 8 can succeed; it creates a distinct intent. If that could double-pay one obligation, a cross-epoch obligation rule is missing from the requirements. The memo deliberately does not equate an approval round with an economic obligation. Assessment: Preserve durable state consistently and never invent a new payment identity after a lost reply. Explain why reopen does not undo an already dispatched external effect.

With neither deduplication nor authoritative status, H0 (no effect) and H1 (effect, lost reply) leave the same local observation. A deterministic automatic decision must act the same way in both. Retrying may complete H0 but duplicate H1. Stopping avoids a new attempt but leaves H0 incomplete. Randomizing the decision does not establish a universal guarantee either. Record outcome_unknown, block automatic resubmission and obtain authoritative reconciliation evidence. A person seeing an empty dashboard is not enough if an old request may still execute. Safe resumption would require, for example, provider confirmation that the original attempt was definitively rejected/cancelled and cannot later execute, or a newly negotiated identity contract that actually covers the old attempt. Otherwise the state remains unresolved. The revised policy withdraws automatic eventual completion while retaining a conservative submission policy. It does not claim universal at-most-once behavior from a provider whose own semantics are unknown. If the business demands both automatic progress and no duplicate effects, this provider contract fails the requirements; change the integration or the requirement explicitly. Assessment: Give the indistinguishable histories and name the surrendered progress claim. “Retry with a new key,” “wait longer,” and “add consensus” do not supply the missing external evidence.

The code models indivisible application/provider transitions and complete restoration of committed state using copies. It does not test actual transaction isolation, flush behavior, network delivery, provider retention or Raft. Crash cuts are boundaries in the model, not injected process failures. The invariant argument explains arbitrary retries under the assumptions; the finite cases catch inconsistent examples and expose broken alternatives. from copy import deepcopy from itertools import permutations class Authority: def __init__(self): self.epoch, self.rev = 7, 2 self.owners, self.receipts, self.intents = {}, {}, {} def approve(self, key, epoch=7, rev=2, amount=100): payload = ('tenant', 'D17', epoch, rev, 'reviewer', 'evidence-2', amount) if key in self.receipts: old, result = self.receipts[key] return result if old == payload else 'key-conflict' if (epoch, rev) != (self.epoch, self.rev): return 'stale' if epoch in self.owners: return 'occupied' # One indivisible durable transition is ASSUMED here. p = ('tenant', 'D17', epoch) result = ('approved/payment_pending', p) self.owners[epoch] = key self.receipts[key] = (payload, result) self.intents[p] = {'amount': amount, 'done': False} return result def reopen(self): self.epoch += 1 class Provider: def __init__(self): self.records, self.effects = {}, [] def pay(self, p, amount): # Assumed atomic provider contract, not its implementation. if p in self.records: old, result = self.records[p] if old != amount: return 'payload-conflict' return result result = ('paid', len(self.effects) + 1) self.effects.append((p, amount)) self.records[p] = (amount, result) return result # All orders of two deliveries of A and one competing B. orders = sorted(set(permutations(('A', 'A', 'B')))) for order in orders: a = Authority() for key in order: a.approve(key) assert len(a.owners) == len(a.receipts) == len(a.intents) == 1 winner = a.owners[7] saved = a.approve(winner) assert a.approve(winner, amount=101) == 'key-conflict' a.reopen() a = deepcopy(a) # restoration assumes complete durable state assert a.approve(winner) == saved # historical, not a new approval assert a.approve('old-new-key') == 'stale' assert a.approve('C', epoch=8)[0] == 'approved/payment_pending' assert len(a.owners) == len(a.intents) == 2 # Cut points: 0 before application commit; 1 before dispatch; # 2 after provider effect before reply; 3 after reply before local done; # 4 after local done. Restart preserves committed state only. for cut in range(5): a, provider = Authority(), Provider() p = ('tenant', 'D17', 7) if cut >= 1: a.approve('A') if cut >= 2: provider.pay(p, 100) if cut >= 4: a.intents[p]['done'] = True a, provider = deepcopy(a), deepcopy(provider) a.approve('A') if not a.intents[p]['done']: assert provider.pay(p, 100)[0] == 'paid' a.intents[p]['done'] = True # Additional concurrent/repeated deliveries, serialized by contract. for _ in range(3): assert provider.pay(p, 100)[0] == 'paid' assert len(provider.effects) == 1 and a.intents[p]['done'] assert provider.pay(p, 101) == 'payload-conflict' assert len(provider.effects) == 1 # Counterexamples: effect-first marker, marker-first effect, expiry. effects, marker = 1, False # crash after external effect if not marker: effects += 1 assert effects == 2 marker, effects = True, 0 # crash before send; marker prevents retry assert marker and effects == 0 provider = Provider() provider.pay('p', 100) provider.records.clear() # identity expiry without ending replay horizon provider.pay('p', 100) assert len(provider.effects) == 2 # Same local observation, different external outcomes, no identity support. observations = [('pending', 'no_reply'), ('pending', 'no_reply')] assert observations[0] == observations[1] for initial_effects in (0, 1): retry_effects = initial_effects + 1 if initial_effects == 1: assert retry_effects == 2 else: assert initial_effects == 0 # no retry leaves H0 incomplete print('PASS: 3 competing-delivery orders; payload binding, stale epoch,') print('historical replay and reopen; 5 crash cuts; provider retries;') print('marker-order and identity-expiry counterexamples; ambiguous histories.') Observed output, 2026-11-07: PASS: 3 competing-delivery orders; payload binding, stale epoch, historical replay and reopen; 5 crash cuts; provider retries; marker-order and identity-expiry counterexamples; ambiguous histories. No real provider was called. Deployment checks still need provider contract review, controlled failure injection, restore tests, retention verification, unauthorized-path tests and obligation-identity decisions. Those are application needs, not evidence of learner mastery.
1.0 — 2026-11-07. Five worked analyses, criteria, hints and executed finite checks corresponding to C01 revision 1.0.

title: Does better model performance improve the customer outcome?

sections.section: Does better model performance improve the customer outcome?
sections.text: Field Value ID / revision / date C02 · 1.0 · 2026-11-11 Title Does better model performance improve the customer outcome? Prerequisites F02/F03, A01/A03/A05, B01 Capability developed Choose an evaluation and a conditional investment decision across component, workflow and customer metrics Source-check status R03 experiment-design sections and R19 customer-interview transcript passages rechecked Experiment status Original hypothetical ledger and executed arithmetic/set checks; no customer study or model benchmark Companion Worked analysis and checks

Keep the current process available and advance the targeted evidence-assistance option A to the next controlled evaluation, rather than choosing the higher-scoring model option B on component accuracy alone. This recommendation is conditional on the constructed assumptions below. It is a decision about what to investigate, not authorization to deploy or evidence that a customer will buy. The fictional purchasing team wants cases correctly resolved with exact evidence before its approval cutoff. The service may prepare drafts, retrieve permitted records and flag exceptions. Human approval remains required for consequential actions. A05’s authority boundary is unchanged. A03 supplies the definition of supporting evidence; A01 supplies the information available at decision time. B01 reminds us that matching may not be the customer’s binding constraint at all. We compare three credible alternatives on the same 100 eligible invoice cases, including every revision and retry within its original case: C: current manual evidence assembly and review. A: fixed evidence workflow with a targeted alternate-extraction branch and human review. B: a model upgrade within the same approval boundary, with additional retrieval/validation work. These names are local to this memo. They are not F03’s pipelines or A05’s W/M/L outcomes. No earlier hypothetical counts are reused as measurements.

sections.section: Separate four claims before comparing them
sections.text: Level Metric and population What it can establish What remains open Component Correct field output on 100 fixed, sufficient-evidence inputs Performance with that supplied context Retrieval, timing, review and customer usefulness Whole task Correct, evidenced disposition by deadline / all 100 eligible cases Contract completion in the evaluated workflow Causal effect on staff behavior and adoption User value Active work, elapsed resolution time, rework and error consequences Whether intended users gain on outcomes they value Budget authority and willingness to change Commercial commitment Authorized trial, repeated use, renewal under explicit terms Behavior toward the particular offer General market demand or profitability A resolvable citation is not necessarily supportive, current or applicable. A reviewer clicking accept is not independently verified correctness. A shorter model response is not a shorter case-resolution time. Log these as distinct variables instead of allowing one convenient event to stand for all four claims. R03 recommends specifying falsifiable hypotheses, success and guardrail metrics, and the experimental unit before interpreting results. R19 recommends reconstructing concrete recent problems and existing alternatives rather than relying on hypothetical enthusiasm. These are practitioner sources guiding the design; neither supplies empirical values for this memo.

sections.section: A common ledger with deliberately invented numbers
sections.text: The initial deadline is one business day from intake, inclusive. For this fixture all cases have an adjudicable expected disposition. Correct means that the final disposition and required evidence satisfy the frozen rubric; it does not mean a payment occurred. Incorrect results and unresolved cases are separate, exhaustive categories. Unauthorized effects are assumed absent under all options, but that assumption requires implementation testing. Assigned quantity across 100 common cases C A B Correct component outputs with sufficient evidence supplied Not applicable 90 96 Correct final dispositions, regardless of lateness 90 92 96 Of those correct dispositions, late at one day 4 4 12 Correct on-time dispositions 86 88 84 Incorrect final dispositions 2 2 1 Unresolved cases 8 6 3 Active staff minutes, including unsuccessful cases 800 400 300 Resource charge in invented units 0 100 200 Component and final correctness are different experiments; a reviewer or fallback can repair a component error, so A’s final correct count may exceed its component count. The component table does not expose the full causal pathway. To investigate the difference, retain intermediate retrieval/context/claim/review records rather than multiplying unrelated aggregate scores. B improves the assigned component score from 90% to 96% and final correctness from 92% to 96%, yet produces four fewer timely correct outcomes. Its 84/100 result is worse than A’s 88/100 for the chosen primary outcome. Correct-but-late work is valuable in some settings, but the initial contract does not count it as timely success. We also report eventual correctness so the deadline metric does not conceal it. For the paired A/B comparison, 76 cases succeed under both, 12 only under A, 8 only under B and 4 under neither. The net change B−A is (8−12)/100=−4 percentage points. Eight improvements coexist with twelve regressions. Inspect their mechanisms and severity before summarizing them as a net number. These are constructed paired outcomes, not a statistical significance test. Assign an active-work value of 0.5 units per minute. Total resource-plus-labor-value charges are C=400, A=300 and B=350. At the one-day deadline, charge per timely correct outcome is respectively 400/86≈4.65, 300/88≈3.41 and 350/84≈4.17. Include failed and late work in each numerator. Released staff time is capacity value, not necessarily cash savings; wages may remain unchanged and the freed time may have no useful alternative use. Service fees, onboarding and error damages are not included. The initial decision rule is: require at least 88 timely correct cases, no more than two incorrect dispositions, no unauthorized effects and a total modeled charge no greater than 360; among feasible options maximize timely correct cases, breaking ties by lower charge. These thresholds are explicit teaching choices, not established customer requirements. A alone satisfies the assigned counts and budget. C fails the outcome and budget gates; B fails the timely-outcome gate despite lower staff effort and fewer errors.

sections.section: Change one constraint, then revise the choice
sections.text: Now the hypothetical customer changes only the resolution deadline to two business days. Keep all cases, evidence, outputs, work and costs fixed. Of the correct cases late at one day, two C cases, two A cases and ten B cases finish by day two. The remaining correct cases are still late. Recomputed result C A B Correct on time at two days 88 90 94 Total modeled charge, unchanged 400 300 350 Charge per timely correct result 4.55 3.33 3.72 Feasible under unchanged remaining gates? No: charge Yes Yes Under the stated maximize-success rule, revise the choice to B: it delivers 94 rather than 90 timely correct cases within the budget. A still has lower charge per success. The recommendation changes because the explicit objective values additional successes subject to a budget; minimizing the ratio would retain A. Do not silently substitute one objective for the other. The extra modeled charge for B versus A is 50 units for four additional timely correct cases, or 12.5 units per incremental success. That is not a price recommendation. If the buyer instead values each additional success at v units in a simple linear net-value model, B beats A only when 4v>50, hence v>12.5. At equality they tie. Real error severity and deadline value may not be linear. This revision is internally consistent because only the classification of arrival-to-completion times changed. It does not assume a faster model, cheaper tool or more accurate reviewer. In a real organization, a relaxed deadline can change queues, staffing or behavior; the frozen-trace calculation would then be only a diagnostic, not a forecast.

sections.section: Evaluation plan that can disprove the recommendation
sections.text: First investigate the problem. Ask operators to reconstruct a recent delayed invoice, identify active work versus waiting, and show the artifacts used. Ask the decision maker who can authorize sample data, process changes and budget. Do not treat praise for an accurate demo as a commitment. A suitable next evidence milestone is an authorized sponsor agreeing to a scoped trial, named reviewer, dates and outcome rubric. No interviews or outreach are performed here. For offline work, choose eligibility at intake before either system affects outcomes. Preserve all offered and excluded counts and reasons. Freeze source snapshots, extraction versions, retrieval configuration, prompts/models, thresholds, call budgets and review rubric. For future cases from known suppliers use a later time holdout; for new suppliers hold out entire suppliers. Keep all revisions/retries together and exclude future evidence. Tune on development cases only. Missing labels require a declared follow-up window and reporting rule, not silent deletion. Run A and B on the same cases with equal prespecified repetitions if stochastic. Measure component quality under common evidence separately from full-system outcomes. Preserve case-level pairing and supplier grouping when quantifying uncertainty; repeated seeds are not independent suppliers. Report effect sizes, regression cases, interval assumptions and subgroup denominators. A balanced failure suite is useful for stress testing but does not establish deployment frequency. Set study size from a minimally useful effect and independent-unit variability; do not treat our 100 invented rows as a power calculation. Before any live trial, validate logging and guardrails in shadow mode, without new approval authority. For a proposed live comparison, randomize stable purchasing teams where reviewers share learning and queues; avoid mixing variants inside one team if that creates spillover. Check for cross-team interference and whether isolated infrastructure would change the intended treatment. Block or match on baseline workload before randomization. Estimate the effect on all assigned eligible cases, preserving assigned treatment even when the tool is not used; separately report usage. Define the analysis horizon and stopping rule before observing outcomes, with immediate operational pauses for critical authority breaches. A trial too small in independent teams can be inconclusive despite many invoices. R03’s counterfactual-logging section motivates comparable exposure definitions in both arms; its engineering-bias section warns about shared components and unequal caches. Our concrete design therefore logs eligibility for both arms from the same pre-treatment rule and records versions/resource conditions. Changing the model and user interface together evaluates the bundle; it cannot attribute the result solely to the model. Measure correct on-time resolution, active review minutes, rework, errors by severity, source support, prohibited attempts/effects and total resource use. Also observe whether released capacity is actually used and whether approvals still wait on an unrelated bottleneck. Verify correctness with evidence-based adjudication, blind to option when practical; investigate judge/person disagreement as A05 specifies. Test the adjudicator on separate cases.

The strongest conclusion here is a logical counterexample: higher component accuracy need not improve the chosen whole-task outcome. The source passages support the evaluation discipline, while the arithmetic follows from invented inputs. They do not prove actual demand, a causal model effect, implementation safety or a revenue forecast. F02 makes error costs and objective changes explicit; F03 separates replay from intervention; A01 protects holdouts; A03 checks source applicability; A05 keeps authority and denominators intact; B01 asks whether the outcome matters enough to change behavior. The next investment should target the weakest link in that chain rather than the most impressive model metric.

Reconstruct the one-day decision, including paired gains/regressions and both cost denominators: per eligible case and per timely correct case. Change only the deadline to two days. Defend the revised choice and explain why minimizing cost per success gives a different answer. Derive the incremental-value threshold. Change the labor-value rate from 0.5 to r and find when B’s modeled charge becomes lower than A’s. Specify an offline and live evaluation that separates component quality, task quality and customer value. Name a leakage and an interference failure. Identify the unsupported customer assumptions and write a concrete evidence milestone that could stop the project even if B’s component score remains highest.

Field Value ID / revision / date C02 answers · 1.0 · 2026-11-11 Title Model performance and customer outcomes — worked analysis Prerequisites F02/F03, A01/A03/A05, B01 and C02 memo Capability developed Defend a conditional choice and an evaluation that could reverse it Source-check status R03/R19 passages recorded in the memo Experiment status Exact arithmetic, paired-set and sensitivity checks executed; no live trial These are reference analyses, not learner responses.

Subtract late-correct cases from eventual correctness; keep every eligible case in the denominator. Preserve outputs and costs when changing the deadline. Apply the stated objective. Compare differences, not just ratios. Staff time is valued capacity, not automatically removed payroll. Offline pairing and live random assignment answer different questions. A model benchmark cannot establish that the buyer’s bottleneck is evidence assembly.

Correct on-time counts are C=90−4=86, A=92−4=88 and B=96−12=84. Correct, incorrect and unresolved counts each total 100 for every option. Late cases are a subset of correct outcomes, not an additional category to add to that total. At 0.5 units per minute, charges are C=0+800×0.5=400, A=100+400×0.5=300 and B=200+300×0.5=350. Per eligible case they are 4,3 and 3.5 units; per timely correct case they are 200/43≈4.65,75/22≈3.41 and 25/6≈4.17. Neither measure is profit. Failed work stays in the numerator. Paired A/B outcomes: 76 both succeed, 12 A-only, 8 B-only, 4 neither. A=88, B=84; B−A=−4 points. Marginal counts alone would conceal the twelve regressing cases. The ledger does not support a p-value or an empirical confidence interval because its inputs were assigned, not sampled. Only A meets all initial gates. C fails the timely-count and charge gates. B passes the charge/error limits but misses the timely-count threshold. A has no established market advantage: this is a conditional next-investigation choice. Criterion: Correct partition and paired arithmetic; distinguish conditional decision from observed superiority.

Add the newly timely correct outcomes: C=86+2=88, A=88+2=90, B=84+10=94. Costs remain 400,300,350. C still exceeds 360; A and B now meet all count/error/budget gates. Maximizing timely correct outcomes chooses B. Cost per success remains lower for A: 300/90=10/3 versus B’s 350/94=175/47≈3.72. This is not a contradiction. Ratio minimization and maximizing success subject to a budget are different objectives. If minimizing charge per success is the true buyer objective, retain A; explicitly revise the objective rather than claiming the original rule selected it. A feasible paired realization is A’s first-day success set 1–88 and B’s set 1–76 plus 89–96. By day two A adds 89–90 and B adds 77–86. Then both succeed on 88 cases, A alone on 2, B alone on 6 and neither on 4. Sets grow monotonically with deadline, while outputs are unchanged. The executable construction demonstrates consistency, not an observed customer trace. Criterion: Change only the constraint, retain gates/costs, and identify the objective responsible for the reversal.

At r=0.5, B costs 50 units more and adds four timely correct outcomes at day two. Under linear value v per success, net-value difference B−A is 4v−50. B wins for v>12.5, ties at 12.5 and loses below it. The chosen v must reflect a real outcome value, not an invented model benchmark score. With staff-value rate r≥0, C costs 800r, A costs 100+400r and B costs 200+300r. B−A=100−100r, so B’s total charge is lower only for r>1. At r=1 they tie. Both can still violate the absolute budget: A requires r≤260/400=0.65; B requires r≤160/300=8/15≈0.5333. Thus B cannot be cheaper than A while both satisfy this fixed 360-unit budget in this model. Sensitivity thresholds must be interpreted with all constraints. In the original r=0.5 setting, lowering the budget from 360 to 300 at day two leaves A feasible and removes B. A favorable value ratio cannot make an unaffordable option feasible. Criterion: Exact crossover, feasible-region reasoning and no claim that labor value equals cash savings.

Offline: freeze versions, evidence available at intake, eligibility, rubric and budgets. Pair options on each case; group revisions and retries. Hold out time or suppliers according to the claim. Repeat stochastic runs under a fixed policy, preserving both within-case variation and between-case diversity. Report all outcomes and severe regressions; use group-aware uncertainty only with defensible independent units and assumptions. Leakage example: retrieving a corrected invoice published after the original decision time. Component correctness can then appear excellent while using unavailable evidence. A separate common-evidence diagnostic isolates answer construction but does not replace the full-system test. Live: establish an authorized, bounded trial with stable team-level assignment when reviewers share learning or queues. Prespecify horizon, outcome, data-quality checks, guardrails, stopping and uncertainty analysis. Determine sample size using independent-team variability and a minimally useful effect. Report all assigned eligible cases, including non-use; do not compare only enthusiastic adopters with all controls. Interference example: treatment changes a shared retrieval cache or review queue, improving or delaying control. Either isolate the unintended sharing or explicitly design an estimand that includes the interaction. Individual-request randomization does not magically remove it. A faster component on replay cannot establish a causal reduction in human work or an adoption effect. Criterion: Separate diagnostic, predictive and causal claims; preserve the clock, unit and missing-outcome rule.

Unknowns include whether matching causes consequential delay, who values released time, whether deadlines can change, what errors cost, who authorizes data use and whether a buyer will adopt. Ask for a recent delayed case and reconstruct active work versus waiting with its artifacts. Compare against the existing workaround, including doing nothing or changing review scheduling. A concrete milestone is a sponsor authorizing a bounded sample, naming a reviewer, agreeing to dates and a success rubric, and specifying how released capacity would be used. This is evidence for one trial, not market validation. Stop or revise the project if matching is already fast, the important delay is elsewhere, safe data access cannot be authorized, or the trial shows no useful outcome despite component gains. A refusal can also reflect recruitment mismatch; record the reason. Criterion: Observable behavior and specific episodes; no invented interview, willingness to pay or commitment.

This script verifies constructed counts and logical implications. It does not run a model, recruit participants, calculate empirical uncertainty or execute payments. from fractions import Fraction as F correct={'C':90,'A':92,'B':96} wrong={'C':2,'A':2,'B':1} unresolved={'C':8,'A':6,'B':3} late={'C':4,'A':4,'B':12} minutes={'C':800,'A':400,'B':300} resource={'C':0,'A':100,'B':200} one={k:correct[k]-late[k] for k in correct} two={k:one[k]+x for k,x in zip(correct,[2,2,10])} cost={k:resource[k]+F(1,2)*minutes[k] for k in correct} assert one=={'C':86,'A':88,'B':84} assert two=={'C':88,'A':90,'B':94} assert cost=={'C':400,'A':300,'B':350} for k in correct: assert correct[k]+wrong[k]+unresolved[k]==100 assert one[k]<=two[k]<=correct[k] assert [cost[k]/one[k] for k in correct]==[F(200,43),F(75,22),F(25,6)] assert [cost[k]/100 for k in correct]==[F(4),F(3),F(7,2)] def choose(success,budget=360): feasible=[k for k in correct if success[k]>=88 and wrong[k]<=2 and cost[k]<=budget] return max(feasible,key=lambda k:(success[k],-cost[k])) if feasible else None assert choose(one)=='A' and choose(two)=='B' assert choose(two,300)=='A' and choose(two,299) is None A=set(range(1,89));B=set(range(1,77))|set(range(89,97));U=set(range(1,101)) def paired(a,b):return (len(a&b),len(a-b),len(b-a),len(U-(a|b))) assert paired(A,B)==(76,12,8,4) A2=A|{89,90};B2=B|set(range(77,87)) assert paired(A2,B2)==(88,2,6,4) assert A<=A2 and B<=B2 assert F(len(B)-len(A),100)==F(-1,25) assert cost['A']/two['A']<cost['B']/two['B'] assert F(cost['B']-cost['A'],two['B']-two['A'])==F(25,2) # 201 labor-value points check charge crossover, plus exact boundaries. for i in range(201): r=F(i,100);a=100+400*r;b=200+300*r assert (b<a)==(r>1) assert (a<=360)==(r<=F(13,20)) assert (b<=360)==(r<=F(8,15)) assert 100+400*F(13,20)==360 assert 200+300*F(8,15)==360 for v in [F(0),F(12),F(25,2),F(13),F(100)]: assert (4*v-50>0)==(v>F(25,2)) print('PASS: partitions, paired sets, deadline reversal, costs, 201 sensitivity points and boundaries')

Field Value ID / title C03 · Which optimization buys useful capacity? Revision / date 1.0 · 2026-11-13 Prerequisites S01 resource models; S05 queues and offered-load accounting; A04 inference memory/scheduling; B02 useful-outcome economics Capability developed Select an optimization using workload, deadline and cost constraints, then revise it when the workload changes Source-check status R16 v1 §§4.1–4.3 and §4.5; R09 chapter 21 resource-capacity discussion inspected Experiment status Deterministic scheduling and exact cost checks executed; no hardware benchmark or model evaluation Companion Worked analysis and reproducible checks

Recommendation under the starting assumptions: test the prompt-processing optimization P before purchasing a second replica R. P delivers all eight offered tasks within the deadline at 30 U per timely correct task, compared with 55 U for R. When the output workload doubles, revise the choice to R: it preserves eight timely tasks while P delivers four. These are conditional results of an invented service model, not deployment claims. The decision owner must first validate the resource and quality assumptions. A cheaper case is not useful if evidence is unsupported, authority is violated or latency is measured at the wrong boundary. This memo combines the earlier modules around one bounded choice; it does not claim that either option is universally optimal.

sections.section: 1. Freeze the job and the comparison
sections.text: The service prepares invoice evidence for an authorized reviewer. It cannot approve payment. A useful task returns the complete supported package within a 90 ms arrival-to-response deadline, inclusive, with unchanged evidence scope and access checks. All eight offered tasks count in the denominator. Late results, refusals and unsupported results do not count as useful successes, although a refusal may be contract-correct in a broader evaluation. The boundary here begins when an eligible prepared input arrives at the serving queue and ends when the validated response is ready. Retrieval, network transit and human consumption are outside this latency boundary. The 90 ms objective is therefore a serving-stage budget, not an end-to-end customer promise. Validation overhead is included in the assigned service durations. A separate illustrative verification charge is counted financially; it does not introduce an unmodeled human wait into the 90 ms clock. All numbers are hypothetical. Eight identical-length requests arrive together at time zero, with IDs 1–8 breaking ties. There are no retries, failures, cancellations, transfers, warmup delays or background interference. Model, precision, input evidence and correctness are held fixed. A task must generate its complete required output; shortening it merely to meet the deadline is not an allowed optimization. Only batch sizes 1–4 are within this fixture’s characterized operating envelope. Batch size eight and more sophisticated continuous scheduling are candidates for later measurement, not assumed impossible. The memo compares three named policies, not every possible schedule. All provisioned replicas are ready at time zero and remain purchased for a common 200 ms window, including idle time. All traces used for the main comparison finish within that window.

Reuse A04’s hypothetical device layout: 24 GiB total, 12 GiB weights, 4 GiB other-memory reserve, leaving 8 GiB for KV state. The cache coefficient is 128 KiB per retained position. Each request has a conservative peak cap of 4,096 positions, including prompt and generated positions for both output scenarios. Thus a request needs at most 512 MiB and four active requests need 2 GiB. Queued requests retain their inputs off-device and hold no KV state. Each replica stores its own weights and cache; its memory is not pooled with another replica. The feasibility check is local to each device: 12 GiB+4 GiB+4(4096)(128 KiB)=18 GiB≤24 GiB. The reserve must actually bound workspace, runtime state and metadata. Memory headroom does not establish a latency guarantee. R16’s block-based mapping separates logical KV positions from physical allocations, and its scheduling discussion addresses growth beyond available blocks. These mechanisms motivate measuring allocation and growth; the paper does not supply our timing law. A memory-only change M that reduces unused allocation but leaves this feasible schedule and its service durations unchanged produces the same timely count as the baseline. That is a counterexample to equating lower allocated bytes with useful throughput. If larger prompts make memory binding, M may matter; the resource condition and timing evidence must then be revisited together. S01’s operation/byte bounds explain what cannot be faster than the available resources permit. Here we additionally assign elapsed service laws so that a trace can be computed. An operation lower bound alone would not justify those durations. R09 chapter 21 cautions that requests differ in resource demand; the same request count need not imply the same capacity requirement.

sections.section: 3. The three policies and their mechanism
sections.text: Let b be batch size and d the number of decode rounds after prefill. In the baseline law, prefill takes 8+2b ms and each decode round takes 4+b ms. Prefill emits the first token; a task returns d+1 tokens in this small abstraction. Sequential phase durations add because there is no overlap. sB(b,d)=8+2b+d(4+b). P halves only prefill time, holding decoding, output quality and all other costs fixed: sP(b,d)=4+b+d(4+b). This is a proposed performance effect to validate, not a claim that a particular kernel or cache will provide it. R uses two unchanged replicas. Each processes one batch of four at time zero. B and P use one replica with two batches of four in FIFO order; the second begins when the first finishes. No batch-formation delay occurs because all requests already exist. At b=4 and d=4, baseline prefill is 16 ms and decoding is 32 ms. Halving a third of the original 48 ms service duration yields 40 ms, a 1.2× batch speedup, not 2×. Even eliminating prefill entirely would leave 32 ms and limit this isolated speedup to 1.5×. This is an original phase-sum derivation; it assumes the change does not move work into decoding or another stage. Starting workload: d=4 B: one baseline replica P: faster prefill, one replica R: two baseline replicas Batch service time 48 ms 40 ms 48 ms Task completion times 48×4, 96×4 ms 40×4, 80×4 ms 48×8 ms Timely correct tasks / offered 4/8 8/8 8/8 Mean serving response 72 ms 60 ms 48 ms Last completion 96 ms 80 ms 48 ms Total busy replica-time 96 ms 80 ms 96 ms Purchased replica-time 200 ms 200 ms 400 ms Here “48×4” means four tasks finish at 48 ms, not a 192 ms response. R halves the last-completion time relative to B without reducing total busy work. P reduces work modestly, but moves the second batch across the deadline, doubling the useful count in this fixture. Threshold effects can make task-level improvement larger than component speedup.

sections.section: 4. Count purchased capacity and unsuccessful work
sections.text: Assign a price of 1 U per purchased replica-ms and a non-overlapping 5 U verification/accounting charge per attempted task, including late tasks. U is an arbitrary currency unit, not a provider price. Total modeled cost is C=200k+5N, where k is replicas and N=8. B and P cost 240 U; R costs 440 U. Divide by timely correct count G, not by tokens or all eventual completions. Costs per useful task are respectively 60, 30 and 55 U. If G=0, retain incurred cost and report no finite cost-per-useful-task ratio. The decision rule is lexicographic: first require all eight offered tasks to succeed within the budget; among qualifying policies choose the lowest modeled cost. P and R pass; P wins. This is not a revenue or profitability model. It excludes implementation, maintenance, procurement, shared infrastructure and other unlisted costs. At unchanged traffic and outcomes, P’s recurring saving relative to R is 200 U per window. If P requires K U of additional engineering expense over R, recovery needs at least K/200 identical windows under these assumptions. Neither workload persistence nor that expense is observed. Counting only busy time would assign much smaller costs and conceal the idle purchased replica. Conversely, a true usage-only billing contract would need another cost model. The common window makes capacity ownership explicit; it is not evidence about a cloud billing minimum.

sections.section: 5. Change one constraint and revise the decision
sections.text: Now require d=8 decode rounds, retaining eight arrivals, the 90 ms deadline, the same 4,096-position cap and the same per-round law. Longer complete outputs are required by the changed workload; prompt processing is unchanged. This is a controlled sensitivity case, not an assertion that real decoding time is independent of growing sequence length. Longer output: d=8 B P R Batch duration 80 ms 72 ms 80 ms Completions 80×4, 160×4 72×4, 144×4 80×8 Timely correct / offered 4/8 4/8 8/8 Mean response 120 ms 108 ms 80 ms Modeled cost / useful task 60 U 60 U 55 U Revise to R because it alone meets the stated all-eight objective. P still reduces elapsed work, but its second batch remains too late. Do not describe P as useless: its improvement simply fails this decision’s threshold. Combining P with R is a fourth option; at the same recurring cost it could reduce latency further, but its additional implementation cost and feasibility are not included in this three-option decision. The exact boundaries make the recommendation auditable. With b=4, B’s second wave finishes at 32+16d, P’s at 16+16d, and R’s only wave at 16+8d. At 90 ms, all eight are timely for integer d≤3, d≤4 and d≤9 respectively. For d≥10 none of these three policies meets the all-eight objective. More capacity does not fix a single task whose own service exceeds the budget; another service law, deadline or complete-output contract is needed.

sections.section: 6. Workload and operational checks that could overturn it
sections.text: At one offered task, there is no second batch to rescue. For b=1,d=4, B takes 30 ms and P 25 ms; both meet the deadline. If R still purchases two replicas for the full window, its extra capacity provides no useful-count gain. More headroom is not automatically a cost saving. For the longer-output case, a second replica ready at delay h completes its batch at h+80. It preserves all eight timely tasks only when h≤10 ms, under a routing rule that assigns that batch to it. “Autoscaling is enabled” is not evidence of readiness. The cost table assumes a warm replica; startup charges and delayed arrivals require a revised ledger and trace. For unequal output lengths, a static batch may run until its longest member finishes; continuous scheduling can remove finished work and admit waiting requests. Those policies require per-request lengths and iteration-level accounting. Average output length is insufficient to reconstruct the queue. Larger prompts can change both memory demand and phase durations. Do not vary the memory cap while silently keeping a timing law outside its characterized range. Validate P against B with the same timestamped offered arrivals, task cases, model, decoding rules and quality rubric. Record accepted/rejected/late/unsupported counts, complete response times, phase durations, peak allocated memory, growth failures, replay/retry work, billed capacity and verification effort. Include idle periods and startup in a declared window. Compare matched quality; one unsupported P result would leave only seven useful tasks and fail the all-eight gate. Eight synthetic tasks do not estimate a production percentile or establish a sustainable arrival rate. Stop rollout on authority or evidence-integrity violations. Reject the optimization claim if speed comes from dropping required output, shifting work outside the clock or excluding hard requests from the denominator. Retain a rollback path and test repeated bursts; the fixture is a decision aid, not a production safety proof.

Reconstruct per-device memory use and explain why a memory-only optimization need not change this decision. Derive all starting-workload finish times, means, useful counts and phase speedup bounds. Rebuild the cost ledger, compare busy versus purchased time, and state what engineering expense does to the recommendation. Apply the longer-output workload, derive integer decode-round thresholds, and evaluate second-replica startup delays of 0, 10 and 11 ms. Design an experiment that can reject P or R. Include sparse traffic, unequal lengths, quality failures and a reason not to report the fixture as a production p99.
