Field Value ID / title C03 answers · Capacity decision analysis Revision / date 1.0 · 2026-11-13 Prerequisites C03 memo, S01/S05, A04, B02 Capability developed Audit the constraints and denominators behind an optimization recommendation Source-check status Uses the memo’s R16/R09 passages; numerical work is original Experiment status Exact scheduling, memory, threshold and cost checks executed; no model or hardware trial Assessment Criteria concern a future answer, not inferred learner mastery

Hint: Count weights once per replica and cached positions once per active request. Worked analysis: Each peak request costs 4,096×128 KiB=512 MiB. Four require 2 GiB. Weights plus other reserve plus request state total 12+4+2=18 GiB, leaving 6 GiB beyond the counted reservation on that device. The original KV pool is 8 GiB; the four requests consume only a quarter of it. Two replicas each need their own 18 GiB budget, not 18 GiB shared between them. This is a conservative cap including output growth, not merely a snapshot of prompt memory. It holds only if the other-memory reserve is sufficient. A memory-only change that preserves the feasible schedule and service law cannot alter completion times. It becomes consequential if allocation previously prevented a useful batch, but that new schedule must still meet the deadline. Physical memory fit does not establish bandwidth, compute or latency capacity. Criteria: Correct byte conversions, per-device accounting and a conditional reason that reducing memory can leave useful capacity unchanged.

Hint: Compute one complete batch, then add queue delay for the second wave. Worked analysis: At b=4,d=4, B is 16+4×8=48 ms and P is 8+4×8=40 ms. One replica finishes its waves at s and 2s: B at 48 and 96, P at 40 and 80. Two B replicas finish all tasks at 48. With four requests per wave, mean response is (s+2s)/2=1.5s for B/P; R’s mean is 48. Means are therefore 72, 60 and 48 ms. Counts within 90 ms are 4,8,8. Prefill is 16/48=1/3 of B’s service. Halving it gives 48/40=6/5 speedup. Removing it entirely leaves 32 ms, limiting this particular phase-only speedup to 48/32=3/2. A 2× component improvement is not a 2× whole-batch improvement. Nor is amortized batch time s/4 the response time of an individual task. Criteria: Correctly distinguishes latency, work and wave scheduling. Does not import a benchmark result into the invented timing law.

Hint: Apply the same purchased window even if a policy stops being busy sooner. Worked analysis: Eight attempted tasks incur 40 U of verification/accounting cost in every policy. B/P each buy 200 replica-ms, so each costs 240 U. R buys 400 replica-ms, so costs 440 U. Dividing by useful counts yields 60,30,55 U. B’s lower total bill than R does not make B acceptable under the all-eight objective. P and R both pass; P is cheaper. Busy replica-time is 96,80,96 ms. R parallelizes the same baseline work; it does not halve total work. A busy-only bill would instead be 136,120,136 U including the common 40, which describes a different pricing assumption. Do not silently switch between the two. If P has additional implementation expense K relative to R, after m identical qualifying windows its saving net of that expense is 200m−K. For positive K, continuous recovery is K/200 windows; whole-window recovery is its ceiling. This calculation omits maintenance and any later workload change. With K=1,000 U, five such windows recover it exactly. This is an illustrative expense, not a quote. If the long-output workload arrives before recovery, the saving premise fails. Criteria: Reports unsuccessful-work costs, idle capacity and excluded costs; keeps quality/coverage as a gate rather than optimizing a ratio at any cost.

Hint: Replace d, not the task count, objective or quality bar. Worked analysis: At d=8, B/R batch time is 16+8×8=80 ms; P is 8+8×8=72. B waves end at 80/160 and P at 72/144; R completes eight at 80. Means are 120/108/80. Useful counts are 4/4/8 and costs per useful result 60/60/55. R is now the only qualifying policy. For all eight to finish: B requires 32+16d≤90, so integer d≤3; P requires 16+16d≤90, so d≤4; R requires 16+8d≤90, so d≤9. These conditions include d=0 if prefill alone supplies the whole output. They do not certify real workloads with the same token count. At d=10, R needs 96 ms, and adding identical replicas cannot reduce an individual batch’s 96 ms under this policy. Smaller batches or a different kernel are separate options. With the second replica ready at h, its four assigned tasks finish at h+80. At h=0,10,11, all-eight counts are respectively 8,8,4. Equality at 90 is allowed. This policy deliberately waits for the second replica for that batch; other routing choices require another trace. Startup costs must be added if the warm-capacity billing premise changes. Criteria: Revises the recommendation and explains the precise constraint causing reversal. Correctly handles inclusive deadlines and does not call requested capacity ready capacity.

Hint: A fair experiment can produce evidence against the optimization you prefer. Worked analysis: Replay matched permitted cases with identical arrival timestamps and output requirements. Freeze model/configuration, data revisions, validation rules and allowed effects. Record phase durations and complete serving response separately; keep retrieval/network/user time in a separate end-to-end measure. Compare ordinary traffic, bursts, sparse single requests, unequal outputs and larger prompts. Count rejected, late and unsupported tasks among all offered tasks. Include provisioned idle time, startup, memory growth, retry costs and verification work. For sparse one-task windows at b=1,d=4, B takes 10+20=30 ms and P 5+20=25; both are useful. A permanently purchased second replica adds cost without adding a timely result. A scale-down policy could change this cost comparison, but is not the stipulated R policy. For unequal outputs, record batch composition and longest-member blocking; an average length does not reconstruct per-task waiting. Inspect continuous scheduling separately. If one P output is unsupported, its eight timely outputs become seven timely-correct results, failing the required gate even if its cost ratio remains attractive. If a model variant omits necessary evidence, lower latency cannot be credited as an equivalent optimization. For production tails, use representative arrivals over repeated windows and an explicit percentile convention and uncertainty analysis. This eight-task deterministic trace is not a sample supporting a production p99 estimate. Criteria: Includes at least one observation that rejects each candidate, matched quality and authority boundaries, explicit units and a fair offered-load denominator. No outreach, model execution or real measurement is implied by this proposed plan.

The standard-library script below ran successfully during production. It independently constructs wave schedules and checks them against the closed-form thresholds. It also checks zero-success handling and exact boundary cases. The 200 ms billing comparison is used only for the two main workloads, whose traces drain inside it; longer synthetic traces below are timing-only sensitivity checks. from fractions import Fraction as Q from math import ceil GiB, KiB = 2**30, 2**10 kv = 4096*128*KiB assert kv == GiB//2 assert 12*GiB + 4*GiB + 4*kv == 18*GiB def service(b,d,fast=False): pre = Q(8+2*b,2) if fast else Q(8+2*b) return pre+d*(4+b) def schedule(n,d,replicas=1,fast=False): free=[Q(0)]*replicas finishes=[] busy=Q(0) remaining=n while remaining: b=min(4,remaining) device=min(range(replicas),key=lambda j:(free[j],j)) elapsed=service(b,d,fast) free[device]+=elapsed finishes.extend([free[device]]*b) busy+=elapsed remaining-=b return sorted(finishes),busy def good(finishes,deadline=90): return sum(t<=deadline for t in finishes) def cost_per(cost,successes): return Q(cost,successes) if successes else None policies=[(1,False),(1,True),(2,False)] for d,expected,means,counts in [ (4,[[48]*4+[96]*4,[40]*4+[80]*4,[48]*8],[72,60,48],[4,8,8]), (8,[[80]*4+[160]*4,[72]*4+[144]*4,[80]*8],[120,108,80],[4,4,8])]: for i,(k,fast) in enumerate(policies): f,busy=schedule(8,d,k,fast) assert f==expected[i] assert sum(f)/8==means[i] and good(f)==counts[i] assert max(f)<=200 assert busy==2*service(4,d,fast) cost=200*k+5*8 assert cost_per(cost,good(f))==([60,30,55] if d==4 else [60,60,55])[i] assert Q(48,40)==Q(6,5) and Q(48,32)==Q(3,2) assert ceil(Q(1000,200))==5 assert cost_per(240,0) is None assert schedule(1,4)[0]==[30] assert schedule(1,4,fast=True)[0]==[25] # 13 decode lengths x 3 policies; compare all-eight success thresholds. for d in range(13): for (k,fast),limit in zip(policies,[3,4,9]): f,_=schedule(8,d,k,fast) assert (good(f)==8)==(d<=limit) # 201 inclusive deadlines x 2 workloads x 3 policies: 1,206 checks. checks=0 for deadline in range(201): for d in [4,8]: for k,fast in policies: f,_=schedule(8,d,k,fast) s=service(4,d,fast) closed=8*int(s<=deadline) if k==2 else 4*(int(s<=deadline)+int(2*s<=deadline)) assert good(f,deadline)==closed checks+=1 assert checks==1206 for h,count in [(0,8),(10,8),(11,4)]: assert good([80]*4+[80+h]*4)==count print('PASS: memory, two full traces, costs, phase bounds, sparse load, zero success, 39 length-policy and 1206 deadline checks, startup boundaries')

title: Which product boundary makes the service viable?

sections.section: Which product boundary makes the service viable?
sections.text: Field Value ID / title C04 · Product-boundary decision memo Revision / date 1.0 · 2026-11-14 Prerequisites B01 customer evidence; B02 economics; B03 distribution and boundary comparison; S06 authority and reliability Capability developed Choose who delivers, operates and controls a service using explicit feasibility gates and two-party economics Source-check status R19 budget/authority, R21 packaging, R11 design principles inspected; locators below Experiment status Hypothetical decision model and exact arithmetic checked; no customer, deployment or security experiment Companion Worked analysis and executable checks

Choose the managed evidence service for the initial six-month planning case. It meets the assigned onboarding constraint and gives greater modeled customer value than the feasible self-serve alternative. When the customer increases available onboarding capacity from four to twelve hours, revise the choice to internal deployment, provided its operating owner and control checks remain satisfied. This is a conditional decision, not a recommendation to buy or deploy an actual product. B03 compared three boundaries around invoice matching. This memo reuses its numbers deliberately, then adds a decision owner, resource constraints, supplier overhead, operational responsibilities and acceptance conditions. It does not repeat B03 as a new lesson or reinterpret its invented inputs as observations. “Viable” here means feasible for this customer and horizon, with acceptable modeled economics for each party that must deliver the offer. It does not mean a validated market or a profitable company. The decision belongs to the fictional purchasing organization’s operations sponsor. The budget owner, data owner, operator and payment approver may be different people. The supplier has a separate decision about whether it can fund delivery. A customer cannot choose a loss-making supplier offer into sustainability by liking it more.

sections.section: 1. One job and a fixed outcome contract
sections.text: The job is to assemble invoice and delivery evidence so an authorized customer reviewer can decide what to do. The unit is one eligible invoice case; retries and document revisions do not create extra customer jobs. An acceptable evidence package identifies the source revision, relevant facts and unresolved discrepancies. It must arrive by the agreed operational cutoff, preserve access restrictions and avoid implying that payment has been approved. All three candidates must meet the same evidence and timeliness rubric on the same case mix. The numerical comparison assumes they do so; that assumption must be tested before a real commitment. Unresolved cases are reported, not silently dropped from cost or success counts. Failure handling and ordinary rework are included in the assigned recurring effort. Unexpected consequential errors are separate stop conditions, not an affordable error allowance. The incumbent manual process remains available. Its modeled incremental value is zero because it defines the comparison baseline. Keeping it may be the right action if every proposed option violates a hard constraint. This prevents a ranking exercise from forcing an unsafe or unfunded change.

sections.section: 2. The contract changes when responsibility changes
sections.text: Responsibility Self-serve hosted tool Managed evidence service Internal deployment Initial route Buyer evaluates a documented trial; customer configures it Buyer receives a bounded service proposal and named operator Sponsor funds internal deployment with an accountable IT owner Mapping and onboarding Customer maps inputs using supplier documentation Supplier performs mapping with customer confirmation Customer integrates and validates the local workflow Day-to-day preparation Hosted software proposes; customer handles exceptions Supplier staff/software prepare and first-review evidence Customer staff/software prepare and resolve exceptions Final business approval Customer reviewer only Customer reviewer only Customer reviewer only Runtime and recovery Supplier operates hosted service Supplier operates service and staffs escalation Customer operates, patches, restores and monitors runtime Data access Explicit hosted-processing grant; support access separately scoped Hosted grant plus named, scoped human access Customer-controlled processing; external calls require separate permission Exit Export mappings, evidence IDs and unresolved work Same plus documented manual handoffs Retain deployable configuration, runbooks and data export R21’s packaging guidance helps distinguish customer offers, but these alternatives differ in responsibility, not just feature limits. Calling an offer “managed” does not automatically transfer approval authority. Calling it “internal” does not prove data stays internal: remote inference, diagnostics and support attachments can cross the boundary. Define one accountable owner for each operational failure. If a source record is missing, the preparation operator returns an unresolved case and the customer’s workflow owner obtains the record. If service processing stalls, the runtime owner restores service or invokes the agreed fallback; the customer owns the decision to resume manual processing. If output support is wrong, the preparation owner investigates and the customer reviewer stops relying on the affected output. These roles should be part of the offer, with escalation contacts and observation windows, not assumptions hidden in a demo.

Apply S06’s separation between proposal and approval. A preparation worker may read the permitted case subset and write a draft. It cannot approve payment, change grants or select an unrestricted identity. The approval service checks authenticated principal, current permission, tenant/object, evidence revision and business state at its decision boundary. Current permission to read a historical result is separate from permission to create a new effect. For example: a supplier analyst reads case A17 under a scoped grant, the customer revokes that grant, and the analyst then tries to retrieve another revision. The new read must be denied under this chosen contract. An old open page or earlier successful login is not fresh permission. Revocation cannot make already disclosed information unread; retention, export and deletion procedures address a different part of the lifecycle. Do not promise instant erasure merely because a token was disabled. R11’s fail-safe defaults, complete mediation and least privilege motivate these requirements. The source supplies principles; our workflow and serialized decision boundary are design applications, not certified implementations. Tests must include support tools, recovery scripts, exports and logs. A restrictive application screen does not constrain a shared administrator credential used behind it. The managed service adds authorized human readers to the trusted surface. The internal option moves more operational responsibility to the customer. Neither label establishes stronger security without checking actual paths, privileges and recovery behavior. If external processing permission is absent, both hosted options are infeasible in this definition regardless of their economic rank. A redacted-data variant would be a new candidate requiring its own quality and cost evidence.

sections.section: 4. State the resource constraints before calculating value
sections.text: Use B03’s hypothetical organization: 100 eligible cases/month, six months of steady use, current handling time eight minutes/case, and customer labor valued at 30 U/hour. U is an invented currency unit. The comparison begins after onboarding; all options are assumed able to start by the same date if they fit the available setup capacity. No launch-delay benefit is inferred. A qualified customer operating owner exists for all options and can fund the recurring time in the table. Initially only four total customer onboarding hours can be released before that date. Supplier setup capacity is available for the two hosted offers. External processing and managed human access are assumed authorized, and all candidates have passed the common quality/control gate for purposes of the model. These are premises, not reported interviews or tests. B03 input, preserved Self-serve Managed Internal Monthly fee paid by customer 120 U 180 U 0 U Recurring customer minutes/case 4 2 3 Customer onboarding hours 4 2 12 Customer infrastructure/month 0 U 0 U 40 U Supplier variable delivery cost/month 40 U 120 U Not an external offer Supplier onboarding cost 60 U 90 U Not applicable Customer recurring time includes review, exception work and allocated operations. In particular, the internal three-minute average must cover recurring maintenance under this fixture; it is not three review minutes plus free administration. Setup hours include integration, training and transition work. Salaried time represents capacity consumed, not automatically cash that can be removed from payroll. Infrastructure and fees are separate from those hours. B01’s distinction between role, problem evidence and commitment matters: a clerk’s willingness to try the service does not release twelve IT hours. R19’s cost, recurrence and authority prompts motivate confirming the allocation with its actual owner. No outreach is performed in this assignment.

For H months, n cases/month, baseline b minutes, new t minutes, hourly labor value w, fee f, infrastructure i and customer setup o hours: V=H[n(b−t)w/60−f−i]−ow. This is modeled net capacity value, not willingness to pay or guaranteed cash savings. The baseline labor value is 100×8×30/60=400 U/month. Self-serve releases 200 U/month before fees, managed 300, and internal 250. Six-month customer result Self-serve Managed Internal Net recurring value/month 80 U 120 U 210 U Setup capacity valued 120 U 60 U 360 U Net value V 360 U 660 U 900 U Fits initial four-hour setup cap? Yes Yes No Internal wins the unconstrained arithmetic but is excluded initially. Among eligible choices, managed gives 300 U more modeled value than self-serve. Its 2-hour setup also leaves 2 hours of the initial allocation unused. Do not invent extra benefit for that slack; it is already reflected in the setup cost. Now require an external supplier to cover its modeled costs over six paid months. Reuse B03’s 200 U acquisition cost per paying organization, then add a new allocated overhead allowance of 10 U/month per organization. This overhead is distinct from variable delivery and onboarding. The supplier remainder is R=H(f−c−a)−u−A, where c is variable delivery, a allocated monthly overhead, u supplier onboarding and A acquisition. Self-serve gives 6(120−40−10)−60−200=160 U. Managed gives 6(180−120−10)−90−200=10 U. Both clear this limited nonnegative gate, but managed has little buffer. These are not company-profit claims; shared overhead allocation must reconcile to actual totals, and unlisted costs remain excluded. Internal deployment has no external supplier revenue in this fixture; its customer infrastructure/operations costs are already counted. The initial decision is therefore managed, conditional on verifying assumptions and explicitly accepting the narrow supplier buffer. A 2 U/month increase in managed overhead changes its remainder from 10 to −2 U. Customer value is unchanged, but the delivery offer fails the stipulated supplier gate. Under that isolated shock, self-serve becomes the feasible positive-value alternative while internal remains setup-constrained.

Now the customer releases twelve onboarding hours instead of four. Change only this capacity constraint: recurring operating skill, permission, quality, fees, demand and the six-month horizon are held fixed. Internal becomes feasible and offers 900 U, exceeding managed by 240 U. Revise the recommendation to internal deployment. The extra allocation is not free labor. The internal option’s full twelve hours are already charged as 360 U; increasing availability does not remove that cost. Conversely, having hours available is insufficient if the owner lacks the competence or ongoing capacity assumed here. In that case the internal option still fails a feasibility gate. Calculate how fragile the revised decision is. Let x be additional internal operations hours/month beyond the original three-minute-per-case allowance. Its value becomes 900−6×30x=900−180x. It ties managed at x=4/3 hours/month, and falls below managed above that point. It remains better than the unchanged incumbent only for x<5 hours/month. The first comparison concerns the best available alternative; the second merely asks whether a positive benefit remains. These are different thresholds. If instead external access is withdrawn while the setup cap stays four hours, both hosted options fail permission and internal fails capacity. Keep the incumbent process and negotiate a new feasible plan. A weighted score must not allow cheap service to compensate for missing authority. Deferring is a valid decision, not a failure to select a product.

sections.section: 7. A bounded evidence plan and handoff
sections.text: Before a real commitment, obtain the sponsor’s actual resource allocation, data owner’s authorized processing scope and operator’s responsibility acceptance. Prepare a permitted representative case set, including missing records, changed revisions and exceptions. Evaluate each candidate against the same completion and evidence rubric. Track total customer time by role and supplier time by activity, without counting the same minute twice. Record startup, mapping, recovery and recurring support separately. Use a small staged pilot as a learning investment, not a market-size estimate. First test non-effecting drafts and permission boundaries. Then, only after the relevant owner authorizes use, evaluate operational cycles with the incumbent fallback available. Record eligible, attempted, timely-supported, unresolved and incorrect cases; classify gaps and preserve disputes. Predefine what constitutes a supported result and when a missed cutoff triggers manual handling. No success-rate number is invented here. Stop on an unauthorized disclosure/effect or inability to preserve source identity. Revisit the offer if actual supplier overhead exceeds its buffer, internal effort crosses the alternative-value threshold, or setup cannot finish within the allocated time. A paid trial alone does not establish retention. A contract alone does not implement mediation. A successful restore drill does not prove every failure mode recoverable. At exit, transfer mappings, evidence references, unresolved cases and runbooks in an agreed format. Revoke access and address retained copies under the agreed lifecycle policy. Count migration effort in the next decision; do not claim a moat from trapped data. C06 will examine supplier changes more fully. Here the scope is allocating responsibility for a viable job.

Build the responsibility and authority map. Trace a revoked supplier reader and explain why an old successful login is insufficient. Recalculate the three customer values and apply the initial setup constraint. Explain why internal’s highest value does not win initially. Rebuild both supplier remainders with the new overhead allowance. Derive the managed overhead ceiling and assess a 2 U/month increase. Change setup capacity to twelve hours and revise the choice. Derive the internal-maintenance thresholds against managed and the incumbent. Specify a pilot, stop conditions and exit handoff. Evaluate the no-external-permission/four-hour-cap case without fabricating a feasible winner.

Basis Verified locator, accessed 2026-11-14 Scope R19 YC / Eric Migicovsky, 2019 Transcript, 30:31–33:44 Cost, frequency, budget and authority discovery guidance; not demand evidence R21 Patrick McKenzie / Stripe Pricing low-touch SaaS, Introduction; Pricing and packaging for things with no physical form Practitioner packaging concepts; historical prices not adopted R11 Saltzer and Schroeder, 1975 Basic Principles, §I.A.3(b), (c), (f) Fail-safe defaults, complete mediation, least privilege; not a modern implementation certification Original synthesis B03 numerical fixture plus explicit setup gate, overhead allocation and constraint changes Checked conditional arithmetic and decision logic, not customer observations or legal/accounting advice Unresolved inputs: actual authority, staffing, quality, demand, costs, maintenance and repeat behavior. No essential blocker remains. No learner answers or mastery are inferred. Reference card: hold the job fixed → assign responsibility → apply permission/quality/resource gates → compare customer value → check delivery economics → change one constraint → revise or defer → preserve an exit path.
1.0 — 2026-11-14. Constraint-first product-boundary memo, supplier overhead check and five analysis tasks.

Field Value ID / title C04 answers · Product-boundary analysis Revision / date 1.0 · 2026-11-14 Prerequisites C04 memo, B01–B03, S06 Capability developed Separate feasibility from preference and test a boundary choice against costs and authority Source-check status Uses the memo’s verified R19/R21/R11 passages; scenarios are original Experiment status Exact arithmetic and finite decision checks executed; no customer or security experiment Assessment convention Criteria apply to future answers, not assumed learner mastery

Hint: Identify the person who performs work separately from the principal allowed to authorize an effect. Worked analysis: The customer sponsor funds the work; the data owner authorizes processing; the preparation operator assembles evidence; the customer reviewer decides on payment. Hosted self-serve leaves exception operations with the customer. Managed adds supplier operators and scoped human access. Internal moves runtime recovery and maintenance to a customer owner. All three retain customer payment approval. A supplier analyst’s grant allows only the named tenant/case scope and operations. After revocation commits, a new protected read must fail under the memo’s contract. Identity still being authenticated does not restore authorization. Access checks need to cover exports, support tools, logs and recovery, not only the ordinary UI. Already disclosed information cannot be recalled by denying the next request; retained copies need separately defined handling. R11 gives principles; the actual revocation enforcement and trustworthy policy state are implementation premises. A generated statement that an administrator approved something does not create a grant. If current policy cannot be established, deny or defer the protected action rather than treating the uncertainty as permission. This can reduce availability while preserving the chosen authority rule. Criteria: Distinguishes identity, authorization, data disclosure and new effects. Names an operational owner without granting it unnecessary payment authority.

Hint: Apply the setup cap after calculating value; do not delete setup cost when more hours become available. Worked analysis: Baseline work is 100×8/60=40/3 hours/month, valued at 400 U. Recurring labor under the three options is 200,100,150 U/month. Including monthly fees/infrastructure gives recurring costs of 320,280,190 U/month. Net monthly benefit relative to baseline is therefore 80,120,210 U. Six-month benefits less setup are 480−120=360 U, 720−60=660 U and 1,260−360=900 U. With a four-hour onboarding cap, self-serve (4) and managed (2) fit; internal (12) does not. Assuming all other gates pass, managed maximizes modeled value among feasible candidates. The 240 U difference between internal and managed is an opportunity that cannot be realized with the initial setup allocation. These values do not prove actual cash savings. Fixed salaries may remain unchanged; released time needs a useful alternative use. Nor do they establish willingness to pay. Common quality and operational-cutoff assumptions must be tested. If one option attains its lower time only by omitting necessary evidence, its numbers are not comparable. Criteria: Gets all three values, excludes the infeasible option, and distinguishes capacity value from observed cash or demand.

Hint: There are separate customer and supplier onboarding costs. They represent different parties’ work. Worked analysis: Self-serve’s monthly contribution after the assigned overhead is 120−40−10=70 U. Across six paid months, subtracting 60 U onboarding and 200 U acquisition leaves 160 U. Managed’s corresponding contribution is 180−120−10=50 U; 300−90−200=10 U remains. For managed monthly overhead a, remainder is 6(60−a)−290=70−6a. Nonnegative remainder requires a≤35/3≈11.67 U/month. At a=12, remainder is −2 U, so managed fails the stated supplier gate. Self-serve’s value stays 360 U and its remainder is 160 U if its own overhead stays ten; it becomes the initial feasible choice. This isolated stress changes managed overhead only. The cost floor for a managed monthly fee at overhead ten is 120+10+290/6=1,070/6≈178.33 U. The assigned 180 U fee is only about 1.67 U above that floor. A price rise could help the supplier but reduce customer value or change adoption; it is a new offer, not an automatic repair. No total-company profitability is established, since the overhead allocation and omitted costs require actual reconciliation. Criteria: Includes acquisition, supplier setup and overhead once; recognizes a narrow buffer and refuses to infer profitability from it.

Hint: Change available setup hours only for the primary reversal. Treat ongoing extra maintenance as a separate sensitivity. Worked analysis: At twelve available hours, internal clears the setup gate. Its 900 U exceeds managed’s 660 and self-serve’s 360. The qualified operating owner and recurring allowance are unchanged premises. The additional eight available hours enable the option but do not lower its twelve-hour setup cost. If additional maintenance is x hours/month, internal value is 900−180x. It ties managed at x=240/180=4/3 hours/month. Below this, internal is preferable if all gates pass; above it, managed has greater value. At x=5, internal value reaches zero, equal to the incumbent. An option can remain better than doing nothing yet lose to another feasible option: x=2 gives internal 540 U, positive but below managed’s 660. Ties should be reported, not concealed with arbitrary precision. A real tie could be resolved by confidence, reversibility or a further test; these preferences are not built into this fixture. With no external processing permission and the initial four-hour cap, both hosted options fail authority and internal fails capacity. The incumbent is the only modeled feasible path. A new timeline, allocation or redacted-data offer requires fresh assumptions. Criteria: Revises the recommendation, preserves counted labor, distinguishes two thresholds and accepts deferral when gates exclude every candidate.

Hint: State what could reject the recommended option before proposing more features. Worked analysis: Confirm the resource allocation with the sponsor, processing permissions with the data owner and ongoing responsibility with each operator. Use a bounded set of permitted cases spanning routine work, missing records, changed revisions and exceptions. Compare complete evidence support and cutoff compliance on matched cases. Log customer and supplier effort separately; classify setup, recurring operations and exceptional rework without overlap. Count unresolved cases and failures rather than filtering them out of the denominator. An initial pilot should produce non-effecting drafts and exercise denied reads, revoked grants and unavailable policy. It should not authorize payments. Stop if an unauthorized disclosure/effect occurs or evidence identity cannot be preserved. Reconsider managed if overhead or support costs exceed the narrow supplier buffer. Reconsider internal if actual maintenance erases its advantage or the operating owner cannot sustain it. No sample size here certifies security, general market demand or long-term retention. For exit, assign an owner to export mappings, evidence identifiers, outstanding cases and runbooks. Verify that the receiving process can interpret the export. Revoke access and handle retained copies according to the agreed lifecycle rules. A deletion request and a completed deletion are different statuses. Migration effort belongs in the next option comparison. A useful pilot can justify another bounded investment without proving the whole service is viable at scale. Criteria: Includes fair quality/cost measurement, authority tests, stop rules, alternative evidence and an actionable exit. Does not invent customer commitments or completed deployment tests.

This standard-library script was executed during production. It checks the ledgers, exact boundaries and a finite decision grid. It does not implement authorization, measure real labor or validate demand. Permission and quality flags represent hypothetical gate outcomes; they are not security-test results. from fractions import Fraction as Q H,n,b,w = 6,100,8,30 spec = { 'self': (4,120,0,4), 'managed': (2,180,0,2), 'internal': (3,0,40,12) } def value(name,extra_internal=Q(0)): t,fee,infra,setup=spec[name] result=H*(Q(n*(b-t)*w,60)-fee-infra)-setup*w return result-H*w*extra_internal if name=='internal' else result def remainder(name,overhead=Q(10)): fee,cost,setup=(120,40,60) if name=='self' else (180,120,90) return H*(fee-cost-overhead)-setup-200 def choose(cap,external=True,extra_internal=Q(0),managed_overhead=Q(10),quality=True): eligible={'incumbent':Q(0)} for name in spec: if not quality or spec[name][3]>cap: continue if name!='internal': if not external: continue a=managed_overhead if name=='managed' else Q(10) if remainder(name,a)<0: continue eligible[name]=value(name,extra_internal) best=max(eligible.values()) return {name for name,v in eligible.items() if v==best} assert [value(k) for k in spec]==[360,660,900] assert [remainder('self'),remainder('managed')]==[160,10] assert choose(4)=={'managed'} assert choose(12)=={'internal'} assert remainder('managed',12)==-2 assert choose(4,managed_overhead=12)=={'self'} assert choose(4,external=False)=={'incumbent'} assert choose(12,external=False)=={'internal'} assert choose(12,quality=False)=={'incumbent'} assert remainder('managed',Q(35,3))==0 assert Q(120+10)+Q(290,6)==Q(1070,6) assert value('internal',Q(4,3))==660 assert value('internal',5)==0 assert value('internal',2)==540 assert choose(12,extra_internal=Q(4,3))=={'internal','managed'} for delta in [Q(-1,100),Q(0),Q(1,100)]: assert (remainder('managed',Q(35,3)+delta)>=0)==(delta<=0) assert (value('internal',Q(4,3)+delta)>=660)==(delta<=0) # 25 setup caps x 49 maintenance values x 2 permission states = 2450 cases. # Extra maintenance ranges 0..4 hours/month in twelfths; all other gates fixed. checks=0 for c in range(25): cap=Q(c,2) for j in range(49): x=Q(j,12) for external in [False,True]: got=choose(cap,external,x) if cap<2: want={'incumbent'} elif cap<12: want={'managed'} if external else {'incumbent'} elif not external: want={'internal'} # value remains positive throughout this grid elif x<Q(4,3): want={'internal'} elif x==Q(4,3): want={'internal','managed'} else: want={'managed'} assert got==want,(cap,x,external,got,want) checks+=1 assert checks==2450 print('PASS: ledgers, overhead/maintenance boundaries, choice reversal, authority/quality gates, 2450 decision cases')
