Field Value ID C05 Title How far should autonomy go? Revision 1.0 Date 2026-11-14 Prerequisites F02/F03; S03/S06; A05 Capability developed Choose an adequate control structure using authority, capacity, expected loss and falsifiable evidence Source-check status R18, R11 and R03 primary passages inspected; locators below Experiment status Executed synthetic arithmetic, sensitivity and controller checks in companion; no deployed agent or learner assessment

Choose a fixed workflow for the initial operating envelope. When reviewer capacity falls below its requirement, conditionally choose a bounded action-taking agent. The condition is evidence that the agent meets the complete task contract and that its authority boundary actually holds. If that evidence is absent, reduce intake or defer work; a staffing shortage does not create permission. A05 prepared invoice evidence without approving payment. This memo extends that fictional service by one explicitly permitted action: place the evidence packet into an internal review queue. It does not authorize payment, email, vendor contact or document deletion. This small extension lets us compare action-taking with suggestion-only assistance while preserving the earlier payment boundary. No real action is performed here. The job is to route each eligible invoice to the correct tenant-local queue, with current revision and supporting passages, within one business day of arrival. Missing evidence produces an unresolved record and counts against timely completion; it must never become invented support. A wrong queue may be reversible but still costs attention, delay and correction. All numerical inputs below are invented planning assumptions, not measurements or vendor claims. F02 supplies the bridge: expected loss is a probability-weighted average of consequences. F03 adds the denominator: count every eligible offered case, including abstentions, failures and retries. S03 supplies a single decision boundary for competing writes; S06 distinguishes permission from a persuasive proposal. A05 supplies the bounded observation/action loop.

Freeze the source snapshot rules, eligible population, business-day clock, tenant scope, allowed destination list and success rubric. There are 1,000 eligible cases per day. Labor costs 0.50 cost units per minute; units are hypothetical common accounting units, not currency quotes. Each option can use the same authorized evidence. Retrieval strategy may differ because it is part of the system being compared. Option Choice of next step Who commits routing? Complete-system limitation W: fixed workflow Code follows version lookup, extraction, rule routing and exception branches Scoped workflow authority; human resolves exceptions Novel evidence layouts may remain unresolved S: suggestion-only assistant Fixed retrieval plus one model suggestion Authorized human checks evidence and submits Human time and queue delay count, not just generation latency A: bounded action-taking agent Model proposes subsequent reads and routing from observations External authority validates a proposed route More operations, recovery states and ongoing evaluation A fixed workflow can mutate state without being model-directed. A suggestion assistant can influence a harmful human decision without owning a write credential. Autonomy, permission and consequence are separate axes. The organizational envelope is identical across all three; identities receive only the subset needed for their role. S’s model has no mutation credential. Its human is not allowed to bypass the same business validation. R18 demonstrates an interaction pattern with search, lookup and finish in Wikipedia knowledge tasks, not an invoice-routing guarantee. The relevant transfer is that later actions can depend on earlier observations. Whether that flexibility improves this service is an empirical question. R11 motivates permission-based defaults, mediation of every access and least privilege. Our controller and capacity model are original applications, not claims proved by those sources.

Partition outcomes into three mutually exclusive categories: wrong route, late/unresolved without a wrong route, and correct on time. Wrong-route loss is 20 units and includes its correction/delay costs even when discovered late. Late/unresolved loss is 5 units. This hierarchy prevents charging the same delay twice. Separate labor numbers include routine review and oversight; the loss amounts exclude that already-counted labor. Unauthorized effects are a disqualifying boundary failure, not an inexpensive fourth category. Input per eligible case W S A Compute/tool cost 0.20 0.35 0.80 Human minutes 1.0 4.0 0.4 Allocated maintenance cost 0 0 0.30 Wrong-route probability 0.020 0.010 0.015 Late/unresolved probability 0.080 0.020 0.030 Correct-on-time probability 0.900 0.970 0.955 Maintenance is incremental to a shared baseline already funded for all options. Zero does not mean W or S need no maintenance. Initial build effort is assumed sunk and equal for this decision horizon; if not, allocate it consistently before choosing. A’s 0.30 allowance is for additional loop evaluation and operations. It is an assumption to validate, not a measured engineering advantage for W. For option j, define cost per eligible case: C(j) = compute(j) + 0.50 × human_minutes(j) + maintenance(j) + 20 × p_wrong(j) + 5 × p_late(j). This gives W = 1.50, S = 2.65 and A = 1.75 units. Daily human demand is respectively 1,000, 4,000 and 400 minutes. Total daily expected costs are 1,500, 2,650 and 1,750 units. Expectation does not require independent cases; uncertainty estimates and daily-tail predictions need additional dependence assumptions. The initial capacity is 1,200 reviewer minutes daily. Require correct-on-time probability at least 0.90 and a verified authority boundary before comparing cost. Assume, only for the numerical decision, that the boundary has been verified for every candidate. W and A pass capacity; S does not. W is the least complex adequate choice and the lower expected-cost choice. We do not select S because its apparent quality excludes the operational impossibility of completing that much human work with this staffing. These are average-work planning gates, not proofs of deadline attainment. The supplied timely rates assume actual arrival patterns, reviewer scheduling and tool limits permit them. A burst could break that premise even if daily totals fit. Deployment must validate the queue, not simply divide total minutes by staff count.

Reduce available reviewer capacity to 500 minutes per day. Hold task, volume, costs, outcome assumptions and permission envelope fixed. W now needs twice the available minutes; S needs eight times as much. A needs 400 and remains adequate under the stated model. Revise the recommendation to A, conditionally on validating those assumptions at the reduced staffing level. Its additional expected cost of 250 units daily buys feasibility, not proven superiority in general. Do not invent lower W error rates or remove human time to preserve the original answer. Nor may A acquire payment credentials to “finish the job.” If the premise that A’s oversight fits 400 minutes fails, none of these candidates is adequate at full intake. Add staffing, reduce admitted volume under a revised service contract, or develop and test a different workflow. Those are new decisions rather than hidden changes to this comparison. Capacity also explains when suggestion-only wins a different decision: if policy prohibits machine-initiated routing but permits reviewed human routing, W and A as defined fail the authority gate. S can be considered only with sufficient staffing. This is a counterexample to choosing autonomy from aggregate quality alone, not the one-constraint revision used above.

The proposed A controller allows at most three evidence calls, three model calls and one routing operation identity per case attempt, inside a ten-second automated-stage deadline. The business-day clock includes waiting for human exceptions. Retries consume the original budgets. Invalid tenant/action proposals terminate the attempt; resource exhaustion yields unresolved. Runtime cancellation is needed for the stage deadline; checking the time only before dispatch is insufficient. A route commit requires authenticated principal, current grant, matching tenant, allowed action and queue, current epoch/revision, valid evidence and an empty routing slot. Validation and insertion of route plus receipt occur atomically in the same serialized authority. Reads are separately permission checked. Tool observations cannot change the principal or grant. The external checker verifies structural/evidence constraints; it does not magically establish semantic correctness, which remains in the outcome ledger. Ordered event Required behavior Agent submits operation K for revision 3 Check current permission and state; commit route and receipt together Reply is lost Mark outcome unknown; do not generate a replacement operation Same K, identical payload, current receipt-read permission Return historical receipt; create no new route Same K, changed destination Reject operation-identity conflict Another operation targets occupied slot Reject competing route Grant revoked before a fresh commit Deny even if proposal was prepared earlier Revision changes before a fresh commit Reject stale proposal; new evidence/review required Revocation after an already committed route does not erase it. Historical receipt retrieval remains subject to current permission. Correction is a separately authorized transition, never blind replay under a new key. This local transaction contract does not promise exactly-once effects across an external payment provider; such effects are outside scope. S03’s concurrency lesson matters even for W: two deterministic workers can still race.

At initial staffing, let A’s wrong-route probability be x with all its other inputs fixed. Then C(A)=1.45+20x. It matches W at x=0.0025, or 0.25%; the assumed 1.5% is higher. At equality retain W for simplicity. This is a threshold conditional on all other inputs and gates, not a target a model’s self-reported confidence can certify. At reduced staffing W remains infeasible even if cheaper. Start with paired offline replay on identical eligible cases and frozen evidence. Score blinded outputs using the shared rubric, report discordant wins/losses and retain all failures. Include ordinary layouts, missing evidence, changed revisions, malicious source instructions and receipt-loss traces. Pairing reduces case-mix confounding; it does not reproduce a live human queue. Repeated retries of one invoice are not independent samples. Then evaluate the complete human/tool workflow under realistic arrivals. Predeclare capacity, correct-on-time, wrong-route, cost and authority guardrails, including stop conditions. Randomize at a stable team or tenant boundary if shared reviewer queues would contaminate invoice-level assignment. R03’s hypothesis, metrics and randomization guidance supports this design; no trial has been conducted. Measure review minutes including corrections, oversight and failures. Inspect distributions and common-mode failures, not only means. A single demonstrated unauthorized path blocks rollout even if average cost improves.

Use these as optional written exercises; no learner response is needed for scheduled production. Hints and worked analysis are in SDE_C05_answers.md. Rebuild the three cost and human-capacity ledgers; choose at both staffing levels. Derive A’s wrong-route break-even rate and explain why it cannot rescue W under reduced capacity. Trace lost response, replay, changed-payload replay, stale revision and revocation. Separate historical evidence from new effects. A dashboard reports 99% correctness among emitted suggestions. Identify the missing denominator and design a fair comparison. Set A’s authority verification to false or its review demand to 600 minutes at reduced staffing. State the decision without silently changing the task. Reference card: freeze the complete job → gate permission and feasibility → count offered cases → compare complete-system loss and cost → change one premise explicitly → reconcile unknown outcomes before retrying → collect evidence that can overturn the choice. C06 next asks how this decision survives a supplier change.

Source Inspected locator Supported use and limit R18: ReAct, v3 §§3.1–3.2, printed p.4 Observation/action interaction in knowledge tasks; no invoice reliability or authorization inference R11: Saltzer and Schroeder §I.A.3(b), (c), (f) Protection design principles; not certification of this proposed controller R03: Microsoft Research Formulate your Hypothesis and Success Metrics; Choose the Appropriate Unit of Randomization First-party experimental-design guidance; not measured gains for this service Original synthesis Ledgers, thresholds, trace and companion script Constructed and executed checks only; no production outcomes Actual loss severity, review time, burst behavior, maintenance, calibrated error rates and authority implementation remain unresolved application inputs. There is no essential production-of-material blocker. The checks do not establish learner mastery or authorize deployment.

Field Value ID C05 answers Title Autonomy decision: hints, solutions and checks Revision 1.0 Date 2026-11-14 Prerequisites F02/F03, S03/S06, A05; SDE_C05.md Capability developed Audit a conditional autonomy recommendation Source-check status Same inspected primary passages and limits as the core memo Experiment status Python script below executed successfully; synthetic inputs and sequential authority model only Read SDE_C05.md first. These are worked solutions, not attributed learner answers.

Hint: price human minutes before adding losses, and use daily minutes for capacity. W costs 0.20 + 0.50×1 + 20×0.020 + 5×0.080 = 1.50 units per eligible case. S costs 0.35 + 2 + 0.20 + 0.10 = 2.65. A costs 0.80 + 0.20 + 0.30 + 0.30 + 0.15 = 1.75. Multiply by 1,000 for daily expected costs of 1,500, 2,650 and 1,750. Human demands are 1,000, 4,000 and 400 minutes. At 1,200 minutes, W and A meet the planning gates; choose W. At 500, only A does; conditionally choose A. All three assigned timely probabilities meet the 0.90 floor, but quality does not make unavailable staff appear. The probabilities are hypothetical full-system assumptions, not outputs derived from total daily capacity. Actual scheduling must validate them. Assessment criterion: correct recommendation plus explicit conditionality. “A is best because agents are faster” supplies neither evidence nor a comparable job.

Hint: keep every A term except wrong-route loss fixed. A’s fixed terms sum to 1.45, so 1.45 + 20x = 1.50 gives x=0.0025. Below 0.25%, A is cheaper if all gates still pass; at equality prefer simpler W. At the original 1.5%, A costs 0.25 more per case. A’s allocated maintenance alone is 0.30; dropping it without justification would change the recommendation by changing the accounting premise. At 500 minutes, cheap W is still infeasible. Conversely A’s higher error or oversight demand could make every option inadequate. Expected loss averages consequences; it does not price permission violations into acceptability. Case independence is not required to sum expected costs. It would matter to a claim about confidence bounds or daily aggregate variability.

Hint: distinguish a committed result from the caller’s knowledge of it. K commits route Q1 for revision 3 but its reply is lost. The caller cannot infer failure. Identical K retrieves the receipt if current read permission permits. K with Q2 conflicts, while a fresh key targeting the occupied slot is rejected. If revision changes before an uncommitted request, stale evidence cannot create a route. Revocation before commit denies; revocation after commit does not erase the historical event. A denied receipt read creates no new effect and does not justify an alternate mutation. Assessment criterion: no fresh operation identity used merely to bypass uncertainty, stale evidence, permission or occupancy. The script models an atomic sequential transition, not a database concurrency protocol, authentication stack or network cancellation implementation. Real tests must exercise those boundaries and all alternate write paths.

Hint: emitted suggestions are a post-treatment subset. 99 correct suggestions among 100 emitted could coexist with 900 unresolved offered cases. That is 99% correctness among outputs but at most 9.9% correct on-time completion over 1,000 eligible cases, before checking human action and deadline. A fair comparison freezes eligibility at arrival, uses the same cases and evidence in offline replay, and includes refusals, retries, human handling and queue delay in full-system results. Report correct-on-time counts, wrong routes, unresolved cases, minutes, costs and authority failures separately. For a live experiment, shared queues can make one invoice’s assignment affect another’s delay. Choose a stable assignment unit consistent with that interference, such as the team, and plan uncertainty analysis at that unit. Neither paired replay nor a small zero-incident sample certifies security. R03’s cited sections in the core support predeclared hypotheses, metrics and attention to randomization units; these particular invoice procedures are original applications.

Hint: apply gates before minimizing cost. At 500 minutes, failed authority verification excludes A. W and S exceed capacity, so the answer is no adequate candidate at full volume. If instead A needs 600 review minutes, the same conclusion follows. An authorized intake reduction or staffing increase would be a separately declared new constraint. Sending payment, omitting evidence or counting only accepted work would change the task covertly. Assessment criterion: preserve the envelope even when that yields an operationally inconvenient answer. No learner score is recorded.

Run the following with Python 3. It uses exact rational arithmetic for monetary boundaries. The 1,501 capacity cases test the decision rule, not a staffing simulation. The authority fixture exposes a single atomic transition for teaching; it does not claim to implement distributed transactions. from fractions import Fraction as F from itertools import product rows = { 'W': (F('.20'), F('1'), F('0'), F('.020'), F('.080')), 'S': (F('.35'), F('4'), F('0'), F('.010'), F('.020')), 'A': (F('.80'), F('.4'), F('.30'), F('.015'), F('.030')), } def cost(row): compute, minutes, maintenance, wrong, late = row return compute + F('.5')*minutes + maintenance + 20*wrong + 5*late def choose(capacity, authority=True, agent_minutes=F('.4')): candidates = [] for name, row in rows.items(): minutes = agent_minutes if name == 'A' else row[1] verified = authority if name == 'A' else True if verified and 1000*minutes <= capacity and 1-row[3]-row[4] >= F('.9'): candidates.append(name) return min(candidates, key=lambda name: (cost(rows[name]), name)) if candidates else None assert [cost(r) for r in rows.values()] == [F('1.5'), F('2.65'), F('1.75')] assert [1000*r[1] for r in rows.values()] == [1000, 4000, 400] assert choose(1200) == 'W' and choose(500) == 'A' assert choose(500, authority=False) is None assert choose(500, agent_minutes=F('.6')) is None threshold = (F('1.5')-F('1.45'))/20 assert threshold == F('.0025') assert F('1.45')+20*(threshold-F('.0001')) < F('1.5') assert F('1.45')+20*(threshold+F('.0001')) > F('1.5') for cap in range(1501): expected = None if cap < 400 else ('A' if cap < 1000 else 'W') assert choose(cap) == expected assert F(99,100) == F('.99') and F(99,1000) == F('.099') class Authority: def __init__(self): self.revision, self.epoch = 3, 7 self.grant, self.read = True, True self.slot, self.receipts, self.effects = None, {}, 0 def route(self, key, payload, authenticated=True, tenant=True, allowed=True, evidence=True): # payload is (revision, epoch, queue); state transition is atomic here. if not authenticated or not tenant: return 'denied' if key in self.receipts: if not self.read: return 'denied' return 'receipt' if self.receipts[key] == payload else 'conflict' if not (self.grant and allowed and evidence): return 'denied' if payload[:2] != (self.revision, self.epoch): return 'stale' if payload[2] not in ('Q1', 'Q2'): return 'denied' if self.slot is not None: return 'occupied' self.slot = payload self.receipts[key] = payload self.effects += 1 return 'committed' p = (3, 7, 'Q1') a = Authority() assert a.route('K', p) == 'committed' # simulate losing this reply assert a.route('K', p) == 'receipt' assert a.route('K', (3,7,'Q2')) == 'conflict' assert a.route('OTHER', p) == 'occupied' a.grant = False assert a.route('K', p) == 'receipt' # existing history, separate read permission assert a.route('NEW', p) == 'denied' a.read = False assert a.route('K', p) == 'denied' and a.effects == 1 b = Authority() b.revision = 4 assert b.route('K', p) == 'stale' and b.effects == 0 for flags in product((False, True), repeat=4): c = Authority() result = c.route('K', p, *flags) assert (result == 'committed') == all(flags) assert c.effects == int(all(flags)) print('PASS: ledgers, thresholds, 1501 capacity cases, recovery trace, 16 guard combinations') The script passed on 2026-11-14. Checks also covered five exercise/answer mappings, required metadata, companion links, balanced fences and absence of draft placeholders. No model inference, production workload, live mutation, concurrency stress test or learner assessment occurred. Unknown real rates and implementation behavior remain explicitly open in the memo.

title: How should architecture respond when a supplier changes?

sections.section: How should architecture respond when a supplier changes?
sections.text: Field Value ID C06 Title Supplier change without losing evidence or control Revision 1.0 Date 2026-11-15 Prerequisites S02/S06, A03–A05, B02/B03 Capability developed Price a migration, preserve authority and evidence, and test whether an advantage survives bundling Source-check status R15 §2.2, R11 §I.A.3(c), R21 packaging section inspected Experiment status Synthetic ledger, sensitivity, paired outcomes and migration-manifest checks executed; no supplier integration or production trial

Retain the incumbent for the initial six-month horizon, while keeping the evidence store, evaluation cases and permission checks under our control. Do not build a universal provider abstraction in advance. Implement a narrow replacement boundary around the specific inference operation. When the incumbent’s recurring charge increases enough, switch the inference component after validating the replacement against the same complete task. Adopting a bundled workflow is a different option because it changes more than inference. The recurring fictional job is preparing invoice evidence for a reviewer: identify the applicable revision, extract the requested reference, attach exact supporting locators and deliver a supported package within one business day. No candidate may approve payment. This memo returns to A05’s evidence-preparation boundary; it does not silently inherit C05’s additional internal routing action. All three options have the same eligible population, evidence rights, output contract, deadline and authority restrictions. A supplier change could mean a price change, model retirement, altered API behavior or a newly bundled feature. Our example changes only a recurring fee. It is not news about any real provider, and all monetary, workload and performance inputs are hypothetical. Business-day completion includes human handling and queues; a fast model response alone is not success.

sections.section: What must remain ours to control?
sections.text: A portable interface is a stable description of the job, not a guarantee of equal behavior. For one inference operation, accept a task ID, schema version, exact evidence references and bounded input; return typed claims, supporting references, unresolved status and usage observations. A provider adapter maps that contract to a particular API. It must expose unsupported capabilities instead of inventing a successful approximation. Asset or rule Authority and migration treatment Source bytes and revision manifests Retain immutable originals and exact document/revision identities; verify export and restore Tenant grants and disclosure policy Enforce in our authority boundary before evidence leaves scope; recheck according to declared revocation rules Extracted facts and locators Keep extractor/rendering versions; a changed extraction creates a new revision under S02’s convention Retrieval index Treat as derived state with a named encoder/chunker/configuration; rebuild and evaluate when incompatible Model prompts and adapter mapping Version explicitly; revise per provider while preserving task semantics Evaluation cases and labels Retain permitted source snapshots, rubrics and holdouts; do not assume data reuse rights Action receipts and operation identity Keep independent of inference vendor; an inference retry cannot become a new business approval S02’s digest checks bytes, but a digest without the bytes cannot restore a source page. Exporting final answers alone loses the ability to inspect what supported them. A03 separates corpus, candidates, supplied context and claims; preserve these intermediate identities so a migration regression can be located. R15 §2.2 describes document/query encoders and inner-product retrieval. That mechanism motivates a concrete compatibility question: do the new query representations match the stored document representations? Equal vector dimensions alone do not answer it. The paper does not establish interoperability between arbitrary providers. R11 §I.A.3(c) calls for authority checks across access paths, including recovery, and cautions about remembered authorization decisions. Our migration application is to test export, replay, support access and rollback as protected paths too. A correctly scoped normal endpoint is insufficient if an export script reads every tenant. These are design obligations, not claims of certification.

Use 1,000 eligible cases per month and six months of service. Labor is valued at 0.50 U/minute. U is a fictional common cost unit. Assume each candidate has passed permission, evidence and deadline gates with at least 95% correct on-time completion under realistic workload. That equal-adequacy premise is provisional and must be tested; the table is a decision model, not results of such a test. Input I: retain incumbent R: replace inference B: adopt supplier bundle One-time migration/validation cost 0 U 900 U 300 U Monthly supplier/infrastructure charge 400 U 250 U 0 U incremental Customer handling minutes/case 2.0 2.2 3.5 Monthly incremental maintenance 100 U 150 U 50 U Control change None Adapter/inference only Retrieval and workflow move to bundle The incumbent’s old setup cost is sunk and excluded. Replacement setup includes mapping, rebuild, evaluation, training and cutover effort. The bundle’s subscription is already purchased for unrelated use, so zero is its incremental charge in this scenario; its labor and maintenance are not free. Recurring human minutes include verification and exceptions, including failures. Maintenance excludes those minutes. Common baseline costs cancel; any noncommon export, overlap or exit fee must be added. Cost is from the customer’s decision perspective, not the supplier’s margin. Define monthly cost M = supplier + cases × minutes × 0.50 + maintenance, then horizon cost T = setup + H × M. Monthly totals are I=1,500, R=1,500 and B=1,800 U. Six-month totals are 9,000, 9,900 and 11,100 U. Retaining I is cheapest among assumed-adequate choices. R’s lower API bill is exactly consumed by 100 U extra handling and 50 U extra maintenance each month; setup then makes it more expensive. B’s free feature does not compensate for extra work. This does not mean switching is always wasteful. It means the reason must survive a complete ledger. No extra monetary value is assigned to optionality here. If planned retirement makes retention impossible, that becomes a feasibility constraint and the comparison must be revised explicitly. Likewise, a cost-only winner cannot excuse worse evidence or forbidden disclosure.

sections.section: One constraint changes: the incumbent fee
sections.text: Change I’s monthly supplier charge from 400 to 700 U, holding everything else fixed. I now costs 1,800 U/month and 10,800 U over six months. R remains 9,900 and B remains 11,100. Revise the choice to R, conditional on the same adequacy gates. R saves 900 U across the horizon after its setup cost. Let x be I’s monthly charge. Then T(I)=6(x+1,100). Equality with R occurs at x=550 U. Above that threshold R is cheaper; at equality retain I to avoid unnecessary migration. The changed x=700 gives recurring savings of 300 U/month, recovering 900 U setup after three full months. For an assured horizon shorter than three months, I is cheaper; at three months the totals tie. This is deterministic accounting under assigned inputs, not a forecast of supplier prices or customer tenure. A different single change illustrates bundling pressure without altering the main scenario. At the original incumbent fee, what bundle handling time t would tie I? Solve 300+6(1,000×0.50t+50)=9,000, giving t=2.8 minutes/case. Below that, an adequate bundle beats I. The additional labor can therefore be measured directly; a claim that “our wrapper is defensible” is irrelevant if the bundle performs the full job with less total cost.

sections.section: Port the evaluation, then rerun it
sections.text: Evaluation portability means carrying the question, population, evidence snapshots and scoring procedure across candidates. It does not mean copying the incumbent’s benchmark score onto the replacement. Freeze eligibility before execution. Each invoice and its retries form one case. Include missing evidence, conflicting revisions, long inputs, unfamiliar layouts, forbidden tenant requests and tool failures. Give candidates access to the same authorized corpus, not necessarily identical retrieval results: retrieval is part of the bundle’s behavior. Use two comparisons. First compare complete deployed candidates under the same service contract. Second, for diagnosis, supply identical sufficient evidence to compatible generators to separate generation from retrieval. Label the second as an intervention; it removes a failure mode the actual deployment may still have. Hold tuning examples apart from the final comparison and record every adapter/model/index version. A constructed paired ledger of 100 cases has 92 successes for both I and R, 4 for I only, 3 for R only and 1 for neither. I succeeds on 96, R on 95. Both meet the assigned 95% sample threshold, but these counts do not prove population adequacy. The same inputs reveal a net loss of one case for R; unpaired headline scores would hide which tasks regressed. Review discordant cases and appropriate uncertainty before changing the production boundary. This is a teaching fixture, not a model benchmark. A04 reminds us to measure resources under actual input/output lengths and offered load. Token counts, cache behavior and context truncation belong to a specific configuration. Compare charged usage and full arrival-to-result delay, including failures, rather than assuming a token or a cache hit has the same cost across suppliers. A05 adds bounded retries and typed unresolved outcomes. An adapter must not conceal repeated calls, timeout fallback or dropped citations to make the schemas look identical.

sections.section: A migration that can be stopped
sections.text: Use a staged plan with explicit exit conditions: Export immutable sources, revisions, facts, grants and evaluation manifests under authorized scope. Verify counts, exact identities and byte digests; restore into an isolated environment. Count agreement alone cannot detect swapped contents. Build replacement derived state under a new configuration identity. Replay frozen cases without business effects. Compare support, permissions, deadlines and full cost, including difficult subgroups. Keep one authoritative publication path. Shadow inference may produce candidate drafts, but it does not create approvals or alter published evidence. Mark outputs by configuration and source revision. Admit a bounded rollout only after gates pass. Keep the old compatible path available for the declared rollback window. Stop on unauthorized access, unresolvable provenance or a predeclared service regression. Retire old credentials and derived stores after reconciliation and retention obligations are satisfied. Preserve historical evidence still referenced by prior decisions. Suppose a new extractor finishes revision 4 while the published head still points to revision 3. A crash before the atomic head change leaves 3 current and 4 unreferenced; recovery must not publish a partial 4. If the head change commits, it must refer to a complete durable revision. This applies S02’s publication rule. Rolling back code does not justify rewriting historical evidence to look as if the new extractor never ran. A lost inference reply may permit another bounded read-only inference call, but duplicate cost and latency remain charged. If future designs add external effects, their receipts and unknown outcomes require their own reconciliation; changing model vendors cannot solve that problem. Failover also is not independent protection when both paths rely on the same unavailable source store or compromised permission service.

sections.section: Does the advantage survive the bundle?
sections.text: R21’s packaging discussion distinguishes feature and usage access across offers. It does not prove that a particular bundle will win or lose. B03 already showed that a cheaper alternative can eliminate the price interval that sustains an offer. Here the defensible hypothesis is narrower: our evidence mapping, exception handling and control integration reduce correct-completion effort enough to justify their cost. Test that hypothesis with the bundle’s complete workflow, permitted exports and the customer’s actual review effort. Reject it if the bundle satisfies the same contract below the total-cost threshold. A reusable evaluation corpus helps only when its rights, relevance and ability to detect consequential failures hold. Proprietary records do not automatically create an advantage. A common JSON interface can reduce adapter work while leaving retrieval tuning, evaluation, operations and user retraining expensive.

Optional written work, with hints and solutions in SDE_C06_answers.md: Rebuild monthly/horizon ledgers and choices before and after the fee change. Derive fee, horizon and bundle-labor thresholds; identify costs excluded by the premises. Explain what the paired 100-case ledger proves and what it cannot prove. Repair an export that has all document IDs but omits one referenced source revision; explain why a matching row count is insufficient. Specify cutover, rollback and authority boundaries, and one observation that disproves the claimed advantage. Reference card: own evidence identities and policy → expose a narrow inference contract → price all migration and recurring work → port the evaluation specification → rerun behavior and load checks → publish only complete revisions → judge the bundle by the complete customer job. Evidence Inspected locator and use Limitation R15: Lewis et al., RAG §2.2, printed p.3: query/document encoders and inner-product retrieval Mechanism only; no arbitrary embedding compatibility claim R11: Saltzer and Schroeder §I.A.3(c): complete mediation and cached authority Design principle, not validation of this migration R21: Stripe / Patrick McKenzie Pricing and packaging for things with no physical form Practitioner guidance, not supplier economics or demand data Original synthesis All tables, thresholds, traces and checks here Hypothetical inputs, not observed production results Actual fees, export rights, retention requirements, rebuild time, error rates, operator capacity and customer handling remain application inputs. No essential blocker remains for producing this material. Next is Audit D across the completed curriculum; learner mastery remains unassessed.

Field Value ID C06 answers Title Supplier-change decision: hints and checks Revision 1.0 Date 2026-11-15 Prerequisites S02/S06, A03–A05, B02/B03; SDE_C06.md Capability developed Audit migration costs, evaluation claims and evidence continuity Source-check status Uses the primary passage locators and limitations in the core memo Experiment status Embedded Python executed; synthetic accounting, paired counts and manifest validation only Read SDE_C06.md before these optional solutions. No response or score is attributed to the learner.

Hint: convert minutes into cost, then add setup once. At 1,000 cases and 0.50 U/minute, recurring labor is I=1,000, R=1,100 and B=1,750 U/month. Supplier plus labor plus incremental maintenance is therefore 1,500, 1,500 and 1,800 U/month. Six months plus setup gives 9,000, 9,900 and 11,100 U. Retain I under the equal-adequacy premise. After only I’s fee becomes 700, its monthly total is 1,800 and horizon total 10,800. R becomes the cheaper adequate choice at 9,900. Savings are 900 U after setup. If R fails the authority or quality gate, the cost comparison cannot authorize migration. If I remains adequate, it stays available at its higher cost; if neither candidate is adequate, state that instead of weakening the task. Assessment criterion: include human work, maintenance and setup, state the horizon, and separate customer cost from supplier margin. These are new C06 inputs, not replacements for B03’s scenario.

Hint: solve equal total costs with just one variable free. For the fee, 6(x+1100)=9900 yields x=550 U/month. R is cheaper strictly above 550 at six months; at equality retain I. At x=700, compare 1800H with 900+1500H: equality is H=3. Only horizons longer than three months recover setup with a strict saving. Monthly payment timing and discounting are excluded from this simple model. For bundle handling, 300+6(500t+50)=9000 gives t=2.8. Below that B is cheaper at the original I fee, provided all gates hold. The threshold is not evidence that such handling time is achievable. A measured extra export fee, migration overlap, training effort or maintenance cost moves the threshold. Add each in the correct period and avoid double-counting effort already included in setup. Assessment criterion: name the fixed assumptions. Quoting a break-even number without its horizon or workload makes it unusable.

Hint: totals include successes shared by both arms. I has 92+4=96 successes and R has 92+3=95. There are seven discordant cases; R gains three and loses four. The paired sample difference is −1 percentage point for R. One shared failure is still in the denominator of 100. Both meet a 95% observed sample floor, but sampling uncertainty, representativeness and dependence remain unresolved. This fixture validates arithmetic only. It does not establish that either real supplier meets a 95% population service objective. Inspect the seven disagreements, preserve held-out evaluation, analyze the relevant sampling unit and test complete workflows under load. Identical evidence supplied directly to both generators is useful diagnosis but bypasses deployed retrieval and cannot replace the whole-system comparison.

Hint: references identify revisions, not just logical documents. Suppose current D17/3 is exported but an old decision references D17/2. Exporting another unrelated revision to keep the total row count unchanged does not repair the missing historical reference. Recover the authorized immutable bytes and manifest for D17/2, validate its digest and locator interpretation, and rerun reference validation. If recovery is impossible, mark the historical evidence gap; do not relabel D17/3 as revision 2. A digest match verifies bytes relative to a trusted expected digest; it does not prove the trusted manifest itself is correct or that access was authorized. The following fixture checks exact keys, byte digests and reference closure. It uses tiny invented bytes, not an actual storage export or encryption/access-control implementation.

sections.section: 5. Cutover, rollback and the advantage claim
sections.text: Hint: the replaceable component and authoritative state have different lifecycles. Shadow execution writes no business effects. A new complete revision becomes current only at the atomic publication boundary. Before publication, a crash leaves the previous head; after publication, the new head must resolve to complete durable evidence. A rollback changes future execution or a valid head under the declared protocol; it never rewrites prior receipts or their evidence. Permission checks cover export, recovery and support paths as well as ordinary requests. The claimed advantage is disproved for this scenario if the bundle meets the same evidence, authority and deadline gates while reducing handling below 2.8 minutes at its assigned costs. Do not respond by counting only the incumbent’s successful cases or by trapping customer records. Usable exports and preserved evidence make the comparison more honest. An adapter’s syntactic compatibility alone does not prove semantic, operational or economic portability.

Run with Python 3. All money uses exact rational arithmetic. The fee sweep checks 1,001 choices; the horizon sweep checks 12 month values. The validator tests a good export, a missing revision, corrupted bytes and a same-count replacement that loses a referenced revision. from fractions import Fraction as F from hashlib import sha256 N, wage = 1000, F('.5') def monthly(fee, minutes, maintenance): return fee + N*wage*minutes + maintenance mI = monthly(400, F(2), 100) mR = monthly(250, F('2.2'), 150) mB = monthly(0, F('3.5'), 50) assert (mI,mR,mB) == (1500,1500,1800) assert (6*mI,900+6*mR,300+6*mB) == (9000,9900,11100) assert 6*monthly(700,F(2),100) == 10800 fee_threshold = F(9900,6)-1100 assert fee_threshold == 550 bundle_threshold = (F(9000-300,6)-50)/(N*wage) assert bundle_threshold == F('2.8') for fee in range(1001): totals = {'I':6*(fee+1100), 'R':9900, 'B':11100} winner = min(totals, key=totals.get) # insertion order retains I at a tie assert winner == ('I' if fee <= 550 else 'R') for months in range(1,13): saving = 1800*months-(900+1500*months) assert (saving>0) == (months>3) assert (saving==0) == (months==3) assert 300+6*monthly(0,bundle_threshold,50) == 9000 assert 300+6*monthly(0,bundle_threshold-F('.01'),50) < 9000 assert 300+6*monthly(0,bundle_threshold+F('.01'),50) > 9000 both, only_i, only_r, neither = 92,4,3,1 assert both+only_i+only_r+neither == 100 assert (both+only_i,both+only_r) == (96,95) assert F(only_r-only_i,100) == F('-0.01') key2, key3 = ('A','D17',2), ('A','D17',3) expected_bytes = {key2:b'reference X',key3:b'reference Y'} trusted = {k:sha256(v).hexdigest() for k,v in expected_bytes.items()} references = {key2,key3} def valid_export(export): return (set(export)==set(trusted) and references <= set(export) and all(sha256(export[k]).hexdigest()==trusted[k] for k in trusted)) assert valid_export(expected_bytes) missing = {key3:expected_bytes[key3]} assert not valid_export(missing) corrupt = dict(expected_bytes); corrupt[key2]=b'reference Z' assert not valid_export(corrupt) swapped = dict(missing); swapped[('A','D99',2)]=b'reference X' assert len(swapped)==len(expected_bytes) and not valid_export(swapped) # Recovery model: publication may point only to a complete revision. for committed in (False,True): durable = {key2,key3} head = key3 if committed else key2 assert head in durable and references <= durable print('PASS: exact ledgers; 1001 fee cases; 12 horizons; paired counts; 4 export fixtures; 2 publication states') Executed successfully on 2026-11-15. Metadata, five exercise/answer mappings, companion links, fences and placeholder checks also passed. These finite fixtures do not exercise a real supplier, concurrency protocol, recovery log, model or live migration. Actual export rights, service quality, costs and operational ownership require evidence before applying the recommendation.
This note compresses the library into a reusable engineering method. It is a map, not a replacement for the worked traces.

sections.section: 1. Define the job before optimizing it
sections.text: A system can look better because its denominator changed. State the eligible population, task identity, output contract, deadline, quality rule and missing-outcome policy before comparing designs. Count offered work, unresolved work, retries and late results. Component accuracy, throughput or token cost is meaningful only after connecting it to a complete outcome. Use F02 for probabilities and expected loss, F03 for fair measurement, and B02 for cost per useful result.

sections.section: 2. Name the invariant and the transition boundary
sections.text: An invariant is a condition that must hold at every protected committed boundary. A correct transition checks its premises and changes protected state atomically. Checking before the boundary and acting later creates a race. A crash-safe write can still commit a decision based on stale information. Ask: What state is protected? Which transition can change it? Which reads are premises of that transition? Can two actors make individually valid but jointly invalid decisions? Which alternate path bypasses the guard? See F01, S03, C01 and S06.

Logical object, revision, attempt, operation and business obligation are different identities. Keep immutable source bytes and exact revision references when later decisions must remain explainable. A digest can verify retrieved bytes but cannot replace the bytes. A “retry” with a new operation identity may duplicate an effect. For an unknown outcome, reconcile the original identity before retrying. A historical receipt proves what happened; permission to read it and permission to create a new effect are separate questions. See S02, S04, C01 and C06.

Model output, user input and tool observations are proposals or data. Authority comes from authenticated context and current policy. Enforce tenant, action, object, revision, epoch, evidence and slot conditions at the effect boundary. A model-supplied actor field is not identity. A timeout is not permission, and an availability target cannot authorize disclosure. Use fail-safe defaults, complete mediation and least privilege as design checks. Test recovery tools, exports, repair scripts and administrative paths, not only the normal UI. See S06, A05, C04 and C05.

A fact may exist in the corpus and still be absent from the index. A retrieved passage may be excluded from context. A cited passage may not support the claim. A supported claim may use a stale revision or be disclosed to the wrong principal. Inspect the chain: available source → eligible source → retrieved candidate → supplied context → claim → supported output → permitted disclosure Evaluation should preserve these intermediate artifacts so a failure can be located. Retrieval makes evidence available; it does not guarantee use, truth or permission. See A03 and C06.

sections.section: 6. Treat evaluation as a deployment model
sections.text: Random rows are often not independent deployment cases. Revisions, templates, organizations, suppliers and reviewer queues can create leakage or interference. Freeze tuning before final evaluation. Use the same cases for paired comparisons when possible, and choose the assignment unit around spillovers. Report uncertainty under the assumptions of the procedure. Randomization does not automatically justify every interval. Repeated retries of one case do not create independent evidence. See F03, A01, A05 and C02.

Track operations, bytes, working set, retained state, temporary workspace and queues separately. Memory feasibility does not establish latency. Throughput does not establish per-request deadlines. Average demand does not reconstruct bursts. Faster prompt processing may have little effect when decoding dominates. For LLM serving, separate weights, KV state and other memory; state the configuration behind every byte estimate. Count all offered work and define the clock. “Autoscaling” is incomplete without startup and routing evidence. See S01, S05, A04 and C03.

Build mutually exclusive cost categories. Include failed attempts, review, support, idle purchased capacity, maintenance, setup, acquisition and dispute work where relevant. Divide by the unit the decision actually values. Cost per token, call or VM can improve while cost per verified timely result gets worse. Customer capacity value is not automatically cash savings. Contribution is not profit. A positive average can hide a capacity tier or severe loss. A free bundled feature can still impose workflow labor. See B01, B02, B03, C03 and C04.

sections.section: 9. Choose the least complex adequate autonomy
sections.text: Autonomy describes who chooses the next step; authority describes what effects are permitted. A deterministic workflow may mutate state. A suggestion-only assistant may consume large human capacity. An action-taking agent can be acceptable only within an externally enforced action set, budget and effect boundary. Apply gates in order: Authority and evidence integrity. Quality and deadline. Capacity. Expected loss and complete cost. Simplicity and operational burden. See A05 and C05.

sections.section: 10. Port the decision specification, then retest behavior
sections.text: A common provider interface reduces adapter work but does not make retrieval, quality, latency, cost or permissions equivalent. Own source identities, grants, evaluation cases and effect receipts when those are central to the product. Treat indexes and caches as versioned derived state. During migration, export and restore evidence, rebuild derived state under a new configuration identity, shadow without effects, publish only complete revisions, and retain rollback long enough to reconcile. Judge a bundle by the complete customer job. See C06.

For any architecture or product choice, write: Decision: the action and owner. Complete job: population, identity, output, deadline and success. Hard gates: authority, evidence, safety, quality and capacity. Options: credible complete systems under shared assumptions. Model: resources, probabilities, consequences and costs. Trace: one normal path, one failure and one counterexample. Changed constraint: alter one premise and revise honestly. Falsifier: evidence that overturns the recommendation. Unknowns: inputs requiring measurement or stakeholder authority. That template is the compact answer to the curriculum’s central question.

New work should deepen a useful decision, connect to existing prerequisites and include inspected primary evidence, a concrete mechanism, counterexamples, separate worked practice and executed checks where appropriate.

title: Invariants, algorithms, and the cost of computation

sections.section: Invariants, algorithms, and the cost of computation
sections.text: Field Value ID / revision F01 / 1.0 Date 2026-11-02 Prerequisites Basic loops and equality; sets and induction bridge below Capability developed Derive an optimization, prove its correctness, and state its cost assumptions Source-check status R01 lecture notes 1, 2 and 4 opened; precise passages listed in §9 Experiment status Python equivalents and bounded exhaustive checks executed; see answer file for reproduction and scope State produced; formal curriculum Audit A still pending Companion Hints and worked answers

sections.section: 1. The decision: what information makes repeated work unnecessary?
sections.text: You receive a batch of document identifiers and need to know whether any identifier appears twice. This is a fictional study case. A duplicate identifier means equal keys under a declared rule; it does not automatically mean two documents contain identical text or two business actions are interchangeable. The useful question is: What can I retain from the processed input so that the next decision is cheaper? Start with a correct, straightforward procedure. Treat its repeated work as evidence about what information is missing. Then choose a representation that answers the repeated question efficiently. This pack develops one example deeply. Named algorithm patterns become easier to learn when you can explain why information may safely be retained or discarded. No diagnostic response or prior mathematical fluency is assumed.

sections.section: 2. A small notation bridge and a precise contract
sections.text: A sequence preserves order: [8, 3, 6, 3]. A set records membership without multiplicity: {8, 3, 6}. The expression x in S asks whether S contains x. A prefix a[0:k] contains positions 0 through k−1; it excludes position k. When k=0, the prefix is empty. An invariant is a statement that remains true at a particular program boundary. Specify that boundary: “before each outer iteration” is meaningful; “the values are correct” is too vague to check. An induction proof establishes a starting case and shows why one valid step preserves the claim. Repeating that argument covers every iteration, however large the input becomes. Our contract: Input: a finite sequence of n immutable keys, with a stable equality rule. Output: True exactly when there exist different positions i and j with equal keys. Empty and one-element sequences return False. The input stays unchanged; the output need not identify the matching positions. For cost analysis initially assume each key fits in a constant number of machine words, equality and hashing cost constant time, and array access costs constant time. These are model premises, not measured facts about arbitrary document strings. Long text and custom equality require another cost model.

sections.section: 3. Build the baseline and count its actual work
sections.text: Compare each new key with every earlier key: def duplicate_pairs(a): for j in range(len(a)): for i in range(j): if a[i] == a[j]: return True return False The inner loop deliberately stops before j, so a key never matches itself. Before outer iteration j, if the function has not returned, the first j keys are pairwise distinct. During that iteration, the inner loop checks every possible earlier partner of a[j]. If a match is found, it supplies two different positions. If none is found, the prefix of length j+1 remains distinct. At termination the prefix is the whole sequence, so False is justified. The finite loop bounds establish termination separately from correctness. Count equality comparisons on an all-distinct input. The iterations perform 0, 1, 2, …, n−1 comparisons. Pair this sum with its reverse: each of the n positions sums to n−1. Therefore 2C(n)=n(n−1),C(n)=n(n−1)2. This is a derivation for this procedure, not a benchmark. At n=1,000 there are 499,500 comparisons; at n=2,000 there are 1,999,000. Doubling n almost quadruples the work. The no-duplicate case is worst-case quadratic, written Θ(n²). Θ describes a tight growth bound up to constant factors for sufficiently large n; O gives an upper bound. Neither notation states milliseconds. Early termination matters. [8, 8] needs one comparison; [8, 3, 6, 3] needs five: one at j=1, two at j=2, then two at j=3. A single fast example cannot establish a general cost claim. The baseline uses O(1) auxiliary space: the input already exists, and only loop indices and temporary references are added.

sections.section: 4. Derive remembered state before choosing a container
sections.text: At every step the expensive question is the same: “Does the next key occur anywhere in the prefix?” Repeated scanning reconstructs membership from scratch. For a yes/no answer, the earlier order and exact occurrence counts are irrelevant. The set of earlier keys is sufficient information. def duplicate_seen(a): seen = set() for x in a: if x in seen: return True seen.add(x) return False Here set() is an illustrative Python implementation. The proof depends on the abstract operations membership and insertion. The performance depends on how those operations are implemented. A container named “set” could internally scan a list; naming the interface does not create a speedup. R01 lecture 2 makes this interface/representation distinction explicit. Next position Key Set before membership check Result 0 8 {} Absent; insert 8 1 3 {8} Absent; insert 3 2 6 {8, 3} Absent; insert 6 3 3 {8, 3, 6} Present; return True The set does not tell us which earlier position contained 3. That information was deliberately discarded because our contract does not ask for it. A changed output contract may require a map from key to earlier index. Use the invariant: Before processing position k, if the algorithm is still running, seen equals the set of keys in a[0:k], and that prefix has no duplicates. At k=0 both claims hold. If the current key is in seen, the membership claim guarantees an earlier equal key, so returning True is sound. If it is absent, inserting it preserves exact membership and distinctness for the next prefix. If the loop ends, all n keys were processed without a repeat. Thus False is sound too. Conversely, if a duplicate exists, its later occurrence must encounter the earlier one in seen; the algorithm cannot miss it. A common bug inserts first, then checks membership. That checks against a state already containing the current item. A singleton [8] exposes the false positive. This is why an invariant belongs to a precise line boundary: changing statement order changes what the state means.

An all-distinct input causes n membership calls and n insertion calls. If membership has expected constant cost and insertion has expected amortized constant cost, the total is expected O(n), with O(n) stored keys. With mandatory inspection of n keys on a distinct input, this becomes expected Θ(n) under our model. The expectation concerns the hashing model; it does not mean every input distribution has been measured. “Amortized” distributes occasional rebuilding costs across a sequence of operations. “Expected” averages over specified randomness. These are different qualifications. One expensive insertion can coexist with a linear expected total. R01 lecture 4, page 4, supplies the hash-table conditions; this pack does not claim that every language runtime implements exactly that design. A hash routes a key to a candidate storage location. Equal hashes do not establish equal keys. Consider a hypothetical table using h(x)=x mod 10: 1 and 11 route to the same bucket but are different. A correct collision-handling table retains enough information to compare actual keys. Keeping only these hash values would incorrectly report a duplicate. In a simple chained table, suppose every distinct key routes to one bucket. The next membership query scans an ever-longer chain. The accumulated work can again grow quadratically. Correctness survives if equality is checked; the promised performance does not. A constant hash is a concrete counterexample to an unconditional “hashing makes this linear” claim. Other boundaries require explicit decisions: If hashing a previously unseen string examines L characters, charging O(1) per key hides input-reading work. Include string lengths in the model and measure the target implementation. Equality and hashing must agree: keys considered equal must route compatibly. Keys must not change their relevant identity while stored. The mathematical contract assumes equality behaves consistently. Special numeric values, case folding, whitespace, and document revisions need a defined business rule before a container can enforce it. Exhausting memory is possible. An online algorithm can process one key at a time while still retaining growing state.

sections.section: 6. Change the constraint and revisit the representation
sections.text: Constraint Defensible option Cost or changed guarantee Evidence that could reverse the choice Small batch, tight auxiliary memory Pairwise baseline Θ(n²) worst-case comparisons; O(1) extra space Actual batch sizes or latency become unacceptable Large batch, sufficient memory, suitable keys Remembered membership with a hash set Expected linear total under stated conditions; O(n) extra keys Measured memory, collision behavior, key costs Known domain of U integer IDs U membership flags indexed by ID Initialize U flags, then scan: O(U+n) time; O(U) flags Domain grows or IDs become sparse/unbounded Only last W items matter Explicit rolling-window contract May forget older duplicates; must manage expiration correctly Requirement actually means “ever seen” Arbitrary long stream, exact all-history answer Retain enough history, possibly externally Memory or external-storage cost grows with information retained Replays, bounded domain, approximation, or time-window requirements become acceptable The domain option follows directly from indexing: initialize every flag to false; on each valid ID inspect its flag, then set it. Domain validation is part of the contract. A tiny domain can make this attractive even when a general-purpose hash table is available. Bounded memory cannot be justified by silently forgetting old values. If a cache retains only the previous two keys, [1, 2, 3, 1] loses the first 1 before the last arrives. It answers a different question. For an exact deterministic all-history membership state over a finite universe, different seen subsets must be distinguishable: choose a key in their symmetric difference and append it; one history now contains a duplicate and the other does not. With at most b bits there are at most 2^b states. More distinguishable subsets than states force an error. This is an original counting argument for the stated one-pass model, not a blanket impossibility statement for replayable input or external storage.

Allow roughly 30–45 minutes if useful; time is a planning suggestion, not an assessment score. Try these before opening the answers. For [4, 9, 1, 7, 9], trace both procedures. Count pairwise equality comparisons and abstract set membership calls. State each return value. Write the remembered-state invariant in your own words. Give initialization, preservation, return reasoning, and termination. Explain the singleton failure of inserting before checking. Calculate the baseline comparison count for n=100 and n=1,000 on all-distinct input. List the assumptions needed for the expected-linear alternative. Explain the difference between membership calls and key comparisons. Modify the contract to return a matching pair of positions. Specify the state and trace the same input. Give the time and space qualifications. You may retain only the previous two IDs. Explain what [1, 2, 3, 1] proves. Give two legitimate requirement or resource changes that permit a solution. In the recurring document service, two workers check the same ID simultaneously, both find it absent, and both perform a payment. Explain why this pack’s single-process proof does not establish duplicate-effect prevention. Write the stronger invariant you would need. Success means explaining the retained information, proof boundary, counted operation, and a failed assumption. Code alone is insufficient. This is the first technical pack; it builds on the initialization map’s themes of state and contracts. S02 will use stored representations to accelerate queries. S03/S04 will examine interleavings and failures. A03 will revisit what a representation retains or loses about evidence.

Write down: contract → baseline → repeated query → sufficient state → invariant → cost model → counterexample. For this example, the repeated query is prefix membership; the state is the set of earlier keys; the check happens before insertion. Pairwise comparison needs n(n−1)/2 comparisons on distinct input. A suitable hash set gives expected linear total work and linear extra keys under explicit assumptions. Tests can expose bugs; the invariant explains arbitrary lengths within the model. Open questions for application: What exactly counts as an equal document ID? How long must history survive? Are inputs adversarial? What is the key-size distribution? Is memory sufficient? These are requirements to resolve before deployment, not blockers to the learning pack. No production performance benchmark or concurrency guarantee is claimed.
