Field Value ID / revision F01 answers / 1.0 Date 2026-11-02 Prerequisites F01 core pack Capability developed Check a proof, trace, and cost claim against a concrete contract Source-check status Same R01 passages as core §9; solutions below are original derivations Experiment status Reproduction block executed under Python 3; bounded exhaustive checks passed

At outer position j, test earlier positions in ascending order. Stop counting when the function returns. State exactly what seen contains before the membership test. Keep “no previous duplicates” as a separate clause. The triangular sum counts comparisons, not elapsed time. A container call may perform multiple comparisons. Which information did a plain set discard? Store just enough to restore the required output. Locate the forgotten key. Decide whether the allowed duplicate horizon can change. A local proof assumes sequential execution. Find the gap between checking and performing a consequential action.

j Current value Pairwise comparisons at this step Set membership result 0 4 0 Absent 1 9 4 vs 9: 1 comparison Absent 2 1 4, 9 vs 1: 2 comparisons Absent 3 7 4, 9, 1 vs 7: 3 comparisons Absent 4 9 4 vs 9, then 9 vs 9: 2 comparisons Present Both return True. The baseline performs 8 equality comparisons. The remembered-state procedure performs 5 membership calls and 4 insertion calls. These are abstract calls; the trace does not imply only 5 equality comparisons inside a real set.

Before processing position k, the set contains exactly the keys at positions below k. If execution has reached this point without returning, those earlier keys are distinct. Empty initialization satisfies this. A successful membership test implies an earlier matching position; an unsuccessful test permits adding the new value while preserving distinctness and exact membership. After the last unsuccessful test, the entire input is distinct. The loop consumes one item per iteration from a finite input, so it terminates. If insertion precedes membership, [8] inserts 8 and immediately finds it, even though the required different position does not exist. The invariant no longer describes an exclusively earlier prefix at the test. A returned positive must have a witness consisting of two distinct positions.

For 100 distinct values: 100×99/2 = 4,950 comparisons. For 1,000: 1,000×999/2 = 499,500. The ratio is 100.909…, rather than exactly 100, because the lower-order term still contributes at finite n. For expected linear total work, assume constant-cost keys/equality/hashing, an appropriate hashing model, controlled load, and a resizing policy whose costs amortize across insertions. Also assume the keys maintain their identity while stored. The abstract membership count is at most n. It does not bound the number of actual equality comparisons by n: collisions can require examining multiple candidates. A constant-hash chained representation is a counterexample to unconditional linear time.

Store a map first_index[key] = earliest processed position. Before position j, the map associates each earlier key with its first index. Check membership before inserting. When present, return (first_index[x], j); otherwise insert j. The example returns (1, 4) using zero-based positions. Because this procedure terminates on its first repeated key, all earlier keys are still distinct. Its first-index convention is unambiguous. If requirements change to all repeated pairs, a single index per key will not preserve enough information; output size may itself be quadratic. Returning one witness retains expected O(n) total time and O(n) extra entries under the same map assumptions as the set. No-match inputs return None.

Before the last key in [1, 2, 3, 1], a previous-two-items cache contains 2 and 3. It misses the duplicate 1. Legitimate alternatives include: Define a last-two-items question explicitly, accepting that older repeats are outside scope. Permit external exact storage that retains earlier keys and defines its lookup/durability guarantees. Restrict IDs to a small known universe and allocate membership flags for that universe. Permit replaying an immutable stored input and compare each new position against earlier positions, trading time and input access for auxiliary memory. These alternatives change different assumptions. “Use a hash” alone does not create unlimited exact history in fixed memory. A probabilistic summary would require a specified error model; no such summary is implemented or analyzed here.

Possible timeline: worker A checks absent; worker B checks absent; A pays; B pays; both record the ID. The membership set may end up containing a single key despite two payments. The final set contents cannot prove that only one effect occurred. A stronger intended invariant is “For each business operation key, at most one committed payment effect occurs.” Its scope must include the durable state and payment boundary, retries, and failures. A coordination mechanism, atomic constraint, or idempotency contract must be chosen and checked in S03/S04 and C01. This answer intentionally does not claim that putting a lock around one process solves cross-process or external effects.

Capability Evidence of a useful answer Formulation Defines equality, distinct positions, empty input, and output shape Derivation Identifies repeated prefix membership and the state needed to answer it Correctness Names the program boundary and handles initialization, preservation, both returns, and termination Analysis Counts an explicit operation and qualifies expected/amortized and key-size assumptions Transfer Explains a changed contract and an invalid extension of the local proof No learner score is recorded. If a step is unclear, revisit that step using a three-element input and manually inspect the state before each test.

The following standard-library-only block is the executed validation code. It checks all sequences of lengths 0 through 7 over {0,1,2}: 3,280 inputs. The oracle uses frequency counting, distinct from the two detection procedures. Assertions verify the remembered-state invariant on every processed prefix. Additional tests check a one-bucket collision model, the insert-before-check bug, the forgetting counterexample, and arithmetic. This is a bounded correctness check, not a performance benchmark or evidence for all possible keys. from itertools import product from collections import Counter def pairs(a): comparisons = 0 for j in range(len(a)): for i in range(j): comparisons += 1 if a[i] == a[j]: return True, comparisons return False, comparisons def seen_check(a): seen = set() for k, x in enumerate(a): assert seen == set(a[:k]) and len(seen) == k if x in seen: return True seen.add(x) return False def witness(a): first = {} for j, x in enumerate(a): if x in first: return first[x], j first[x] = j return None cases = 0 for n in range(8): for a in product(range(3), repeat=n): oracle = any(count > 1 for count in Counter(a).values()) assert pairs(a)[0] == seen_check(a) == oracle w = witness(a) assert (w is not None) == oracle if w is not None: i, j = w assert 0 <= i < j < n and a[i] == a[j] cases += 1 assert cases == 3280 assert pairs([4, 9, 1, 7, 9]) == (True, 8) assert pairs([8, 3, 6, 3]) == (True, 5) assert witness([4, 9, 1, 7, 9]) == (1, 4) for n in (0, 1, 2, 10, 100, 1000, 2000): assert pairs(list(range(n))) == (False, n * (n - 1) // 2) # Explicit one-bucket chained model; each contains scan checks keys. # Append follows a confirmed miss, so no second search is needed. bucket = [] checks = 0 for x in range(100): for y in bucket: checks += 1 assert x != y bucket.append(x) assert checks == 4950 assert 1 % 10 == 11 % 10 and 1 != 11 def insert_first_bug(a): seen = set() for x in a: seen.add(x) if x in seen: return True return False assert insert_first_bug([8]) is True assert pairs([8])[0] is False def previous_two(a): recent = [] for x in a: if x in recent: return True recent.append(x) recent = recent[-2:] return False assert previous_two([1, 2, 3, 1]) is False assert seen_check([1, 2, 3, 1]) is True print(f"PASS: {cases} exhaustive inputs; traces, counts, witnesses, and counterexamples") Source and review limits: R01 passages support the abstract foundations; all exercise inputs and calculations are original. No current Python hash implementation details were inspected, and no claim about its precise collision or resizing policy is needed for these checks. Audit A remains queued.

title: Probability, base rates, and decisions under uncertainty

sections.section: Probability, base rates, and decisions under uncertainty
sections.text: Field Value ID / revision F02 / 1.0 Date 2026-11-02 Prerequisites Fractions and elementary algebra; bridge in §2 Capability developed Translate detector evidence into conditional probabilities and choose an action under explicit losses Source-check status R02 §§6.2.1, 6.3, 6.4.1 inspected in author PDF, draft 2024-01-15; calibration supplement R23 §2 inspected Experiment status Exact arithmetic and decision-boundary checks executed; no empirical detector evaluation Companion Hints and worked answers

sections.section: 1. A probability is an input to a decision
sections.text: In the recurring fictional document service, an automated check flags a submitted record as potentially incorrect. Should the workflow pass it, pause it, or ask a reviewer? A statement such as “the detector catches 90% of errors” does not answer that question. You need to know what population the record came from, what a flag means in that population, and the consequences of each permitted action. This pack uses invented counts and loss units to derive the decision. They are teaching inputs, not observed accuracy, pricing, or business loss estimates. “Pause” is a reversible workflow action in the example; permission for consequential actions remains a separate system requirement. A low expected loss does not authorize a system to exceed its authority. The central distinction is between a measurement about a detector, an estimate about a particular case given available evidence, and a rule for acting on that estimate. Keeping these separate lets you change policy when costs change without pretending the detector itself changed.

An event is a condition that may be true: let E mean “the record contains the defined error,” and A mean “the detector alerts.” The complement ¬E means no such error. A probability of 0.01 is 1%, or one out of 100 under the specified model. Multiply a proportion by a population count to obtain the corresponding count: 0.01×10,000=100. Write P(E) for the probability of error before observing this alert. The base rate, also called prevalence, is this error proportion in the population under discussion. Write P(A|E) for the probability of alert among erroneous records. The vertical bar means “given”; it changes the denominator. P(E|A) asks a different question: among alerted records, what proportion are erroneous? R02 defines discrete conditional probabilities using restricted row or column totals, then derives Bayes’ theorem using the product rule. Its expectation definition weights each possible result by its probability. We will apply those foundations to original count tables and a two-action loss model. The nonzero-denominator condition matters: a conditional fraction over an empty alert group is undefined, not zero.

sections.section: 3. Two populations, the same assumed detector
sections.text: Assume the detector alerts on 90% of erroneous records and 5% of clean records. These are respectively sensitivity (true-positive rate) and false-positive rate. Specificity is the clean-record non-alert rate, here 95%. All rates are hypothetical and assumed identical in the two populations. Population L contains 10,000 records with a 1% error rate. Therefore 100 are erroneous and 9,900 are clean. Population L Error E Clean ¬E Total Alert A 90 495 585 No alert ¬A 10 9,405 9,415 Total 100 9,900 10,000 The 90 true alerts come from 0.90×100. The 495 false alerts come from 0.05×9,900. Of the 585 alerts, only 90 are errors: P(E|A)=90/585=2/13≈15.38%. Most alerts concern clean records even though sensitivity is high. There are so many clean records that a small false-positive fraction creates many alerts. Population H has the same size but a 20% error rate: 2,000 erroneous records and 8,000 clean records. Population H Error E Clean ¬E Total Alert A 1,800 400 2,200 No alert ¬A 200 7,600 7,800 Total 2,000 8,000 10,000 Now P(E|A)=1,800/2,200=9/11≈81.82%. The alert is much stronger evidence of an actual error in this population. This does not prove real detector rates remain unchanged after a population shift; that is an explicit premise of the comparison. Different document types or label definitions could change the conditional rates too. For no-alert records, use the other row: P(E|¬A)=10/9,415≈0.1062% in L and 200/7,800≈2.5641% in H. Absence of an alert is not proof of absence of error.

sections.section: 4. Derive the update instead of memorizing it
sections.text: Let b=P(E), s=P(A|E), and f=P(A|¬E). The fraction that both has an error and alerts is sb. The fraction that is clean and alerts is f(1−b). Those groups are disjoint and together contain every alert, so P(A)=sb+f(1−b). Dividing the first group by all alerts gives P(E∣A)=sbsb+f(1−b). This is Bayes’ rule expressed for this binary detector. It follows from counting the same joint event in two ways: P(E and A)=P(A|E)P(E)=P(E|A)P(A). Division by P(A) requires P(A)>0. No independence assumption between error and alert is needed; their dependence is exactly what makes the detector useful. To obtain the no-alert version, replace s by 1−s and f by 1−f. A useful check is to reconstruct the base rate by weighting the two posteriors by the sizes of their groups. In L, the erroneous counts recovered from the alert and non-alert rows must sum to 100. This catches a denominator swap that can otherwise look plausible. Here is the tempting mistake: calling 90% sensitivity “90% of alerts are correct.” In L the two fractions share the numerator 90 but divide by 100 and 585 respectively. Before manipulating a percentage, write the group after the word “among.”

sections.section: 5. Derive a decision threshold from losses
sections.text: Suppose the only available choices are pass and pause. Set correct decisions to zero loss for this model; assign loss C_FN=100 to passing an erroneous record and C_FP=20 to unnecessarily pausing a clean one. Costs are in a common invented loss unit. They can represent an agreed combination of delay, rework, and harm, but comparable units and complete consequences must be justified in a real application. For a record with error probability p given all information being used, the loss table is: Action Error, probability p Clean, probability 1−p Expected loss Pass 100 0 100p Pause 0 20 20(1−p) Expected loss means multiply each loss by its chance and add. It is an average under the model, not a promise about any individual outcome. Choose pause when C_FP(1−p)<C_FN p. Expanding and collecting the p terms gives p>CFPCFP+CFN. The denominator is positive here. At equality both actions have the same modeled loss; define a tie policy explicitly. With our numbers the threshold is 20/120=1/6≈16.67%. For alerts in L, p=2/13 is below the threshold: passing loses 200/13≈15.38 versus pausing 220/13≈16.92. For alerts in H, pausing loses 40/11≈3.64 versus passing 900/11≈81.82. The same alert leads to different actions because its conditional meaning differs. Now increase only the missed-error cost to 200. The threshold becomes 20/220=1/11≈9.09%. Both alert groups should now be paused in the two-action model. The detector and probability estimates have not changed; the losses have. A universal 0.5 threshold would ignore the asymmetry. These comparisons assume p captures the information available to the policy. If you have case-level features, an entire alert group’s average need not be appropriate for each record. They also assume independent decisions without a shared capacity constraint. Limited reviewers or an overall pause budget create a coupled allocation problem.

sections.section: 6. Asking a person is a third action with a cost
sections.text: Add review at cost 4 per record. First assume, unrealistically but transparently, that a reviewer always resolves the error status correctly and has no other delay or downstream cost. The expected review loss is 4. Review beats pass when 4<100p, or p>0.04. It beats pause when 4<20(1−p), or p<0.8. Therefore: Probability region Minimum-loss action under the ideal-review model p<0.04 Pass 0.04<p<0.8 Review p>0.8 Pause p=0.04 or p=0.8 Tie between adjacent choices; apply declared policy For the L alert group, review at 4 beats both automatic choices. For the H alert group, pause at about 3.64 beats review. Review is valuable when its information can change the action enough to justify its cost; it need not be best for every uncertain case. Remove the perfect-review assumption. If review misses 5% of actual errors and incorrectly pauses 10% of clean records, its expected loss becomes Lreview=4+0.05p(100)+0.10(1−p)(20)=6+3p. Those residual error rates must describe the cases actually routed to review. At p=0.2, review loses 6.6, pass loses 20, and pause loses 16. Review still wins there, but the old 0.04 and 0.8 boundaries no longer apply. “Human in the loop” is a workflow description, not a numerical guarantee. An abstention policy that defers action needs its own delay, escalation, and unresolved-case losses.

sections.section: 7. Estimate, calibration, and policy are different objects
sections.text: A numeric score in [0,1] is not automatically an established probability. Calibration asks whether stated probabilities match observed event frequencies in an appropriate population. For a binary event predictor, predictions around 0.8 should correspond to an error frequency around 80% if they are calibrated there. The R23 supplement formalizes calibration of confidence in a predicted class; here we use the analogous binary-event formulation, not a claim about that paper’s empirical performance. As an original counterexample, imagine two equally sized groups all assigned score 0.5. Their error rates are 10% and 90%. The overall rate is 50%, matching the score, while each subgroup is poorly served by it. Aggregate calibration does not establish subgroup calibration or individual certainty. Even a predictor that emits the population base rate for every record can be calibrated in aggregate while providing no useful ranking within that population. Calibration evidence needs labeled examples relevant to intended use, with counts and uncertainty recorded. A bucket containing two predictions is much weaker evidence than its precise-looking percentage suggests. Changing the population can invalidate old calibration evidence. Choosing a cost-based threshold does not repair a biased probability estimate. Conversely, improving calibration does not choose your loss function or resolve an authority restriction.

Before trusting the calculation, check the error definition and label quality; the population and base rate; stability of sensitivity and false-positive rate; omitted loss categories; reviewer accuracy and capacity; and whether group averages conceal important differences. Near a decision boundary, plausible uncertainty in either p or cost can reverse the choice. Investigate the parameter that matters to the decision rather than reporting extra decimal places. F01 established the habit of declaring a model before claiming a guarantee. B01 separated observed evidence from assumptions and identified whose outcome matters. F02 adds a conditional model for uncertainty. F03 will test how rates are estimated and comparisons designed. A05 will reuse abstention and review decisions; B02 will connect failures and human work to delivery economics. Try these six tasks before opening the answers. All inputs are hypothetical. Rebuild both 10,000-record tables from b, s, and f. Calculate both alert precision and non-alert error probability. Explain each denominator. A third population has 10% errors, 80% sensitivity, and 2% false-positive rate. Build its table and compute P(E|A). At p=0.2, compare pass and pause for costs (C_FN,C_FP)=(100,20), then (100,40). Derive each threshold and explain the reversal. Derive the perfect-review boundaries for cost 4 and costs (100,20). Then derive the imperfect-review boundaries using the rates in §6. Explain how the two 0.5-score subgroups can look calibrated together. Propose a check before applying one common threshold. An evaluation set was constructed with equal error and clean counts, while deployment prevalence is 1%. Explain what can and cannot be transferred, and list three deployment measurements needed before enabling automatic decisions. Success means reconstructing the counts, stating loss assumptions, and identifying evidence that would change the action. No learner answers or mastery are recorded.

Write the denominator first. Sensitivity is P(A|E); alert precision is P(E|A). Compute the latter from base rate and both conditional alert rates. Expected loss sums probability×loss. The two-action threshold is C_FP/(C_FP+C_FN) only for the stated zero-correct-loss model. Review adds an action and its own cost and residual errors. Calibration concerns probability validity; policy concerns choices under losses and constraints. Author PDF obtained directly after web reader size limit. Page references are printed pages. R23: Guo, Pleiss, Sun, Weinberger (2017), On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks Conference PDF, §2, PDF p. 2, eq. 1 and Reliability Diagrams paragraphs Definition and finite-sample estimation context only; no contemporary-model or benchmark claim Count tables, threshold derivations, imperfect review, subgroup counterexample Original §§3–7; exact checks in answer file Conditional results from invented inputs; no empirical validation Open application questions: actual prevalence, conditional detector performance, case-level probability quality, loss values, reviewer behavior, and capacity. They are unresolved empirical inputs, not blockers to F03. Audit A remains pending.

Field Value ID / revision F02 answers / 1.0 Date 2026-11-02 Prerequisites F02 core Capability developed Reconstruct conditional probabilities and audit an action rule Source-check status Same R02 and R23 passages as core §9; solutions are original derivations Experiment status Exact rational arithmetic and boundary checks executed; no empirical experiment

Split the population into error and clean groups first, then split each by alert status. Divide true alerts by all alerts, including clean-record alerts. Write both expected losses before rearranging an inequality. Review must beat both alternatives. For imperfect review, include the fee and residual errors. Average the equally sized groups, then inspect them separately. A deliberately balanced test set has an assigned prevalence, not necessarily the deployment prevalence.

For L, true alerts=100×0.9=90; missed errors=10; false alerts=9,900×0.05=495; correct non-alerts=9,405. Precision is 90/585=2/13≈15.3846%. Non-alert error probability is 10/9,415=2/1,883≈0.1062%. For H, true alerts=2,000×0.9=1,800; missed errors=200; false alerts=8,000×0.05=400; correct non-alerts=7,600. Precision is 1,800/2,200=9/11≈81.8182%. Non-alert error probability is 200/7,800=1/39≈2.5641%. Each table sums to 10,000. Sensitivity divides true alerts by all erroneous records; precision divides them by all alerted records. Their equal numerator does not make the ratios interchangeable. Recover the base rate by weighting each row’s error probability by its share of the population.

Outcome Error Clean Total Alert 800 180 980 No alert 200 8,820 9,020 Total 1,000 9,000 10,000 P(E|A)=800/980=40/49≈81.6327%. The no-alert error probability, if needed, is 200/9,020=10/451≈2.2173%. The table is a designed scenario. Observing exactly these counts in a future sample is not guaranteed merely by specifying rates.

At p=0.2, with missed-error cost 100 and unnecessary-pause cost 20: pass loss=20; pause loss=16. Pause wins. Threshold=20/(100+20)=1/6. Raise only the unnecessary-pause cost to 40: pass loss remains 20; pause loss becomes 32. Pass wins. Threshold=40/140=2/7≈28.5714%. The probability estimate and detector evidence stayed fixed. The loss of interrupting a clean case changed the decision. At either threshold, the alternatives tie; state a tie policy rather than claim a strict preference. More generally, if correct actions also have nonzero costs, compute each action’s full expected loss. Do not insert the old threshold formula without checking its premises.

Perfect review at cost 4 beats passing when 4<100p, so p>1/25=0.04. It beats pausing when 4<20(1−p), so p<4/5=0.8. Review is strictly best inside that interval. Outside it, the relevant automatic action is cheaper; endpoints are ties. Imperfect review has loss 6+3p. Against passing: 6+3p<100p ⇒ p>6/97≈0.061856. Against pausing: 6+3p<20−20p ⇒ p<14/23≈0.608696. The review region narrows to (6/97,14/23). Below its lower endpoint, pass is best; above its upper endpoint, pause is best. The two automatic losses cross at 1/6, which lies inside this review region, so there is no overlooked interval where one of them defeats review. At p=0.2, review loss is 6.6, less than both 20 and 16. This calculation assumes reviewer error rates conditional on true status remain the stated values among routed records. Selection can change those rates: difficult cases sent to review may not resemble cases in a general reviewer assessment.

With equal-sized groups, (0.1+0.9)/2=0.5. All predictions have score 0.5, so aggregate event frequency agrees with that score. Within the first group it overstates risk by 0.4; within the second it understates risk by 0.4. This is an exact hypothetical construction, not a sampled finding. Check event frequencies by relevant subgroup and score range on suitable labeled cases. Record sample sizes, label definitions, uncertainty, and whether the data represent deployment. A common action threshold may still be appropriate when losses match, but the input probabilities need to represent the information used. Apparent aggregate calibration cannot certify that property for subgroups.

Precision computed on a 50%-error evaluation set uses that set’s prevalence. It cannot simply be reported as deployment precision at 1%. If sensitivity and false-positive rate transfer unchanged, substitute the deployment base rate in Bayes’ expression. That transfer assumption itself needs checking across document types, sources, and time. Before automatic decisions, measure or otherwise justify at least: deployment prevalence with an appropriate sampling design; conditional detector rates on relevant labeled inputs; and the losses and operational consequences of permitted actions. Review accuracy, queue capacity, and subgroup calibration are further relevant measurements. Do not label only alerted cases if you also need to estimate missed errors: that selection leaves an important denominator unobserved. F03 develops the sampling and experimental design needed to investigate these questions.

Capability Evidence in an answer Conditional reasoning Names the population after “among” and uses the correct denominator Mechanism Builds joint counts and derives the Bayesian update Decision analysis Includes every modeled action/state loss and treats ties explicitly Transfer Explains how changed prevalence, losses, or reviewer errors affect policy Evidence discipline Distinguishes hypothetical rates, measured estimates, calibration, and decisions No learner score or readiness judgment is recorded.

from fractions import Fraction as F def table(b, s, f): errors, clean = 10000*b, 10000*(1-b) return errors*s, clean*f, errors*(1-s), clean*(1-f) cases = [ (F(1,100),F(9,10),F(1,20),(90,495,10,9405),F(2,13)), (F(1,5),F(9,10),F(1,20),(1800,400,200,7600),F(9,11)), (F(1,10),F(4,5),F(1,50),(800,180,200,8820),F(40,49)), ] for b,s,f,expected,precision in cases: tp,fp,fn,tn = table(b,s,f) assert (tp,fp,fn,tn) == expected assert tp+fp+fn+tn == 10000 assert tp/(tp+fn) == s and fp/(fp+tn) == f assert tp/(tp+fp) == precision == s*b/(s*b+f*(1-b)) assert (tp+fp)/10000*precision + (fn+tn)/10000*fn/(fn+tn) == b assert F(10,9415) == F(2,1883) assert F(200,7800) == F(1,39) assert F(200,9020) == F(10,451) p=F(1,5) assert (100*p,20*(1-p),40*(1-p)) == (20,16,32) assert F(20,120)==F(1,6) and F(20,220)==F(1,11) assert F(40,140)==F(2,7) assert 4+F(1,20)*p*100+F(1,10)*(1-p)*20 == F(33,5) for k in range(1001): p=F(k,1000) automatic = (20*(1-p) < 100*p) assert automatic == (p > F(1,6)) for review,lower,upper in [(F(4),F(1,25),F(4,5)), (6+3*p,F(6,97),F(14,23))]: assert (review < min(100*p,20*(1-p))) == (lower < p < upper) for p in [F(1,25),F(4,5)]: assert min(100*p,20*(1-p)) == 4 for p in [F(6,97),F(14,23)]: assert min(100*p,20*(1-p)) == 6+3*p assert (F(1,10)+F(9,10))/2 == F(1,2) print('PASS: three tables; Bayes reconstruction; losses; 1001 grid points; exact boundary ties') These assertions check arithmetic and the derived rule on the stated examples and a finite grid. Algebra establishes the continuous boundary under the model. No experiment establishes that the invented rates or costs hold in a real system. Audit A is pending.

title: Did the pipeline improve, or did the measurement change?

sections.section: Did the pipeline improve, or did the measurement change?
sections.text: Field Value ID and revision F03 · 1.1 Date 2026-11-03 Prerequisite F02, especially conditional proportions and the cost of errors Capability Design a comparison, identify which claim it supports, and decide what evidence would justify rollout Source check Microsoft Research R03 and the R13 Python edition’s Chapter 5 author lab. Passage locators appear at the end. Experiment status Constructed data and executed arithmetic. The live study is a proposed design. Companion Hints and worked answers

sections.section: Start with the case that fools the dashboard
sections.text: A purchasing team is comparing two pipelines that extract invoice evidence for an approver. A handles today’s workflow. B adds a retrieval step and attaches supporting passages. Imagine the team introduced B in the exceptions queue first. A dashboard then compared their success rates. Every number in this lesson is a teaching input. Document type A, correct / eligible B, correct / eligible Routine 72 / 80 = 90% 19 / 20 = 95% Exception 12 / 20 = 60% 52 / 80 = 65% All 84 / 100 = 84% 71 / 100 = 71% Would you cancel B? Take a pencil and mark the denominator for each percentage. The comparison of totals gives B a 13 percentage point deficit. Within both document types, B leads by 5 points. A handled mostly routine cases. B handled mostly exceptions. The overall rate depends on the difficulty mix as well as the pipeline. Use a hypothetical target workload of 80% routine and 20% exception documents. For every 100 target cases, A’s estimated successes are 80 × 0.90 + 20 × 0.60 = 84. B’s are 80 × 0.95 + 20 × 0.65 = 89. At a common mix, the difference is +5 percentage points. At a 50/50 mix it is still +5 because both within-type differences happen to be equal. If the differences had opposite signs, the target mix could change which pipeline you preferred. The adjusted result answers a deliberately narrow question. It describes what the given rates imply at the chosen mix. Routing may also have depended on supplier, reviewer experience, or document quality within each type. Any of those differences could account for the apparent gain. Weighting by type fixes one imbalance. To investigate the remaining uncertainty, use the same documents for both pipelines.

sections.section: Specify what a win would mean
sections.text: Write the decision before selecting a metric. Here it is whether B should enter a limited live trial, followed by whether it should replace A for the intended teams. Those decisions need different evidence. In this example, a case consists of one invoice, its revisions, and any retries. Define success as a correctly resolved case with the required source evidence within two business days of arrival. A blinded adjudicator applies the same frozen rubric to both arms. A timeout or unresolved case at the deadline counts as a failure. Counting only completed outputs would allow B to improve its displayed accuracy by quietly dropping difficult work. Specify the population as invoices from participating purchasing teams, supported languages, and the agreed intake dates. Determine eligibility at receipt, before either pipeline has influenced the case. Record the reason for every predeclared exclusion. An unsupported input can be outside this target population while still deserving a separate count for readers who need to know what fraction of incoming work the claim covers. A useful metric has a unit, a denominator, a clock, and a rule for missing outcomes. Use correct on-time cases divided by eligible cases as the primary metric. Count staff review minutes and compute charges for failures as well as successes. Report total cost per eligible case and total cost divided by verified successes. The second ratio is undefined if there are zero successes. Report severe erroneous recommendations separately. An average gain can coexist with an unacceptable error that the average conceals. F02’s denominator discipline applies directly. A low error fraction among cases that produced answers does not give the error fraction among all eligible cases. B01 supplies another check. If the buyer cares about evidence reaching the approver, a faster extractor helps only when that step changes the eventual outcome.

sections.section: Replay both pipelines under controlled conditions
sections.text: Build a locked historical set from the intended intake population. Keep revisions of the same invoice together. If the intended claim concerns unfamiliar suppliers, reserve entire suppliers for the final test. If it concerns future cases from existing suppliers, use a later time window and keep future revisions out of earlier tuning. Those designs answer different questions. Choose the split that matches deployment. Freeze prompts, models, decision thresholds, retrieval index snapshot, rubric, and compute budget before looking at final labels. Exclude information that would become available only after the original request. A retrieval snapshot containing the eventual corrected invoice could make B appear remarkably accurate while giving it evidence unavailable at decision time. Use development folds to tune choices. Repeatedly tuning on the final set turns it into development data. R13’s validation example illustrates why a held-out estimate itself can vary with the split. Run both pipelines on each eligible case. Counterbalance execution order if caches warm up, isolate caches if they would otherwise pass information between pipelines, and report cold and warm workloads if both matter. Give a stochastic pipeline the same prespecified number of attempts per case. Multiple attempts on one invoice still represent one underlying case. Here is a second constructed comparison on 100 common cases. Both pipelines succeed on 76, only A succeeds on 8, only B succeeds on 13, and both fail on 3. A succeeds on 84 and B on 89. The gain is (13 − 8) / 100 = 5 points. This paired view adds information that the two totals hide. Eight cases regress. Reading those eight cases may reveal a severe evidence error that makes the candidate unsuitable even with a positive average. For uncertainty, decide which observations could reasonably vary independently. In a workload sampled by supplier, one supplier template may generate dozens of nearly identical invoices. To estimate workload sampling variability, resample suppliers with replacement, keeping all of each selected supplier’s cases and both pipeline outputs together. Recompute the chosen statistic per replicate. If the target is a typical case, sum successes and denominators over the resampled suppliers before taking their ratio. A typical-supplier target weights suppliers equally instead. Few suppliers, rare events, or an unrepresentative sample limit what a bootstrap interval can tell you. It cannot recover a missing supplier population. If your claim concerns exactly the fixed 100-case suite and the outputs are deterministic, the descriptive difference is known for that suite. Replay can establish differences on those inputs under that resource policy. It leaves open what happens when reviewers trust suggestions, queues back up, or customers change their submissions. Those effects require observation of the workflow under each policy.

sections.section: A live experiment plan, written before results
sections.text: Design choice Proposed specification for the fictional teams Effect of interest Difference in the mean participating team’s fraction of eligible cases correctly resolved within two business days under assignment to B versus A. Each team gets equal weight. Assignment Use stable team IDs. Form pairs of teams using baseline volume, exception share, and historical success rates. Randomly assign one team in each pair to B and its partner to A. Exposure and unit A team and its dedicated reviewer queue stay in one arm throughout. The case is the measurement unit. The team is the assignment unit. Shared reviewers or queues require regrouping before launch. Duration and size Candidate window of four working weeks plus two business days for final outcomes. Before launch, use historical team-level variability to plan enough independent pairs for a meaningful gain. Freeze the required team count and duration. If the size is infeasible, call the study a pilot. Outcomes Primary as defined above. Secondary measures include active review time per eligible case, cost per verified success, and the distribution of resolution times. Guardrails include severe errors and missing telemetry. Exclusions and missing data Apply the same intake rules to both arms. Retain crossovers, retries, failures, and unverified cases in their assigned arm. Flag missing adjudication separately and show sensitivity to its assumed outcome. Analysis For each pair subtract A’s team success rate from B’s. Average those differences. Display pair-level data and a 95% interval accounting for pairing, plus counts for each arm. Prespecify routine/exception and new/existing supplier summaries. Decision and stop One efficacy analysis after outcomes mature. Example gate agreed in advance: lower interval bound above +2 points, cost within budget, and acceptable severe-error rate. Define actual budget and severity limits with owners before launch. Pause exposure immediately for a severe unauthorized recommendation or broken assignment logging. For an optional uncertainty bridge, let d_i be B minus A in team pair i, with m independent pairs. Their average is d_bar. The sample standard deviation s_d measures the spread of these differences around d_bar. The standard error s_d/sqrt(m) estimates how much the average varies under a model of independent, comparable pair differences. A two-sided t interval is d_bar ± t_(0.975,m−1) s_d/sqrt(m). The multiplier depends on m−1 degrees of freedom, so substituting 1.96 for every study size is inappropriate. NIST documents the mean-interval formula and its repeated-sampling interpretation in R24, §1.3.5.2. Applying it to pair differences is our modeling choice. Exact t coverage requires independent identically distributed normal differences; for bounded team rates this is an approximation, whose adequacy needs enough independent pairs and no dominating outliers. Random assignment alone does not establish that sampling model or transport the result to other teams. A 95% confidence procedure aims to cover its target in 95% of repeated samples under its assumptions. It does not assign a 95% probability to the fixed target lying in this particular observed interval. Additional documents within a team do not create more independent assignments. For a few pairs, display raw differences. Under the sharp null that assignment changes no team’s outcome, no interference, and independent fair assignment within each pair, enumerate the 2^m possible within-pair label swaps. Each assignment is equally likely by design. Compare the absolute observed mean difference with that enumeration for a two-sided randomization test, including equally extreme values. This tests that sharp null; it does not directly supply a confidence interval for a heterogeneous average effect. The derivation follows from the specified randomization mechanism, rather than from the R13 bootstrap example. Randomization makes assignment independent of potential outcomes under the design, in expectation. It can still produce imbalance in one draw. Historical metrics, an A/A rehearsal, and checks that IDs keep their assignment help uncover faults. An A/A rehearsal routes both arms to the same pipeline to test instrumentation. An unexplained arm-count discrepancy calls for checking the assignment mechanism and missing logs. With paired team assignment, equal team counts are expected while document counts may differ naturally. Request-level assignment would be inappropriate here. A reviewer can learn B’s evidence-checking technique and apply it to A cases. B can also fill a shared queue and delay A cases. Either path lets one assignment affect another case’s outcome. Separating teams works only if the separation contains the important spillovers. If both arms depend heavily on one central reviewer pool, redesign the assignment around genuinely separate pools or revise the question to what can be learned from replay.

sections.section: Read a result and decide what to do
sections.text: Imagine the planned live analysis yields +5 points with a 95% interval from −1 to +11. The interval includes a small decline and gains above the +2-point gate. Under that rule the evidence is inconclusive for rollout. A broad interval is compatible with meaningful benefit and meaningful uncertainty. If the instrument lost more completion events in B, first quantify the differential loss and repair the measurement before using the estimate. Look at distributions as well as means. In an illustrative set of ten waits, nine one-minute waits and one 21-minute wait average three minutes. Ten three-minute waits also average three. The implications for a ten-minute deadline differ. When reporting latency quantiles, name the eligible population, timeouts, quantile convention, and sample size. When reporting stakeholder value, ask whether delays occur before or after the customer’s deadline. Before deciding, inspect candidate explanations for the result. Selection bias can enter when participation depends on having easy documents. Confounding can enter when more experienced reviewers receive B and would have done better with either pipeline. Leakage can enter when test labels influence tuning or a later correction enters the retrieval corpus. Interference can enter when treatment changes control’s queue or reviewer behavior. Each failure calls for a different repair. More rows drawn through the same broken mechanism can sharpen the wrong estimate.

Allow roughly 35 minutes. Prepare a one-page comparison plan before consulting the separate solutions. Reproduce the dashboard difference and the 80/20 adjusted difference. Give one remaining explanation for the gap within each document type. Reconstruct the paired replay from its four counts. Which cases deserve inspection first? Which uncertainty question calls for supplier-level resampling? Write the live study’s assignment, measurement, and analysis units. Explain how the shared reviewer pool would change the design. Suppose A verifies 84 correct cases for 420 cost units, and B verifies 89 for 480 units, out of 100 eligible cases each. Calculate cost per eligible case and per verified success. Propose a decision if the budget ceiling is 5.2 units per verified success. Draft eligibility, exclusions, missing-outcome handling, subgroup summaries, stopping rules, and the rollout gate. Apply it to the hypothetical interval above. Explain what an offline win and a live win would each justify. Transfer the plan to an AI assistant for debugging. Identify an independent unit, one leak, one spillover, and one whole-task success metric.

Keep the case ID, eligibility rule, clock, and denominator visible. Compare pipelines on common cases for a workload claim. Assign treatment where spillovers can be contained for a causal claim. Match the uncertainty calculation to the independent units. Record a useful effect size and the conditions for rollout before results arrive. A01 revisits generalization, S05 revisits latency distributions, and A05 reuses whole-task outcomes for AI evaluation. Basis Inspected passage How this pack uses it R03 · Machmouchi, Gupta, Zhang and Fabijan, Microsoft Research (2020) “Formulate your Hypothesis and Success Metrics,” “Choose the Appropriate Unit of Randomization,” “Set Up Counterfactual Logging,” and “Review Engineering Design Choices to Avoid Bias.” Primary article Practitioner guidance on units, guardrails, consistent exposure definitions, and shared infrastructure. The proposed invoice study is an application of these ideas. R13 · James, Witten, Hastie, Tibshirani and Taylor, ISL with Python (2023) Chapter 5 author lab, “The Validation Set Approach,” alternative split, and “The Bootstrap,” function boot_SE. Author notebook Holdout variability and resampling with replacement. The paired supplier resampling design is our adaptation to related documents. R24 · NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook §1.3.5.2, Confidence Limits for the Mean, definition and interpretation, inspected 2026-11-04 Mean-interval formula. Pair-level application and randomization enumeration are explicitly qualified original analysis. Original examples and study design Tables, arithmetic, interval scenario, protocol, and solutions in this pack All counts, thresholds, and costs are hypothetical. The companion contains the executed checks. Open questions for deployment include the actual supplier mix, independent reviewer pools, outcome completeness, baseline variance, and acceptable cost and harm limits. These determine whether the proposed live study can proceed. Curriculum Audit A completed on 2026-11-04; see SDE_Audit_A.md for scope.

All data below are constructed. Check status Exact arithmetic executed on the included examples. The live experiment is a design exercise.

Ask which pipeline saw more exceptions. Compare both at one agreed mix. Start with the cases on which the pipelines disagree. Follow what the reviewer learns and which queues they share. Include the cost of failed work in the numerator. Decide what happens to an eligible record when its final label is missing. Follow a debugging task from issue intake to an independently verified fix.

sections.section: 1. The dashboard and the common workload
sections.text: A’s observed total is 84% and B’s is 71%, giving B −13 percentage points. At an 80% routine mix, A scores 0.8 × 0.9 + 0.2 × 0.6 = 0.84. B scores 0.8 × 0.95 + 0.2 × 0.65 = 0.89. Both within-type comparisons give +5 points. The direction reverses because B was disproportionately assigned difficult cases. Even within exceptions, B might have seen suppliers whose supporting documents were more complete. Establish whether those documents were available at receipt, then replay both versions against the same point-in-time evidence. The observed change in case mix is visible in the table. Supplier completeness is a proposed rival explanation, not an observed fact about these cases.

Both succeed on 76 cases, only A on 8, only B on 13, neither on 3. A’s 84 and B’s 89 are compatible with 21 disagreements. Net change is 13 − 8 = 5 additional successes per 100 cases. Inspect the eight regressions for severe unsupported actions, then inspect the thirteen gains to understand the mechanism. Comparing error severity can change a decision even at the same success rate. For the fixed suite the difference is exactly five points. If estimating variability across future suppliers drawn by a similar sampling process, resample whole suppliers, preserve paired outputs, and recompute the difference on each draw. Log how many suppliers there are and whether one supplies most cases. If there is only one supplier, the observed suite gives no between-supplier variation to estimate. Repeated runs of the same stochastic pipeline address a separate source of variation.

Assign teams within matched pairs. Measure each eligible invoice case once, linking all revisions and retries. Aggregate to team-level success rates, then average within-pair treatment differences. The target weights each participating team equally. If the target changes to a typical invoice, define volume weighting in advance and still account for team-level assignment. A central reviewer shared across both teams may learn treatment practices or experience treatment-induced delay. Reassigning individual cases leaves both paths open. If stable, sufficiently numerous non-overlapping reviewer pools exist, consider pool assignment and plan power at that level. If there is only one shared pool and carryover cannot be controlled, continue with paired replay for the offline question and record the live effect as unresolved.

Measure A B Cost per eligible case 420 / 100 = 4.20 480 / 100 = 4.80 Cost per verified success 420 / 84 = 5.00 480 / 89 ≈ 5.39 Extra cost per net extra verified success on this suite — (480 − 420) / (89 − 84) = 12.00 At a hard ceiling of 5.2 per verified success, B exceeds the budget despite better quality. Keep A for the stated decision, or redesign B and evaluate a fresh version. If the business owner explicitly revises the budget because a correct outcome is worth more, the decision can change. These costs include all 100 cases by construction. Using only successful cases’ processing costs would hide wasted work.

Include all supported invoices arriving during the frozen enrollment window. Exclude only predeclared ineligible records identifiable at intake, such as synthetic test traffic. Keep timed-out cases and crossovers in their assigned arm. Count successful outcomes only when verified by the deadline. Separately report the fraction with unavailable labels. For a sensitivity check, bound each arm’s rate between verified successes divided by eligible cases and (verified successes + unknown cases) divided by eligible cases. A pessimistic bound for the treatment difference gives A the favorable missing-case assumption and B the unfavorable one. Report routine and exception cases and supplier familiarity as prespecified subgroups, with their denominators. Keep subgroup findings exploratory unless the study was designed to test them. Freeze team count, enrollment horizon, deadline, meaningful effect, budget, and severity limits before the trial. Use a single final efficacy analysis after outcomes mature. Stop exposure for prespecified safety or data-integrity failures and document the interruption. The example interval [−1, +11] points fails a gate requiring its lower bound to exceed +2 points. A +5 point estimate alone cannot pass the gate. Keep the decision inconclusive and inspect uncertainty and guardrails. A replay win supports improved performance on the tested workload. A successful randomized trial supports an effect of assignment in the participating teams under its operating conditions. Expansion to new teams needs evidence about their workload and constraints.

Define an issue as one task, including its reopened attempts. Require a reproducer or failing test before eligibility. Success might mean a fix that passes an independent regression test, preserves the specified behavior, and survives a defined reopen window. Compare on historical issues using repositories as split groups when the claim concerns unfamiliar repositories. A retrieval index containing the eventual merged fix leaks the answer. A developer who learns a diagnosis from the assistant on one ticket can reuse it on a control ticket. For a live evaluation, consider assignment by collaborating team, subject to enough independent teams and contained collaboration across arms. Measure time to verified resolution and regressions along with completion. The number of generated patches alone gives little evidence about successful debugging.

A complete plan names the decision, population, case, assignment unit, denominator, outcome window, data split, independent units, exclusions, guardrails, cost, stopping rule, and inference boundary. It identifies a concrete mechanism for leakage, selection, or interference and changes the design to address it. The rubric describes an answer a learner could produce. No learner assessment was performed.

from fractions import Fraction as F a, b = (F(72, 80), F(12, 20)), (F(19, 20), F(52, 80)) assert F(71, 100) - F(84, 100) == F(-13, 100) for routine_weight in (F(4, 5), F(1, 2)): def total(rates): return routine_weight * rates[0] + (1 - routine_weight) * rates[1] assert total(b) - total(a) == F(5, 100) assert sum((76, 8, 13, 3)) == 100 assert (76 + 13) - (76 + 8) == 5 assert F(420, 84) < F(52, 10) < F(480, 89) assert F(480 - 420, 89 - 84) == 12 waits = [1] * 9 + [21] assert sum(waits) == sum([3] * 10) assert sum(t > 10 for t in waits) == 1 print("PASS: workload mix, paired counts, budget, marginal cost, and deadline example")

sections.section: Which document should the reviewer see first?
sections.text: A reviewer needs a delivery reference to verify an invoice. Suppose each passage is represented by two counts in a fixed order: delivery references first, payment references second. Passage A contains two delivery references and no payment references. Passage B contains three delivery references and four payment references. If the reviewer can open just one passage, should the service show A or B? Two plausible requirements lead to different answers. A reviewer assembling every available delivery reference might prefer the passage with the larger raw count. A reviewer trying to find a passage devoted to delivery might prefer one whose references all concern delivery. The arithmetic below makes each choice explicit. A real reviewer’s success would also depend on whether the references were correct, distinct, and from the right invoice. The counts are invented so we can inspect what the calculation preserves.

sections.section: Write the shape beside each quantity
sections.text: A scalar is a single number. A vector is an ordered collection of coordinates. Here a document vector has two coordinates. Write vectors as columns, so A = (2, 0)ᵀ has shape 2 × 1. The superscript T means transpose, which swaps rows and columns. Put documents in rows of a matrix D. Its first row is [2, 0], its second is [3, 4], and its third is [0, 2] for a payment-only passage C. The column vector q = (1, 0)ᵀ describes the delivery query. To calculate Dq, take one row at a time. Multiply corresponding coordinates by the query weights and add. The first row gives 2 × 1 + 0 × 0 = 2. The second gives 3 and the third gives 0. This row-by-column calculation is a dot product. In one multiplication we have a score for each passage. Quantity Shape Meaning of one entry D 3 × 2 Count for one passage and one reference type q 2 × 1 Query weight for one reference type Dq 3 × 1 Score for one passage DᵀD 2 × 2 Sum across passages of products of two feature counts The shared dimension tells you which coordinate you sum over. The dimensions that survive identify the output. Try writing qᵀD with the shapes above. Its inner dimensions are 2 and 3, so the intended multiplication fails a shape check. A subtler bug survives that check. If the query encoder puts payment first, q = (1, 0)ᵀ now describes a different request even though every multiplication still runs. A one-feature test query with a known result catches this disagreement. A production interface should record the feature order and the encoder version used on each side. A matrix can also change the representation. Apply the row matrix T = [1, 1] to each document column. The result is one scalar, the total number of references. Passages (2, 0)ᵀ and (0, 2)ᵀ both become 2. Once the service retains only that total, even a perfect downstream scoring function of the total must give those two passages the same score. Before accepting a compact representation, identify a pair of inputs your application must distinguish and take both through the transformation.

The Euclidean norm is a vector’s length. Square its coordinates, add them, and take the square root. Passage B has length √(3² + 4²) = 5. Its unit vector is (3/5, 4/5)ᵀ. Dividing each coordinate by the same positive length preserves its proportions and makes its length one. For nonzero q and d, the dot product of their unit vectors is the cosine of the angle between them. Passage Raw score against q Length Cosine against q A (2, 0) 2 2 1 B (3, 4) 3 5 3/5 C (0, 2) 0 2 0 Raw overlap ranks B above A. Cosine ranks A above B. Which result is defensible depends on what makes evidence useful to the reviewer. Try duplicating every reference in B. Its raw score doubles. Its unit vector still has coordinates (3/5, 4/5). In general, multiplying a nonzero document by a positive scalar multiplies its dot product and norm by that same scalar, which cancels in the cosine. This invariance helps when document length is a nuisance. It discards information when the magnitude represents multiple independently verified pieces of evidence. Deduplication and verification are separate design choices. An empty passage maps to (0, 0)ᵀ. Its norm is zero, so cosine would require dividing by zero. Define what the application does here. One policy is to mark the passage unscorable, exclude it from ranking, and retain its ID in coverage reports. Silently dropping such cases from evaluation can flatter a system that struggles on empty or poorly parsed documents. F03’s denominator rule applies. The same shape arithmetic applies to learned embeddings, where coordinates are learned from training data and need not have names that a reviewer can interpret. A cosine of 0.6 expresses a geometric relationship under the chosen representation. Estimating a 60% chance that the passage answers a question would require a defined event and labeled outcomes, as in F02. A02 will reuse dot products when comparing queries and keys. A03 will return to ranking passages and checking whether the selected passage supports an answer.

sections.section: Fit one parameter and inspect its units
sections.text: Suppose the same service wants to estimate active review time. Let x count pages and y measure review minutes. Choose the model ŷ = wx, where w is minutes per page. The model assumes proportionate time and a zero intercept. An intake task with a fixed setup cost could violate that assumption. Use two constructed training cases, (x, y) = (1, 2) and (2, 4). The design matrix now has shape 2 × 1, with rows [1] and [2]. Multiplying by the single weight gives two predictions. Start at w = 1. The predictions are 1 and 2 minutes. Subtract the targets to get residuals −1 and −2 minutes. Average their squares to obtain a mean squared error of (1 + 4)/2 = 2.5 minutes². Squaring prevents an underestimate from canceling an overestimate and makes a two-minute error contribute four times as much as a one-minute error. A stakeholder who cares mainly about missed deadlines may want a different evaluation measure. Keeping w symbolic exposes the whole loss curve: L(w)=[(w−2)2+(2w−4)2]/2=(5/2)(w−2)2. The square reaches zero at w = 2, so this dataset has an exact fit. Knowing that answer makes this an effective debugging case. We can check whether the update heads toward a known minimum and calculate how far it goes.

sections.section: Derive the slope before choosing a step
sections.text: Perturb w by a small nonzero amount h. Expanding the square gives L(w+h)−L(w)=5(w−2)h+(5/2)h2. Divide by h to get the change in loss per unit change in w. The quotient is 5(w−2) + (5/2)h. As h approaches zero the last term vanishes. The derivative is therefore L′(w) = 5(w−2). At w = 1 the slope is −5. Increasing w a little lowers the loss. After crossing w = 2 the slope becomes positive and a further increase raises the loss. With several weights, the gradient collects one partial derivative per weight, each calculated with the other weights fixed. Here one scalar gives the entire gradient. Gradient descent uses the update w_new = w − ηL′(w), with a positive step size η. For η = 0.1, the first step goes from 1 to 1.5. The two predictions become 1.5 and 3. Their residuals are −0.5 and −1, so the new mean squared error is (0.25 + 1)/2 = 0.625 minutes². Verify the loss both ways, from the predictions and from the simplified quadratic. Agreement catches mistakes such as missing the division by two. What makes this particular step safe? Subtract the optimum from both sides of the update: wnew−2=(1−5η)(w−2). Each update scales the distance from the optimum by |1−5η|. Starting away from the optimum, the loss decreases exactly when that factor is less than one, or 0 < η < 0.4. At η = 0.2 the update lands on the optimum in one step. At η = 0.4 it bounces to the other side at the same distance. A larger step can increase the loss even though the slope was correct. This range comes from the curvature of this specific quadratic and the chosen units. Changing the loss scaling changes its derivative and the suitable step size.

sections.section: Decide whether the fit earns a trial
sections.text: Consider one invented held-out two-page invoice that takes two minutes because its evidence is already assembled. At w = 1 the prediction is exact. After the training step, w = 1.5 predicts three minutes and the squared error rises from zero to one minute². That single case establishes a counterexample to the claim that every new case improves when training loss falls. Estimating an average effect across new invoices requires a representative evaluation set. For the retrieval choice, compare raw overlap and cosine on identical queries and passage collections. Have a reviewer judge whether each selected passage contains the required source evidence. Include duplicates, mixed-topic passages, and empty inputs. For time prediction, compare against a simple baseline on later invoices or held-out suppliers, according to the intended deployment. Record absolute errors in minutes alongside squared loss, and separate underestimates on deadline-sensitive cases. A01 will revisit how fitting, validation, and final evaluation answer different questions.

Calculate the three scores when q = (0, 1)ᵀ. Give the shape of Dq and explain a feature-order bug that this query could expose. Rank A, B, and C by raw and normalized overlap for the original delivery query. Repeat after tripling B. Give an explicit policy for a zero-vector query. Apply T = [1, 1] to A and C. Can any function of the resulting scalar alone recover which passage contains delivery evidence? Justify your answer. Starting at w = 1, calculate a second gradient step after the worked first step, using η = 0.1. Verify its loss from residuals and from the closed form. Try η = 0.5 from w = 1. Compare the new loss with the old loss. Explain why the sign of the gradient alone cannot select a step size. A teammate asks to deploy based on lower training loss and a higher average top-ranked cosine. Use the held-out counterexample and propose a separate acceptance check for each task.

Write the coordinate meaning and shape beside every input. For a score, test what happens when you duplicate a document or erase its features. For an update, write down the target, units, loss, slope, step size, and next loss. For a deployment decision, name the outcome on unseen cases that would change your choice. Claim or calculation Source and inspected locator Scope Product dimensions and row-by-column sum R02 §2.2, printed pp. 22–23, equations 2.13–2.14 Matrix multiplication Euclidean length, dot product, angle R02 §§3.1–3.2.1, p. 72, equations 3.4–3.5, and §3.4, p. 76, equations 3.24–3.25 Cosine uses two nonzero vectors Derivative as limiting slope R02 §5.1, pp. 141–142, definitions 5.1–5.2 Scalar differentiable function Gradient descent update R02 §7.1, p. 228, equations 7.5–7.6 Book uses a row gradient and transposes it for a column update. The scalar case has one component. Document ranking, loss curve, stable step interval, held-out case Original constructed examples above and checks in the companion Conditional arithmetic. Actual relevance labels, time distributions, and operating costs require application evidence. R02 is Deisenroth, Faisal, and Ong, Mathematics for Machine Learning, Cambridge University Press, 2020.
