title: Hints, worked answers, and reproducible checks

sections.section: Hints, worked answers, and reproducible checks
sections.text: Field Value ID, revision, date F04 answers · 1.0 · 2026-11-05 Prerequisite F04 learning pack Capability Check the feature contract, ranking, update direction, step size, and evaluation boundary Source check R02 passage locators in the core pack. Numerical cases and derivations are original. Experiment status Executed the Python 3 checks below on the constructed inputs.

The query assigns one unit of weight to the second coordinate. A positive scaling factor appears in both the numerator and the denominator of cosine. A deterministic function returns the same output when given the same input. Evaluate the derivative at the current weight before taking the second step. Compare distances to the optimum on both sides of the step. Separate the task of finding supporting evidence from the task of estimating minutes.

Multiplying each document row by (0, 1)ᵀ returns its payment-reference count. The output is (0, 4, 2)ᵀ, a 3 × 1 column indexed by passage. If a caller says it requested payment evidence but receives (2, 3, 0)ᵀ, it may have emitted (1, 0)ᵀ. Check the encoded query, the stored column order, and the expected output for a passage with only payment references. Shape validation alone accepts both query vectors.

For delivery q = (1, 0)ᵀ, the raw scores in document order are 2, 3, 0. Their descending order is B, A, C. Divide each by its document length and by the unit query length to obtain 1, 3/5, 0. Cosine orders them A, B, C. After tripling B its vector is (9, 12)ᵀ, its length is 15, and its raw score is 9. Its normalized score is 9/15 = 3/5. Both rankings retain their respective orders, although B’s raw lead grows. A zero query provides no direction. One defensible policy is to return an explicit “insufficient query features” status and ask for a usable reference type. Include that outcome when computing the fraction of all queries served successfully. Assigning a numerical score to every passage would require a separate fallback rule and a way to evaluate its relevance.

T times A gives 1 × 2 + 1 × 0 = 2. T times C gives 1 × 0 + 1 × 2 = 2. For any function g using only the transformed count, g(2) must serve both passages. Delivery evidence occurs in A and is absent from C. Consequently at least one answer must be wrong if g always chooses present or absent. Keep the delivery coordinate or the original reference data if this distinction is part of the contract. The total still answers a question about overall volume.

After the first step w = 3/2. The current derivative is 5(3/2 − 2) = −5/2. With η = 1/10 the next weight is 3/2 + 1/4 = 7/4. Predictions of 7/4 and 7/2 minutes have residuals −1/4 and −1/2. The mean of their squared residuals is (1/16 + 1/4)/2 = 5/32 minutes². Substituting in (5/2)(7/4 − 2)² gives the same result. A fresh gradient matters because the remaining error shrinks at each step.

From w = 1 the slope is −5. A step size of 1/2 sends the weight to 7/2, which lies 3/2 from the optimum. The new loss is (5/2)(3/2)² = 45/8 minutes², larger than the initial 5/2. Increasing w from 1 initially moves downhill. The step travels past the minimum far enough to lose the whole gain. Under repeated updates the error multiplier is 1−5η = −3/2, so the weight alternates sides and its distance grows. In the worked convention, dividing the entire loss by two would also halve each gradient and double the corresponding stable step-size interval.

In the constructed holdout, a two-page invoice took two minutes. Training reduced squared loss from 5/2 to 5/8, yet held-out squared error went from 0 to 1. For a workload claim, freeze a representative test population before selecting weights. Compare predictions with independently recorded active minutes, report mean absolute error by supplier type, and check the fraction of critical cases underestimated beyond an agreed tolerance. Decide beforehand what improvement and tolerance the workflow requires. A higher top score can also reward repeated words without finding an applicable source. Use the same frozen queries, candidate passages, and eligibility rules for both rankers. Have blinded reviewers check the selected passage against the original invoice and required fact. Count cases with missing evidence and cases the ranker declines. A decision can then use the fraction of all eligible queries with verified supporting evidence and the observed cost of review. Self-assessment. A complete solution preserves the document and feature axes, explains the scale invariance and zero case, derives the next weight using the current slope, and names a held-out outcome for each task. The numerical checks below can be run after attempting the exercises.

from fractions import Fraction as F from math import isqrt docs = [(2, 0), (3, 4), (0, 2)] def dot(x, y): assert len(x) == len(y) return sum(a*b for a, b in zip(x, y)) def cosine(x, y): squared = dot(x, x) * dot(y, y) if squared == 0: return None root = isqrt(squared) assert root*root == squared # exact roots in these examples return F(dot(x, y), root) q = (1, 0) assert [dot(d, q) for d in docs] == [2, 3, 0] assert [dot(d, (0, 1)) for d in docs] == [0, 4, 2] assert [cosine(d, q) for d in docs] == [1, F(3, 5), 0] assert cosine((9, 12), q) == F(3, 5) and dot((9, 12), q) == 9 assert cosine((0, 0), q) is None assert dot(docs[0], (1, 1)) == dot(docs[2], (1, 1)) == 2 def loss(w): return sum((w*x-y)**2 for x, y in [(1, 2), (2, 4)]) / F(2) def step(w, eta): return w - eta * 5*(w-2) w1 = step(F(1), F(1, 10)) w2 = step(w1, F(1, 10)) assert (w1, w2) == (F(3, 2), F(7, 4)) assert [loss(w) for w in (1, w1, w2, 2)] == [F(5, 2), F(5, 8), F(5, 32), 0] assert loss(step(F(1), F(1, 2))) == F(45, 8) assert (1*2-2)**2 == 0 and (w1*2-2)**2 == 1 for k in range(51): eta = F(k, 100) for w in [F(-1), F(1), F(3)]: assert loss(w) == F(5, 2)*(w-2)**2 assert (loss(step(w, eta)) < loss(w)) == (0 < eta < F(2, 5)) h = F(1, 100) assert (loss(w+h)-loss(w-h))/(2*h) == 5*(w-2) print('All F04 checks passed.') The symmetric difference equals the derivative exactly here because the loss is quadratic. The algebra in the learning pack establishes the step-size interval for every starting weight away from the optimum. The finite sweep checks the implementation on both sides of each boundary.

Prepared for Vinit · 1 November 2026 Purpose: Develop the ability to reason about, design, evaluate, and economically justify reliable software and AI systems. Build transferable engineering judgment that survives changes in languages, frameworks, vendors, and models. What this edition contains: a curated source catalog, 18 connected module briefs, six synthesis assignments, a worked example, a finite 30-run production plan, and reusable production/audit prompts. It is the foundation and specification for the deeper library; the 18 full learning packs have not yet been generated. Original papers remain at their linked sources; this file is not an offline collection of those papers. Evidence status: Source pages were opened on 1 November 2026. The catalog distinguishes full-text access, abstract access, and course/book indexes. Those statuses establish source identity and relevance, not an exhaustive technical audit of each work. Read the actual supporting passage before citing a paper’s detailed result. Pedagogical choices, sequencing, exercises, and workload sizes below are recommendations, not empirically optimal prescriptions.

How do I turn an uncertain customer problem into a system whose behavior, reliability, and economics I can defend? This question creates a useful intersection of software engineering, cloud, AI, and business. It allows breadth while requiring the same ideas to recur. The desired capabilities are to: Formulate a problem, define an invariant, and reason from a baseline to a better solution. Predict important resource and failure constraints before selecting a technology. Separate measurements from assumptions, and evidence from plausible explanations. Read a paper and identify its mechanism, experimental scope, and limitations. Evaluate an AI system at the level of the complete customer task. Explain how architecture changes cost, risk, maintenance, and the offer a customer buys. Write a clear decision memo, including what evidence would reverse the recommendation. Framework fluency still matters when building and debugging a real system. In this library, implementation is a way to test a principle. It does not define the curriculum.

Area Core question Modules Tangible evidence of progress Reasoning and mathematical models What follows from the assumptions, and how would I find out whether they hold? F01–F04 Proof sketches, counterexamples, estimates, experiment designs Systems and cloud What state exists, where can it fail, and which resource limits the design? S01–S06 Execution traces, failure models, capacity estimates, isolation boundaries AI systems What does the model learn, what can the surrounding system guarantee, and how is quality measured? A01–A05 Evaluation sets, baseline comparisons, retrieval diagnoses, serving estimates Product and business judgment Who benefits, what will they change, and can the economics support delivery? B01–B03 Customer evidence plans, unit models, pricing hypotheses, distribution choices The business area is intentionally smaller. Its role is to shape engineering decisions, not to start a second general MBA curriculum.

sections.section: Repeated concepts that make the areas compound
sections.text: Concept First use Later reuse Invariants and contracts Algorithm correctness Transactions, replicated logs, agent permissions, billing rules State and information Data structures and representations Caches, indexes, model parameters, external knowledge, audit trails Uncertainty and expected loss Probability Evaluation, incident diagnosis, customer research, economic sensitivity Scarce resources Time and memory Queues, network bandwidth, GPU memory, engineer time, support effort Measurement and feedback Experiments Model selection, deployment, product adoption, pricing changes Boundaries and incentives Abstraction and ownership Security, organizational handoffs, supplier dependence, customer switching Each new pack should name an earlier concept it reuses and a later decision it enables. A source earns its place through that connection, not through fame alone.

Use one recurring fictional case: a business service that receives documents, extracts evidence, proposes an action, and requires approval for consequential changes. The case is only a study vehicle. It is not a product recommendation, a commitment to document AI, or evidence of market demand. Use other examples to test transfer.

Core: Understand the mechanism; reproduce a small example; explain one failure condition. Application: Apply it under changed constraints and defend a decision. Research extension: Read a difficult proof, reproduce a published experiment, or compare recent methods when a real question justifies it. Complete Core and Application before collecting additional papers on the same subject. A historical paper teaches a mechanism or argument; it does not establish the best current implementation.

Vendor certification paths, framework surveys, daily AI news, broad lists of tools, exhaustive distributed-system algorithms, training a frontier model, unrelated scientific fields, general investing, and startup biographies. Add one only when it resolves a concrete gap in an existing module.

Do not infer mathematical readiness from years of employment. Begin with a small diagnostic: Given a duplicate-detection loop, state its invariant and count its work. Calculate a conditional probability from a small contingency table. Multiply a small matrix by a vector and explain the shape of the result. Explain why a benchmark with more successes can still be a worse comparison. Use the result to generate short bridges in logic, algebra, probability, and derivatives. These are preparation, not a pass/fail judgment about engineering ability. The MIT algorithms course explicitly lists discrete mathematics as a prerequisite [R01]. The mathematical reference is a shelf of selected chapters, not a cover-to-cover assignment [R02].

The questions and exercises below are original curriculum designs. Source labels point to the catalog in section 5. Each exercise includes a criterion for a useful answer; the later learning pack should supply a separate worked solution.

sections.section: F01 — Invariants, algorithms, and the cost of computation
sections.text: Question: How do I improve a brute-force solution while preserving its correctness? Starting scope: One problem, a correct baseline, repeated work, a useful representation, and an invariant. Introduce asymptotic analysis alongside the specific operation being counted. Add hashing or a monotonic two-pointer example only after deriving why the operation is safe. Sources: R01, beginning with algorithms/computation, data structures, and hashing. Return to dynamic programming later rather than treating every pattern as required first reading. Exercise: Solve duplicate detection by pairwise comparison, then with remembered state. Give a loop invariant. Explain the assumptions behind the time and memory claims. Change the task to bounded memory or a stream. Exit criterion: Derive the improvement, identify what information must be retained, and give a case where a stated performance assumption fails. Connections: S02 indexes, S04 safety properties, A03 retrieval representations. Prerequisites: basic loops; a bridge in sets and induction if needed.

sections.section: F02 — Probability, base rates, and decisions under uncertainty
sections.text: Question: When should a system act, abstain, or ask a person? Starting scope: Conditional probability, expected value, base rates, and unequal error costs. Use small count tables before symbolic notation. Distinguish a probability estimate from a calibrated estimate and from a decision threshold. Source: R02, probability and distributions. Use R13 for later connections to classification. Exercise: Construct two populations with different event prevalence. Apply the same detector characteristics to both. Compare the proportion of alerts that are correct. Then change the cost of a missed event versus an unnecessary intervention. Exit criterion: Explain why the action rule can change without changing the detector, and list the assumptions that would make the calculation misleading. Connections: F03 experiment interpretation, A05 evaluation, B02 expected cost. Prerequisites: fractions and elementary algebra.

sections.section: F03 — Measurement, experiment design, and evidence quality
sections.text: Question: Did the change improve the system, or did the measurement change? Starting scope: Sampling, distributions, uncertainty, confounding, randomization, and metric definitions. Keep a performance benchmark distinct from a causal product experiment. Record workload and population boundaries. Sources: R03 for experiment design checks; R13 for resampling and model assessment. Exercise: Design a comparison between two document-processing pipelines. Specify the experimental unit, dataset, outcomes, important subgroups, cost metric, exclusions, and a stopping/analysis plan before observing results. Explain when randomizing individual requests would be inappropriate. Exit criterion: Identify plausible leakage, selection bias, or interference, and explain what the experiment can and cannot conclude. Connections: S05 latency measurement, A01 generalization, A05 evaluations, B01 demand evidence. Prerequisites: F02.

Question: What computation sits underneath embeddings and learning? Starting scope: Vectors, dot products, norms, matrix shapes, derivatives, and a small gradient update. This is a bridge to later AI mechanisms, not a survey of all linear algebra. Source: R02, selected material from linear algebra, analytic geometry, vector calculus, and continuous optimization. Exercise: Compute similarity for a few small vectors; show how normalization changes the comparison. Fit a one-parameter linear model using a tiny dataset and calculate a gradient step by hand. Exit criterion: Track dimensions, explain what the loss measures, and describe why lowering training loss alone does not establish usefulness on new inputs. Connections: A01 learning, A02 attention, A03 retrieval. Prerequisites: algebra and a short derivative bridge; F02 for probabilistic interpretation.

sections.section: S01 — Resource models, locality, and abstraction costs
sections.text: Question: Why can two implementations of the same algorithm have very different costs? Starting scope: CPU work, data movement, working sets, memory representation, virtualization, and locality. Separate an abstract cost model from an implementation measurement. Never transfer an unsourced latency table between machines. Source: R04, selected CPU scheduling, address-space, paging, and translation material. The later GPU connection is supplied by R16. Exercise: Compare contiguous scanning, pointer traversal, and batched work. Predict the dominant resource for a stated workload, then specify a benchmark that could disprove the prediction. Exit criterion: State machine/workload assumptions and distinguish algorithmic complexity, wall-clock time, and throughput. Connections: S02 storage, S05 capacity, A04 inference. Prerequisites: F01.

sections.section: S02 — Data organization, indexes, and recovery
sections.text: Question: What must be stored so reads are useful and acknowledged changes survive the stated failures? Starting scope: Logical data versus physical layout, access paths, write cost, and recovery records. Study a small index and a small recovery trace. Relational reasoning is a durable model, not allegiance to a database product. Sources: R05, storage, indexes/filters, logging, and recovery; R04 persistence as a bridge. Exercise: Design storage for facts extracted from documents, preserving source identity and revisions. List two important queries and estimate which records each access path touches. Trace a crash between successive writes. Exit criterion: Explain the read/write/storage trade-off and identify what the acknowledgement actually promises. Connections: S03 transactions, S04 replication, A03 evidence provenance. Prerequisites: F01, S01.

sections.section: S03 — Concurrency, transactions, and logical time
sections.text: Question: Which interleavings can violate the application’s invariant? Starting scope: Shared state, histories, concurrency control, and causal ordering. Keep transaction isolation, wall-clock order, and logical time as distinct concepts. Sources: R05 concurrency-control theory and selected mechanisms; R06 for event ordering. Exercise: Draw two concurrent attempts to consume the same limited resource. Produce one violating history, then explain which constraint or protocol excludes it. Add a delayed message from another process. Exit criterion: Show the history explicitly and explain what is guaranteed across the boundary of each mechanism. Connections: S04 consensus, S06 permission changes, A05 tool side effects. Prerequisites: F01, S02.

sections.section: S04 — Replication, consensus, and partial failure
sections.text: Question: What can a group of machines safely agree on when some communication fails? Starting scope: Replicated state machines, logs, leader election, safety versus liveness, and the declared failure model. Use Raft as one worked design. Avoid treating it as a universal answer to all consistency problems. Sources: R07, sections 2 and 5 and the state/transition summary; R06 as prerequisite context. R10 helps separate transport behavior from application guarantees. Exercise: Trace a leader failure during an update and a later retry from a client. Identify the distinct questions of log commitment, client knowledge, and duplicate business effects. Exit criterion: State a safety property, show why a naive alternative violates it, and identify a failure outside the model. Connections: S06 reliability, A05 workflows, B02 reliability expense. Prerequisites: S03.

sections.section: S05 — Queues, tail latency, and cloud elasticity
sections.text: Question: What happens when demand varies and work waits for a scarce resource? Starting scope: Arrival/service rates, concurrency, latency distributions, admission control, and provisioning. Connect workload shape to the decision to reserve, share, or elastically obtain capacity. Sources: R08 for latency tails; R09 handling overload; R12 for the original cloud economics argument. Read R12 as a historical model, not a current price guide. Exercise: Specify a bursty workload and a service-time distribution. Draw what happens to waiting work when offered load exceeds processing capacity. Compare rejecting, queueing, batching, and adding capacity under the same objective. Exit criterion: Explain why an average alone is insufficient; define the population and percentile; identify a constraint autoscaling cannot remove instantly. Connections: A04 serving, B02 unit economics, B03 offer design. Prerequisites: F02, F03, S01.

sections.section: S06 — Reliability, isolation, and authority boundaries
sections.text: Question: What limits damage when a component fails, lies, or acts with too much authority? Starting scope: Service objectives, error budgets, observability, isolation, least privilege, and complete mediation. Keep an availability failure distinct from an authorization failure. Sources: R09 embracing risk and service-level objectives; R11 introductory protection principles; R10 for function placement. Exercise: For the recurring case, draw principals, data boundaries, and permitted actions. Identify which checks belong outside the language model. Define an observable service objective and an explicit trade-off between additional safeguards and operating cost. Exit criterion: Identify a failure that retries cannot fix, and explain what remains true if the model proposes an unauthorized action. Connections: A05 agents, B02 cost of failures, B03 customer trust. Prerequisites: S03–S05.

sections.section: A01 — Learning, generalization, and distribution change
sections.text: Question: What does evidence on past examples justify about future examples? Starting scope: Objectives, baselines, fitting, validation, overfitting, leakage, and distribution change. Begin with a small conventional predictor before reasoning about a language model. Source: R13, statistical learning, resampling, and regularization; R02 as mathematical support. Exercise: Design a split for documents with repeated organizations, templates, and revisions. Compare it with a random row split. Specify a simple baseline and explain what each comparison would establish. Exit criterion: Explain a high-scoring but invalid evaluation and describe an alternative that matches the intended deployment. Connections: F03 evidence, A03 retrieval, A05 monitoring. Prerequisites: F02–F04.

sections.section: A02 — Attention and the Transformer mechanism
sections.text: Question: How does a representation of one token incorporate information from other tokens? Starting scope: Queries, keys, values, shapes, attention weights, masking, and the distinction between training and inference. Trace one small operation before studying a full architecture. Source: R14. The original architecture and experiments are historical; do not infer that every current model has all of its design choices. Exercise: Calculate a tiny attention operation with explicit matrices. Change a mask and identify which outputs may change. Describe where sequence length enters the chosen computation. Exit criterion: Explain the operation and its assumptions without relying on an API or an anthropomorphic explanation. Connections: F04 transformations, A03 representations, A04 memory cost. Prerequisites: F04, A01.

sections.section: A03 — Retrieval, external knowledge, and provenance
sections.text: Question: When should information live in stored evidence rather than only in a model’s parameters? Starting scope: Candidate retrieval, ranking, evidence selection, freshness, access control, and answer support. Separate retrieval quality from generation quality. Source: R15 for a concrete retrieval-augmented model. Use S02 concepts for storage and S06 for access boundaries. The paper’s design is not interchangeable with every product called RAG. Exercise: Construct cases where the correct document is missing, present but not retrieved, retrieved but ignored, and cited without supporting the answer. Design a check for each failure. Exit criterion: Localize the failure stage and explain what a citation verifies and what it does not. Connections: S02 indexes, F03 measurement, A05 evaluation. Prerequisites: S02, A01, A02.

sections.section: A04 — Inference serving and memory economics
sections.text: Question: How do memory management and scheduling change the cost of serving a model? Starting scope: Model storage, per-request state, batching, throughput/latency constraints, and memory fragmentation. Derive estimates only for a stated architecture and numeric precision. Source: R16, PagedAttention. Reuse R04 and R08 for the systems connection. Treat published speedups as workload-specific results, not a prediction for a current provider. Exercise: Write a symbolic memory budget for model state plus active requests. Vary sequence length and concurrency. Compare two serving policies under a fixed latency objective and an explicitly assumed workload. Exit criterion: Identify the limiting resource and list what must be measured before claiming a cost improvement. Connections: S01 locality/virtualization, S05 queues, B02 unit economics. Prerequisites: S01, S05, A02.

sections.section: A05 — Evaluation, workflows, and controlled autonomy
sections.text: Question: When is a system capable enough, and constrained enough, to perform the intended task? Starting scope: End-to-end success, baselines, failure categories, repeated trials, tool contracts, action budgets, and authority. Distinguish a fixed workflow from model-directed action selection. Sources: R18 as one early tool-interaction design; R17 for system-level dependencies; R03 for evidence discipline. S06 supplies the authority model. Exercise: Compare a deterministic workflow, a single model call, and a tool-using loop on the same task set. Include explicit failure cases, costs, and side-effect rules. Explain how you would investigate disagreement between an automated judge and a person. Exit criterion: Defend the simplest design supported by the evidence and identify what an offline evaluation misses. Connections: F02/F03 uncertainty and measurement, S03 retries, S06 permissions, B02 cost. Prerequisites: A01, A03, S06; A04 for serving estimates.

sections.section: B01 — Customer problems, alternatives, and evidence of demand
sections.text: Question: What problem is costly enough that someone will change their behavior? Starting scope: User versus buyer, current workaround, frequency, consequences, adoption friction, and observed commitments. Keep customer observations separate from founder interpretations. Source: R19, the customer-interview segment. This is practitioner guidance, not experimental evidence that a given business will succeed. Exercise: Choose a business workflow you can observe. Prepare questions about a recent real instance, its costs, alternatives, and decision process. Define stronger and weaker forms of evidence before speaking with anyone. No outreach is performed by this library. Exit criterion: State a falsifiable demand hypothesis and distinguish politeness, stated interest, trials, payment, and repeated use. Connections: F03 measurement, A05 success definitions, B03 distribution. Prerequisites: none; revisit after F03.

sections.section: B02 — Unit economics, pricing units, and sensitivity
sections.text: Question: Which unit of useful work creates value, and what does delivering it actually cost? Starting scope: Revenue, variable cost, fixed cost, support and review effort, contribution, and uncertain demand. Separate technical units such as tokens from business outcomes such as resolved cases. Sources: R20 for unit metrics; R21 for pricing/packaging hypotheses. Reuse R12 for capacity assumptions. Exercise: Model a service per attempted job and per verified successful job. Include failures and human review. Vary success probability, workload size, customer price, and support burden. State what is hypothetical versus observed. Exit criterion: Explain why a lower model price can still yield a worse overall service, and why positive contribution is not the same as company profitability. Connections: S05 capacity, A04 inference, A05 outcomes, B03 customer offer. Prerequisites: F02, B01, A05.

sections.section: B03 — Distribution, product boundaries, and defensibility
sections.text: Question: Why would a customer find, adopt, keep, and pay for this offering when alternatives improve? Starting scope: A narrow initial customer, acquisition path, onboarding, workflow fit, switching friction, supplier dependence, and maintenance burden. Treat a claimed moat as a hypothesis requiring evidence. Sources: R22 on early manual recruitment and service; R21 on segmentation/packaging; R19 on problem evidence. Exercise: Compare a self-serve tool, a managed service, and an internal deployment for the same customer job. Specify the buyer, distribution route, required trust, variable labor, and effect of a supplier bundling your main feature. Exit criterion: Explain which assumptions make an option attractive and identify evidence that would overturn the recommendation. Connections: S06 reliability commitments, A05 evaluation, B01 demand, B02 economics. Prerequisites: B01, B02.

Read modes: “Read” means a selected passage is an initial assignment; “Reference” means consult only to resolve a question. A course link is not an instruction to finish the course. Access labels: “Full text opened” means the text was accessible to the retrieval tool and relevant portions were inspected, not that every page was exhaustively reviewed. “Index opened” means the host’s description/contents were verified, with chapter-level verification left to pack production. “Abstract opened” supports source selection, not detailed experimental claims. ID Source and primary link First reading and role Access checked / limitation R01 MIT 6.006: Introduction to Algorithms, Spring 2020 — Demaine, Ku, Solomon Selected opening lectures and hashing; use problems to practice proof and cost analysis Course index/syllabus opened. Prerequisite mathematics may need a bridge. R02 Mathematics for Machine Learning — Deisenroth, Faisal, Ong, 2020 Reference: chapters on linear algebra, geometry, calculus, probability, optimization Author index/contents opened; free PDF linked. Not a beginner-first cover-to-cover assignment. R03 Patterns of Trustworthy Experimentation: Pre-Experiment Stage — Microsoft Research, 2020 Read experiment-design patterns; ask which apply to the chosen unit of analysis Primary practitioner article opened. Platform experience is contextual evidence. R04 Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces — Remzi and Andrea Arpaci-Dusseau Reference: scheduling, address spaces/paging, concurrency, persistence Author index opened; free chapters available. Implementation exercises may use C without making C the learning goal. R05 CMU 15-445/645, Fall 2025 schedule — Andy Pavlo Reference: storage, indexes, concurrency theory, logging/recovery Course index/schedule opened with lecture-note links. Use the archived edition consistently. R06 Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System — Leslie Lamport, 1978 Read event ordering and logical clocks before distributed histories Full-text PDF opened. Scope is the paper’s formal model, not all modern distributed-system behavior. R07 In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm, extended version — Ongaro and Ousterhout, 2014 Read replicated state machines and core Raft sections; trace the state summary Full-text PDF opened. Defer membership changes and full proofs until the core trace is clear. R08 The Tail at Scale — Dean and Barroso, 2013 Read the motivation and mechanism of latency tails; compare with workload measurements Publisher record/abstract opened. Linked ACM full text returned an access error during this session; detailed claims need a verified accessible copy. R09 Site Reliability Engineering — Google, 2016 Selected chapters: Embracing Risk, Service Level Objectives, Handling Overload Contents and selected full chapters opened. Adapt practices to scale and context. R10 End-to-End Arguments in System Design — Saltzer, Reed, Clark, 1984 Read argument and examples; use it to locate correctness responsibilities Full-text PDF opened. An architectural argument, not a mechanical prohibition on lower-layer functionality. R11 The Protection of Information in Computer Systems — Saltzer and Schroeder, 1975 Selected introductory protection/design principles Author-hosted entry/overview opened. Historical mechanisms require contextual reading; principles are the intended focus. R12 Above the Clouds: A Berkeley View of Cloud Computing — Armbrust et al., 2009 Read the elasticity/economics argument and assumptions University record/abstract opened. Its prices, market picture, and provider details are historical. R13 An Introduction to Statistical Learning — James, Witten, Hastie, Tibshirani; Python edition also Taylor Selected statistical-learning, resampling, and regularization material Author index/contents opened; free book PDFs linked. Choose one edition consistently. R14 Attention Is All You Need — Vaswani et al., 2017 Read model architecture after F04; reproduce one attention calculation Author-submitted abstract/metadata opened; full paper linked. Historical translation results do not establish present product quality. R15 Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks — Lewis et al., 2020 Read model formulation and evidence evaluation Author-submitted abstract/metadata opened; full paper linked. Original training/model formulation differs from many later RAG workflows. R16 Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention — Kwon et al., 2023 Read memory problem, mechanism, and evaluation conditions Author-submitted abstract/metadata opened; full paper linked. Published speedups are not universal serving guarantees. R17 Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems — Sculley et al., 2015 Read system boundaries, dependencies, and feedback risks Conference full-text PDF opened. Systems analysis, not a new model algorithm or current agent benchmark. R18 ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models — Yao et al., 2022/2023 Read the action/observation approach and evaluation setup Author-submitted abstract/metadata opened; full paper linked. Treat as one research design, not proof of general agent reliability. R19 Startup School Week 1: evaluating ideas and talking to users — YC / Hale / Migicovsky, 2019 Start with the user-interview segment, then evaluate its fit to a local customer Primary transcript opened. Practitioner advice with a startup-selection context. R20 FinOps Framework: Unit Economics — FinOps Foundation Read distinctions between resource units and business outcomes Current framework page opened. A living practice framework, not a causal study of profitability. R21 Pricing low-touch SaaS — Patrick McKenzie / Stripe Read segmentation and packaging examples; turn them into testable hypotheses Primary practitioner guide opened. Historical case prices are not current market recommendations. R22 Do Things that Don’t Scale — Paul Graham, 2013 Read manual recruitment and early customer-service argument Author essay opened. Anecdotal founder guidance; assess survivorship and context.

Create a short card with: problem; assumptions; mechanism; evidence; limitations; one derivation or trace; and a decision it informs. Read the actual relevant section before promoting a claim from “author says” to “supported within this setup.” For empirical papers, record dataset, baseline, metric, compute/workload, and uncertainty where reported. For formal papers, record the model and statement proved. For practitioner essays, record the experience and possible selection bias. These are different kinds of evidence. When a paper is too hard, write down the precise missing concept. Request a bridge on that concept and return to the same passage. Avoid generating an unrelated beginner course.

sections.section: 6. Worked seed: connect performance, reliability, and economics
sections.text: This example is original and hypothetical. Every input below is chosen for teaching, not measured in production. Arithmetic has been checked; no system benchmark was run.

sections.section: A. A local optimization has a system-level ceiling
sections.text: Assume a request takes one normalized unit of serial time. A stage uses fraction f of that time. Everything else is unchanged. If that stage becomes s times faster: T_new = (1 − f) + f/s Speedup = 1 / ((1 − f) + f/s) For f = 0.30 and s = 4, T_new = 0.775 and the total speedup is about 1.29. The fourfold stage improvement is not a fourfold request improvement. Derivation: Split the original time into improved and unchanged portions; divide only the improved portion by s; compare old to new time. Boundary: This model excludes overlap, changes in queueing, different request mixes, and resource contention. Optimizing the stage may change those factors, so measurements can differ. Do not present this calculation as a p99 forecast.

sections.section: B. More stages can impose a success requirement
sections.text: Assume eight stages must all succeed. Let each stage succeed with probability 0.97 and assume independent outcomes. Then: P(all succeed) = 0.97^8 ≈ 0.7837 This is a consequence of the assumed probability model. It is not a measured success rate for any agent. Without independence, use conditional probabilities: P(all succeed) = P(S1) × P(S2 | S1) × … × P(S8 | S1,…,S7) Boundary: Shared bad inputs, common dependencies, retries, and recovery can invalidate the simple independent-stage model. An extra verification stage can improve the full outcome even while adding another component. Evaluate the complete task.

sections.section: C. The cheapest attempt need not produce the cheapest useful outcome
sections.text: Assume each attempted job has the stated variable cost, and a “success” is an actually correct, usable, billable result. There are no retries, review costs, refunds, or fixed costs in this toy model. Hypothetical pipeline Variable cost per attempt Success probability Expected variable cost per success over many comparable attempts A ₹1.00 0.70 ₹1.00 / 0.70 ≈ ₹1.43 B ₹1.30 0.95 ₹1.30 / 0.95 ≈ ₹1.37 For N comparable attempts, expected cost is Nc and expected successes are Np; their ratio is c/p. This ratio of expectations is a planning metric, not a guarantee about a small batch’s realized ratio. If revenue is hypothetically ₹3 per successful job, expected contribution per attempt is p×₹3−c: ₹1.10 for A and ₹1.55 for B. Neither figure is profit after fixed costs, and neither establishes customer willingness to pay ₹3. Boundary: Review labor, correlated failures, accepted-but-wrong outputs, usage distribution, and pricing rules can change the result. Replace assumptions with evidence before a real decision.

F01 supplies decomposition; F02 supplies probability; S05 forces workload assumptions; A05 defines success; B02 makes the denominator economically meaningful. The same case is examined through several connected ideas rather than through several unrelated tutorials. Transfer exercise: Introduce an optional human-review stage. State which inputs you need to decide whether it improves the offer. A useful answer includes its effect on false acceptance, completion rate, turnaround time, variable labor, and what customers will pay—not just model accuracy.

These assignments connect modules after their prerequisites have been produced. They are proposed future work, not completed experiments. ID Decision Inputs to reuse Required output C01 Where must duplicate-effect prevention live? F01, S02–S04, R10 A failure timeline; invariant; responsibility boundary; counterexample to an inadequate fix C02 Does better model performance improve the customer outcome? S01/S05, A04, B02 Resource model; workload sensitivity; effect on latency and cost per successful task C04 Which product boundary makes the service viable? sections.section: 8. Finite production plan for the subscription period
sections.text: Production and learning are separate schedules. The runs below commission and check future study assets. They do not assert that the learner can master this material in a month. A run is a unit of work, not a guaranteed daily quota or an enabled automation. There are 18 core packs, six synthesis assignments, four audits, one map/diagnostic run, and one final packaging run. If fewer runs fit the actual allowance or remaining subscription period, preserve prerequisite packs and audits, and defer additional synthesis. Verify the real expiration date before setting a schedule. Run Work item Deliverable / stopping point 01 Map and diagnostic This architecture, source registry, prerequisite questions, stable IDs 02 F01 Invariant and algorithm-improvement pack 03 B01 Customer-evidence pack; no invented interviews 04 F02 Probability and expected-loss pack 05 F03 Measurement and experimental-design pack 06 S01 Resource-model pack 07 Audit A Check sources, derivations, prerequisite gaps in runs 02–06 08 F04 Mathematical bridge pack 09 S02 Storage/index/recovery pack 10 S03 Concurrency and ordering pack 11 S04 Replication and failure pack 12 S05 Queues/cloud elasticity pack 13 C01 Duplicate-effect decision memo 14 S06 Reliability and authority pack 15 Audit B Check systems traces, failure assumptions, and cross-links 16 A01 Learning/generalization pack 17 A02 Attention mechanism pack 18 A03 Retrieval/provenance pack 19 A04 Inference-serving pack 20 A05 Evaluation/autonomy pack 21 C02 Customer-outcome evaluation memo 22 Audit C Check AI evidence, math, benchmark scope, and unsupported generalizations 23 B02 Economics and sensitivity pack 24 B03 Distribution/product-boundary pack 25 C03 Capacity and cost memo 26 C04 Product-boundary memo 27 C05 Autonomy decision memo 28 C06 Supplier-change decision memo 29 Audit D Cross-library contradictions, broken prerequisites, missing answers, missing sources 30 Package and handoff Index, consolidated notes, separate solutions, reference cards, open-questions ledger, export

Maintain a simple index with: run ID, module ID, status, artifact path, source-verification date, unresolved issues, and prerequisites. Suggested states are queued, drafted, checked, and needs-revision. These track artifact production, not the learner’s mastery. The worker must inspect this index at each run. If a prerequisite or earlier artifact is unavailable, repair the missing link or report the block; do not fabricate continuity. If a run fails, retry that run before advancing. Use a finite run count and an end date matching the actual subscription window when configuring an automation. Store original explanations, source metadata, derivations, exercises, and answers in downloadable formats. Keep references to originals and make lawful local copies only where access and rights allow. Public links and a list of paper titles alone do not satisfy deferred offline study.

Each core pack should be independently usable later: Orientation: Decision it enables, prerequisites, notation, and a short entry route. Mechanism: A concrete example, explicit assumptions, and a trace, derivation, or useful diagram. Boundary: An invariant or claim, a counterexample, and the conditions where the model stops applying. Evidence: Primary sources with exact supporting locations; distinguish proofs, experiments, and practitioner judgment. Transfer: One prior concept reused, one future use, and one changed-constraint question. Practice: A bounded task with setup, success criteria, and separate hints/solutions. Reference: Compact recall card, assumptions, and unresolved questions. Use a short orientation, a moderate core explanation, and optional deeper material. Avoid a mandatory length floor. Depth should follow the question. Give mathematical bridges before derivations that require them. For each important source claim, keep a ledger row containing claim, source, locator, evidence type, and applicability limit. A citation title alone is not evidence. A second review by the same model is useful but is not independent verification; grounding still comes from source inspection, valid derivations, tests, or external measurements.

Act as a research editor and engineering tutor building a durable foundation for an individual SDE with roughly two years of experience. The goal is transferable judgment in software systems, cloud, AI, and technology business. The user’s current languages and frameworks are not curriculum boundaries. Read the supplied library index, the assigned module brief, and the prerequisite packs before writing. Work on exactly the assigned run ID: [RUN_ID]. Topic/module: [MODULE_ID]. If required material is unavailable, identify the gap and produce the smallest useful repair rather than inventing prior state. Optimize for understanding mechanisms, testing claims, and making decisions. Start with the concrete question in the module brief. Explain necessary prerequisites and notation; do not infer mathematical proficiency from years of experience. Browse and open the relevant primary sources. Use original papers, author textbooks, university materials, original postmortems, and first-party technical documentation. For business, distinguish practitioner experience from empirical evidence. Record source title, authors, date/version, URL, relevant location, and access limitations. Cite only inspected material. An abstract is insufficient support for a detailed experimental claim. Produce one self-contained learning pack: orientation; mechanism with a worked example; assumptions and failure boundary; evidence; a trade-off that changes a decision; connections to earlier modules; a bounded exercise; and separate hints/solutions. Add a concise reference card. Use the lowest level of explanation necessary for the question—bytes, execution traces, mathematical models, or incentive/cost models as appropriate. Prefer one primary anchor and at most two necessary supplements per pack. Use one illustrative implementation or pseudocode when useful. Compare additional implementations only when they reveal a meaningful design trade-off. A source count or engine count is not a quality target. Distinguish sourced facts, derivations with explicit premises, hypothetical inputs, observed experimental results, and unresolved claims. Source empirical numbers and implementation constants. Show derivations for calculated results. State versions/workloads for implementation-dependent facts. Mark code as executed or untested accurately. Include a production incident only if a primary account supports its relevance. Otherwise use a clearly labeled hypothetical counterexample. Keep historical research results separate from current product claims. For current technical claims, verify current primary documentation. Audit consequential claims and calculations before finalizing. Correct discovered errors. List remaining uncertainties with specific verification steps; do not manufacture a quota of questionable claims. Evidence gaps must not silently become core facts. Keep the core readable without repeated claim labels on every sentence. Put detailed provenance in a claim ledger. Do not pad to a word count. Preserve the chosen scope and stop when this run’s deliverable is complete. Save the pack and separate solutions in durable, downloadable form using the environment’s supported storage. Update the index with actual artifact locations, source-check date, prerequisite links, checks performed, and unresolved issues. Never claim a save or test that did not succeed.

Audit the supplied packs [IDS] against their original sources and stated assumptions. Treat the drafts as claims to check, not as authority. Prioritize claims that affect correctness, causal interpretation, security boundaries, performance, or economic decisions. Open the cited passage; verify that it supports the wording. Check mathematical premises and arithmetic. Where feasible, run the relevant small experiment. Distinguish source existence, source support, reproducibility, and applicability to a different setting. Look for invented precision, mixed versions, missing prerequisites, inconsistent terminology, benchmark generalization, undefined success metrics, and solutions that contradict the exercises. For business claims, separate assumptions and anecdotes from observed demand. Do not invent an independent reviewer or claim independent validation merely because this is another model pass. Return a correction log with location, issue, evidence, change, and residual uncertainty. Apply supported corrections, preserve source provenance, and update cross-links. Record checks not possible in this environment. Finish with a corrected pack and an honest verification status.

sections.section: 12. Use the library at your own pace
sections.text: Pick one question relevant to your curiosity or a real decision. Follow its prerequisite links rather than reading in a rigid calendar. Begin with the short orientation. Attempt the example or exercise before opening the solution. On a later visit, change one assumption and see whether your explanation still works. Track learning separately from production: can recognize, can explain, can derive/trace, can transfer. A packet can be checked while your own understanding is still at the recognition stage. Neither a large archive nor a completed reading count establishes skill. When time is scarce, favor revisiting one useful decision and its supporting mechanisms. Expand the library when a concrete question exposes a missing concept. This keeps a versatile foundation connected to increasingly capable reasoning.

sections.section: Scheduled task prompt: Build the SDE Foundations Library
sections.text: Use the following as the task’s instructions. Make SDE_Foundations_Library_v1.md accessible to the scheduled task. Set the cadence, end date, and model in the task configuration separately. This document does not create a schedule. Act as my research engineer, technical editor, and curriculum architect. Build a durable Markdown knowledge library that I can study later at my own pace.

Develop my transferable reasoning and engineering judgment across mathematical foundations, software systems, cloud, AI, and technology business. I am an SDE with roughly two years of experience. Do not organize the curriculum around my current languages, frameworks, employer, or certifications. Explain prerequisites rather than assuming mathematical fluency. Use SDE_Foundations_Library_v1.md as the curriculum authority. Its Library reference is libfile_5d05587b7cd481918fb66c263ba6df00. Read the actual file, especially the module briefs, source catalog, and 30-run plan. Treat its source list as a researched starting point, not as proof that every paper has already been fully read or every claim verified. The central question is: How do I turn an uncertain problem into a system whose behavior, reliability, and economics I can defend?

At the start of every run, read the curriculum, SDE_INDEX.md, and the relevant existing artifacts. Rely on saved files, not assumed chat memory or a persistent scratch directory. On the first run, initialize the index and source register from the curriculum. Include the planned run sequence, module dependencies, and diagnostic questions; no learner response is required to proceed. When readiness is unknown, include optional prerequisite bridges. Never invent my diagnostic answers or learning progress. On subsequent runs, complete the next unfinished work item in this sequence: 01 Map/index; 02 F01; 03 B01; 04 F02; 05 F03; 06 S01; 07 Audit A; 08 F04; 09 S02; 10 S03; 11 S04; 12 S05; 13 C01; 14 S06; 15 Audit B; 16 A01; 17 A02; 18 A03; 19 A04; 20 A05; 21 C02; 22 Audit C; 23 B02; 24 B03; 25 C03; 26 C04; 27 C05; 28 C06; 29 Audit D; 30 Final packaging. Repair a blocking error or missing prerequisite before advancing. Reuse existing completed work. If saving was interrupted, reconcile existing artifacts before creating duplicates. If essential input is inaccessible, report the specific block; do not replace the agreed curriculum with an invented one. Complete one substantial work item per execution. A difficult item may continue across executions: save a clear checkpoint, identify what remains, and resume it next time. Do not silently truncate a lesson or claim the whole sequence is finished because 30 executions have elapsed.

Open and inspect primary sources: original papers, author textbooks, university material, first-party documentation, and original incident reports. Use a few strong sources per topic, adding others only when they resolve a meaningful question or contradiction. For consequential factual claims, provide a supporting URL and precise section, page, theorem, figure, or other verified locator. Distinguish sourced facts, derived results, hypothetical inputs, measured results, practitioner judgment, and unresolved claims. Keep empirical findings within their reported workload, population, and experimental conditions. Verify current details when a claim depends on present implementations. An abstract is insufficient evidence for detailed experimental claims. When access fails, seek an accessible primary alternative or mark the limitation. Historical papers teach mechanisms; their prices and benchmark results are not current forecasts. Business anecdotes are not proof of demand. Show premises for derivations and label invented example numbers. Check arithmetic and consequential technical claims. Accurately distinguish executed experiments from untested code. Write original synthesis and link to source material; respect access and reproduction rights.

Use stable filenames: SDE_INDEX.md: curriculum progress, artifact links/IDs, dependencies, revisions, and next action. SDE_SOURCES.md: source register and access/verification status. SDE_<MODULE_ID>.md: each core pack or synthesis assignment. SDE_<MODULE_ID>_answers.md: hints, worked answers, and assessment criteria where applicable. SDE_Audit_<A|B|C|D>.md: audit findings and corrections. SDE_START_HERE.md: final reading routes and handoff. Each pack begins with a compact metadata table: ID, title, revision, date, prerequisites, capability developed, source-check status, and experiment status. Keep detailed claim provenance in an evidence table, not repetitive labels on every sentence. For a core pack, cover: The question and decision this knowledge enables, with a short orientation and prerequisite bridge. A substantial explanation of the mechanism, using a worked example, derivation, or execution trace. Assumptions, invariants where applicable, failure conditions, and a counterexample. Meaningful trade-offs and the evidence that would change the choice. Connections to earlier concepts and later applications. A bounded exercise plus application questions, with separate hints and worked answers. A compact reference card, supporting sources, and unresolved questions. You may reorder, combine, or rename sections and choose prose, equations, tables, pseudocode, or Mermaid diagrams. Use byte-level detail when it explains the mechanism; use mathematical, system, or economic models when those are more appropriate. Add a small prerequisite appendix if necessary. State a significant scope adjustment and its reason in the index. Keep the overall curriculum intact. Make the core independently understandable. Aim roughly for 1,500–2,500 words when justified, with no minimum and no padding. Put optional depth in an appendix. Avoid compressing several difficult ideas into an impressive but unexplained survey. An actual production incident or comparison of several engines is optional, never a quota. For synthesis items, use a decision memo suited to the assigned question. Combine the specified earlier modules, compare credible options under the same assumptions, defend a choice, and revise it after a constraint changes. Include a separate worked analysis for later self-assessment.

On audit runs, inspect the relevant original passages, recheck derivations, and examine counterexamples. Look for unsupported precision, mixed versions, missing prerequisites, misleading benchmarks, inconsistent terminology, and mismatches between exercises and answers. Record the original issue, evidence, correction, affected artifacts, and remaining uncertainty. Apply supported corrections to the existing files while preserving their identities and revision history. A second model pass is not independent validation. Track artifact states as queued, in_progress, produced, audited, or needs_revision. These describe the files, not my mastery. Preserve useful open questions without treating every minor uncertainty as a blocker. Repair consequential errors before dependent material uses them. Save outputs in durable storage available to future runs, then update the index with actual artifact links or identifiers. Preserve existing files and avoid overwriting unrelated work. Mark an item produced only after the required files are successfully saved. If durable saving is unavailable, report it and retain the completed draft where possible; do not claim persistence.

After the planned work and blocking repairs are complete, produce SDE_START_HERE.md, verify the index and answer links, and provide a downloadable archive or consolidated Markdown export if supported. Mark the program complete. Future triggers should report completion without generating filler or restarting the curriculum. Disable the task only if that capability is available and authorized by its setup. End every run with a short report: item completed or checkpointed; saved file links; checks performed; material uncertainties or blocks; and the next item. Produce the actual Markdown files, not only a plan or a chat essay.

These questions are intentionally unresolved. They need measurements, stakeholder authority or experience from a real system. Do not fill them with confidence alone.

What are the offered-arrival, burst, input-length and output-length distributions? Which deadlines are component budgets and which are customer promises? How often do timeouts leave an unknown external outcome? Which failures share a dependency and therefore cannot be multiplied as independent? How long must receipts, source revisions and recovery logs remain available?

What is the actual deployment unit: row, revision, document, customer or organization? Which templates, suppliers and revisions connect nominally separate cases? Who produces labels, with what disagreement and adjudication process? How often does evidence exist but fail at eligibility, retrieval, context selection or support? How stable are quality and calibration across segments and time? Can the evaluation corpus legally and operationally be reused across suppliers?

Which principal is authenticated at every read and effect boundary? How fresh must revocation be, and which cached decisions can outlive a policy change? Which support, export, repair and recovery paths bypass the normal application route? Which effects require two distinct conditions or people? What is the contract for historical receipt reads after access changes?

What are the measured memory peaks, phase curves, startup delay and queue behavior? Which costs are variable, committed, tiered, shared or already sunk? What labor is released capacity, and what becomes actual cash savings? What is the cost per verified timely result, including failures and review? Where do capacity tiers or acquisition/setup costs reverse the apparent optimum?

Which segment experiences the problem recently and repeatedly? Who uses, operates, approves, owns data and controls budget? What current workaround is the real competitor? What proportion activates and repeats after enough follow-up time? Does a bundle solve the complete job or only the visible component? Which claimed advantage survives exportability and a credible alternative?

In the insurance POS or claims system, where can a stale rule or revision survive into a financial decision? Which report or transaction has an implicit invariant that is checked too early? Where does a retry create a new business identity instead of reconciling the first attempt? Which metric at work counts only completed cases and hides dropped or delayed work? Which AI-generated code review needs evidence about the actual runtime, database or authority boundary? Add dated answers and evidence beneath each question as you encounter real examples. Keep facts, hypotheses and decisions visibly separate.

title: Resource models, locality, and abstraction costs

sections.section: Resource models, locality, and abstraction costs
sections.text: Field Value ID / title S01 · Resource models, locality, and abstraction costs Revision / date 1.1 · 2026-11-04 Prerequisites F01 operation counts and invariants. Optional units bridge below. F03 helps with the benchmark design. Capability developed Predict a limiting resource, expose representation costs, and design a measurement that could overturn the prediction Source-check status R04 author-hosted OSTEP chapters inspected. Exact passages and version limits appear in the evidence ledger. Experiment status Original address-trace simulator and arithmetic executed. No hardware timing experiment performed. Companion Hints, worked answers, and reproducible checks

The fictional document service must sum eight integer evidence counts before presenting a batch to an approver. One implementation scans a packed array. Another follows a list of records. Each visits every value once and performs eight additions. F01’s operation model gives both linear growth, Θ(n). That leaves a practical question unanswered. Which representation meets the latency and memory budget on the intended machine? Use three descriptions together. The algorithm specifies the logical work. The representation determines which addresses must be accessed to do it. The execution environment determines how those accesses compete for resources. An optimization can change one without improving the whole task. The goal here is to write a falsifiable resource prediction before choosing an implementation. For the sum, require immutable input, every record visited exactly once, and an integer total that fits the chosen accumulator. A list must be finite, acyclic, and terminate at its declared end. Reordering is harmless for this exact integer sum. It may change floating-point rounding or violate an order-sensitive workflow. Preserving F01’s contract comes before comparing costs.

sections.section: A units bridge and a useful cost model
sections.text: A byte is an addressable storage unit in our model. A record has fields occupying several bytes. A cache line is the fixed block our toy data cache transfers at once. A page is the separately chosen unit of virtual-memory translation. Those two units serve different purposes. Let W be counted operations and r an assumed upper bound on the rate of those same operations per second. W/r has units of seconds. Let D be required bytes transferred across a named boundary and b an assumed upper bound on that boundary’s bytes per second during the task. D/b is another time demand. Both rates must bound the resources available to this workload. A measured rate from a different workload is only a planning estimate, not automatically a valid upper bound. For a simplified machine where both resource limits apply, T≥max(W/r,D/b). This is a lower bound under the declared rates, not a runtime estimator. Perfect overlap would be needed to reach the larger term with no other cost. Dependencies, translation work, scheduling, setup, or waiting can lengthen execution. Summing the terms also requires assumptions about overlap. “Bytes accessed” must identify whether it counts requested field bytes, cache-line fills, or traffic from main memory. A miss in one cache can be served by another. Elapsed latency measures a specified start-to-finish interval for one task. CPU time counts time executing on the CPU, including execution stalls charged while scheduled. Throughput counts completed tasks per elapsed interval. A task waiting to be scheduled can have greater elapsed time without doing more algorithmic work. OSTEP’s scheduling chapter also distinguishes arrival-to-completion turnaround from arrival-to-first-scheduling response time. Use the intended clock explicitly. R04, chapter 7 §§7.2, 7.6–7.8

sections.section: Follow the bytes through a small machine
sections.text: Caches retain copies of data. Temporal locality means reusing a recently accessed item. Spatial locality means accessing nearby locations. These are workload properties that can make caching useful. They are not guarantees supplied by a container’s name. R04, chapter 10 §10.1, pp. 2–3 Here is an intentionally tiny, hypothetical machine. Every numerical result below is derived from these assumptions. Values occupy 8 bytes. A list node contains an 8-byte value followed by an 8-byte next pointer. The data cache holds four 32-byte lines, is fully associative, and evicts the least recently used line. Fully associative means any line can occupy any slot. Pages contain 64 bytes. A separate translation cache, the TLB, holds two page translations with the same replacement rule. Both caches start empty. Every page is resident and accessible. For counting data-cache lines, use an identity page mapping in this toy machine. A miss loads the requested block. Ignore instructions, stack accesses, page-table traffic, prefetching, writes, and other processes. Count each value or pointer load once. No field crosses a line boundary. Compare three layouts with values 1 through 8 in logical traversal order. Layout Addresses visited for values Additional accesses Packed array 0, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 56 None Packed linked nodes 0, 16, 32, 48, 64, 80, 96, 112 Next pointer at each value address + 8 Scattered linked nodes 0, 256, 64, 320, 128, 384, 192, 448 Next pointer at each value address + 8 For byte address a, the line number is floor(a/32), the virtual page is floor(a/64), and the page offset is a mod 64. “Floor” means discard the fractional part. The packed array’s line sequence is 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1. Only its first access to each line misses. Its eight values all share one page translation. For a packed list, each pair of nodes shares a line. Loading a node’s pointer reuses the line containing its value. The scattered list visits eight different lines and eight different pages. Each pointer still hits the same line and page as its preceding value. A list pointer carries the address of the next node, so the next value address depends on a previous load. An array’s next address follows from its base and index. That dependency difference motivates a latency hypothesis even when both access the same number of values. Derived count Array Packed list Scattered list Value / pointer loads per pass 8 / 0 8 / 8 8 / 8 First-pass data-cache misses 2 4 8 First-pass line-fill bytes 64 128 256 First-pass TLB misses 1 2 8 Second-pass data-cache misses 0 0 8 Second-pass TLB misses 0 0 8 The second pass immediately repeats the same traversal without clearing caches. The array and packed list fit. The scattered list cycles through more lines and translations than the capacities allow. By the time it returns to a block, that block has been evicted. The answer file executes this trace and checks the totals against independent block counts. All three sums equal 36. The first-pass fill-byte ratio of 4 between scattered list and array is not a fourfold speedup. We have supplied no timings, overlap model, or real cache hierarchy. Nor is 256 bytes the scattered list’s allocated memory. It is transferred data under this model. Its field storage totals 128 bytes, spread across eight pages covering a 512-byte virtual span. A real allocator adds its own layout and bookkeeping.

A process sees virtual addresses. Paging maps virtual pages to physical frames while preserving the within-page offset. Adjacent virtual pages need not occupy adjacent physical frames. Contiguous virtual storage therefore does not promise one physically contiguous allocation. R04, chapter 13 §13.3, pp. 3–5 and chapter 18 §18.1, pp. 1–4 The TLB caches translations. A missing translation requires translation work. It does not by itself imply that the data page must be read from storage. OSTEP treats nonresident pages through a separate present-bit and page-fault mechanism. Our trace deliberately keeps every page resident. R04, chapter 19 §19.1, pp. 1–3 and chapter 21 §§21.2–21.3 For this lesson, call the distinct data and translations needed over a specified interval the working set. Always specify that interval. Repeatedly scanning a small representation can reuse cached state. Growing the representation or interleaving unrelated work can remove that benefit. OSTEP’s array example makes the analogous connection between layout, page crossings, and translation reuse. R04, chapter 19 §19.2, pp. 3–5 Virtualization also lets processes share CPU time. A private address space and runnable thread do not promise exclusive physical resources. This lesson covers OS process and memory abstractions. It does not estimate hypervisor or container overhead. A benchmark must state its actual sharing conditions.

sections.section: Batching trades setup work for waiting
sections.text: Suppose entering a document-validation operation has a fixed hypothetical cost h = 24 microseconds, followed by c = 3 microseconds per record. A batch of k records costs h + kc. With a permanently backlogged single worker and no overlap, throughput is k/(h+kc), and amortized service cost per record is c+h/k. One record takes 27 microseconds. Eight take 48 microseconds total, or 6 per record. The saturated throughput ratio is 27/6 = 4.5. Every record in a batch released together still waits for that batch’s 48-microsecond service. Dividing service by eight does not give each record’s elapsed latency. This is an original application of fixed-cost amortization, a technique also discussed in OSTEP’s scheduling chapter. R04, chapter 7 §7.7, p. 8 Now change the arrival pattern. Eight records arrive 100 microseconds apart, starting at time zero, and processing starts only when the batch fills. The first waits 700 microseconds for assembly and 48 for service. The last waits 48. Their mean arrival-to-completion latency is 398 microseconds. Immediate processing would finish each in 27 because arrivals are farther apart than service time. The high-load throughput advantage and low-load latency penalty are compatible. Choose a batch size and a maximum wait together. Also budget batch memory and define partial-batch behavior. In the exact deterministic scenario, a 750-microsecond first-record deadline permits k=8, while k=9 takes 851 microseconds. Real arrival variability needs measurement. Reordering batches must still preserve approval and output-association rules.

sections.section: Turn the prediction into a disprovable comparison
sections.text: For a long, read-only scan with little arithmetic and a working set larger than cache, predict that data movement matters. For one scattered dependent chain, predict that waiting on dependent loads matters. For costly per-record computation, predict CPU execution may dominate. These are hypotheses. The tiny simulator establishes none of their real-machine rankings. Use this proposed benchmark protocol, adapted from F03’s emphasis on a common workload and declared measurement rules. Freeze values, record counts, checksum, integer semantics, and output contract. Compare the same logical work. Verify each output before accepting a timing. Implement an array scan, packed-node traversal, and scattered-node traversal. Record actual field sizes, padding, allocation method, and pointer order. Keep construction outside traversal timing, then report a separate end-to-end measurement including construction. Record CPU, memory, OS, compiler/runtime and optimization settings, process/thread count, CPU placement, and other load. Ensure the compiler cannot discard the computed result. Inspect the executed code where optimization could invalidate the comparison. Sweep sizes from small reusable data to much larger working sets. Define warmup and cache conditions. Initializing input can already warm it, so “first timed run” is not proof of a cold cache. Run repeated comparisons in interleaved, randomized order using the same datasets. Report timing distributions and sample counts. If accessible, record CPU time, cache/translation events, and measured traffic with their precise counter definitions. Separately test batching under stated arrival patterns. Include assembly waiting in per-record latency and count completed records over a stated interval. Track memory and correctness alongside throughput. If packing does not improve time, investigate whether arithmetic, dispatch, or waiting elsewhere dominates. If scattered traversal approaches scan speed, inspect residency, layout, and actual dependencies before concluding locality is irrelevant. A low byte rate can coexist with waiting on a serial dependency. Changing one factor at a time and checking the mechanism makes the result more useful than a single fastest-run ratio.

Try these six tasks before opening the companion. Reproduce the first-pass cache and TLB misses for all layouts. Explain why the scattered list has eight TLB misses across sixteen field loads. Derive the second-pass counts. Then reduce the data cache to two lines while retaining the two-entry TLB. Which counts change? Map virtual address 136 with 64-byte pages when virtual page 2 maps to physical frame 7. Explain why a TLB miss alone establishes neither a data-cache miss nor storage I/O. Reproduce batching costs, throughput ratio, and the first/last/mean latencies. Find the largest full batch meeting the 750-microsecond first-record limit under the specified arrivals. Propose a benchmark that could reject the claim that scattered traversal is slower because of data access. Name one confound, one mechanism measurement, and one changed-workload test. Change the workload to frequent insertions at known list nodes, then change it again to a repeatedly scanned, immutable snapshot. Defend a representation for each and identify costs omitted by traversal-only timing. A useful answer names the logical contract, counted resource, machine assumptions, and evidence that would change the choice. F01 supplies correctness and abstract work. F03 supplies comparison discipline. S02 will revisit layout for storage and indexes. S05 will add queues and capacity. A04 will apply resource reasoning to inference using its own sources and workloads. CPU examples here establish no GPU speedup.

Record the contract, representation, working-set interval, transfer boundary, rate assumptions, and clock. Count operations and bytes separately. Distinguish a cached translation from cached data. Treat throughput and task latency as separate outcomes. Recheck correctness after batching or reordering. R04 is Remzi H. and Andrea C. Arpaci-Dusseau’s Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces. The author index identifies version 1.10, November 2023. Individual free chapters receive updates. The inspected chapter 10 and 18 PDFs include 2025 copyright footers. The locators below identify the author-hosted snapshots accessed 2026-11-04, rather than asserting every PDF is the original 2023 text. Page numbers are chapter-local PDF pages, counting from 1. Claim / role Inspected location Evidence type and boundary Scheduling clocks, time sharing, fixed-cost trade-off Ch. 7 §§7.2, 7.6–7.8, pp. 2, 6–10 Textbook mechanisms. No quoted latency table or current scheduler claim. Cache hierarchy and locality Ch. 10 §10.1, pp. 2–3 Only this background is used. Multiprocessor coherence algorithms are outside S01. Virtual address-space abstraction Ch. 13 §13.3, pp. 3–5 Process view versus physical placement. Pages, frames, translation Ch. 18 §18.1, pp. 1–4 Mechanism. Our page size and mapping are hypothetical. Translation caching and locality Ch. 19 §§19.1–19.2, pp. 1–5 Translation control flow and array example. Our numerical trace is independently constructed. Nonresident page handling Ch. 21 §§21.2–21.3 Distinguishes translation misses from absent data pages. No fault-cost estimate. Resource bound, layouts, batching, benchmark design Derivations in this pack and checks in companion Original models and proposed protocol. Executed simulation checks model bookkeeping, not hardware behavior. Unresolved application inputs are actual cache and translation behavior, memory layout, workload sizes, arrival variability, contention, and latency limits. They are measurement needs, not blockers to this pack. Audit A completed on 2026-11-04; see SDE_Audit_A.md for scope and checks. No learner response or mastery is inferred.
