title: Hints, worked answers, and reproducible checks

sections.section: Hints, worked answers, and reproducible checks
sections.text: Field Value ID / revision / date S01 answers · 1.0 · 2026-11-04 Companion Resource models, locality, and abstraction costs Prerequisites / capability F01 and S01’s declared toy machine. Explain resource counts, latency, and a falsifiable comparison. Source-check status Uses R04 passages and evidence boundaries recorded in the core pack. Experiment status Python 3 model checks below executed successfully. No measured hardware performance. Assessment status Suggested criteria only. No learner answers received or mastery inferred.

Divide an address by the block size and discard the remainder. Track data lines and translated pages separately. A node has two loads. Keep the cache contents after pass one. Ask how many distinct blocks are touched before a block is revisited. Preserve the offset when changing a virtual page number to a physical frame number. Separate assembly waiting, whole-batch service, and service cost divided by record count. Design a comparison where the suspected mechanism changes while useful work stays the same. Include how positions are found, how storage is allocated, and whether a compact snapshot must be built.

For the array, the line IDs are four 0s followed by four 1s. All eight page IDs are 0. There are two line misses and one translation miss. For packed nodes, the sixteen field loads have four accesses per line, covering lines 0–3. Pages 0 and 1 each hold four nodes. There are four line misses and two translation misses. For scattered nodes, value addresses give line IDs 0, 8, 2, 10, 4, 12, 6, 14 and page IDs 0, 4, 1, 5, 2, 6, 3, 7. Each next-pointer load repeats its value’s line and page. There are eight misses of each kind, eight data hits, and eight TLB hits. A 50% TLB hit rate here reflects one hit on every node’s pointer. It does not establish good absolute performance. Multiplying data misses by the hypothetical 32-byte fill unit gives 64, 128, and 256 bytes. The pointer values contain the next addresses, including a terminating sentinel stored at the final node. Reading that sentinel counts as a load. Following it does not occur. Criterion. Explain every miss and hit using the access sequence. Keep field storage, virtual span, requested bytes, and transferred bytes distinct.

sections.section: 2. Capacity changes and the second pass
sections.text: With four cache lines, the array’s two lines and the packed list’s four lines remain resident after pass one. Neither has another data miss. Their one and two translations also fit, so their second-pass TLB misses are zero. The scattered layout exceeds both capacities and reuses blocks only after eviction. It incurs eight of each kind again. With only two data-cache lines, the array still fits and has zero second-pass data misses. The packed list finishes its first pass with lines 2 and 3. Reading lines 0 and 1 evicts those, then reading 2 and 3 misses again. Its second pass has four data misses. The scattered list still has eight. Translation capacity is unchanged, so second-pass TLB misses remain 0, 0, and 8. This is a concrete counterexample to “a second run is warm, therefore every access hits.” Warmth requires the relevant state to survive. It is also a counterexample to “every linked list has poor locality.” The packed list fits the original cache and translation capacities, though it still loads pointers and occupies more bytes than the array. Criterion. Show which state survives and which is evicted. Do not infer time from miss counts alone.

136 = 2 × 64 + 8, so the virtual page number is 2 and the offset is 8. Mapping page 2 to frame 7 yields physical address 7 × 64 + 8 = 456. The TLB remembers a mapping. The data cache remembers data. A TLB miss can be resolved from page tables for an already-resident page. It says nothing by itself about whether the resulting physical data line is cached. Storage I/O requires a separate condition such as fetching a nonresident backed page. Our simulation excludes that condition. It also excludes the page-table memory traffic needed to repair a translation miss. Criterion. Preserve the offset and distinguish translation work, data-cache lookup, and nonresident-page handling. The R04 chapter 19 and 21 passages in the core ledger support this boundary.

The one-record service cost is 24 + 3 = 27 microseconds. For eight records it is 24 + 8 × 3 = 48, or 6 per record. With an indefinitely backlogged worker, throughputs are 1,000,000/27 ≈ 37,037 records/s and 8,000,000/48 ≈ 166,667 records/s. Their ratio is 4.5. These are conditional model outputs, not benchmark results. At 100-microsecond arrival spacing, eight arrivals occur at 0, 100, …, 700. The full batch completes at 748. Latencies are 748, 648, 548, 448, 348, 248, 148, and 48 microseconds. Their mean is (748 + 48)/2 = 398. Each immediately processed record takes 27 because service completes before the next arrival. For general positive integer k in this scenario, first-record latency is 100(k−1)+24+3k=103k−76. The requirement 103k−76 ≤ 750 gives k ≤ 826/103 ≈ 8.019. Thus the largest permitted full batch is eight. Nine would take 851. A wait timeout can cap assembly time when arrivals vary, but must leave time for actual service and any queueing. It does not guarantee a deadline on its own. Criterion. Name the arrival and load conditions. Never call the amortized 6-microsecond service cost a 6-microsecond batch-member latency.

sections.section: 5. A test that can overturn the explanation
sections.text: A useful hypothesis is that dependent scattered accesses cause longer traversal time for the target record sizes. Start with one compiled implementation and the same immutable records and checksum. Measure packed and scattered node traversal at several sizes. Use the same field representation so pointer overhead is not confused with array-versus-node layout. Separately include the packed array as the practical alternative. Allocation inside only one timed region is a confound. So is placing one candidate’s data in a different memory region or running it under different competing load. Report construction-inclusive and traversal-only times with matching boundaries. Check warmup, compiler elimination, generated dependencies, and output correctness. Where the platform exposes suitable counters, compare cache misses, translation events, and memory traffic using their documented meanings. Test a small working set that fits, then enlarge it. A small-set speed gap that persists without the predicted miss difference weakens a cache-miss-only explanation. Add identical expensive per-record arithmetic as a separate sensitivity test. If arithmetic then dominates, layout may matter less to whole-task time. A null result with noisy measurements is inconclusive, so include repeated-run variation. Criterion. State a predicted change, a controlled comparison, a mechanism observation, and a result that would change the explanation. This is a proposed experiment, not an executed one.

For frequent insertion after already-known nodes, a linked representation can avoid shifting a packed array’s suffix. That conclusion assumes node references are already available and storage can be allocated. Searching for the insertion point, allocation, ownership, and concurrent mutation can dominate or invalidate a simple constant-work splice story. A segmented or slack-filled representation is another candidate if scans and updates both matter. For a repeatedly scanned immutable snapshot, a compact array is a reasonable starting choice. Measure the cost of constructing the snapshot and how many scans reuse it. If compacting costs C and each subsequent scan saves Δ, the simple serial break-even condition is mΔ > C for m scans, assuming Δ > 0 and no other changes. Include extra peak memory while both forms coexist. If only one scan occurs, conversion can lose overall despite a faster scan. An integer sum invariant remains that after k logical visits the accumulator equals the sum of exactly those k values. A cycle, missed node, duplicate visit, overflow, or reordering that violates the actual task contract invalidates the comparison before speed matters. Criterion. Defend a conditional choice and include construction, memory, and correctness. A representation name alone is not an explanation.

The following standard-library Python 3 block was executed on 2026-11-04. It models references to explicitly assigned addresses. The Python runtime’s own memory layout and execution time have no role in these results. It verifies list termination and sums, cache and TLB counts over two passes, changed capacity, translation arithmetic, batch deadlines, and units-based throughput ratios. LRU state is retained between passes and reset between layouts. from collections import OrderedDict from fractions import Fraction class LRU: def __init__(self, capacity): assert capacity > 0 self.capacity = capacity self.items = OrderedDict() def touch(self, block): miss = block not in self.items if not miss: self.items.move_to_end(block) else: self.items[block] = None if len(self.items) > self.capacity: self.items.popitem(last=False) return int(miss) def linked_trace(addresses): nodes = { a: (i + 1, addresses[i + 1] if i + 1 < len(addresses) else None) for i, a in enumerate(addresses) } trace, seen, total = [], set(), 0 p = addresses[0] while p is not None: assert p in nodes and p not in seen seen.add(p) value, nxt = nodes[p] trace.extend([p, p + 8]) total += value p = nxt assert len(seen) == len(addresses) and total == 36 return trace traces = { 'array': list(range(0, 64, 8)), 'packed': linked_trace(list(range(0, 128, 16))), 'scattered': linked_trace([0, 256, 64, 320, 128, 384, 192, 448]), } assert sum(range(1, 9)) == 36 def two_passes(trace, cache_capacity=4): cache, tlb = LRU(cache_capacity), LRU(2) results = [] for _ in range(2): data_misses = translation_misses = 0 for address in trace: assert address % 8 == 0 assert address // 32 == (address + 7) // 32 data_misses += cache.touch(address // 32) translation_misses += tlb.touch(address // 64) results.append((data_misses, translation_misses)) return results expected = { 'array': [(2, 1), (0, 0)], 'packed': [(4, 2), (0, 0)], 'scattered': [(8, 8), (8, 8)], } for name, trace in traces.items(): result = two_passes(trace) assert result == expected[name] # Independent first-pass counts work because no block is revisited # after moving on from its contiguous run in these particular traces. assert result[0][0] == len({a // 32 for a in trace}) assert result[0][1] == len({a // 64 for a in trace}) print(name, result, 'fill bytes', result[0][0] * 32) assert two_passes(traces['array'], 2) == [(2, 1), (0, 0)] assert two_passes(traces['packed'], 2) == [(4, 2), (4, 0)] assert two_passes(traces['scattered'], 2) == [(8, 8), (8, 8)] assert divmod(136, 64) == (2, 8) assert 7 * 64 + 8 == 456 h, c, k, spacing = 24, 3, 8, 100 service = h + c * k arrival = [i * spacing for i in range(k)] finish = arrival[-1] + service latencies = [finish - t for t in arrival] assert service == 48 and Fraction(service, k) == 6 assert Fraction(k, service) / Fraction(1, h + c) == Fraction(9, 2) assert (latencies[0], latencies[-1]) == (748, 48) assert Fraction(sum(latencies), k) == 398 def first_latency(size): return (size - 1) * spacing + h + c * size assert first_latency(8) == 748 and first_latency(9) == 851 assert max(s for s in range(1, 101) if first_latency(s) <= 750) == 8 # A monotone expression establishes the bound beyond the tested range. assert spacing + c > 0 assert h + c < spacing print('All S01 model checks passed.') Expected printed rows are array [(2, 1), (0, 0)] fill bytes 64, packed [(4, 2), (0, 0)] fill bytes 128, and scattered [(8, 8), (8, 8)] fill bytes 256, followed by the success line. These checks establish the declared model’s bookkeeping, not production speed, physical memory consumption, or a real scheduler’s behavior.

sections.section: What should an approval point to?
sections.text: A reviewer approved a payment using page 2 of invoice D17. A week later the supplier sends a corrected invoice with a different total. The reviewer needs both the current total and the evidence behind the earlier decision. A table keyed only by invoice ID makes overwriting the old value easy. Once that happens, an audit that joins the approval to today’s invoice can produce a plausible but false account of yesterday’s decision. Give the logical document a stable ID and give each accepted revision its own identity. Keep the source bytes retrievable under an immutable reference. A digest can help verify retrieved bytes, but reproducing the page requires the bytes themselves. In this design a revision includes one frozen extraction result. Re-extracting the same bytes with a changed extractor creates a new revision that may share the same content reference. This is a design convention that makes the history unambiguous. Relation Key Other information and constraints Revision (doc, rev) Immutable source reference, content digest, extractor version, completion manifest such as the expected fact slots Fact (doc, rev, slot) Name, typed value, source locator. Foreign key to Revision. Slot identifies one occurrence within the frozen extraction. Head doc Chosen published rev. The pair (doc, rev) references Revision. ApprovalEvidence (approval_id, evidence_no) Exact (doc, rev, slot) used, with a foreign key to Fact. Multiple pieces of evidence can support one approval. At every published boundary, Head must select a complete revision. Its facts must resolve to evidence in the same source version. Existing approvals must continue to resolve even when Head advances. A foreign key establishes that the target row exists. Completeness additionally requires checking the expected slots before publication. For an invoice with no extractable facts, an explicit empty manifest distinguishes a completed empty result from an extraction still in progress. Store amounts with a currency and an agreed exact numeric representation. Preserve a locator such as page number plus coordinates in the frozen page image. An offset into a newly generated text rendering would also require its rendering version. Publish Revision, Fact, and Head within one database transaction after validating the manifest. Assume a single publisher for now. If the source is in separate object storage, make the immutable object durable and verify it before publishing the database reference. A crash between those operations can leave an unreferenced object. Retention and later cleanup must protect every revision used as evidence.

sections.section: Put two questions to the same twelve rows
sections.text: The reviewer opens D17 revision 2 and asks for all its facts, including their source locators (Q1). An investigator instead asks for every historical occurrence of delivery reference X, including the document and source locator (Q2). Those questions place the same rows in different groups. “Historical” matters. A later correction may remove X from the current revision while an older occurrence still answers Q2. Here is a hypothetical heap, an unordered collection of pages holding records. The numbers are physical row identifiers for this example. Each fact label below abbreviates one fully identified fact with its own slot and locator. A vertical ordering across pages reflects insertion order, with revisions interleaved as they arrive. Page Four records in slot order, shown as row ID, document/revision, fact P1 1 D17/1 total · 2 D17/1 delivery X · 3 D08/1 total · 4 D08/1 delivery Y P2 5 D17/2 delivery X · 6 D09/1 total · 7 D09/1 delivery Z · 8 D10/1 total P3 9 D10/1 delivery Y · 10 D17/2 total · 11 D11/1 total · 12 D11/1 delivery X With a full scan, inspect all twelve records on three heap pages. Q1 returns rows 5 and 10. Q2 returns rows 2, 5, and 12. Scan predicates are simple enough to use as an oracle when testing an index. For example, changing Q1 to filter only on doc would accidentally return revision 1 as well. A faster path that returns that larger set has changed the question. An index stores another route to the records. Imagine two ordered indexes. One groups physical row IDs by (doc, rev). The other includes only delivery facts and groups their row IDs by reference value. In our small model, each lookup follows one root separator to one leaf page holding the complete matching entry and its short list of row IDs. Assume a cold cache and count each distinct page read once during the query. The caller needs the source locator, which lives in the heap. These assumptions describe a constructed two-level tree. A real tree may fit in a single page or span many levels. Query Lookup trace Distinct pages Candidate heap rows inspected Q1 by revision Root → leaf for (D17,2) → row 5 on P2 and row 10 on P3 2 index + 2 heap = 4 2 Q2 by delivery Root → leaf for X → rows 2, 5, 12 on P1, P2, P3 2 index + 3 heap = 5 3 Either by scan P1 → P2 → P3 3 heap 12 The index saves predicate evaluations, yet both indexed paths touch more pages than the scan on this layout. S01’s question about the unit being counted changes the recommendation. On a much larger heap, a selective lookup might still lead to only two data pages. Conversely, a popular delivery reference might lead to nearly every page. A widely scattered result also changes how the storage device can serve the reads. Page counts alone do not determine elapsed time. One alternative is to put frequently requested output fields in the leaf. In a read model where all required fields and visibility information are available there, Q2 could finish after the index lookup. The wider entries take more space and may reduce the number that fit per page. Another option is to store a revision’s facts together, so Q1 fetches them from fewer pages. Q2 might still reach many pages because delivery references cut across documents. Choose after measuring the query mix, common and rare keys, cache state, and required output columns. The CMU notes explain leaf entries and the distinction between record IDs and tuple payloads. R05, lecture 08 §§1–2

sections.section: What a new index costs the writer
sections.text: Suppose revision 3 adds a total and a delivery reference Y. Those two facts require two base rows and two row-ID associations in the revision index. The delivery-only index gains one association. That is five logical additions in this fact-storage model, plus the revision metadata and Head update. A batch could share a leaf write, and a full leaf could split, so five additions do not predict five device writes. Index keys and row IDs consume storage for every retained revision. Returning historical X matches remains correct even after the head moves to Y. Before adding the delivery index, ask how frequently investigators actually search by reference and how selective the common values are. Measure extra bytes per revision, ingestion time, and the distribution of lookup times under the same workload. Include maintenance and recovery in the comparison. If approvals mostly open known revisions and historical investigations are rare, a revision index and occasional scan may suffice. If selective investigations must finish within a deadline, the secondary index earns a trial against the scan.

sections.section: Crash after the reply, before the last page write
sections.text: A server has published D17/2 and now wants to publish D17/3. Consider two persistent logical objects in a small recovery model. F3 is the complete immutable revision bundle, including its facts and locators. H is the head pointer. The old revision remains accessible. Representing the new bundle as one object keeps the trace short. An implementation with several fact pages must log all of them. For this trace the indexes are derived and rebuilt from recovered facts before reads resume. Assume a single transaction, a trusted initial snapshot, atomic writes of each modeled object, and stable storage that retains completed flushes through power loss. The source bytes are already durable. Volatile memory is lost in a crash. The durable log is a valid prefix of complete records in order. This toy protocol prohibits uncommitted updates from reaching home pages (NO-STEAL) and allows committed pages to reach home after acknowledgement (NO-FORCE). A home page is the normal storage location for the object. These choices allow a compact redo-only demonstration. Stage the full bundle and new head in memory. Append log records setting F3 to the complete bundle and H to 3. The writer can flush those records before it decides to commit. Append COMMIT for this transaction and flush the log through COMMIT. An ordered flush makes both earlier updates durable with it. Publish both changes as a unit for subsequent readers, then send the success reply. Later write the committed objects to their home locations. For the example, F3 goes home first. Retain the log until a durable checkpoint includes both objects. After a crash, recover before accepting reads. Apply the assignments of each fully committed transaction in log order. An incomplete transaction has no durable home updates under the stated policy. Replaying the same full-value assignment twice gives the same state here. Last event before power loss What survives State after recovery Updates flushed, COMMIT absent Update records and old home pages D17/2 is current COMMIT flushed, reply still in transit Complete transaction log, old home pages D17/3 is current. Client needs to resolve the uncertain outcome. Client received success, only F3 reached home Complete log, new F3, home H still 2 Replaying H publishes D17/3 with its evidence Both objects reached home, log still retained Complete log and new home values Repeated assignments preserve D17/3 Move the reply earlier as a counterexample. If the server replies after appending COMMIT only in volatile memory, power loss can leave an update-only durable prefix. Recovery correctly retains revision 2, contradicting the promise the client heard. A transaction ID or stable publication key lets a retry query the committed result after a lost reply. Protecting an external payment from duplicate effects requires its own contract in C01. A system that lets uncommitted updates reach home must also handle their effects during recovery. CMU’s ARIES lesson describes analysis, replaying history, and undoing incomplete transactions. The toy protocol deliberately buys a shorter proof by restricting flushes. OSTEP’s data-journaling trace provides the related file-system intuition: persist the journal contents, persist the commit marker, then install the updates at their home locations. Each layer has its own transaction boundary. R05, lectures 21 §§2, 6 and 22, recovery phases · R04, chapter 42, p. 11

An approval cites only D17 and “total.” Show what happens on a join after the total changes. Specify the missing keys and one source-retention assumption. Trace Q1 and Q2 using the table. Count candidate heap records and distinct cold pages for each access path. Explain how a cached root changes each indexed count. Q2 becomes “all current invoices citing X.” Assume each document’s highest listed revision is its published head. Which rows qualify? Explain how to implement the changed query and which extra reads were absent from the original count. For the two-fact revision 3, count logical additions with each index. Name one observed change in workload that would reverse your recommendation. Crash after the success reply with only F3 installed. Recover by hand. Then remove the rule that prevents uncommitted home writes and construct a state the toy algorithm fails to repair. Formulate the acknowledgement in one sentence. Explain what the client can conclude after a timeout, and what additional mechanism you would need if the storage device itself were lost.

Keep four things on the page: the stable logical identity, the query predicate and output, the unit of physical work, and the durable event preceding success. At the end of a recovery trace test both an old approval and a fresh Head lookup. S03 considers interleaved writers, S04 broadens the failure boundary to replicas, and A03 reuses revision identity for evidence retrieval. Basis Inspected locator Use and limit R05, CMU Fall 2025 03, §§7–10, pp. 3–4 Pages, heap layout, record IDs. Page sizes and occupancy here are assigned. R05, same edition 08, §§1–2, pp. 1–2 Keys, routing, leaf payloads, insertion. Our posting lists and two-level counts are conditional. R05, same edition 21, §2 pp. 1–2 and §6 pp. 4–5 and 22, pp. 5–6 Buffer policies, log-before-data ordering, durable commit, scope of ARIES redo and undo. R04, OSTEP Crash Consistency, chapter-local p. 11, data-journaling protocol and Recovery File-system analogy for commit versus checkpoint. Original design and executed checks Companion below the six solutions Synthetic history and failure model. Actual storage barriers, corruption handling, concurrent publication, workload selectivity, and latency need separate verification.

Experiment Executed SQLite queries against synthetic facts and enumerated a separate redo-only recovery model in Python.

Follow the approval after the head moves. Which row and which source bytes does it identify? Translate each row ID into a page before adding index reads. Distinguish a revision that exists from one selected by Head. Count row-ID associations before estimating bytes or writes. List the durable prefix and the two home values separately. Consider a crash immediately before the reply and immediately after dispatch.

sections.section: 1. Keep the evidence behind an approval
sections.text: Suppose D17/1 records a total of 90 and D17/2 records 95 in the same currency. Joining an old approval to the current head returns 95 even if the reviewer approved 90. Joining only by doc and name across history can return both totals. Store the approved evidence’s (doc, rev, slot) and join by that key. Resolve its page locator against the immutable source reference attached to that same revision. Keep the source version readable throughout the evidence-retention period. A checksum alone cannot reconstruct a deleted page.

sections.section: 2. Count what each path actually reads
sections.text: Q1 finds row 5 on P2 and row 10 on P3. Its indexed path inspects two candidate records and reads four distinct cold pages including root and leaf. Q2 finds 2, 5, 12 on P1, P2, P3. It inspects three candidate records and reads five distinct cold pages. Scanning either query inspects twelve records over three pages. A resident root reduces the respective cold reads to three and four under the same other assumptions. The root lookup still occurs. If the leaf contains every requested field and sufficient visibility information, the heap fetches could also disappear. The count includes only facts that pass the exact index predicate as candidate heap records. An index keyed just on doc would return four D17 candidates and require a revision check. The narrower key may be useful for other queries. It answers a different performance question.

Historical X hits are 2, 5, 12. D17/1 has been superseded by D17/2, so only 5 and 12 survive the current-revision filter under the assigned heads. After publishing D17/3 with Y, only 12 survives. Join each candidate’s (doc, rev) to (doc, published_rev) in Head. A cached Head entry for D17 can serve two candidate checks. Additional cold reads depend on Head’s index and data layout. The given fact-page model has insufficient information to assign an exact cold total to the join. A current-only secondary index could accelerate this query, at the cost of removing obsolete entries and installing new ones atomically when Head changes.

Two base inserts are required. Keeping only the revision index adds two revision associations, for four logical additions. Keeping only the delivery index adds one delivery association, for three. Keeping both gives five. Revision metadata and Head updates are outside those figures. Old revision entries stay available for historical queries. If X becomes ubiquitous and each investigation needs full locators from nearly every page, compare a scan against the secondary lookup. If selective historical investigations become frequent, measure how much the secondary index saves under that mix and whether ingestion can absorb the cost.

The durable prefix contains SET F3, SET H=3, and COMMIT. Home contains F3 and H=2. Reapply the complete bundle assignment, then assign H=3. Rebuilding derived indexes from the recovered facts restores their query results. The immutability of old revisions preserves approvals pointing to D17/1 or D17/2. Now allow H=3 to reach home before COMMIT. A crash with the update-only log leaves H=3 but F3 missing. The toy recovery skips incomplete transactions and therefore preserves the dangling reference. Valid fixes include preventing this flush or retaining undo information and using a recovery protocol that restores the prior state. Replaying every update unconditionally would expose an uncommitted revision.

sections.section: 6. State the promise and its boundary
sections.text: A success reply promises that after a process or power failure with the modeled stable storage intact, recovery will expose the complete published revision and preserve earlier evidence. A timeout is compatible both with a transaction that never committed and with one whose reply was lost. Look up a stable operation key before deciding to retry. The write protocol must enforce the operation-key constraint at the same transaction boundary if a retry is to reuse the existing result. Surviving loss of the device requires an independently durable copy with a tested recovery procedure. If every acknowledged revision must survive that loss, success must wait for sufficient data to be durable outside that failure domain. A nightly backup alone leaves a window of acknowledged changes at risk. S04 will specify the replication and failure assumptions in detail. Assessment criteria. A defensible answer names the revision key, states the query semantics, counts pages and matching rows separately, identifies the durable commit boundary, and gives a crash or workload that defeats an overbroad claim.

Run this block under Python 3. SQLite checks the logical query results. The assigned heap layout and cold-page counts are calculated separately. The recovery function models ordered durable records and atomic home writes. These are three different checks. import sqlite3 from itertools import product data = [ (17,1,'total','90'), (17,1,'delivery','X'), (8,1,'total','55'), (8,1,'delivery','Y'), (17,2,'delivery','X'), (9,1,'total','48'), (9,1,'delivery','Z'), (10,1,'total','70'), (10,1,'delivery','Y'), (17,2,'total','95'), (11,1,'total','75'), (11,1,'delivery','X'), ] db = sqlite3.connect(':memory:') db.execute('CREATE TABLE fact(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, doc INT, rev INT, name TEXT, val TEXT)') db.executemany('INSERT INTO fact(doc,rev,name,val) VALUES(?,?,?,?)', data) q1 = 'SELECT id FROM fact WHERE doc=17 AND rev=2 ORDER BY id' q2 = "SELECT id FROM fact WHERE name='delivery' AND val='X' ORDER BY id" def ids(query): return [row[0] for row in db.execute(query)] assert ids(q1) == [5,10] and ids(q2) == [2,5,12] db.execute('CREATE INDEX by_rev ON fact(doc,rev)') db.execute("CREATE INDEX by_delivery ON fact(val) WHERE name='delivery'") assert ids(q1) == [5,10] and ids(q2) == [2,5,12] db.execute('CREATE TABLE head(doc INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, rev INT)') db.execute('INSERT INTO head SELECT doc, MAX(rev) FROM fact GROUP BY doc') current = "SELECT id FROM fact JOIN head USING(doc,rev) WHERE name='delivery' AND val='X' ORDER BY id" assert ids(current) == [5,12] def heap_pages(row_ids): return {(row_id-1)//4 + 1 for row_id in row_ids} assert len(heap_pages(range(1,13))) == 3 assert 2 + len(heap_pages(ids(q1))) == 4 assert 2 + len(heap_pages(ids(q2))) == 5 db.executemany('INSERT INTO fact(doc,rev,name,val) VALUES(?,?,?,?)', [(17,3,'total','98'), (17,3,'delivery','Y')]) db.execute('UPDATE head SET rev=3 WHERE doc=17') assert ids(current) == [12] and ids(q2) == [2,5,12] assert db.execute('SELECT val FROM fact WHERE id=1').fetchone() == ('90',) # One transaction and one complete, ordered log prefix. bundle = ('total=98','delivery=Y') log = [('bundle',bundle), ('head',3), ('commit',True)] old = {'head':2,'bundle':None} new = {'head':3,'bundle':bundle} def recover(home, prefix): state = home.copy() if prefix and prefix[-1] == ('commit',True): state.update(prefix[:-1]) return state for length in range(3): # no durable commit, NO-STEAL assert recover(old, log[:length]) == old for wrote_bundle, wrote_head in product((False,True), repeat=2): home = {'head':3 if wrote_head else 2, 'bundle':bundle if wrote_bundle else None} assert recover(home, log) == new assert recover(recover(home, log), log) == new # Illegal flush breaks the invariant when there is no durable COMMIT. assert recover({'head':3,'bundle':None}, log[:2]) == {'head':3,'bundle':None} print('S02 query, page-count, publication and recovery checks passed.') The toy log uses full after-values. An operation such as “increment a balance” would require a replay guard or a different log encoding to tolerate repeated application. Real device flush behavior and database crash handling require a deployment-specific test.

Field Value ID / revision / date S03 · 1.0 · 2026-11-06 Prerequisites F01 invariants and S02 revision identity, transactions, and recovery. Notation bridge below. Capability developed Expose a violating interleaving, choose an enforcement boundary, and separate causality from request validity. Source-check status R05, CMU Fall 2025 lectures 17, 18, 20, and R06, Lamport 1978. Supporting passages inspected 2026-11-06. Experiment status Executed finite Python history and state-machine checks in the companion. No concurrent database or network deployment tested. Companion Hints, worked answers, and reproducible checks

The document service has published invoice D17/2. Two reviewers submit competing approval proposals. The service permits at most one accepted proposal in an approval round. Acceptance here records a decision and its exact evidence in the database. Any later payment is a separate effect. S02 preserved complete revisions through a crash under a single-publisher assumption. We now remove the single-writer assumption. A transaction can survive a crash exactly as written and still contain a decision based on obsolete information. F01’s sequential check-then-insert proof needs a boundary that prevents another actor from changing the premise between the check and the update. Use two existing candidate rows, A and B, for one document and round. Each has an accepted bit, initially zero. The invariant at committed boundaries is a+b≤1,a,b∈{0,1}. Each transaction reads both bits and, if their sum is zero, sets its own bit to one. In isolation, either transaction preserves the invariant. The case and all values in this pack are hypothetical. A history lists operations in execution order. R_A(b)=0 means transaction A read zero from b. W_A(a)=1 is A’s proposed write, and C_A means its commit. An abort discards its database changes. A serial history finishes one transaction before starting the other. A serializable history has an equivalent serial execution, even if its operations overlap. A concurrency protocol controls which histories can commit. R05, lecture 17 §6

Assume each transaction reads a committed snapshot taken at its first read, sees its own writes, and stages writes privately until commit. Concurrent writers to the same row cannot both commit, but no rule validates the other rows they read. This is the simplified snapshot-isolation model used for the example. Step Transaction A Transaction B Committed (a,b) 1 Read a=0, b=0 (0,0) 2 Read a=0, b=0 (0,0) 3 Stage a=1 (0,0) 4 Commit (1,0) 5 Stage b=1 using its snapshot (1,0) 6 Commit (1,1) The write sets are disjoint. Atomic commit of each transaction does not reject this history. Neither reviewer observed dirty data. The failure comes from combining two individually valid decisions whose premises cannot both remain true. Try both serial orders. If A finishes first, B reads (1,0) and declines. If B finishes first, A reads (0,1) and declines. Neither reaches (1,1). This is write skew, a possible anomaly under snapshot isolation. MVCC stores versions but needs a concurrency protocol to determine allowed behavior. Its presence alone does not promise serializability. R05, lecture 20 §1, Snapshot Isolation The dependency test explains the conflict. A read b before B wrote b, so preserving that observation requires A before B. B read a before A wrote a, requiring B before A. The cycle excludes a conflict-equivalent serial order. In this fixed-object read/write model, conflicts occur across transactions on the same object when at least one operation writes. An acyclic precedence graph characterizes conflict serializability. R05, lecture 17 §6, p. 4 Checking accepted IN (0,1) on each row permits the bad result. Giving each candidate a unique ID also permits it. A constraint must encode the contested resource. A separate Acceptance relation with a unique (doc, round) key can directly exclude two acceptance records, provided the system records acceptance only through that relation and handles a rejected insertion as failure.

sections.section: Put the check and change behind one boundary
sections.text: For a small, auditable design, create a guard row for every document. Every operation that changes its approval round, selected revision, or acceptance first obtains the same exclusive transaction lock. Keep that lock through commit or abort. After acquiring it, read the current committed state, validate the request, and write the complete decision with its S02 evidence references in the same transaction. Precomputed extraction can happen outside this boundary. Step A B 1 Acquire D17 guard, read free slot Request guard, wait 2 Record acceptance and evidence, commit Still waiting 3 Release guard Acquire guard, read occupied slot 4 Decline, finish, release guard This protocol depends on a current read after the wait. Reusing a snapshot taken before acquiring the guard can restore the stale premise. An implementation must refresh the relevant read or abort and restart when its isolation rules cannot provide that view. The pseudocode specifies a contract, not portable SQL behavior for every engine. In two-phase locking, lock acquisition precedes a phase that only releases locks. Holding all transaction locks until termination is the rigorous variant. Locking can introduce waiting and deadlock. R05, lecture 18 §§1–3 Our single-document protocol has just one guard. Extending it to two documents creates a new case. A holds D17 and waits for D18 while B holds D18 and waits for D17. Requiring ascending document-ID acquisition excludes that cycle because a chain of waits would have to keep increasing and return to its start. The argument assumes every participant follows that order and does not acquire hidden conflicting resources in another order. An optimistic alternative performs an atomic conditional transition on a shared token row. It succeeds only if the slot is still empty and the request’s round and revision still match. Approval evidence and the successful result must commit with that transition. A separate client-side comparison followed by an unconditional write does not provide this contract. A full serializable transaction is another option when invariants span several rows or predicates, with the application prepared to retry an aborted transaction from fresh reads. Choice Useful condition Cost to investigate Evidence that would change the choice Shared guard held through commit Short decisions for one document Wait time and long lock holders Most latency is waiting on unrelated work inside the transaction Conditional token transition Invariant fits one token and atomic receipt Repeated failed attempts under contention Retries dominate useful completions Serializable multirow transaction Invariant spans changing rows or predicates Aborts, retries, implementation semantics Measured contention or an incomplete transaction boundary A unique acceptance key remains a useful additional constraint. A local mutex in one worker cannot coordinate other workers unless every write is routed through that one authority. Measure contention before asserting a performance winner. Safety alone says nothing about bounded waiting or fairness.

A slot can be reopened after a correction. Represent the document state as (epoch, published_rev, owner), initially (7,2,empty). Epoch is a never-reused approval-round number. Reopening increments it, clears the current owner, and preserves historical receipts and immutable evidence. Publishing a changed revision also advances the epoch under the same guard. No operation clears the owner within an existing epoch. An approval request carries a stable operation key, expected epoch, expected revision, actor, and exact evidence payload. The authority validates all of them inside the guarded transaction. Accepted receipts bind the key to that payload. A replay with identical inputs returns the historical result without consuming again. Reusing a key for different inputs is rejected. A historical success receipt does not assert that the approval is still current after reopening. Now hold an old request in the network. Authority order Received operation State/result 1 Reopen D17 after correction (8,3,empty) 2 Old approval expecting (7,2) arrives Reject stale request, leave state unchanged 3 New approval expecting (8,3) Accept if still free, bind evidence to D17/3 Checking only “slot empty” accepts the old request at step 2. Checking only the revision also fails if the round was reopened while revision 2 stayed published. An epoch distinguishes two free states with different histories. Requests obtain epochs from the authority, and cannot choose an arbitrary higher epoch to overwrite it. Permission to approve is a separate check developed in S06. The proof is short. Initially each epoch has no acceptance. The sole accepting transition requires an empty owner and writes one owner and its receipt atomically. Subsequent attempts in that epoch fail the empty check or return an existing receipt. Reopening starts a fresh epoch and retains the previous record. Thus each (doc,epoch) has at most one accepted proposal. Version validation additionally prevents acceptance against the wrong published revision at the decision boundary. It does not cancel an external action already executed.

sections.section: Logical clocks explain order, not validity
sections.text: Lamport’s happened-before relation includes process order, message send before receipt, and their transitive consequences. Two events are concurrent when neither reaches the other by those relations. A logical clock preserves this order, but a smaller timestamp does not prove causation. R06, pp. 559–560 Use counters starting at zero. Increment for local/send events. On receipt of timestamp t, assign max(local,t)+1. In this constructed trace P is the old requester, Q the administrator, and D the authority. Event Action Logical clock p1 P sends old approval to D, delayed 1 p2 P performs unrelated local work 2 q1 Q sends reopen to D 1 d1 D receives q1 2 d2 D applies reopen 3 d3 D receives p1 4 d4 D rejects the old approval 5 There is a path p1→d3→d4, but none from p2 to d2 or back. Although 2<3, those latter events are concurrent in this modeled communication history. The send timestamp remains 1 even though its receipt gets 4. The receipt’s larger number cannot make epoch 7 valid again. Ordering known events by (clock, process-ID) breaks ties and extends happened-before. It does not establish that an unseen earlier message is absent. Lamport’s mutual-exclusion construction adds queues, acknowledgements, and delivery assumptions beyond counters. R06, pp. 560–561 We use the centralized guarded decision above, without claiming to implement that distributed protocol. Wall-clock values serve deadlines and human chronology only under stated clock and delay assumptions. Logical counters measure neither seconds nor freshness. Likewise, a serializable database history promises an equivalent serial order, without by itself proving that this order matches independently observed wall clocks.

Expand the bad history into separate reads and writes. Show both dependency edges and both serial outcomes. Explain why row-local validity checks permit the violation. Trace the guarded protocol with B winning first. Then release the guard immediately after reading. Construct a violating execution and state the missing guarantee. Reopen epoch 7 as epoch 8 while retaining revision 2. An old request carries (7,2). Compare a revision-only check with the complete conditional transition. State the invariant over historical acceptances. Recompute all seven logical clock values. Identify a timestamp-ordered concurrent pair. Explain why sorting received requests cannot prove no earlier request is still in transit. An accepted transaction commits, its reply is lost, and the client retries. Specify what must be saved with the acceptance. Then add an external payment before commit and identify the failure the database cannot undo. A job now reserves one slot on each of D17 and D18. Construct a deadlock, propose an acquisition order, and state which guarantee still requires deployment evidence. Choose between the guard and conditional transition for a highly contended document and name measurements that would reverse your choice.

sections.section: Reference card, evidence, and open questions
sections.text: Write the invariant before choosing isolation. List reads as well as writes. Find an impossible serial order. Protect the whole decision, including its receipt. Reject stale epochs at the authority. Treat clocks as ordering metadata with a declared model. Separate the database commit from any external effect. Basis Inspected locator Supported use and limit R05, CMU Fall 2025 17, §3 p. 2 and §6 pp. 3–4 Transaction boundary, schedules, conflict graph. External actions fall outside database rollback. R05, same edition 18, §§1–3 pp. 1–3 Exclusive locks, 2PL, rigorous retention, deadlock. No engine-specific SQL contract asserted. R05, same edition 20, §1 pp. 1–2 Versions, snapshot isolation, write skew. The two-bit history is original. R06, Lamport 1978 Printed pp. 559–561, Partial Ordering, Logical Clocks, Ordering the Events Totally Formal event model, clock condition, implementation rules, tie breaking, protocol assumptions. Original design and derivation Histories, guard, epoch/receipt contract, clock trace, companion checks Constructed inputs and bounded executed models. No empirical throughput or deployed correctness claim. Before deployment, verify actual isolation and lock behavior, every path that can mutate the guard state, evidence retention, retry-key retention, and failure handling around commit. Test long waits and retries under the real workload. The finite checks do not simulate hardware, database internals, or a lossy network. These are application unknowns, not blockers for the next pack. F01 supplies the invariant proof, and S02 supplies durable revision identity. S04 will add replicated authorities and partial failure. S06 will revisit permission changes at the decision boundary. A05 and C01 will carry the separation between accepted intent and external tool effects.
1.0 — 2026-11-06. Original S03 pack with a write-skew history, shared-guard repair, stale-epoch counterexample, and logical-time trace.

Field Value ID / revision / date S03 answers · 1.0 · 2026-11-06 Prerequisites Concurrency, transactions, and logical time, F01, S02 Capability developed Test a history against an invariant and identify where a guarantee ends Source-check status R05 and R06 primary passages and locators recorded in the core pack Experiment status Finite Python models executed. These checks do not test an actual database, lock manager, network, or external payment service.

Include the row each transaction reads but does not write. Ask whether another transaction can change the state before the first decision commits. Two occurrences of “empty” can belong to different approval rounds. Follow process and message arrows before comparing numbers. A timeout describes client knowledge. It does not identify the commit outcome. Draw who waits for whom. Then separate safety, eventual progress, and observed latency.

sections.section: 1. Read dependencies can defeat disjoint writes
sections.text: One expanded history is R_A(a)=0, R_A(b)=0, R_B(a)=0, R_B(b)=0, W_A(a)=1, C_A, W_B(b)=1, C_B. The writes become visible at their respective commits. Both transactions base their decisions on (0,0). R_A(b) precedes W_B(b), giving A→B. R_B(a) precedes W_A(a), giving B→A. Preserving both read dependencies requires a cycle, so this history is not conflict serializable. The direct serial comparison is even more specific to the application. A then B produces (1,0), and B then A produces (0,1). The actual (1,1) is neither. Both rows are valid bits and both candidate IDs are unique. The violated condition spans the pair. A unique key on (doc,epoch) in the authoritative Acceptance relation can encode the one-slot invariant. The rule must apply to every acceptance path, and the rejected transaction must not report success or execute a payment.

sections.section: 2. Hold the guard across the decision
sections.text: B obtains the guard, reads (0,0), stages its acceptance and evidence, commits, then releases the guard. A waits, acquires it, reads current committed (0,1), and declines. If either transaction aborts, all of its database changes are discarded before the guard becomes available. Early release gives this counterexample. A acquires, reads (0,0), releases. B acquires, reads (0,0), releases. A commits a=1. B commits b=1. Each read held a lock, but the decision was not protected through the update. The missing property is exclusion across the whole read/validate/write/commit interval, or an atomic revalidation at the write boundary. Holding the guard while using an old snapshot is also insufficient. B must read state that includes A’s committed acceptance after waiting, or restart. All acceptance, reopening, and publication writers must participate in the same protocol. A lock on an unrelated row creates no such exclusion.

State changes from (7,2,empty) to (8,2,empty). A delayed request expecting (7,2) passes a revision-only comparison because both revisions are 2. It fails the epoch comparison because 7 differs from 8. Checking both fields at the same atomic decision boundary rejects it without altering the current round. Let Accepted(d,e) be the set of accepted operation keys for document d and epoch e. The invariant is |Accepted(d,e)| <= 1 for every historical epoch. Never clear an owner and reuse the epoch. Reopening creates a new epoch, and old receipts remain historical facts. An immutable evidence key still points to D17/2 even after D17/3 is published. If an old request had already succeeded, replaying its operation key returns that previous receipt. It must not create another acceptance in epoch 8. Return enough information to distinguish “accepted in epoch 7” from “currently selected approval.” If the same key carries a different payload, reject the key reuse. The examples assume keys remain available for the entire possible retry period. Deciding that period is a deployment requirement.

P increments from 0 to 1 for p1, then to 2 for p2. Q independently increments to 1 for q1. D receives q1 at max(0,1)+1=2, performs d2 at 3, receives p1 at max(3,1)+1=4, and rejects at 5. The events p2 and d2 have timestamps 2 and 3 but no happened-before path in either direction. A clock comparison therefore does not prove causal dependence. In contrast, p1→d3 follows the actual message, and d3→d4 follows D’s process order. The clock inequality holds along both edges and their transitive consequence. The table’s row placement is one possible display order, not an extra communication edge. A physical observer could record a chronology that is absent from the modeled processes’ information. Neither a wall-clock timestamp nor a Lamport timestamp grants permission to accept an old epoch. If D has only received one request, sorting its received set cannot distinguish a world with no other request from a world with an earlier request still delayed. A policy promising causal request order needs additional information or waiting assumptions. The pack’s authority instead decides using validated current state. It promises the capacity and epoch invariants, without promising that the earliest sender wins.

sections.section: 5. The response and the effect are separate boundaries
sections.text: Store the acceptance, exact evidence references, operation key, payload binding, and result in one database transaction. After an uncertain reply, query or retry that key. An identical accepted retry returns its receipt with no new consumption. An aborted transaction leaves no accepted receipt in this model. Durability of a successful commit still depends on S02’s storage/failure assumptions. A stable key stored in a worker’s volatile memory is insufficient. Writing a receipt in a later transaction leaves a gap after acceptance in which a retry cannot find it. Writing a receipt first in a separate transaction can claim success even if the later acceptance fails. Now send a payment before committing, then abort the database transaction. The payee may already have received the money while the local transaction disappears. Retrying can send again. Database rollback cannot reverse that external service’s state. An atomic record of intent plus a dispatcher can make delivery recoverable, but duplicate delivery still requires a suitable receiver-side effect contract. C01 develops that boundary. This pack does not claim exactly-once payment from a local receipt or logical timestamp.

A holds D17 and wants D18. B holds D18 and wants D17. A waits for B and B waits for A. Neither can reach its release step unaided. Require every transaction to acquire guards in ascending document order, D17 then D18, and retain them through the combined commit. B then waits for D17 before it can hold D18, excluding the constructed cycle. Atomic acceptance of both reservations still requires one transaction encompassing both. For one very hot document with short validations, begin by testing the guarded design because its waiting behavior and proof are simple. Keep slow extraction or remote requests outside the lock. A conditional transition is attractive when collisions are rare and validation is cheap to repeat. At high contention, aborted attempts may consume significant work. The recommendation is practitioner judgment to test, not a universal ranking. Measure useful committed decisions, retries per success, wait-time distribution, transaction duration, and fairness under the same arrival pattern. A guard might cause unacceptable waits behind a slow holder, or optimistic retries might waste more time than waiting. Neither protocol proves a latency bound. The real database’s conflict handling, recovery, and all write paths need validation before deployment. Assessment criteria. A useful response supplies a concrete violating history, checks the aggregate invariant, identifies a protocol that excludes the history, and states the boundary of that protocol. It distinguishes serializability, causal order, wall-clock time, stale request validity, and external effects. Artifact checks do not establish learner mastery.

Run the following block under Python 3. Each two-candidate history contains three ordered operations per transaction. R takes a snapshot and decides, W stages that candidate’s bit, and C commits the staged value. There are 20 interleavings preserving each transaction’s order. In 18, both snapshots precede the other candidate’s commit, so the model permits both acceptances. The two serial histories accept only one. These counts describe enumerated histories, not their probability in a real scheduler. The guarded model uses a single indivisible current-state transition, representing the contract the implementation must supply. Its finite tests cannot prove a database implements that contract. The separate invariant argument is in the core pack. from itertools import combinations, permutations from collections import Counter # All interleavings of R,W,C for each of two candidates. histories = [] for positions_a in combinations(range(6), 3): aset = set(positions_a) actors = ['A' if i in aset else 'B' for i in range(6)] pc = dict(A=0, B=0) history = [] for actor in actors: history.append((actor, ('R','W','C')[pc[actor]])) pc[actor] += 1 histories.append(history) def snapshot_run(history): state = dict(A=0, B=0) decisions, staged = {}, {} for actor, operation in history: if operation == 'R': decisions[actor] = sum(state.values()) == 0 elif operation == 'W': staged[actor] = int(decisions[actor]) else: state[actor] = staged[actor] return state assert len(histories) == 20 bad = sum(sum(snapshot_run(h).values()) > 1 for h in histories) assert bad == 18 serial_a = [(a,s) for a in ('A','B') for s in ('R','W','C')] serial_b = [(a,s) for a in ('B','A') for s in ('R','W','C')] assert snapshot_run(serial_a) == dict(A=1, B=0) assert snapshot_run(serial_b) == dict(A=0, B=1) # Fixed-object precedence graph for the expanded violating history. rw = [('A','R','a'), ('A','R','b'), ('B','R','a'), ('B','R','b'), ('A','W','a'), ('B','W','b')] edges = set() for i, (t1,op1,x1) in enumerate(rw): for t2,op2,x2 in rw[i+1:]: if t1 != t2 and x1 == x2 and 'W' in (op1,op2): edges.add((t1,t2)) assert edges == {('A','B'), ('B','A')} # Single document. Each method is an assumed atomic guarded transaction. # The receipt payload's rev stands for already-validated immutable evidence. class Authority: def __init__(self): self.epoch, self.rev, self.owner = 7, 2, None self.receipts = {} # key -> (actor, expected_epoch, expected_rev) def approve(self, key, actor, epoch, rev): payload = (actor, epoch, rev) if key in self.receipts: if self.receipts[key] != payload: raise ValueError('operation key reused for different inputs') return 'replay' if (epoch,rev) != (self.epoch,self.rev): return 'stale' if self.owner is not None: return 'occupied' self.owner = key self.receipts[key] = payload return 'accepted' def reopen(self, rev): self.epoch += 1 self.rev, self.owner = rev, None def check(self): per_epoch = Counter(p[1] for p in self.receipts.values()) assert all(n <= 1 for n in per_epoch.values()) if self.owner is not None: assert self.receipts[self.owner][1:] == (self.epoch,self.rev) for order in permutations(('A','B')): d = Authority() results = [d.approve(a,a,7,2) for a in order] assert results == ['accepted','occupied'] d.check() # A and B target epoch 7; C targets epoch 8. N reopens with the same revision. for order in permutations(('A','B','C','N')): d = Authority() for op in order: if op == 'N': d.reopen(2) else: expected = 8 if op == 'C' else 7 before = len(d.receipts) result = d.approve(op,op,expected,2) if result == 'accepted': assert d.epoch == expected and d.rev == 2 assert len(d.receipts) == before + 1 else: assert len(d.receipts) == before d.check() d = Authority() d.reopen(2) assert d.rev == 2 # revision-only check would pass an old request assert d.approve('old','A',7,2) == 'stale' and d.owner is None assert d.approve('new','B',8,2) == 'accepted' d = Authority() assert d.approve('k','A',7,2) == 'accepted' # Lost reply, retry, then reopen, and retry again. assert d.approve('k','A',7,2) == 'replay' d.reopen(3) assert d.approve('k','A',7,2) == 'replay' and d.owner is None assert len(d.receipts) == 1 try: d.approve('k','A',8,3) except ValueError: pass else: raise AssertionError('key reuse was accepted') assert d.approve('wrongrev','B',8,2) == 'stale' d.check() # Clock trace and transitive happened-before closure. clock = dict(P=0,Q=0,D=0) timestamps = {} events = [('p1','P',None), ('p2','P',None), ('q1','Q',None), ('d1','D','q1'), ('d2','D',None), ('d3','D','p1'), ('d4','D',None)] hb, previous = set(), {} for event,process,sent in events: if process in previous: hb.add((previous[process],event)) if sent is not None: hb.add((sent,event)) clock[process] = max(clock[process], timestamps[sent]) + 1 else: clock[process] += 1 timestamps[event] = clock[process] previous[process] = event while True: closure = hb | {(a,d) for a,b in hb for c,d in hb if b == c} if closure == hb: break hb = closure assert [timestamps[e] for e,_,_ in events] == [1,2,1,2,3,4,5] assert all(timestamps[a] < timestamps[b] for a,b in hb) assert ('p2','d2') not in hb and ('d2','p2') not in hb assert timestamps['p2'] < timestamps['d2'] assert ('p1','d4') in hb print('20 snapshot histories checked; 18 violate capacity.') print('2 guarded orders and 24 reopen/request orders preserve capacity.') print('Stale epoch/revision, replay, payload binding, and clocks passed.') The 24 orders enumerate all placements of four modeled atomic calls, including a future-epoch request arriving before reopening. Such a request fails rather than forcing the authority to advance. The tests also cover accepted-key replay after a round ends. They do not prove fairness, bound network delay, or establish crash durability of a production implementation. No learner answers have been inferred.
1.0 — 2026-11-06. Six worked answers and executable finite-history, epoch, replay, and logical-clock checks.

Field Value ID / revision / date S04 · 1.0 · 2026-11-06 Prerequisites S03 histories, epochs and receipts; S02 durable commit and immutable evidence Capability developed Trace a leader failure, defend a commitment boundary, and distinguish client uncertainty from repeated effects Source-check status R07 extended Raft paper and R10 author-hosted paper inspected. Exact locators below. Experiment status Executed finite quorum, voting, log-repair and application-replay checks. No live cluster tested. Companion Hints, worked answers, and checks

S03 gave D17 one authority for deciding which approval occupies a round. That authority checked the epoch, selected revision and operation key together. Now its machine fails after accepting a request. A replacement must distinguish a decision that must survive from a speculative update that can disappear. Merely copying files to another server does not define that distinction. We will replicate an ordered sequence of commands across three servers A, B and C. A command is input to a deterministic state transition. Given the same initial state and command sequence, each server must compute the same results. For example, Approve(k,D17,epoch=7,rev=2,actor=R) either records an acceptance and receipt or returns a defined rejection. It cannot call a changing external model during replay and still promise identical results. Store the chosen evidence identity in the command and validate it against replicated state. A log index is a position in the sequence. A term is a leadership generation. An approval epoch is the business round introduced in S03. These are three different numbers. Electing a new leader does not reopen D17’s approval round. A log entry records its index, term and command. Raft is our worked mechanism, using the paper’s fixed-membership core. Its persistent state includes term, vote and log; its voting and append rules constrain successors. Current-term entries advance commitment through a majority, with earlier entries covered by the committed prefix. The detailed rules are in R07 Figure 2 and §§5.2–5.4. This pack constructs one trace to explain why those restrictions matter rather than reproducing a full implementation.

sections.section: Declare the world before claiming reliability
sections.text: Assume three fixed members with stable identities. Servers may stop and recover. Messages may be lost, delayed, duplicated or reordered. Stable storage retains completed writes across the modeled restart. Servers follow the protocol; malicious replies and undetected corruption are outside the model. Required persistent changes reach stable storage before success responses to protocol RPCs. Progress needs a communicating majority and enough stability to elect and retain a leader. A network timeout is evidence that a response did not arrive by a deadline, not proof that the other machine stopped. An isolated old leader can remain alive while the other two elect a successor. Our safety target is that different servers never apply different commands at the same log index. Our application target is at most one acceptance per document/approval epoch. Those properties differ. An agreed command that erroneously ignores the epoch could be replicated perfectly and still violate the business rule. The replicated state transition must preserve S03’s invariant. For three members a majority has two. Any two such majorities overlap because two disjoint sets of size two would require four members. More generally, two subsets of size q in N members intersect in at least 2q−N members. Intersection provides a witness shared by two decisions. Rules about what that witness may approve supply the safety argument. Counting copies alone does not.

sections.section: A committed approval with no reply
sections.text: Start with the same committed prefix through index 4 on all servers. Its last term is 1. D17 is at epoch 7, published revision 2, with no owner. A is leader in term 2. The following values and events are an original hypothetical case. Event A B C Client knowledge 1 Persist entry 5, term 2, approval k Prefix through 4 Prefix through 4 Waiting 2 Send entry 5 Check predecessor (4,1), persist entry 5, reply Unreachable Waiting 3 Receive B’s success; majority A+B holds entry 5 Has entry 5, may not know it is committed Still through 4 Waiting 4 Advance commitment, apply approval, then crash before reply No commit notification received Still through 4 Timeout 5 Down Seek election in term 3 Vote for B Outcome unknown 6 Down Replicate no-op at index 6, term 3, to C after entry 5 Persist entries 5 and 6 Outcome unknown 7 Down Commit through 6, apply 5 then 6 Learn commit boundary, apply in order Retry k can receive original result At event 3, the original leader’s term-2 entry has reached a majority. Its protection does not depend on whether the client hears about it. B’s uncertainty about the commit boundary also does not make that entry disposable. Why can B win? Its last entry is (term 2,index 5), while C ends at (term 1,index 4). C can vote for B. In the reverse attempt, B rejects C’s older log, so C cannot obtain two votes while A is down. The up-to-date comparison examines last term first, then last index for a tie. A long log with an older last term is not automatically preferred. Why include the no-op? B must not simply infer that an inherited entry is committed by counting its copies under the new term. B replicates an entry from its own term at index 6. Committing that entry establishes the whole preceding prefix, including approval k. A no-op changes no business state. It still occupies a log position and establishes a commitment boundary. R07 §5.4.2 and Figure 8 explain why the general rule needs the current-term restriction. If A returns, observing term 3 makes it step down. A follower checks the index and term of the preceding entry before accepting an extension. Conflicting uncommitted suffixes can be replaced. That repair operation is not permission to erase an arbitrary committed entry; election restrictions prevent a valid successor from lacking committed history.

Change only event 2. Suppose B never persisted entry 5, so A alone has it when A crashes. B and C both end at index 4. They can elect B and commit a different term-3 entry at index 5. On recovery A’s uncommitted suffix is replaced. This does not violate the safety target because A must not have applied or reported success for its speculative entry. An early reply after A’s local append would create a false promise. The client would have heard “accepted” for a decision that a legitimate replacement leader could discard. This is S02’s acknowledgement discipline extended across machines. A durable local log protects against one kind of restart; it does not by itself establish replicated commitment. A different naive rule lets whichever server times out become leader and accept locally. Partition A from B+C. A accepts proposal k, while B accepts competing proposal j for the same epoch. If both return success, merging the histories later cannot make both original promises true. Under our contract the minority cannot commit new approvals. It can return an unavailable response or offer a clearly labeled stale view, but cannot call that view an authoritative current decision.

sections.section: Retry the operation, preserve its identity
sections.text: Replaying k can append another log entry. Log consensus alone does not identify that entry as the same business request. Our deterministic application retains key → (payload,result) with the acceptance. Reapplying the identical key returns its stored result. Reusing the key for a different payload is rejected. The receipt state must survive recovery and any snapshot that discards older log entries. Suppose an approval round was reopened after k succeeded. A retry still receives the historical result for k, without accepting anything in the new epoch. The response must distinguish a past accepted decision from a currently active approval. A client that generates a new key after every timeout loses this protection. This contract prevents repeated application of the same recorded operation within the retention boundary. It does not make an external payment atomic with the log. If a dispatcher sends a payment and crashes before recording its response, another dispatcher may send again. The destination needs an effect-level identity and contract, or the workflow needs explicit reconciliation. R10’s duplicate-message discussion shows why lower-layer duplicate suppression cannot recognize every application retry. C01 will develop that responsibility boundary. Likewise, a server that calls itself leader cannot safely answer every “is k accepted?” query from local memory. It may be isolated and superseded. R07 §8 describes additional safeguards for authoritative reads. For this lesson, route result resolution through a protocol that establishes current authority and applies the required committed prefix. A stale “not found” response is not evidence that a retry should receive a new key.

Design choice What it buys under its model Cost or remaining gap Evidence that changes the decision One durable server with recovery Simple local persistence Machine/device failure can halt service or lose unavailable data Required recovery window and actual restore tests Three-member consensus group Majority progress despite one unavailable member Durable replication and communication on the critical path Storage latency, network delay, correlated outages Five-member consensus group Majority of three can remain after two unavailable members More replicated storage and operational work Failure-domain analysis justifies the extra tolerance Async copy plus early success Lower acknowledgement dependency Latest acknowledged decisions can be absent after failover Acceptable data-loss window explicitly permits that outcome Three processes on one failed host do not provide three independent failure domains. Replicating a bad command also creates three copies of the same bug. Backups, restore procedures, authorization and application validation remain separate needs. Measure acknowledgement latency, election disruption, follower lag, disk flush behavior and retry outcomes under the intended workload. Do not translate the historical paper’s timing examples into a production timeout. Safety requires the rules to hold even during long delay; useful progress additionally requires favorable communication and scheduling conditions. No universal recovery-time bound is derived here.

List all two-member majorities of A,B,C. Show their intersections. Explain why overlap alone cannot stop conflicting decisions if a voter may vote twice in one term. Trace the main failure through B’s election. Identify when entry 5 becomes committed, when B can establish its commit boundary, and what the client knows at each point. Crash A before B stores entry 5. Show a legitimate replacement at index 5 and explain which earlier success reply would be invalid. Compare candidate logs ending at (term 2,index 9) and (term 3,index 6). Then explain why counting a majority of copies of an inherited entry is insufficient as the general commitment rule. Retry k before and after reopening D17. Specify receipt retention and payload binding. Give one duplicate-payment failure this cannot exclude. Partition A from B+C and then partition all three separately. State safety and progress expectations. Name one failure outside the model and a measurement needed before choosing three versus five members.

Basis Inspected locator Use and scope R07, Ongaro/Ousterhout, extended version, May 20, 2014 Paper, §2 pp. 1–2; Figure 2 p. 4; §§5.1–5.4 pp. 4–9 Replicated state, durable protocol state, election and log rules, current-term restriction. Fixed membership here. R07, same edition §5.6 pp. 9–10; §8 p. 13 Timing/progress distinction, client retries and authoritative reads. No benchmark result adopted. R10, Saltzer/Reed/Clark, 1984 Author copy, PDF p. 6 Duplicate message suppression; p. 7 Transaction management Application-level retry and acknowledgement meaning. No historical performance figure adopted. Original case and checks Trace tables, majority arithmetic, companion model Constructed inputs. The checks are not a full Raft implementation or proof. Recall the sequence: persist → replicate under the protocol → establish commitment → apply deterministically → reply. Separate log index, leadership term, business epoch and operation key. After a timeout, resolve the same operation identity. Keep the external-effect boundary visible. S03’s invariant is now replicated; S02’s durability promise applies to each required persistent write. S06 will add authority and damage boundaries. B02 will price reliability and recovery. Open deployment questions include storage failure modes, read semantics, receipt retention, evidence availability, membership changes and snapshot correctness. The last two are deliberately deferred implementation depth, not removed curriculum items.
1.0 — 2026-11-06. Fixed three-member trace, majority derivation, two crash boundaries, retry contract, and separate finite checks.

Field Value ID / revision / date S04 answers · 1.1 · 2026-11-08 Prerequisites Replication, consensus, and partial failure, S03 and S02 Capability developed Separate replicated commitment, client knowledge and repeated business effects Source-check status R07 and R10 locators in the core pack Experiment status Python finite checks executed; no distributed deployment or complete protocol simulator

Write AB, AC and BC before making a general claim. Separate where the entry exists from who knows it is committed. Compare the surviving logs before holding an election. Term is the first comparison key. An inherited entry retains its original term. The operation key belongs to the business request, not the network connection. A process can be alive while unreachable. A majority must be able to communicate.

The majorities are {A,B}, {A,C}, {B,C}. Distinct pairs intersect in A, B or C. For N members and q-member sets, their union has size at most N, so the intersection has size at least 2q−N. With N=3 and q=2 the bound is one. With N=5 and q=3 it is also one. If A votes for both B and C in the same term, B+A and C+A can each claim a majority. Intersection has not helped because the shared member contradicted itself. Persisting the vote before responding is essential across restarts. The majority calculation also does not prove the elected log contains every committed entry; the log freshness restriction and log-matching properties supply further structure.

Entry 5 becomes committed once A, its term-2 leader, has durably replicated it on A+B. A learns that threshold was reached from B’s successful response. B can still be unaware of commitment because no commit notification reached it. The client times out and cannot distinguish this history from one in which A never committed. B wins term 3 with its own vote and C’s. C has an older last log term. A candidate C cannot win using B because B’s log is more up-to-date. In this particular trace A is down, so C’s own vote is insufficient. B’s term-3 no-op at index 6 reaches B+C. B can advance its commit boundary through 6 under the current-term rule and apply entry 5 before 6. B reconstructs the acceptance and receipt even if it had never applied them before the election. An identical retry of k returns that receipt. The term-3 no-op does not change D17’s epoch 7 or selected revision 2.

If only A stored entry 5 before crashing, B and C retain the common prefix through 4. B can win term 3 and append command j at index 5, then commit it on B+C. When A rejoins as a follower, an AppendEntries extension whose predecessor is (4,1) can replace A’s conflicting term-2 entry with term-3 j. No committed entry has been removed in this branch. A’s success reply after only its local append would have been invalid because the promised result can disappear during valid failover. The correct client outcome before replicated commitment is still pending or failed/unknown, depending on the exact API contract; a timeout alone remains unknown.

sections.section: 4. Log freshness and an inherited entry
sections.text: (term 3,index 6) is more up-to-date than (term 2,index 9), because term is compared first. Within the same last term, the higher last index wins. This is a log comparison, distinct from the candidate’s current election term and distinct from a wall-clock timestamp. R07 Figure 8 constructs a history in which a previous-term entry reaches a majority through later replication yet can still be overwritten. Therefore the general replica-count rule requires an entry from the current leader’s term. Once that newer entry commits, the preceding prefix is committed with it. In the main case entry 5 had already committed under A; the extra step lets B establish a safe boundary without assuming knowledge it did not receive. It does not change the historical fact of commitment.

Retain k with its canonical input payload and result in replicated application state. Apply acceptance and receipt together. A repeat with matching inputs returns the stored result. A repeat with different inputs is an error. Retain enough receipt history to cover the supported retry period, including snapshots and restores. The lesson’s model retains every receipt indefinitely; a bounded production policy must define what happens to expired keys. After reopening, return “accepted in epoch 7” for k without consuming the new round. A fresh key targeting epoch 7 fails epoch validation. The key-reuse check must not silently reinterpret an old request against today’s evidence. A payment dispatcher can send once, crash before recording the response, then send again after recovery. The local receipt cannot prove how many effects the destination performed. Replicated intent helps recover pending work; safe retry at the payment boundary needs the destination’s identity/effect contract or explicit reconciliation.
