title: Cache correctness, invalidation, and stale fills

sections.section: Cache correctness, invalidation, and stale fills
sections.text: Field Value ID / revision / date X01 · 1.0 · 2026-11-20 Prerequisites F01 invariants; S02 revision identity; S03 interleavings. S06 and A03 are useful follow-ups. Capability developed Find a stale-fill race, choose a cache consistency contract, and identify the assumptions a generation guard cannot enforce. Source-check status XR01, original USENIX paper §3.2.1; XR02, RFC 9111 §§4.2, 4.4 and 6. Passages inspected 2026-11-20. Experiment status Finite interleaving and boundary checks executed in the companion. No distributed cache or production workload tested. Companion Hints, worked answers, and executable checks Explore the stale-fill race Compare the same events with and without a generation guard. Each step is atomic in this teaching model. Scenario Delayed fill after invalidationValid token, lagging replicaGuard metadata forgotten Previous stepNext stepRestart trace The scripted explorer needs JavaScript. The complete trace and boundaries are explained in the lesson below.

You have a correct database and an expensive read. A cache seems like a performance decision: retain the answer and reuse it. But it adds a second place where a previous answer can outlive the assumptions that made it valid. Our question is specific: after an update has invalidated a cached object, can an earlier reader put the previous revision back? If yes, reducing database latency may have increased the duration of an incorrect result. This extension uses a fictional document D17. Revision 7 is replaced by revision 8. All times, rates and histories below are constructed teaching inputs. The cache is an application cache; its rules are ours to specify, not automatic consequences of an HTTP header or a particular product. If concurrency is unfamiliar, think of each row in a history as one indivisible step. Different requests can take turns between rows. A request that started first need not finish first. A revision identifies data; a generation identifies a period in which a cache fill is permitted. They are different counters with different owners.

sections.section: A successful invalidation that still fails
sections.text: The initial cache is empty. The database holds revision 7. A reader uses the familiar sequence: check cache, read database on a miss, store the result. A writer commits to the database and then deletes the cache entry. Step Reader A Writer B Database Cache 1 Cache miss 7 empty 2 Read revision 7 into local memory 7 empty 3 Paused before cache fill Commit revision 8 8 empty 4 Delete cached D17; report success 8 empty 5 Store local revision 7 8 7 6 New reader C uses cached revision 7 8 7 No failed delete is needed. No dirty database read is needed. The delete worked on the state that existed at step 4. The late fill is a new mutation after the delete. Moving the delete before the database commit also admits a counterexample: delete, reader misses and reads 7, reader fills 7, writer commits 8. Changing the order of two separately coordinated systems does not by itself close every gap. The invariant we want for this lesson is deliberately limited: Once invalidation advances this key’s generation, a fill carrying an older generation must not become a usable cache entry. This is a cache-publication property. It does not yet say that every response after a database commit returns the latest revision.

sections.section: Remember enough to reject a late fill
sections.text: Give the cache a per-key generation, initially 0. On a miss, A obtains token 0 before reading the database. Invalidation atomically increments the generation and clears the value. Filling atomically checks the token and writes only if it still matches. miss: return current generation as token invalidate: generation = generation + 1; value = empty fill(t, v): if t == generation, store v; otherwise reject Each line describes an atomic cache-side operation in our model. Separate network calls to read the generation and later set the value do not implement the final line: invalidation could occur between them. A lock, transaction or equivalent conditional operation must actually enforce the boundary. Now step 4 advances the generation from 0 to 1. Step 5 presents token 0. The cache rejects it and stays empty. The next reader can fetch revision 8. If A fills before invalidation instead, invalidation clears its entry. Both orderings protect the stated publication invariant. The original Facebook memcache paper describes a related lease mechanism: a miss can return a key-bound token that is checked on a subsequent fill, and a delete can invalidate that token. The same section discusses regulating lease issuance to reduce competing fills. XR01, §3.2.1, printed p.388. Our generation model is an original simplified exercise, not a reproduction of that production protocol or its performance results. The order of token acquisition matters. Reading revision 7, then observing generation 1 after invalidation, and presenting that new token with the old data defeats the guard. A token is evidence about a particular operation’s ordering, not a stamp you can attach after the fact.

sections.section: What this guard does not prove
sections.text: Consider three changes to the premises. Delayed invalidation. The database commits revision 8, but the invalidation arrives later. During that interval, an old cache entry can still be served. Even after a fill is rejected, the initiating reader might return its local revision 7 to its caller. Protecting cache publication alone does not repair that response path. A requirement such as “every read beginning after a successful write sees at least that write” needs an acknowledgement/read protocol that enforces that relationship. One option is to return a required revision to the writing client and validate or bypass entries below it; the authority used for that validation must itself meet the contract. A lagging database replica. A reader obtains generation 1 after invalidation but reads revision 7 from a replica that has not applied revision 8. The token matches, so the fill is accepted. The guard has not been violated; its premises were weaker than the application’s freshness goal. A version floor carried with invalidation could reject revisions below 8, but only if that floor is trustworthy, available and atomically checked with publication. Waiting, bypassing or failing must be specified when no suitable read is available. Evicted guard metadata. An old reader holds token 0. Invalidation advances to 1. The cache loses its generation record and recreates the key at 0. The old token now matches again: an ABA-style reuse of identity. Keeping a generation only as long as its value is cached is insufficient. Use a design that prevents old tokens from becoming valid after eviction or restart—for example, an incarnation identity that cannot be reused within the outstanding-token lifetime. Prove the lifetime and recovery assumptions rather than assuming a counter is durable. These are reasons to state the contract precisely. A mechanism can correctly enforce its own invariant while the whole application remains incorrect.

Suppose A reads revision 7 at time 0. Revision 8 commits at time 1. A fills the cache at time 100 with a 60-second TTL measured from insertion. The entry expires at time 160. It has a full remaining TTL at insertion although its source observation is already 100 seconds old. In this constructed history, the old revision can be served during [100, 160), including almost 159 seconds after the update. That is a 60-second serving interval, not 159 seconds of continuous cached service. For an insertion-based application TTL, if an observation happens at time r, fill is delayed by d and the TTL is T, expiry is r + d + T. At time t, observation age is t − r, while cache residence is t − (r + d). The difference is d. A bounded TTL alone therefore does not bound observation age without a bound on fill delay and the age of the source read. Do not apply that insertion-only formula to HTTP caches. RFC 9111 defines freshness using response age and freshness lifetime; its age accounting includes transit and residence. It also limits the scope of invalidation and distinguishes HTTP caching from an application’s later reuse of data. XR02, §§4.2–4.2.3, 4.4 and 6. HTTP freshness still should not be mistaken for a proof that the underlying business object has never changed.

sections.section: Choose a contract before choosing a cache
sections.text: Use Acceptable contract to investigate Evidence that could change the choice Public descriptive text Explicitly bounded age may be acceptable Actual update frequency and cost of stale text A document revision selected by ID Immutable revision content may be reusable Whether identity is immutable and all dependencies are included Current “latest revision” pointer Needs its own freshness/ordering contract Writer acknowledgement, invalidation delay and replica lag Approval permission Must match the declared revocation boundary Whether permission is checked at the protected action Generated answer from documents Reuse only under the required evidence and access context Source revisions, principal scope, retrieval/model configuration and current permission The last two rows connect to S06 and A03. A cache key containing a user or policy version does not discover that permission has changed. The serving path still needs a valid authority decision. Likewise, immutable document content does not make the mutable pointer “latest” immutable. There is a cost trade-off. In a hypothetical workload of 1,000 reads per second, one source query per miss and a 95% hit rate imply 50 source queries per second. At 80%, that becomes 200: four times the source demand despite a 15-percentage-point change in hit rate. This arithmetic assumes no retries, coalescing or refresh traffic. It is not a latency prediction. For a burst of 100 simultaneous misses on the same key, ideal coalescing could use one fetch if that result is valid for all callers and the leader finishes in time. A stalled leader needs bounded waiting and recovery. If every timeout triggers an independent fetch, the database can receive the original burst after a delay. A generation guard alone neither coalesces requests nor limits backend load. This is the link to S05: enforce the source’s capacity budget even when the cache is cold or unavailable.

Attempt these before opening the worked companion. Reconstruct the stale-fill history from an empty cache. State why a successful delete is insufficient. Criterion: the database read precedes commit, while fill follows invalidation. Interleave the reader’s token/read/fill steps with the writer’s commit/invalidate steps while preserving each actor’s order. Compare unguarded and guarded publication. Criterion: distinguish the invariant after invalidation from freshness after commit. Make generation checking fail by changing either token acquisition order, source-read consistency or metadata retention. Criterion: give a complete history and identify the violated premise. Recompute the TTL example with fill at time 120 and TTL 30. Criterion: give expiry, observation age at fill and the possible stale-serving interval after the update; label the TTL convention. Compare source demand at 95% and 80% hit rates. Then give a case where coalescing is unsafe. Criterion: preserve denominators and identify differing keys or permission contexts. Choose a cache policy for “latest document” and a separate policy for “may approve.” Criterion: name authority, invalidation/validation boundary, failure behavior and a measurement that could reverse your design.

A delete removes a value; it does not automatically cancel a reader already in flight. Acquire the fill token before the source observation; validate it atomically with publication. Generation fencing protects an ordering boundary. Source freshness, response freshness and authority need additional contracts. Cache residence, source observation age and business revision age are different quantities. Treat a cold cache, lost invalidation and forgotten guard metadata as explicit cases. Measure useful outcomes and source load, not hit rate alone.

ID / type Inspected support Boundary XR01 · primary historical paper Nishtala et al., Scaling Memcache at Facebook, NSDI 2013, §3.2.1, printed p.388: original PDF Token-check and delete-invalidation mechanism; no current implementation claim or reused benchmark XR02 · primary standard RFC 9111, §§4.2–4.2.3, 4.4, 6: full text HTTP age/freshness and invalidation scope; not a specification for our application cache Original derivation Histories, generation proof, TTL arithmetic and hit-rate arithmetic in this lesson and companion Finite atomic model with stated assumptions; not a distributed correctness proof Continuity F01, S02, S03, S05, S06 and A03 Existing mechanisms reused; no learner mastery assumed Before implementing this in a real system, determine maximum read/fill delay, which replica serves misses, how invalidation survives process failure, how generation state survives eviction and restart, and what the caller receives after a rejected fill. Those inputs remain unknown here.

title: Hints, worked answers, and finite checks

sections.section: Hints, worked answers, and finite checks
sections.text: Field Value ID / revision / date X01 companion · 1.0 · 2026-11-20 Lesson Cache correctness, invalidation, and stale fills Experiment status Python checks below executed. They enumerate ten legal single-reader/single-writer schedules and explicit failure fixtures. No live cache or concurrent deployment tested.

For 1–2, distinguish where the reader holds its result from where the cache holds a value. For 3, change only one premise at a time. For 4, put observation, update, insertion and expiry on one clock. For 5, write source demand as offered reads multiplied by miss fraction. For 6, define what event makes a previous answer invalid.

sections.section: 1. Delete succeeds and an old value returns
sections.text: Start with database revision 7 and no cached value. A misses and reads 7. B commits 8 and deletes the cache. A then inserts its local 7. C starts after B has finished and reads 7 from cache. The defect is not a failed delete: the earlier request performs a later write. A second timed delete only moves the deadline unless it is tied to a proven maximum lifetime of all earlier fills and successfully delivered.

sections.section: 2. Ten schedules and one final stale fill
sections.text: Label token acquisition T, database read R, fill F, commit C and invalidation I. Require T < R < F and C < I. There are ten ways to interleave chains of lengths three and two: choose three of five positions for the reader. In the unguarded model, T R C I F leaves revision 7 cached after invalidation. With an atomic generation check, F is rejected. If F happens before I, I clears the entry. If T happens after I, then R also happens after I and C; our latest-committed source-read assumption returns 8. These cases explain the result independently of enumeration. This does not guarantee immediate freshness after C: the history T R C F I temporarily exposes 7 before I. Nor does rejecting F stop the application returning its local 7 directly. The checked property is specifically cache state after I, not all response behavior.

Late token: R observes 7, C commits 8, I advances generation, T obtains the new generation, F publishes 7. Fix the ordering or use an independently validated source revision. Lagging source: C, I, T, then R reads 7 from a delayed replica. F has a valid token but old data. Require a suitable source read or validated revision floor, and define behavior while the replica catches up. Forgotten generation: T obtains 0, R observes 7, C commits 8, I advances to 1. Metadata disappears and resets to 0. F passes. The missing premise is identity retention/non-reuse across the lifetime of outstanding work. An incarnation token is useful only if restart, eviction and failover actually preserve its uniqueness contract.

With observation at 0, update at 1, fill at 120 and insertion TTL 30, expiry is 150. Observation age at insertion is 120 seconds. The cache could serve the obsolete revision during [120, 150), a 30-second interval whose end is nearly 149 seconds after the update. This assumes no later valid replacement or invalidation. An HTTP cache’s age rules are different; the original lesson explicitly limits this example to an insertion-based application TTL.

At 1,000 reads/s, 5% misses imply 50 source queries/s; 20% misses imply 200 source queries/s. The multiplier is four. Offered traffic, retry traffic and refresh work must be measured separately before using this as a capacity estimate. Coalescing two requests just because their query strings match is unsafe if their tenants, permissions or required revisions differ. Even when one immutable blob can be shared, authorization to disclose it must be evaluated under the required contract. Under ideal coalescing of 100 equivalent requests, one source fetch suffices; a failed leader or retry storm changes that count.

For a “latest document” display, an explicitly declared bounded-age policy may be adequate if the user can tolerate it. Record source revision and observation time, reject fills with invalid generations, and measure invalidation delay and outdated responses. If the user requires read-your-write behavior, carry the committed revision and validate/bypass entries below it against an adequate source. For “may approve,” follow S06’s action-time authority boundary: an approval ordered after revocation must not commit under the revoked grant. A presentation cache is not that authority. On unavailable authority, defer the protected action under this policy. A policy allowing bounded revocation delay would be a different, explicitly weaker contract. Useful evidence includes source-read lag, guard-state recovery behavior, rejection rate, source saturation during cache outages and end-to-end latency with permission checks enabled. Correctness requirements and measured costs together can reverse the cache choice. No actual permission system is tested here.

Run with Python 3. Each model step is atomic. Schedules omit network loss, multiple writers, replication, crash recovery and real concurrency. The negative fixtures deliberately violate one premise and must expose the defect. The unit tests establish behavior of this model, not a deployed protocol. from itertools import permutations from fractions import Fraction def simulate(order, guarded): db, generation, cache = 7, 0, None token = observed = None invalidated = False violations = [] for step in order: if step == "T": token = generation elif step == "R": observed = db elif step == "C": db = 8 elif step == "I": generation += 1 cache = None invalidated = True elif step == "F": if not guarded or token == generation: cache = observed if invalidated and cache is not None and cache < db: violations.append(step) return cache, violations orders = [p for p in permutations("TRFCI") if p.index("T") < p.index("R") < p.index("F") and p.index("C") < p.index("I")] assert len(orders) == 10 bad = ["".join(p) for p in orders if simulate(p, False)[1]] assert bad == ["TRCIF"], bad assert all(not simulate(p, True)[1] for p in orders) assert simulate("TRCIF", True)[0] is None assert simulate("CITRF", True)[0] == 8 # Broken ordering: source observation before token acquisition. assert simulate("RCITF", True)[0] == 7 assert simulate("RCITF", True)[1] == ["F"] def guarded_fill(generation, token, observed): return observed if token == generation else None # Fresh token, stale replica: token validity does not prove data freshness. assert guarded_fill(1, 1, 7) == 7 # A reset generation makes an old token valid again. assert guarded_fill(0, 0, 7) == 7 assert guarded_fill(1, 0, 7) is None def fresh(now, inserted, ttl): return now < inserted + ttl assert 100 + 60 - 1 == 159 assert 120 + 30 - 1 == 149 assert fresh(149, 120, 30) assert not fresh(150, 120, 30) assert not fresh(151, 120, 30) assert not fresh(120, 120, 0) assert 1000 * (1 - Fraction(95, 100)) == 50 assert 1000 * (1 - Fraction(80, 100)) == 200 assert Fraction(200, 50) == 4 print("PASS: 10 schedules; expected stale-fill counterexample; guarded invariant;") print("late-token, replica and reset fixtures; TTL boundaries; exact load arithmetic")

A useful answer reproduces the failure without appealing to a vague “race condition,” locates the atomic boundary, and names at least one assumption that the fix cannot enforce. A stronger transfer applies the same reasoning to a generated-answer cache or a mutable revision pointer. These criteria do not record your level automatically.

title: When does a retry prevent recovery?

sections.section: When does a retry prevent recovery?
sections.text: Field Value ID / revision / date X02 · 1.0 · 20 November 2026 Prerequisites S05 queues, S06 reliability and C03 useful capacity Capability developed Decide whether to spend a remaining deadline and a shared capacity budget on one more attempt. Evidence XR03 and XR04. Primary passages and scope below. Experiment Deterministic queue and deadline checks in the worked companion.

sections.section: Why a quiet minute can contain a busy second
sections.text: Marc Brooker describes an operational pattern on Amazon EBS and AWS Lambda. Clients running periodic jobs lined up near clock boundaries. Looking at per-second traffic exposed bursts obscured by longer averages. The team worked with clients to stagger periodic work and reported processing the same work with less server capacity. The report gives no universal percentage saving. For periodic work they used a repeatable offset per host so recurring patterns remained diagnosable. For retrying clients, the same paper describes randomizing the backoff delay. AWS Builders’ Library, “Jitter,” final five paragraphs This case gives us two different engineering decisions. Spreading a fixed batch changes when its work arrives. Retrying a timed-out call can also change how much work arrives. A timeout tells the caller that it stopped waiting. The original attempt may still occupy a worker. Ask which of those two quantities is causing the problem before tuning a delay.

Imagine a retrieval service that can finish 100 equal-cost attempts per second. At the start of recovery it has 40 queued attempts. Every second 90 new requests arrive. An upstream client also has a pool of previously timed-out requests eligible for retry. Treat arrivals as a batch before service, assume a work-conserving queue and retain unfinished work. These values are invented. S05 explains why real requests can have very different costs. With no extra attempts, ten slots per second drain old work. With 15 retries per second, the queue grows by five even though fresh traffic alone is below capacity. Compare end-of-second queue lengths. Extra attempts admitted each second Start After 1 s After 2 s After 3 s After 4 s 0 40 30 20 10 0 5 40 35 30 25 20 10 40 40 40 40 40 15 40 45 50 55 60 Compute each cell as max(0, previous queue + fresh attempts + retries − capacity). At exactly ten retries per second the queue stops growing, yet never drains. To clear all 40 within eight seconds under constant rates, reserve five slots per second for recovery. That leaves at most five for retries. This is a budget for the entire dependency in this model. Giving each of ten callers its own five attempts per second would permit fifty. The table holds retry arrivals fixed to isolate their cost. In a running service the loop can feed itself. More attempts lengthen the queue. More callers hit their deadline and resubmit, increasing arrivals again. Google SRE documents this pattern and recommends both per-request attempt limits and an aggregate retry budget. Its numeric overload example illustrates the mechanism. Google SRE, chapter 22, “Retries”

Suppose an AI assistant has 800 ms to return evidence. Its first retrieval attempt times out at 560 ms. It needs 150 ms for another retrieval and 60 ms to assemble a response, using invented deterministic costs. Before backoff it has 240 ms left, of which 30 ms can be spent waiting. A 40 ms backoff puts the earliest modeled finish at 810 ms. The request should stop even if the dependency has spare retry tokens. Conversely, satisfying the deadline cannot create backend capacity. In production the stage times are distributions. Measure the joint end-to-end outcome under load and reserve slack for scheduling. A workable policy has one layer own the retry. It checks whether the failure is transient, whether a repeated operation is safe, whether enough deadline remains, and whether the shared budget admits it. It propagates the remaining deadline downstream and records both attempts against one logical request. Two layers that each allow three attempts can send nine attempts to the bottom service on the all-fail path. Jitter spreads those attempts. A cap limits their number. For a read-only retrieval, duplicate computation may be tolerable. For an agent issuing a billable or externally visible action, a missing reply can leave an unknown outcome. Reconcile using the operation identity and the provider’s actual guarantees before reissuing it. See C01. Even read-only inference can be expensive if the original generation keeps decoding. Verify how cancellation propagates and when accelerator capacity is actually released.

With 40 queued attempts, 90 fresh arrivals and capacity 100, find the largest constant integer retry rate that drains the queue in five seconds. Show why the next integer fails. A retry needs 150 ms plus 60 ms for response assembly. Find the latest time at which it can start under an inclusive 800 ms deadline. What changes if the first attempt timed out at 610 ms? An SDK and gateway each permit two retries after an initial attempt. Bound downstream attempts and choose which layer should own retries for this workload. Identify the information it needs. Design a replay for the retrieval endpoint. Which metric would convince you that retries are helping users? Which measurement would make you stop them?

Source Inspected locator Application boundary XR03 · Marc Brooker, AWS Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter, “Jitter,” EBS/Lambda periodic workload account, and “Retries and backoff” Production experience with burst timing and guidance for retries. The model’s capacity and deadlines are original assumptions. XR04 · Mike Ulrich, Google Addressing Cascading Failures, “Retries” and “Queue Management” Describes retry feedback, aggregate limits and waiting costs. The service in our trace is hypothetical. Before choosing a budget, measure per-dependency headroom during recovery, attempts still running after a timeout, actual retries inside SDKs, and the fraction of logical requests delivering supported evidence by the deadline. An improving attempt success rate can coexist with fewer users receiving timely results.
Return to the lesson. Try drawing a single time axis for the user and a separate queue for the dependency. Each retry consumes space on both.

Five seconds to drain 40 attempts requires eight net completions per second beyond incoming work. With ten spare slots, at most two can go to retries. At two the queue follows 40, 32, 24, 16, 8, 0. At three it ends at five. A shared per-second limit assumes equally expensive requests and enforcement over all callers. A token bucket with accumulated burst tokens can briefly exceed that rate. Account for burst size when making a five-second guarantee.

Latest modeled retry start is 800 − 150 − 60 = 590 ms. At 560 ms, waiting exactly 30 ms consumes all slack. Waiting 31 misses the deadline. At 610 ms even immediate dispatch is 20 ms too late. If the caller can cheaply return a useful partial result, evaluate that separately under the same evidence requirement. Returning unsupported evidence would change the task.

Each layer permits three attempts including the first. The worst case sends nine downstream calls for one logical request. If the gateway knows the user’s deadline, dependency budget and operation identity, it can own the retry and configure the SDK for one attempt. That reduces the modeled ceiling to three. A different layer can own it if that layer has equivalent information. Verify effective SDK and proxy settings by tracing a controlled failing request.

Replay the same arrival trace against policies with zero retries and a bounded retry budget. Include a short transient disconnect and a sustained capacity loss, then restore capacity with a queue still present. Count logical requests that return valid evidence by their deadline divided by all eligible original requests. Alongside it record attempts per logical request, outstanding work after cancellation, peak queue and time to drain. Control model version, output requirements and cache state. A retry that rescues the disconnect but prolongs overload calls for different treatment of those failure classes. Stop admitting retries when the added load prevents the queue from draining within the recovery target. Production thresholds require measured service curves and an agreed recovery target.

The following checks use a deterministic teaching model with a single queue and inclusive deadline. def trace(retries, seconds): queue = 40 history = [queue] for _ in range(seconds): queue = max(0, queue + 90 + retries - 100) history.append(queue) return history assert [trace(r, 4)[-1] for r in (0, 5, 10, 15)] == [0, 20, 40, 60] assert trace(2, 5) == [40, 32, 24, 16, 8, 0] assert trace(3, 5)[-1] == 5 assert max(r for r in range(101) if trace(r, 8)[-1] == 0) == 5 assert 560 + 30 + 150 + 60 == 800 assert 560 + 31 + 150 + 60 > 800 assert 610 + 150 + 60 == 820 assert (1 + 2) ** 2 == 9 A complete answer explains both limits on another attempt, shows where the time goes, and states which real measurements would change the decision.

title: Approximate membership and the price of forgetting

sections.section: Approximate membership and the price of forgetting
sections.text: Field Value ID / revision / date X03 · 1.0 · 20 November 2026 Prerequisites F01 invariants, F02 base rates and S02 state identity Capability developed Decide when a one-sided probabilistic membership filter saves expensive negative work without turning incomplete state into false certainty. Evidence XR05 and XR06. Primary passages and scope below. Experiment Deterministic sizing, load and stale-snapshot checks in the worked companion.

Suppose an AI retrieval service receives a document identifier and may need an object-store read before it can retrieve or rerank chunks. Most requested identifiers are absent from the tenant’s current index. An exact in-memory set would avoid wasted reads, but its memory cost may be too high. A Bloom filter stores a compact summary of the identifiers that were present when a snapshot was built. For an insert-only filter constructed from every live identifier, the answers mean different things: Filter answer What follows Safe action At least one tested bit is 0 The identifier was not inserted Skip the expensive lookup, provided the filter belongs to the same complete snapshot All tested bits are 1 The identifier may have been inserted Check the authoritative index or store The second row is a false-positive boundary. It spends extra work but does not invent a record if the caller verifies the result. A false negative would skip a real record. The mathematical structure avoids false negatives only under its premises. A stale filter, an incomplete build, different key encoding, corruption or publishing the filter before its matching data can violate them. Burton Bloom’s original paper frames this as an allowable error of commission followed by a secondary test. It explicitly rules out uses requiring error-free performance. Its method 2 starts with a bit array set to zero, maps each stored message to several bit addresses and sets them to one. A query is rejected when any tested bit is zero; all ones only accept it for the follow-up test. Bloom 1970, printed pp. 422–423, especially “A Sample Application” and “Method 2”

Let m be the number of bits, n the inserted keys and k the number of independent bit probes per key. Start with m zero bits. For each key, compute k bit positions and set all of them to one. For a query, compute the same positions. Any zero means definitely absent under the snapshot premises. All ones mean maybe present. With uniform independent positions, the approximate false-positive probability is p≈(1−e−kn/m)k. For a fixed number of bits per inserted key, b = m/n, the useful integer probe count is near b ln 2. Adding probes beyond that point sets too many bits and can make the filter worse. Bloom derives the corresponding occupancy and false-acceptance relationship in equations 16–17 and identifies the minimum-space point where half the field remains zero. Bloom 1970, printed pp. 425–426 The formula is a model. Real hash construction, small filters, uneven key distributions and implementation layout can change observed behavior. Measure the implementation used in production.

Consider an invented retrieval snapshot with 1,000,000 document identifiers, 10 bits per identifier and 7 probes. The filter uses 10,000,000 bits, about 1.25 MB. The approximation gives p = 0.00819, or about 0.819%. If 3,000,000 definitely absent identifiers are queried each day, the filter sends about 24,581 of them to the authoritative lookup and rejects about 2,975,419. At an invented 2 ms of service time per slow lookup, that avoids about 5,951 service-seconds per day. These figures are deterministic teaching inputs, not a capacity claim about object storage or vector databases. Moving from 10 to 12 bits per key uses another 0.25 MB. With 8 probes, the modeled false-positive probability falls to about 0.314%, so the same negative workload sends about 9,427 lookups through. The extra memory prevents roughly 15,154 additional slow lookups. Whether that is worthwhile depends on the measured latency, I/O, cache churn and memory opportunity cost. Optimize the whole path rather than the false-positive rate alone. The expected useful saving for negative queries can be sketched as qnegative(1−p)cslow−qallcprobe−cmemory−cbuild. Use distributions for the real decision. One disk miss, remote request or GPU-side retrieval stage can have a heavy-tailed cost that an average hides.

sections.section: Production decision — Bigtable reads across SSTables
sections.text: Google’s Bigtable implementation stored a tablet’s state across SSTables. A read could therefore require accesses to all of them, and an SSTable outside memory could cause disk I/O. The team let clients request Bloom filters for SSTables in a locality group. The filter answered whether an SSTable might contain a row/column pair. They reported that, for certain applications, a small amount of tablet-server memory drastically reduced disk seeks and that most lookups for nonexistent rows or columns did not touch disk. Bigtable, §6 “Bloom filters,” proceedings p. 211 / PDF printed p. 7 The constraint was repeated negative work across immutable files. The choice kept a compact summary near the reader and treated a positive result as permission to inspect the SSTable. The paper reports the direction of the operational outcome, not a universal percentage or configuration. The filters were configurable per locality group because the payoff depends on workload. To transfer this decision, collect the negative-lookup fraction, number of candidate files or partitions per read, actual cost of a rejected slow lookup, filter memory and probe cost, observed false-positive rate, and cache effects. Then compare end-to-end read latency and resource use with and without the filter under the same trace.

An ordinary Bloom filter cannot safely delete by clearing a bit. Other keys may share it, so clearing it can create false negatives. Immutable SSTables avoid this particular mutation problem because a filter can be built for a fixed file and discarded with that file. Mutable systems need a different lifecycle, such as rebuilds, versioned snapshots or a deletion-capable structure whose extra state and concurrency rules are understood. For an AI corpus, bind the filter to the exact index manifest: Build the data snapshot and membership filter from the same enumerated key set. Validate inserted count, checksum and a sample of known members before publication. Publish one manifest that names both artifacts, then switch readers atomically. If the filter is missing, older than the data, or has an unknown version, fall back to the authoritative lookup. Record filter negatives separately from verified positives so a rollout can be replayed and audited. A filter can prove absence only inside the set it summarized. “Not in tenant index snapshot 42” does not mean “the document never existed,” “the user lacks access,” or “no relevant evidence exists.” Those are different claims with different authorities.

For 1,000,000 keys at 10 bits per key, reproduce the modeled false-positive probability using 7 probes. Estimate false positives among 3,000,000 negative queries. Compare 10 bits and 12 bits per key for that workload. State the incremental memory and avoided authoritative lookups. Which real cost would decide whether to upgrade? A data snapshot is version 43 while its filter is still version 42. A query for a key added in version 43 returns negative. Classify the failure and design the serving rule that prevents it. Design an A/B replay for a retrieval service. Which measurements establish saved work, and which check that the optimization did not hide valid documents? Decide whether to use this filter to deny an authorization request. Identify the invariant that makes the proposed use unsafe.

Source Inspected locator Application boundary XR05 · Burton H. Bloom Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors, printed pp. 422–423 and 425–426, equations 16–17 and Table I Defines the one-sided membership mechanism and modeled trade-off. Independence and uniformity are analytical assumptions; system freshness is outside the paper. XR06 · Chang et al., Google Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data, §6 “Bloom filters,” proceedings p. 211 / PDF printed p. 7 Documents a deployed storage decision and qualitative outcome. It does not provide a universal bits-per-key setting or measured percentage reduction. Before trusting a negative, verify the filter and authoritative data share a version, the build covered every live key, readers use identical canonical encoding, and fallback behavior is safe during rollout and recovery. Before buying more filter memory, verify negative lookups dominate enough expensive work to matter.
Return to the lesson. Keep two questions separate: how often a complete filter admits unnecessary work, and whether the deployed filter is complete for the data being served.

The invented snapshot has n = 1,000,000, m = 10,000,000 and k = 7, so m/n = 10 bits per key. p≈(1−e−7/10)7=0.0081937. That is about 0.819%. Among 3,000,000 queries for absent keys, the expected count admitted to the authoritative lookup is 3,000,000 × p ≈ 24,581. The remaining roughly 2,975,419 are useful negatives. Expected counts are workload averages, not a guarantee for a particular day.

Twelve bits per key needs 12,000,000 bits, or about 1.50 MB, versus 1.25 MB at ten bits. The incremental memory is 0.25 MB using decimal units. With k = 8, the modeled false-positive probability is about 0.003142, so approximately 9,427 of the 3,000,000 negative queries reach the slow path. The additional memory avoids about 24,581 − 9,427 = 15,154 slow lookups per day. At the invented 2 ms each, this is only about 30.3 service-seconds beyond the 10-bit filter’s saving. Decide using measured end-to-end tail latency, I/O and cache churn, memory pressure, filter probe CPU and rebuild cost. A lower isolated false-positive rate is not itself the product outcome.

The version-42 filter never received the key added to data version 43. Its negative is a system-created false negative even though the mathematical insert-only filter kept its promise for version 42. The serving invariant should be filter.manifest_version == data.manifest_version before a negative can skip the lookup. On mismatch, perform the authoritative lookup or fail the snapshot switch before it becomes visible. Publish the filter and data through one immutable manifest reference so readers cannot independently select versions.

Use one captured trace with stable tenant, index snapshot, canonical key encoding and cache starting state. Run it against the unfiltered path and the candidate filter. Record total queries, true absent queries, filter negatives, filter positives, verified true positives, verified false positives, authoritative lookups, bytes read, CPU, cache misses and latency distributions. To detect hidden valid documents, independently enumerate the authoritative snapshot and assert that every present key returns “maybe.” Include keys added at each publication boundary and force version mismatch, partial-build and fallback fixtures. Compare retrieval recall and final evidence-bearing answers on a labeled set as a downstream check. The membership check establishes whether a document identifier is in one snapshot; it does not establish semantic relevance.

Do not deny authorization from a Bloom-filter negative unless the filter’s completeness and freshness are themselves part of the authorization system’s proven invariant. A stale or partially published filter could deny an allowed subject. The safer optimization is to use a positive only to trigger the authoritative policy lookup and to fall back on any version uncertainty. Authorization also has revocation semantics that a basic insert-only filter cannot represent safely.

The checks use deterministic invented inputs and the standard independent-uniform approximation. from math import exp, log def modeled_fpr(bits_per_key, probes): return (1 - exp(-probes / bits_per_key)) ** probes p10 = modeled_fpr(10, 7) p12 = modeled_fpr(12, 8) assert abs(p10 - 0.0081937221) < 1e-10 assert abs(p12 - 0.0031423503) < 1e-10 assert round(3_000_000 * p10) == 24_581 assert round(3_000_000 * p12) == 9_427 assert round(3_000_000 * (p10 - p12)) == 15_154 assert 10_000_000 / 8 / 1_000_000 == 1.25 assert 12_000_000 / 8 / 1_000_000 == 1.5 assert round((24_581 - 9_427) * 0.002, 3) == 30.308 assert round(10 * log(2)) == 7 assert round(12 * log(2)) == 8 def may_skip(filter_version, data_version, bits): return filter_version == data_version and 0 in bits assert may_skip(42, 42, [1, 0, 1]) assert not may_skip(42, 43, [1, 0, 1]) assert not may_skip(43, 43, [1, 1, 1]) A complete answer names the authoritative follow-up, quantifies avoided work, and treats freshness, completeness and key encoding as premises of every “definitely absent” result.
